Module 1·LLD · week 1Must

Design principles

14 topics · about 1.5 h of reading

Design principles are the habits that keep code easy to change. A program that works today but breaks in three places whenever a requirement moves is a badly designed program, even if every test passes. This module gives you the vocabulary (cohesion, coupling, SOLID, DRY, KISS, YAGNI) and the practical skills (clean code, spotting code smells, drawing UML) that every design discussion and every code review uses.

It builds on Core Java · Module 2 (OOP), which explains how classes, interfaces and polymorphism work. Here the question changes from "how does it work?" to "how should I arrange it so it survives change?". The next module, Design patterns, shows ready-made solutions that apply these principles, and LLD interview problems asks you to use both.

  • Judge a design with two ideas: high cohesion and low coupling.
  • Explain each SOLID principle in 30 seconds and show a violating and a fixed version in Java.
  • Tell DRY from accidental duplication, and use KISS and YAGNI to stop over-engineering.
  • Refactor messy code using clean-code rules and name the code smell you are fixing.
  • Draw class diagrams and sequence diagrams and map each arrow to Java code.

What good design means: cohesion, coupling and designing for change

Good design means code that is cheap to change: each class does one focused job (high cohesion), classes know as little as possible about each other (low coupling), and details are hidden behind interfaces (encapsulation).

Nobody can predict every future requirement. Tomorrow the business adds a new payment method, a new tax rule, or moves from MySQL to PostgreSQL. A design is good when such a change touches few places and breaks nothing else. A design is bad when one small change forces edits in ten files. Almost every principle in this module is a way to measure or improve this one property: cost of change.

Cohesion: things that belong together

Cohesion measures how strongly the parts inside one module (a method, a class, a package) belong together. In a highly cohesive class, every field and method serves one clear purpose. You can describe the class in one sentence without using "and".

Low cohesion: a grab-bag

public class Utils {
    public static String formatRupees(long paise) { /* ... */ return ""; }
    public static boolean isValidPan(String pan) { /* ... */ return true; }
    public static void sendSms(String phone, String text) { /* ... */ }
    public static byte[] zip(byte[] data) { /* ... */ return data; }
}

High cohesion: one purpose each

public final class MoneyFormatter {
    public String rupees(long paise) { /* ... */ return ""; }
}
public final class PanValidator {
    public boolean isValid(String pan) { /* ... */ return true; }
}
public interface SmsGateway {
    void send(String phone, String text);
}

Names like Utils, Helper, Manager and Common are warning signs: they attract unrelated code because nobody knows where else it should go. Cohesion also applies to methods: a method validateAndSaveAndEmail() has three purposes.

Coupling: how much one part knows about another

Coupling measures how much one module depends on another. When class A is tightly coupled to class B, a change in B forces a change in A, and you cannot test or reuse A without B. Some coupling is unavoidable (parts must talk), so the goal is loose coupling: depend on a small, stable contract rather than on details.

Kind of couplingWhat A depends onExample
Tight (bad)The concrete classnew MySqlOrderRepository() inside a service
Tight (bad)Another class's internalsorder.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity()
Tight (bad)Shared mutable stateA public static Map that many classes edit
Loose (good)An interfaceOrderRepository passed to the constructor
Loose (good)A message or eventPublishing OrderPlaced instead of calling five services

Here is a tightly coupled class and a loosely coupled one:

// Tight: the service creates its own dependency, so you cannot swap or fake it
class ReportService {
    private final PdfWriter writer = new PdfWriter();       // hard-wired
    void publish(String text) { writer.write(text); }
}

// Loose: the service only knows the small interface it needs
interface DocumentWriter {
    void write(String text);
}

class LooseReportService {
    private final DocumentWriter writer;                    // any implementation
    LooseReportService(DocumentWriter writer) { this.writer = writer; }
    void publish(String text) { writer.write(text); }
}

class PdfWriter implements DocumentWriter {
    public void write(String text) { System.out.println("PDF: " + text); }
}

The goal: high cohesion, low coupling

These two travel together. When each class has one focused job, it needs fewer collaborators and talks to them through small interfaces. When responsibilities are mixed, classes reach into each other and coupling rises. If you remember only one sentence from this module, remember this one.

Encapsulation: the root of good design

Encapsulation means hiding data and implementation behind a small public interface (see Core Java). From a design view, it is what makes low coupling possible. If other classes cannot see your fields, they cannot depend on them, so you are free to change them later.

// Exposed: every caller can break the rule and depends on the representation
class WalletBad {
    public long balance;
}
// caller: wallet.balance -= 500;   // overdraft possible, rules scattered in callers

// Encapsulated: the rule lives in one place, the field can change type later
class Wallet {
    private long balanceInPaise;

    void debit(long paise) {
        if (paise <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        if (paise > balanceInPaise) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
        balanceInPaise -= paise;
    }
    long balance() { return balanceInPaise; }
}

Rule of thumb: expose behaviour (debit), not data (setBalance). Every public getter and setter is a small leak of your design.

Program to an interface, not an implementation

Declare variables, parameters and return types with the most general type that gives you the methods you need. Write List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();, not ArrayList<Order> orders = .... Write a method that accepts Collection<Order> when it only loops. On the larger scale, a service depends on a PaymentGateway interface, and the Razorpay or Stripe class is a detail chosen at the edge of the program. The caller then survives any change of implementation, because it never named one.

Designing for change

  1. Find what varies. Payment methods, tax rules, notification channels, report formats: these change often. Business names and core flows change rarely.
  2. Hide what varies behind an interface. Callers depend on the interface and never know which version runs.
  3. Keep the stable part stable. The flow "validate, price, pay, notify" should not be edited when a new payment method arrives.
  4. Do not predict, prepare. You cannot guess every change. Keep code simple and decoupled, then refactor when a real change arrives (see YAGNI).

A quick test for any design: "If requirement X changes, how many files do I edit?" If the answer is one or two, the design is doing its job.

Coupling cannot be zero

  • A system with no coupling does nothing. The aim is to couple to stable abstractions, such as List, PaymentGateway, or a domain event, and not to volatile details.
  • Too many tiny classes can raise coupling too, because readers must hop between files. Balance both goals.
  • Coupling across a network (microservices) is costlier than inside a JVM; see distributed system patterns.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Calling a class "cohesive" because it is in one file. Cohesion is about purpose, not location.
  • Making every field public "for convenience" and every class depend on new ConcreteClass().
  • Creating an interface for every class by habit. Add an interface when there are, or will really be, several implementations or when you need a seam for tests.

Interview: good design

  • What is cohesion and coupling? Cohesion: how well the inside of a module belongs together. Coupling: how much modules depend on each other. Aim for high cohesion and low coupling.
  • How do you reduce coupling? Depend on interfaces, inject dependencies, hide data, communicate with events, and follow the Law of Demeter.
  • How does encapsulation help design? It lets you change internals without touching callers.

The OOP pillars revisited with design in mind

Encapsulation hides change, abstraction names what matters, inheritance reuses a true is-a contract, and polymorphism lets you replace if/else on type with objects that each know their own behaviour: together they are the tools every design principle uses.

Core Java explains how the four pillars work: Core Java · Module 2 has the syntax, rules and examples. This article asks a different question: what does each pillar buy you in a design? Think of them as tools, and of the principles in this module as the instructions for using them.

PillarDesign question it answersPrinciple that depends on it
EncapsulationHow do I stop callers depending on my internals?Low coupling, Tell, Don't Ask
AbstractionWhat is the smallest contract callers need?ISP, DIP
InheritanceWhich types are truly substitutable?LSP, composition over inheritance
PolymorphismHow do I add behaviour without editing old code?OCP, Strategy

Encapsulation: hide what may change

Every private field is a decision you may change later without telling anyone. Design for it: make fields private, make objects immutable when possible (records, final fields), return unmodifiable views or copies of collections, and put the rules next to the data they protect. An Order should expose addItem() and cancel(), not getItems().add(...) and setStatus(...).

Abstraction: name the idea, hide the how

An abstraction is a promise: "give me an Order and I will return a Receipt". The caller does not care about databases or HTTP. A good abstraction is small (few methods), stable (does not change when internals change) and honest (it does not leak details such as SQLException in a method that has nothing to do with SQL). In Java you express abstractions with interfaces and abstract classes; Core Java compares the two.

Inheritance: use sparingly, and only for real is-a

Inheritance is the strongest coupling Java offers. A child sees and depends on its parent's behaviour. Use it when the child truly is a parent in every situation the parent is used (the Liskov test, see LSP) and when the parent was designed to be extended. For code reuse alone, prefer composition.

Polymorphism: replace conditionals with objects

Polymorphism is the engine of design for change. Instead of one method with an if or switch on a type code, you define an interface and let each type implement its own behaviour. Adding a new type then means adding a class, not editing a switch in five places.

// Before: every new shape means editing this method (and every other switch like it)
static double area(String type, double a, double b) {
    switch (type) {
        case "CIRCLE":    return Math.PI * a * a;
        case "RECTANGLE": return a * b;
        default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(type);
    }
}

// After: each shape knows its own area; adding Triangle edits nothing existing
interface Shape { double area(); }
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {
    public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}
record Rectangle(double w, double h) implements Shape {
    public double area() { return w * h; }
}

Java 21 adds sealed interfaces with pattern-matching switch as a second tool: when the set of types is closed and fixed, a sealed hierarchy with an exhaustive switch is also good design, because the compiler tells you every place to update when you add a type. Choose polymorphic methods when new types are likely; choose sealed types plus switch when new operations are likely.

Design habits from the pillars

  • Private fields, behaviour-rich classes, few setters.
  • Small interfaces named after the role (PaymentGateway), not the technology (RazorpayService).
  • Default to final classes; open a class for extension on purpose.
  • Any switch or instanceof chain on a type is a hint to ask whether polymorphism fits (see code smells).

Interview: OOP pillars from a design view

  • Do not recite definitions only. Say what each pillar protects: encapsulation protects against change in data, abstraction against change in implementation, polymorphism against change in behaviour.
  • Mention that inheritance is the one to be careful with, and say why (fragile base class; see composition over inheritance).

S: Single Responsibility Principle

A class should have only one reason to change: it should serve one actor or one concern, so that a change in business rules, storage or notifications touches only the class that owns that concern.

SOLID is a set of five principles popularised by Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob"): Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion. They are guidelines, not laws, but they appear in almost every design interview and code review. We take them one at a time, each with a violating version and a fix.

The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) says: a class should have one, and only one, reason to change. Martin later restated it as: a module should answer to one actor, meaning one group of people who ask for changes. If the finance team and the marketing team both ask for changes to the same class, that class has two responsibilities, and their edits will collide.

The violation: a class that does everything

Look at a typical first draft of order placement. It validates, calculates the price, writes to the database and sends an email, all in one place.

import java.sql.*;
import java.util.List;

record OrderItem(String sku, long unitPaise, int qty) { }
record Order(String id, String customerEmail, List<OrderItem> items) { }

public class OrderService {
    public void placeOrder(Order order) throws SQLException {
        // 1. validation rules (changes when the business rules change)
        if (order.items().isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Order has no items");
        }
        if (!order.customerEmail().contains("@")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Bad email");
        }
        // 2. pricing (changes when the finance team changes discounts or GST)
        long total = 0;
        for (OrderItem i : order.items()) total += i.unitPaise() * i.qty();
        if (total > 500_000) total = total * 95 / 100;
        // 3. persistence (changes when the database or schema changes)
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:postgresql://db/shop");
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
                 "INSERT INTO orders(id, email, total) VALUES (?, ?, ?)")) {
            ps.setString(1, order.id());
            ps.setString(2, order.customerEmail());
            ps.setLong(3, total);
            ps.executeUpdate();
        }
        // 4. notification (changes when marketing wants SMS or a new template)
        System.out.println("Mail to " + order.customerEmail() + ": order " + order.id());
    }
}

There are four reasons to change this class: validation rules, pricing, the database, and the message. Each belongs to a different person or team. The problems are practical:

  • Merge conflicts and regressions. A discount change can accidentally break the SQL.
  • Hard to test. To test the discount you need a live database.
  • No reuse. The pricing logic cannot be used by the "show cart" page.
  • Hard to read. Four concerns are mixed in one method.

The refactoring: one class per reason to change

import java.util.List;

class OrderValidator {
    void validate(Order order) {
        if (order.items().isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Order has no items");
        }
        if (!order.customerEmail().contains("@")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Bad email");
        }
    }
}

class PriceCalculator {
    long totalInPaise(List<OrderItem> items) {
        long total = 0;
        for (OrderItem i : items) total += i.unitPaise() * i.qty();
        return total > 500_000 ? total * 95 / 100 : total;
    }
}

interface OrderRepository {
    void save(Order order, long totalInPaise);
}

interface OrderNotifier {
    void orderPlaced(Order order);
}

public class OrderService {
    private final OrderValidator validator;
    private final PriceCalculator pricing;
    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final OrderNotifier notifier;

    public OrderService(OrderValidator validator, PriceCalculator pricing,
                        OrderRepository repository, OrderNotifier notifier) {
        this.validator = validator;
        this.pricing = pricing;
        this.repository = repository;
        this.notifier = notifier;
    }

    public void placeOrder(Order order) {                 // the workflow, nothing else
        validator.validate(order);
        long total = pricing.totalInPaise(order.items());
        repository.save(order, total);
        notifier.orderPlaced(order);
    }
}

OrderService now has one job: coordinate the steps. Its reason to change is "the order workflow changes". The JDBC code lives in a JdbcOrderRepository, the email in an EmailOrderNotifier. You can test PriceCalculator with plain JUnit and no mocks, and replace the notifier with a fake in a test of the service.

How Spring helps

In Spring Boot, the layered structure is SRP at work: @RestController handles HTTP, @Service holds business rules, @Repository talks to the database. Spring's dependency injection then wires the small classes together, so splitting a class into four costs you almost nothing: you declare the collaborators as constructor parameters and the container supplies them.

Common misunderstandings

  • "One class = one method." Wrong. A class may have many methods if they all serve the same responsibility. BigDecimal has dozens of methods and one purpose: decimal arithmetic.
  • "Split everything." Splitting too far creates dozens of tiny classes that each do nothing and are hard to follow. Split along reasons to change, not along lines of code.
  • It is about change, not size. A 400-line class with one reason to change can be fine; a 60-line class that mixes SQL and email is not.
  • Entities and DTOs: a JPA entity that is also the JSON response and also the form object has three reasons to change. Use separate DTOs at the API boundary.

Tip: how to find responsibilities

Describe the class in one sentence. If you need "and" or "or", split it. Ask: "Who would ask me to change this?" If the answer lists several roles (finance, ops, security), you have several responsibilities. Another signal: the class imports packages from unrelated areas (java.sql and javax.mail in one file).

Interview: explain SRP in 30 seconds

"SRP says a class should have only one reason to change. If validation, pricing, database access and email are in one class, any of four teams can break it. I split them so that each class serves one concern, and a coordinator class calls them. It makes code easier to test and to change. It does not mean one method per class; it is about reasons to change." Follow-up: "How do you know when to split?" Answer: when you see unrelated imports, a hard-to-name class, or tests that need heavy setup.

O: Open/Closed Principle

Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification: you add new behaviour by writing new classes that plug into an existing abstraction, without editing the tested code that already works.

Every time you edit a working class, you risk breaking it. The Open/Closed Principle (OCP), from Bertrand Meyer and popularised by Uncle Bob, says design the code so that new behaviour arrives as new code, not as edits to old code. "Open for extension" means you can add behaviour. "Closed for modification" means the existing, tested source stays untouched.

It is not magic. It works only along the lines of change you anticipated (or have already seen once). You build the abstraction around something that varies, such as a discount rule, and then new variations are new classes.

The violation: a switch that grows forever

enum CustomerType { REGULAR, PREMIUM, STUDENT }

public class DiscountCalculator {
    public long discountInPaise(CustomerType type, long amountInPaise) {
        switch (type) {
            case REGULAR:
                return 0;
            case PREMIUM:
                return amountInPaise * 10 / 100;
            case STUDENT:
                return amountInPaise * 5 / 100;
            default:
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown type " + type);
        }
    }
}

Marketing now wants a FESTIVE discount, then EMPLOYEE, then FIRST_ORDER. Each one means editing this method, recompiling and retesting every existing branch, and probably editing similar switch blocks elsewhere (the invoice printer, the report). This is a sign that OCP is violated: every new variant edits old code.

The fix: an abstraction and one class per rule

public interface DiscountPolicy {
    boolean appliesTo(CustomerType type);
    long discountInPaise(long amountInPaise);
}

class RegularDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public boolean appliesTo(CustomerType type) { return type == CustomerType.REGULAR; }
    public long discountInPaise(long amount) { return 0; }
}

class PremiumDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public boolean appliesTo(CustomerType type) { return type == CustomerType.PREMIUM; }
    public long discountInPaise(long amount) { return amount * 10 / 100; }
}

class StudentDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public boolean appliesTo(CustomerType type) { return type == CustomerType.STUDENT; }
    public long discountInPaise(long amount) { return amount * 5 / 100; }
}

public class DiscountCalculator {
    private final java.util.List<DiscountPolicy> policies;

    public DiscountCalculator(java.util.List<DiscountPolicy> policies) {
        this.policies = policies;
    }

    public long discountInPaise(CustomerType type, long amountInPaise) {
        return policies.stream()
                .filter(p -> p.appliesTo(type))
                .findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No policy for " + type))
                .discountInPaise(amountInPaise);
    }
}

To add a festive discount you write FestiveDiscount implements DiscountPolicy and add it to the list. DiscountCalculator is closed: it never changes. The set of rules is open: it grows by adding classes. This is the Strategy pattern (Strategy).

How Spring makes OCP easy

Spring can inject all beans of an interface as a List, or as a Map keyed by bean name. You write a new @Component and the calculator finds it, with no registration code:

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import java.util.List;

@Component
class FestiveDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {          // new class only
    public boolean appliesTo(CustomerType type) { return type == CustomerType.FESTIVE; }
    public long discountInPaise(long amount) { return amount * 15 / 100; }
}

@Service
class DiscountService {
    private final List<DiscountPolicy> policies;           // Spring injects every bean

    DiscountService(List<DiscountPolicy> policies) { this.policies = policies; }
    // same logic as above
}

(The example assumes CustomerType has a FESTIVE constant, added as part of the new feature; adding an enum constant is not editing the calculator.)

Other ways to get OCP

  • Inheritance and the Template Method: a base class fixes the algorithm; subclasses fill in steps (Template Method).
  • Decorator: wrap an object to add behaviour without changing it (Decorator).
  • Plugins and ServiceLoader: new JARs on the classpath add implementations of an interface.
  • Lambdas: pass a Predicate or Comparator instead of hard-coding a rule.

Common misunderstandings and limits

  • You cannot close code against every change. Pick the likely axis of change. If you guess wrong, the abstraction does not help, so wait for the second or third variant before building it (see YAGNI).
  • "Never modify a class" is not the rule. Fixing a bug in PremiumDiscount is a normal edit. The rule is about adding features.
  • A switch over a closed, stable set (days of the week) is fine. The smell is a switch that you keep editing and that is copied in several places.
  • A good test: does adding a feature require editing existing if/else or switch blocks? If yes, OCP is violated.

Mistake: building the framework first

Writing a PolicyFactoryProvider with a plugin system for a rule that has one variant is over-engineering. Write the simple if first. When the second variant arrives, refactor to an interface. When the third arrives, you will thank yourself.

Interview: explain OCP in 30 seconds

"OCP says classes should be open for extension and closed for modification. If I have a switch on customer type for discounts, every new type edits that method. I introduce a DiscountPolicy interface, one class per rule, and the calculator loops over the policies. A new rule is a new class; old code stays untouched. In Spring I inject List<DiscountPolicy> so a new @Component is picked up automatically." Common follow-up: "Is it always possible?" Answer: only along anticipated axes of change; do not abstract early.

L: Liskov Substitution Principle

If S is a subtype of T, you must be able to use an S anywhere a T is expected without breaking the program: a subclass may do more than its parent promises, but never less, and it must not surprise callers.

Barbara Liskov's principle protects the main promise of inheritance and interfaces: code written against the parent type keeps working with every child. If a method takes a Shape, it must work for every Shape you ever create. When a subclass breaks this promise, callers start writing if (x instanceof Special) checks, and polymorphism is lost.

"Is-a" in English is not enough. A square is a rectangle in geometry, but a Square class is not a valid subtype of a mutable Rectangle class. The test is behavioural: can the child stand in for the parent in all the parent's contracts?

The classic violation: Rectangle and Square

class Rectangle {
    protected int width;
    protected int height;

    void setWidth(int w)  { this.width = w; }
    void setHeight(int h) { this.height = h; }
    int area() { return width * height; }
}

class Square extends Rectangle {              // "a square is a rectangle"
    @Override void setWidth(int w)  { this.width = w; this.height = w; }
    @Override void setHeight(int h) { this.width = h; this.height = h; }
}

public class LspDemo {
    static void resize(Rectangle r) {
        r.setWidth(5);
        r.setHeight(4);
        System.out.println(r.area() + " (expected 20)");
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        resize(new Rectangle());
        resize(new Square());
    }
}
20 (expected 20)
16 (expected 20)

The method resize is correct for a Rectangle. With a Square it gives a wrong answer, because Square changed the meaning of setWidth (it also changes the height). The subtype broke the parent's implied contract: "setting the width does not change the height".

Fix: do not model it as inheritance of a mutable class. Make both implement a common read-only abstraction, or make them immutable so the problem disappears.

interface Shape { int area(); }

record Rectangle(int width, int height) implements Shape {
    public int area() { return width * height; }
}

record Square(int side) implements Shape {
    public int area() { return side * side; }
}

Violation 2: the unsupported method

A very common LSP break is a subclass that throws UnsupportedOperationException (or does nothing) for a method it inherited.

// Violating
abstract class Bird {
    abstract void eat();
    abstract void fly();
}
class Sparrow extends Bird {
    void eat() { /* ... */ }
    void fly() { /* ... */ }
}
class Penguin extends Bird {
    void eat() { /* ... */ }
    void fly() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Penguins cannot fly"); }
}

static void migrate(java.util.List<Bird> birds) {
    for (Bird b : birds) b.fly();           // crashes when a Penguin is in the list
}

The callers of Bird believe every bird flies. The fix is to split the hierarchy so that the contract matches reality:

interface Bird { void eat(); }
interface Flyer { void fly(); }

class Sparrow implements Bird, Flyer {
    public void eat() { /* ... */ }
    public void fly() { /* ... */ }
}
class Penguin implements Bird {
    public void eat() { /* ... */ }
}

static void migrate(java.util.List<? extends Flyer> flyers) {
    for (Flyer f : flyers) f.fly();         // only things that can fly are accepted
}

Now a Penguin cannot even be passed to migrate: the compiler enforces the contract.

The rules behind LSP

The contract of a method has a before part (preconditions), an after part (postconditions), and rules that always hold (invariants). A valid subtype follows these:

RuleMeaningViolation example
Preconditions: do not strengthenChild accepts at least what the parent acceptsParent takes any amount; child rejects amounts above 10,000
Postconditions: do not weakenChild promises at least what the parent promisesParent never returns null; child returns null
Invariants: keep themRules that always hold, still holdParent keeps balance at 0 or more; child allows negative
Exceptions: no new surprisesChild throws only what the parent's contract allowsChild throws UnsupportedOperationException from an inherited method
History: no new mutationChild must not change what the parent treats as fixedAn immutable parent whose child adds setters

Java helps with some of this: an overriding method cannot throw broader checked exceptions, cannot reduce visibility, and may only narrow the return type (covariance). It cannot enforce the rest. Contracts live in Javadoc, in tests, and in your head.

A realistic example: payment methods

interface PaymentMethod {
    /** Charges the amount. Never returns null; throws PaymentFailedException if declined. */
    Receipt charge(long amountInPaise);
}

class UpiPayment implements PaymentMethod { /* ... */
    public Receipt charge(long amountInPaise) { return new Receipt("UPI", amountInPaise); }
}

// Violating child: returns null for small amounts and refuses large ones silently
class WalletPayment implements PaymentMethod {
    public Receipt charge(long amountInPaise) {
        if (amountInPaise < 100) return null;            // postcondition weakened
        if (amountInPaise > 1_000_000) return null;      // surprise
        return new Receipt("WALLET", amountInPaise);
    }
}
record Receipt(String mode, long paise) { }
class PaymentFailedException extends RuntimeException { }

The checkout code written for PaymentMethod calls receipt.mode() and gets a NullPointerException. The honest fix: WalletPayment throws PaymentFailedException, exactly as the contract says.

Misunderstandings and JDK examples

  • LSP is about behaviour, not syntax. A class can compile as a subtype and still violate LSP.
  • The JDK itself bends LSP: List.of(...), Arrays.asList(...) and Collections.unmodifiableList(...) implement List but throw UnsupportedOperationException on some mutators. It is documented as an "optional operation", and it is a known trade-off. In your own code, avoid it; split read-only and mutable interfaces instead.
  • A subclass that overrides a method with an empty body ("do nothing") is often a violation too: callers expect the effect.
  • Frequent instanceof checks in client code ("if it is a Penguin, skip") are the symptom.

Tip: test the contract once, run it for every subtype

Write an abstract JUnit test class for the interface (PaymentMethodContractTest) with an abstract create() method, and extend it once per implementation. Any subclass that breaks the contract fails the same tests.

Interview: explain LSP in 30 seconds

"LSP says a subtype must be usable wherever its parent type is, without the caller noticing. The standard example: a Square extending a mutable Rectangle breaks code that sets width and height separately. Another sign is a child that throws UnsupportedOperationException. A subclass must not require more, promise less, or throw surprises. The fix is usually to change the hierarchy: smaller interfaces, immutable types, or composition."

I: Interface Segregation Principle

Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use: prefer several small, role-specific interfaces over one fat interface.

An interface is a contract the implementer must fulfil and the client sees. When one interface has twenty methods, every implementer must write all twenty (many as empty stubs), and every client sees methods it should never call. A change to a method that a client never uses can still force that client to recompile and retest. The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) says: split the interface by client role.

The violation: a fat interface

interface MultiFunctionDevice {
    void print(Document d);
    void scan(Document d);
    void fax(Document d);
    void staple(Document d);
}

class OfficePrinterPro implements MultiFunctionDevice {      // can do all
    public void print(Document d)  { /* ... */ }
    public void scan(Document d)   { /* ... */ }
    public void fax(Document d)    { /* ... */ }
    public void staple(Document d) { /* ... */ }
}

class BasicPrinter implements MultiFunctionDevice {          // can only print
    public void print(Document d)  { /* ... */ }
    public void scan(Document d)   { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    public void fax(Document d)    { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    public void staple(Document d) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}
class Document { }

Three methods in BasicPrinter lie. That also breaks LSP: callers of MultiFunctionDevice cannot trust scan. A fat interface is usually the cause of an LSP violation.

The refactoring: role interfaces

interface Printer  { void print(Document d); }
interface Scanner  { void scan(Document d); }
interface Fax      { void fax(Document d); }

class BasicPrinter implements Printer {
    public void print(Document d) { /* ... */ }
}

class OfficePrinterPro implements Printer, Scanner, Fax {
    public void print(Document d) { /* ... */ }
    public void scan(Document d)  { /* ... */ }
    public void fax(Document d)   { /* ... */ }
}

class ReportJob {
    private final Printer printer;                 // needs only printing
    ReportJob(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; }
    void run(Document d) { printer.print(d); }
}

ReportJob asks only for a Printer. It works with both devices, and a change in Fax cannot affect it. Java lets a class implement many interfaces, so splitting costs nothing for implementers who do everything.

A backend example: the repository

Suppose you start with this interface:

// Fat: login code, admin code and report code all see everything
interface UserStore {
    User findById(long id);
    User findByEmail(String email);
    void save(User user);
    void delete(long id);
    List<User> searchAll(String text);
    void exportToCsv(Path file);
}

// Segregated by client role
interface UserReader { User findById(long id); User findByEmail(String email); }
interface UserWriter { void save(User user); void delete(long id); }
interface UserSearch { List<User> searchAll(String text); }
interface UserExporter { void exportToCsv(Path file); }

The login service gets only a UserReader. If someone injects a mock in a test, there is one method to fake, not six. The read-only report job cannot call delete by accident, because the type does not allow it. That is also a security benefit.

(Assumed types for the fragment: User, java.util.List, java.nio.file.Path.)

ISP in the JDK and Spring

  • Java Collections: Iterable, Collection, List, RandomAccess are layers. A method that only loops should take Iterable or Collection, not ArrayList.
  • Functional interfaces: Runnable, Supplier, Comparator each have one method: the smallest possible role interface.
  • Spring Data: Repository, CrudRepository and PagingAndSortingRepository are separate layers, so you extend only what you need. A custom repository can extend plain Repository and declare just the two query methods the service needs.
  • Servlet and Spring listeners: callbacks like ApplicationListener have a single method.

Limits and misunderstandings

  • ISP does not mean "one method per interface" for everything. Group methods that always change together and are used together.
  • Too many micro-interfaces make code hard to navigate. Split when two kinds of clients use different subsets.
  • It applies to classes too: a class with a wide public API forces clients to know too much. Expose a narrow API.
  • Java 8 default methods can hide a fat interface: adding a new default method to a widely used interface is easier than splitting it, but the interface is still fat.

Mistake: empty or throwing implementations

If you write throw new UnsupportedOperationException() or an empty body to satisfy an interface, stop. Either the interface is too big (ISP) or the subtype is wrong (LSP). Fix the interface.

Why the principle exists

Robert C. Martin formulated ISP while helping a company with a printer system in which one big Job class served every kind of client: print jobs, staple jobs and fax jobs all used the same class. Any change to the stapling code forced a rebuild and redeploy of the code that only printed. The cost was not the bad design itself; it was the ripple. A client that depends on a method it never calls still depends on the interface as a whole, so every change to the interface reaches it.

You feel the same pain today: a unit test must fake six methods when the class under test uses one, a new method on a shared interface breaks twelve implementers, and a junior developer calls delete() on a repository handed to a read-only report. ISP asks you to design the interface from the client's point of view: "what does this caller need?", not "what can this implementation do?".

A second example: payments

A payment service starts with one interface. Checkout needs charge, the support team needs refund, and a nightly job needs settle. Putting them in one PaymentOps interface looks tidy, until you add a cash-on-delivery provider that cannot do online refunds and has no settlement. Now it must throw from two methods.

interface Charger  { String charge(String orderId, long paise); }
interface Refunder { void refund(String paymentId, long paise); }
interface Settler  { void settle(java.time.LocalDate day); }

// An online provider plays all three roles
class CardProvider implements Charger, Refunder, Settler {
    public String charge(String orderId, long paise) { return "PAY-" + orderId; }
    public void refund(String paymentId, long paise) { /* call the bank */ }
    public void settle(java.time.LocalDate day)      { /* send the batch file */ }
}

// Cash on delivery only plays one role: no fake methods
class CashOnDelivery implements Charger {
    public String charge(String orderId, long paise) { return "COD-" + orderId; }
}

class CheckoutService {
    private final Charger charger;                    // sees one method only
    CheckoutService(Charger charger) { this.charger = charger; }
    String pay(String orderId, long paise) { return charger.charge(orderId, paise); }
}

Wiring is easy: one CardProvider object is passed to the checkout as a Charger, to the support tool as a Refunder and to the job as a Settler. The object is the same; the view of it is narrow. A test for CheckoutService can even use a lambda: new CheckoutService((id, p) -> "FAKE"), because a single-method interface is a functional interface.

ISP in the JDK, honestly

The JDK is not perfect. Collection.add is an "optional operation": List.of(...) and Collections.unmodifiableList return lists whose add throws UnsupportedOperationException. That is a fat interface leaking into an LSP problem, and the JDK accepted it for convenience in 1998. Functional interfaces such as Supplier and Comparator show the opposite style: one method, one role. Use these examples to show you can see the trade-off, not only the textbook case.

ISP, SRP and LSP: how they differ

PrincipleLooks atQuestion it asks
SRPA classDoes it have more than one reason to change?
ISPAn interface, from each client's sideDoes any client depend on methods it does not use?
LSPA subtypeCan it replace its parent without surprises?
DIPThe direction of a dependencyDoes high-level code own the abstraction?

A fat interface is often an SRP problem in disguise: an interface that mixes reading, writing and exporting has several reasons to change. Splitting by client role usually fixes both at once.

Wrong: the client takes the fat type

class ReportJob {
    private final UserStore store;          // can also delete and export
    ReportJob(UserStore store) { this.store = store; }
    long countActive() {
        return store.searchAll("").size();
    }
}

Right: the client asks for its role

class ReportJob {
    private final UserSearch search;        // exactly what it uses
    ReportJob(UserSearch search) { this.search = search; }
    long countActive() {
        return search.searchAll("").size();
    }
}

Rules for applying ISP

  • Design the interface for the caller. Write the client first, see which calls it makes, and shape the interface to match.
  • Declare parameters, fields and constructor arguments with the narrowest type that works.
  • If an implementation must throw UnsupportedOperationException or leave a body empty, the interface is wrong.

Conventions

  • Name role interfaces after what the client wants: Charger, UserReader, Notifier. Avoid IManager and Handler2.
  • Keep one fat implementation class if it is natural; the segregation is in the interfaces, not necessarily in the classes.
  • Put an interface in the package of the client that uses it (the DIP habit), not next to the implementation.

When NOT to split

  • Methods that every client uses together, such as open, read and close of one resource, belong in one interface.
  • A small public library interface with one implementer and one client gains nothing from three tiny interfaces. Split when a second kind of client or a second implementation appears.
  • Splitting a published interface breaks every user of it. For a public API, add a new narrower interface and let the old one extend it.

Interview: explain ISP in 30 seconds

"No client should depend on methods it does not use. A fat MultiFunctionDevice forces a basic printer to implement scan and fax as empty methods. I split it into Printer, Scanner and Fax, and each class implements only the roles it has. The benefits: fewer fake methods, easier mocking, smaller change impact. In Spring Data, the layered repository interfaces follow the same idea."

Interview: follow-up questions on ISP

  • ISP vs SRP? SRP is about reasons to change of a class. ISP is about what each client is forced to see of an interface. They often fix the same code.
  • How do you spot a violation? Empty or throwing methods, mocks with many unused stubs, and clients that import an interface for one call.
  • Does ISP mean one method per interface? No. Group methods by client role.
  • Show a real example. The payment roles above, or Spring Data's layered repositories.

D: Dependency Inversion Principle (and DI, and IoC)

High-level business code should not depend on low-level details such as a database or an email library; both should depend on an abstraction that the high-level code owns, and the concrete detail is supplied from outside.

In a normal top-down program, the high-level class (OrderService, the business rules) calls the low-level class (MySqlOrderRepository, SmtpMailer). The source code of the high level then mentions the low level, so a change of database edits the business code. The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) reverses the arrow of the source dependency:

  1. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.
  2. Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions.

"Inversion" means that the low-level class now implements an interface which the high-level module defines. The arrow that used to point from business to database now points from database to business.

The violation

public class OrderService {
    private final MySqlOrderRepository repository = new MySqlOrderRepository();   // concrete
    private final SmtpMailer mailer = new SmtpMailer("smtp.example.com");          // concrete

    public void place(Order order) {
        repository.insert(order);
        mailer.send(order.customerEmail(), "Order placed");
    }
}

Problems: you cannot unit-test place without MySQL and an SMTP server; moving to PostgreSQL or SES means editing the service; the service decides how its collaborators are built.

The refactoring: abstraction + constructor injection

// The high-level module owns these abstractions
public interface OrderRepository {
    void save(Order order);
}
public interface Mailer {
    void send(String to, String message);
}

public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final Mailer mailer;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository, Mailer mailer) {   // injected
        this.repository = repository;
        this.mailer = mailer;
    }

    public void place(Order order) {
        repository.save(order);
        mailer.send(order.customerEmail(), "Order placed: " + order.id());
    }
}

// Low-level details implement the abstractions
class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    public void save(Order order) { /* JDBC code */ }
}
class SmtpMailer implements Mailer {
    public void send(String to, String message) { /* SMTP code */ }
}

Now a unit test needs no infrastructure:

class FakeRepository implements OrderRepository {
    final java.util.List<Order> saved = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
    public void save(Order order) { saved.add(order); }
}

@Test
void savesAndNotifies() {
    var repo = new FakeRepository();
    var sent = new java.util.ArrayList<String>();
    var service = new OrderService(repo, (to, msg) -> sent.add(to));   // lambda as Mailer

    service.place(new Order("O1", "asha@example.com", java.util.List.of()));

    assertEquals(1, repo.saved.size());
    assertEquals(java.util.List.of("asha@example.com"), sent);
}

(JUnit 5 imports omitted. Mailer has one method, so a lambda can implement it.)

DIP vs DI vs IoC

These three terms are confused in every interview. They are related but different.

TermWhat it isLevel
DIP Dependency Inversion PrincipleA design rule: depend on abstractions, owned by the high-level codePrinciple (the "why")
IoC Inversion of ControlA broad idea: a framework or container calls your code, and controls creation and flow, instead of your code controlling everythingArchitecture style
DI Dependency InjectionA technique: an object receives its collaborators from outside (constructor, setter, field) instead of creating themTechnique (the "how")

DI is one way to achieve IoC. DIP is the design goal that DI makes easy. You can follow DIP without a framework (pass objects in main), and you can use a Spring container and still violate DIP by injecting concrete classes everywhere.

How Spring helps

The Spring container is an IoC container: you declare components, and Spring creates them and injects the dependencies. Constructor injection is the recommended style because it makes dependencies visible and fields final:

@Repository
class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    JdbcOrderRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbc) { this.jdbc = jdbc; }
    public void save(Order order) {
        jdbc.update("INSERT INTO orders(id, email) VALUES (?, ?)",
                    order.id(), order.customerEmail());
    }
}

@Service
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;      // the interface, not the JDBC class
    private final Mailer mailer;

    OrderService(OrderRepository repository, Mailer mailer) {   // one constructor: no @Autowired
        this.repository = repository;
        this.mailer = mailer;
    }
}

With one implementation per interface, Spring picks it automatically. With two, use @Primary or @Qualifier. Switching from JDBC to JPA is a new @Repository class, with no change to OrderService. More on wiring in the Spring notes (Spring fundamentals).

Misunderstandings

  • "DIP = using @Autowired." No. Injecting JdbcOrderRepository (a concrete class) into the service is DI without DIP.
  • "Every class needs an interface." No. Value objects, records, DTOs and simple stable utilities (String, List) do not need one. Add an abstraction at boundaries: database, network, clock, file system, email, payment gateways.
  • The interface must be shaped by what the business needs (save(Order)), not copied from the library API (executeUpdate(String sql)). Otherwise the abstraction leaks details.
  • Injecting the clock (java.time.Clock) is a small DIP win: tests can fix the time.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Calling new on a collaborator inside a service, or using a static singleton (Mailer.getInstance()) that cannot be replaced.
  • Field injection (@Autowired private Foo foo;), which hides dependencies and blocks final fields and plain-Java tests.
  • Circular dependencies (A needs B needs A): the abstractions are split wrongly; extract a third class.

Interview: explain DIP in 30 seconds

"High-level policy should not depend on low-level detail; both depend on an abstraction. My OrderService depends on an OrderRepository interface that it owns; JdbcOrderRepository implements it. So I can swap the database or test with a fake. DI is the technique that supplies the implementation through the constructor, and IoC is the idea that the container, not my code, builds and wires the objects." Be ready to separate the three terms.

DRY, KISS and YAGNI

DRY says every piece of knowledge should live in one place; KISS says choose the simplest design that works; YAGNI says do not build features or flexibility until you actually need them. They pull against over-engineering and against copy-paste.

SOLID tells you how to structure code. Three shorter slogans tell you when to stop. They sound obvious, but a surprising amount of real damage comes from ignoring them or from applying them blindly.

DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself

The principle comes from The Pragmatic Programmer: every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation in the system. The key word is knowledge, not text. If the GST rate is 18% and you write 0.18 in the cart, the invoice and the report, then one business fact lives in three places. When the rate changes, you will miss one, and the invoice will disagree with the cart.

Wrong: the same rule copied

// CartService
long tax = amount * 18 / 100;
// InvoiceService
long gst = amount * 18 / 100;
// ReportService
long taxPart = amount * 18 / 100;

Right: one authoritative place

public final class TaxPolicy {
    private static final int GST_PERCENT = 18;
    public long gstOn(long amountInPaise) {
        return amountInPaise * GST_PERCENT / 100;
    }
}
// every service calls taxPolicy.gstOn(amount)

DRY also covers: constants and enums (not repeated strings), shared validation rules, database schema versus entity classes (generate one from the other or keep them in sync with tests), documentation that restates code, and build configuration.

DRY is about knowledge, not identical-looking code

Two code blocks may look the same today but represent different knowledge. Merging them couples two unrelated things. Example: a shipping-address validator and a billing-address validator are both "check pincode has six digits". If the rule for billing later allows foreign postal codes while shipping stays Indian only, the shared function now needs flags and conditions. That is accidental duplication, and removing it was the mistake.

SituationSame knowledge?Action
GST rate used in three servicesYes, one business ruleExtract to one place
Two DTO classes with the same three fieldsNo, different API contracts that may divergeKeep separate
Same 6-line loop in two methods, same reason to changeYesExtract a method
Two validators that look alike but belong to different featuresProbably notWait; see the rule of three

The rule of three

Copy once: fine. Copy a second time: you have three copies, so now refactor. Duplicating twice shows you the real shape of what is common and what differs; abstracting after the first copy is a guess. Martin Fowler describes it as: "the first time you do something, you just do it; the second time you wince but do it anyway; the third time you refactor". Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

KISS: Keep It Simple, Stupid

Among designs that work, prefer the simplest one. Simple means few moving parts, easy to read, easy to debug, and easy for a new teammate to follow, not "fewest lines". A clever one-liner with nested ternaries and streams is not simple.

Wrong: clever

return users.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(u -> u.age() > 17 ? u.city() != null
        ? u.city() : "NA" : "MINOR", Collectors.counting()))
    .entrySet().stream().max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue())
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey).orElse(null);

Right: boring and clear

Map<String, Long> countByCity = new HashMap<>();
for (User u : users) {
    if (u.age() < 18) continue;
    String city = u.city() == null ? "NA" : u.city();
    countByCity.merge(city, 1L, Long::sum);
}
return mostFrequent(countByCity);      // a small named method

KISS in design: a method call before a message queue, a monolith before microservices, a HashMap before a distributed cache, an if before a rules engine. Add complexity only when a measured problem demands it.

YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It

From Extreme Programming: do not add functionality until it is necessary. Developers love building "just in case" features: a plugin system, a generic base class, ten configuration flags, support for MongoDB "in case we change". Unused code still costs: it must be written, tested, read, and kept compatible, and your guess about the future is usually wrong.

// Over-engineered for a service with one payment gateway
interface PaymentGatewayFactoryProvider { PaymentGatewayFactory get(String region); }
interface PaymentGatewayFactory { PaymentGateway create(Map<String, Object> config); }
// ... 6 more types, an XML config loader, a registry

// What the team needed on day one
class RazorpayClient {
    Receipt charge(long paise, String token) { /* call the API */ return null; }
}
// Add an interface when the second gateway is really planned (then it is easy)

YAGNI is not "never plan". It means: do not implement speculative features. Good habits (small classes, tests, loose coupling) keep change cheap, so you do not need to predict it.

The tension between them

DRY pushes you to abstract; KISS and YAGNI push you to wait. A balanced working rule: write the simple version first; duplicate once if unsure; abstract when the third case appears and the shared knowledge is clear; delete code that is not used.

Other short principles

Separation of concerns
Keep different jobs in different places (UI, business rules, data access). See next article.
Law of Demeter
Talk only to your direct friends. See the next article.
Principle of least astonishment
A method should do what its name says and nothing surprising. getUser() that creates a user breaks it.
Fail fast
Check inputs early and throw a clear exception, instead of letting bad data travel deep.
Boy Scout rule
Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it.
Premature optimisation
Do not optimise without measuring; Knuth: "premature optimization is the root of all evil" (in the 97% of cases where it does not matter).

Mistakes to avoid

  • Merging two similar-looking methods with a boolean flag parameter to "stay DRY"; the result is harder to read than the duplicates (see clean code).
  • Building a generic framework "for the next project" inside the current one.
  • Using KISS as an excuse for one 600-line method.

Interview: DRY, KISS, YAGNI

  • What is DRY? One authoritative place for each piece of knowledge; example the GST rate. Add: it is about knowledge, not identical lines.
  • When does DRY go wrong? When you merge code that looks similar but changes for different reasons; mention the rule of three.
  • YAGNI vs designing for change? I keep the code loosely coupled so change is cheap, but I do not build the features until they are needed.

Law of Demeter, Tell Don't Ask and separation of concerns

Talk only to your direct collaborators (Law of Demeter), tell objects what to do instead of pulling their data out and deciding for them (Tell, Don't Ask), and keep different concerns such as web, business and data in different layers (separation of concerns).

These three ideas all reduce coupling. They say the same thing in different words: do not let one class know the inner structure of another.

Law of Demeter ("don't talk to strangers")

The Law of Demeter (LoD), also called the principle of least knowledge, says a method should call methods only on:

  • its own object (this),
  • its parameters,
  • objects it creates, and
  • its direct fields (its friends).

It should not reach through one object to get another and call that one. The warning sign is a chain of getters, sometimes called a train wreck:

Wrong: knows the whole chain

// OrderPrinter knows Order has a Customer, which has an Address, which has a City
String city = order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity();
if (city.equals("Mumbai")) {
    surcharge = 50;
}

Right: ask your friend

// Order hides how the city is found
if (order.isShippedTo("Mumbai")) {
    surcharge = 50;
}

// in Order
boolean isShippedTo(String city) {
    return customer.livesIn(city);       // Customer hides Address
}

With the first version, a change in how Customer stores an address (say, a list of addresses with a default one) breaks every caller that walked the chain. With the second, only Customer.livesIn changes.

When chains are fine

  • Fluent APIs and builders return the same object: sb.append("a").append("b"), stream.filter(...).map(...), HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(...).build(). These are not Demeter violations, because every call is on the same kind of object.
  • Plain data structures (records, DTOs, JSON trees) are meant to be navigated: response.user().name().
  • Do not add dozens of one-line wrapper methods mechanically (getCustomerAddressCity()). Ask what the caller really wants to know (isShippedTo), and name that.

Tell, Don't Ask

"Ask" style code pulls data out of an object, makes a decision outside, and pushes the result back. "Tell" style code sends a command and lets the object, which owns the data, decide. The first scatters business rules across callers; the second keeps each rule next to its data. This is encapsulation applied to behaviour.

// ASK: the caller owns the rule, and every caller must repeat it
if (account.getBalance() >= amount && account.getStatus() == Status.ACTIVE) {
    account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount);
} else {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot withdraw");
}

// TELL: the account owns the rule
account.withdraw(amount);

// in Account
void withdraw(long amount) {
    if (status != Status.ACTIVE) throw new IllegalStateException("Account not active");
    if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
    balance -= amount;
}

Notice the symptoms of "ask": many getters and setters, and "service" classes full of ifs that inspect entities. Such an entity with no behaviour is sometimes called an anemic domain model. It is not always wrong (simple CRUD apps live with it), but when rules become complex, move them into the objects that own the data.

Edge cases

  • Queries are fine: order.total() asks for a value. The problem is asking for data in order to decide something the object could decide.
  • Strict Tell, Don't Ask can push presentation logic into entities. Keep formatting and UI decisions out of domain classes.
  • JPA entities and DTOs need getters for frameworks; the principle still applies to the methods you add by hand.

Separation of concerns (SoC)

A concern is a distinct job: showing data, applying business rules, storing data, logging, security. Separation of concerns means each concern lives in its own part of the system with a clear boundary. It is SRP at the scale of layers and modules.

The rules of layering: a controller never builds SQL; a repository never decides discounts; a service never touches HttpServletRequest. Cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, security, caching) are separated through aspects and filters, not repeated in each method. In Spring that is what @Transactional and Spring Security do for you, using proxies.

@RestController
class OrderController {
    private final OrderService service;
    OrderController(OrderService service) { this.service = service; }

    @PostMapping("/orders")
    ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> place(@RequestBody @Valid PlaceOrderRequest req) {
        Order order = service.place(req.toCommand());      // no business rules here
        return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(OrderResponse.from(order));
    }
}

Mistakes to avoid

  • Business rules inside controllers or in JavaScript only, because "it was quick".
  • Returning JPA entities from controllers, so the database shape leaks into the public API.
  • Putting @Transactional or SQL in controllers.
  • Splitting into so many layers that a simple field copies through six classes (accidental complexity; KISS).

Interview: coupling principles

  • Law of Demeter? A method should talk only to itself, its parameters, its fields and objects it creates. Avoid a.getB().getC().doIt(). Mention fluent builders as an allowed exception.
  • Tell, Don't Ask? Put the rule in the object that owns the data: account.withdraw(x) rather than reading the balance and setting it from outside.
  • Separation of concerns? Controller, service and repository layers, each with one job; cross-cutting concerns handled by aspects.

Composition over inheritance: from inheritance explosion to Strategy

Use inheritance for a few real is-a relations; for behaviour that varies along several independent directions, hold the behaviours as fields (composition) and combine them at run time, which avoids a class explosion.

The basics are in Core Java · Module 2: has-a versus is-a, the fragile base class, aggregation and composition. This article is the design view: how a hierarchy grows out of control, and the standard refactoring that fixes it.

The problem: inheritance explosion

You are building a notification system. First it sends email. Then SMS. Then someone asks for urgent messages, which must be sent immediately and logged. A natural first design extends the class for every combination:

There are two independent axes: the channel (email, SMS, push) and the priority (normal, urgent, scheduled). With 3 channels and 3 priorities, inheritance needs 9 classes, and each new channel adds 3 more. The urgent logic is copied in every urgent class. This is the class explosion. Worse, the behaviour is fixed at compile time: a message cannot be switched from normal to urgent while running.

The refactoring: extract each axis and compose

  1. Find each direction of variation: channel and delivery policy.
  2. Make an interface for each one.
  3. Give the main class one field per interface, set in the constructor.
  4. Delete the subclasses; combine by passing different parts.
interface Channel {
    void deliver(String to, String message);
}

class EmailChannel implements Channel {
    public void deliver(String to, String message) {
        System.out.println("EMAIL to " + to + ": " + message);
    }
}
class SmsChannel implements Channel {
    public void deliver(String to, String message) {
        System.out.println("SMS to " + to + ": " + message);
    }
}

interface DeliveryPolicy {
    void send(Runnable deliverAction);
}

class Immediate implements DeliveryPolicy {
    public void send(Runnable deliverAction) { deliverAction.run(); }
}
class Delayed implements DeliveryPolicy {
    private final long millis;
    Delayed(long millis) { this.millis = millis; }
    public void send(Runnable deliverAction) {
        java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture
            .runAsync(deliverAction, java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture
                .delayedExecutor(millis, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS));
    }
}

class Notification {
    private final Channel channel;                // composed behaviour 1
    private final DeliveryPolicy policy;          // composed behaviour 2

    Notification(Channel channel, DeliveryPolicy policy) {
        this.channel = channel;
        this.policy = policy;
    }

    void send(String to, String message) {
        policy.send(() -> channel.deliver(to, message));
    }
}

public class NotificationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Notification(new EmailChannel(), new Immediate()).send("asha@x.com", "Hi");
        new Notification(new SmsChannel(), new Immediate()).send("98100", "OTP 4521");
    }
}
EMAIL to asha@x.com: Hi
SMS to 98100: OTP 4521

Now there is one Notification class, two small channel classes and two small policy classes: 3 + 3 = 6 classes instead of 9, and adding a push channel is one class, not three. Any combination is possible, and you can change either part at run time. This is the Strategy pattern, and also the shape behind Spring dependency injection.

When to choose which

Use inheritance whenUse composition when
There is a true is-a that passes the Liskov testBehaviour varies along more than one axis
The parent is designed for extension (Template Method)You want to change behaviour at run time
You want to share a stable skeleton of an algorithmYou want to test with fake parts
The hierarchy is shallow (2 levels)You want to reuse code from a class that is not a real parent

Rule of thumb

Use interfaces to say what a thing can do, composition to get the code that does it, and inheritance only for a small, stable skeleton. If you cannot say "a B is always usable as an A", do not write B extends A.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Extending a utility class to get its methods (class OrderService extends BaseService with 40 helper methods). Inject helpers instead.
  • "Base" classes that grow into a god-class every subclass depends on.
  • Composition with no interface: holding a concrete PdfWriter field. You get has-a but not swappability.

Why inheritance is risky: the fragile base class

Explosion is only one problem. The deeper one is that a subclass depends on how its parent works inside, not just on what it promises. When the parent changes an internal detail, the child breaks even though no public signature changed. This is the fragile base class problem. The classic case is a set that counts how many elements were ever added:

Wrong: inherits and depends on internals

import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.HashSet;

class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    private int added = 0;
    @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        added += c.size();
        return super.addAll(c);     // calls add() for each item inside!
    }
    int added() { return added; }
}
// addAll(List.of("a","b","c")) -> added() == 6, not 3

Right: wraps and delegates

import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

class CountingSet<E> {
    private final Set<E> inner = new HashSet<>();
    private int added = 0;
    boolean add(E e) { added++; return inner.add(e); }
    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        added += c.size();
        boolean changed = false;
        for (E e : c) changed |= inner.add(e);
        return changed;             // we control exactly what happens
    }
    int added() { return added; }
}

The inherited addAll calls add for every element, so the count doubles. If the JDK ever changed that internal call, the child would break again in the other direction. With composition you depend only on the public contract of Set. For a version that is also a Set, use a Decorator that implements the interface and forwards calls.

The idea in one picture

A second example: order pricing

An e-commerce team writes FestivalOrder extends Order to apply a festival discount, then PrimeFestivalOrder extends FestivalOrder for members, then a GstExemptPrimeFestivalOrder. Each rule multiplies the tree. With composition, an Order holds a PricingRule and a TaxRule, and you assemble the combination per request:

interface PricingRule { long apply(long subtotalPaise); }
interface TaxRule     { long taxOn(long amountPaise); }

class Order {
    private final long subtotal;
    private final PricingRule pricing;
    private final TaxRule tax;

    Order(long subtotal, PricingRule pricing, TaxRule tax) {
        this.subtotal = subtotal;
        this.pricing = pricing;
        this.tax = tax;
    }
    long payable() {
        long net = pricing.apply(subtotal);
        return net + tax.taxOn(net);
    }
}

class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PricingRule festival = s -> s - s / 10;          // 10% off
        PricingRule member   = s -> festival.apply(s) - 5_000;
        TaxRule gst18        = a -> a * 18 / 100;
        System.out.println(new Order(100_000, festival, gst18).payable());
        System.out.println(new Order(100_000, member, gst18).payable());
    }
}
106200
100300

Rules are plain lambdas here, which is the lightest form of composition: behaviour passed as a value.

Composition, delegation and default methods

  • Composition: the object holds other objects and uses them. The parts' lifetime usually belongs to the whole (see the UML note in UML class diagrams).
  • Delegation: the object forwards a call to the held part. This is the mechanism of composition.
  • Interface default methods give shared code without a parent class, but they cannot hold state. They help for small helpers, not for the main logic.
  • Sealed hierarchies (Java 17+) keep inheritance safe by listing the allowed subclasses. Use them for closed sets of variants such as payment results.

In the JDK and Spring

  • Stack extends Vector is a well-known JDK mistake: a stack exposes add(int, E) and get(i). ArrayDeque is the modern choice and does not inherit them.
  • Collections.synchronizedList and the Java I/O wrappers (BufferedReader around a Reader) compose instead of subclassing.
  • Thread versus Runnable: pass a Runnable to a thread instead of extending Thread.
  • Spring: JdbcTemplate and RestTemplate take callbacks and converters; constructor injection of collaborators is composition. Spring Data repositories are interfaces, not base classes you extend with logic.

Comparison

InheritanceComposition
Relationshipis-ahas-a / uses
Bound atCompile timeRun time (swap the part)
CouplingTo the parent's implementationTo an interface
TestingHard to fake the parentInject a fake part
CostLittle codeSome forwarding boilerplate

Rules

  • Never inherit only to reuse code. Inherit only when the Liskov test passes and the parent was designed for extension.
  • If you do design a class for extension, document which methods call which (self-use), or make the class final.
  • Each composed part should be an interface, so it can be replaced.

Conventions

  • Default to final classes; open them to extension on purpose.
  • Pass parts through the constructor and keep them private final.
  • Name the parts by role (Channel, PricingRule), not by kind of class.

When NOT to prefer composition

  • Frameworks that expect you to extend a base class: HttpServlet, OncePerRequestFilter, Exception. Extend them, but keep the subclass thin and move logic into injected collaborators.
  • A real is-a with a stable parent: ArrayList is a List; a Circle is a Shape.
  • Forwarding every method of a wide interface by hand is noise. Use a small IDE-generated delegate, or reconsider (ISP, I: Interface Segregation).

Interview: composition over inheritance

  • Give the reason: inheritance couples the child to the parent's implementation and is fixed at compile time; composition couples to an interface and can change at run time.
  • Use the notification example: channel × priority makes N × M subclasses; composition gives N + M classes.
  • Say which pattern it leads to: Strategy (also Decorator and State).
  • Concede that inheritance is still right for real is-a and designed-for-extension classes.

Interview: follow-ups on composition

  • What is the fragile base class problem? A child that relies on the parent's internal calls breaks when the parent changes. Use the HashSet.addAll counting example.
  • Composition vs aggregation? Both are has-a. In composition the part cannot live without the whole; in aggregation it can.
  • Does "prefer composition" mean never inherit? No. It is a default, not a ban.
  • Which patterns follow from it? Strategy, Decorator, State, Adapter, and dependency injection.

Clean code: naming, small methods, no magic numbers and more

Clean code reads like clear prose: names say what things are, each function does one thing, there are no unexplained numbers, errors are handled separately from the main flow, and comments explain why, not what.

You write code once, and read it many times: when you fix a bug, add a feature, or review a pull request. Clean code (the title of Robert C. Martin's book) optimises for the reader. Each rule below comes with a before and after.

1. Meaningful names

A name should answer what it is, why it exists and how it is used, so that no comment is needed. Use nouns for classes and variables, verbs for methods, and the vocabulary of the business (the domain).

Wrong

int d;                       // elapsed time in days
List<int[]> list1 = getThem();
void proc(Order o, boolean f) { }
class DataManager { }

Right

int elapsedDays;
List<Cell> flaggedCells = findFlaggedCells();
void cancel(Order order, boolean refundIssued) { }
class InvoiceGenerator { }
  • Classes: nouns (OrderValidator); methods: verbs (calculateTotal); booleans: questions (isPaid, hasStock).
  • Avoid noise words (Data, Info, Manager, Util) and encodings (strName, IOrderService is debated; follow your team).
  • Use one word per concept: do not mix fetch, get and retrieve for the same idea.
  • Use searchable names. A name like MAX_RETRIES is easy to find; 3 is not.
  • Length matches scope: i in a three-line loop is fine; a field used across a class needs a full name.

2. Small functions that do one thing

A function should do one thing, at one level of abstraction, and be short enough to see on one screen (many teams aim for under 20 lines). If you can extract a piece with a name that is not just a restatement of the code, extract it.

Wrong: one long method mixing levels

void checkout(Cart cart) {
    for (Item i : cart.items()) {
        if (i.qty() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    }
    long total = 0;
    for (Item i : cart.items()) total += i.price() * i.qty();
    if (total > 100000) total -= total / 10;
    System.out.println("Charging " + total);
}

Right: reads like an outline

void checkout(Cart cart) {
    validate(cart);
    long total = applyBulkDiscount(sum(cart));
    charge(total);
}

3. Few parameters; parameter objects

Zero to two parameters are easy; three is the practical limit; more is a smell. Group related values into an object (parameter object), usually a record:

Wrong: long list, order easy to mix up

createUser("Asha", "Rao", "asha@x.com", "98100", "Pune", "411001", true);

Right: named, grouped, extendable

record Address(String city, String pincode) { }
record NewUser(String firstName, String lastName, String email,
               String phone, Address address, boolean newsletter) { }

createUser(new NewUser("Asha", "Rao", "asha@x.com", "98100",
                       new Address("Pune", "411001"), true));

For many optional values, use a Builder.

4. No boolean flag arguments

A boolean parameter means the method does two things. The call site render(true) says nothing. Split into two methods, or pass an enum.

Wrong

sendMessage(user, text, true);      // true = what?

Right

sendUrgentMessage(user, text);
sendNormalMessage(user, text);
// or: sendMessage(user, text, Priority.URGENT);

5. Guard clauses and early return

Handle the invalid cases first and return or throw. The main path then stays at the left margin without deep nesting (the "arrow anti-pattern").

Wrong: nested

double payment(Employee e) {
    double result;
    if (!e.isDead()) {
        if (!e.isRetired()) {
            result = e.salary();
        } else {
            result = e.pension();
        }
    } else {
        result = 0;
    }
    return result;
}

Right: guard clauses

double payment(Employee e) {
    if (e.isDead()) return 0;
    if (e.isRetired()) return e.pension();
    return e.salary();
}

6. Constants and enums, not magic numbers or strings

A magic number is a literal whose meaning is not obvious. Replace it with a named constant; replace sets of related strings with an enum, so the compiler checks them.

Wrong

if (user.getStatus().equals("A")) { ... }
if (retries > 3) { ... }
long fee = amount * 18 / 100 + 25;

Right

enum AccountStatus { ACTIVE, BLOCKED, CLOSED }
private static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3;
private static final int GST_PERCENT = 18;
private static final long FLAT_FEE_PAISE = 25;

if (user.status() == AccountStatus.ACTIVE) { ... }
if (retries > MAX_RETRIES) { ... }
long fee = amount * GST_PERCENT / 100 + FLAT_FEE_PAISE;

Values like 0, 1 and -1 in obvious contexts (i + 1, list.size() == 0) do not need names. Configuration that differs per environment (URLs, timeouts) belongs in application.yml, not in constants.

7. Comments explain why, not what

If a comment restates the code, delete it or rename the code. Use comments for intent, warnings, a business rule, or the reason for a surprising choice. Javadoc is for public APIs.

// Bad: says what the code already says
i++;   // increment i

// Better: explains a decision the code cannot
// Banks settle on working days only, so a weekend due date moves to Monday (RBI rule).
LocalDate due = nextWorkingDay(requested);

Do not leave commented-out code; version control remembers it (see Git basics). A TODO needs an owner or a ticket number.

8. Error handling as a separate concern

Main logic should not be buried under try/catch blocks and error-code checks. Use exceptions, not magic return values like -1 or null. Keep error mapping in one place (in Spring, @RestControllerAdvice).

// Bad: error codes mixed with the flow
int code = service.transfer(from, to, amount);
if (code == -1) { ... } else if (code == -2) { ... }

// Good: the happy path is clean, the failure is an exception
service.transfer(from, to, amount);      // throws InsufficientFundsException

@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiExceptionHandler {
    @ExceptionHandler(InsufficientFundsException.class)
