    ResponseEntity<ErrorBody> onInsufficient(InsufficientFundsException e) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(409).body(new ErrorBody(e.getMessage()));
    }
}
  • Do not catch Exception and ignore it. At least log it, or let it propagate.
  • Return empty collections, not null; use Optional for "maybe a value" return types.
  • Throw specific exceptions with a message that says what failed and with which ID.

9. Small classes and consistent formatting

Keep classes small and focused (SRP). Order members the same way in every file (constants, fields, constructors, public methods, private methods). Use one formatter for the whole team (Google Java Style, Spotless or the IDE formatter in CI) so that diffs show real changes, not whitespace arguments. Keep lines to about 100 to 120 characters.

Checklist before you open a pull request

  • Could a new teammate understand each method name without reading the body?
  • Is any method longer than a screen, or doing "X and Y"?
  • Any literal number or string that has a meaning? Name it.
  • Any boolean parameter, more than three parameters, or deep nesting?
  • Is there dead code, a commented-out block, or a comment that repeats the code?

Cautions

  • Rules are guidelines. A 40-line method that reads as one clear story can beat ten tiny methods that make you jump around.
  • Do not extract a method for every line; extract when the new name adds meaning.
  • Refactor under test. Change structure, not behaviour, and run the tests after each step.

Interview: clean code

  • What is clean code? Code that is easy to read, change and test: good names, small focused functions, no duplication, no magic values.
  • How do you handle a 300-line method? Write tests first, then extract methods with intent-revealing names (Extract Method), group data into objects, and replace conditionals with polymorphism.
  • Why avoid boolean arguments? Call sites are unreadable and the method does two things.

Code smells and the refactoring that fixes each

A code smell is a surface sign that the design has a problem; learn the common smells (long method, large class, primitive obsession, feature envy, shotgun surgery, switch on type, duplicated code, data clumps) and the standard refactoring for each.

A code smell is a pattern in code that is not a bug but hints at a deeper design weakness. The term comes from Kent Beck and Martin Fowler's book Refactoring. A refactoring is a small change that improves structure without changing behaviour. The rule: smell, then test, then refactor in small steps, then test again.

SmellHow it looksRefactoringPrinciple
Long method50+ lines, many levels of nesting, comments marking sectionsExtract Method; guard clausesSRP
Large class (god class)Hundreds of lines, many fields, unrelated methodsExtract ClassSRP
Primitive obsessionString email, long amount everywhereReplace with value objects (Email, Money)Encapsulation
Feature envyA method uses another class's data more than its ownMove MethodTell, Don't Ask
Shotgun surgeryOne change forces small edits in many classesMove Method / Move Field into one classDRY, cohesion
Switch on typeswitch or if/else on a type code, repeatedReplace Conditional with Polymorphism (Strategy, State)OCP
Duplicated codeSame logic in several placesExtract Method; Pull Up Method; Template MethodDRY
Data clumpsThe same group of fields or parameters travels togetherIntroduce Parameter Object / Extract ClassCohesion
Long parameter list4+ parametersParameter object; BuilderClean code
Divergent changeOne class changes for many unrelated reasonsExtract ClassSRP
Message chaina.getB().getC().getD()Hide DelegateDemeter
Speculative generalityUnused hooks, flags and abstract classes "for later"Remove it; inlineYAGNI

Example 1: primitive obsession → value object

Primitive obsession means using String, int and long for domain ideas. A String can hold anything, so every method that receives an email must check it again, or forget to.

// Smell: any string is accepted; amount might be rupees or paise?
void register(String email, String phone, long amount) { /* ... */ }
register("98100", "asha@x.com", 5);        // arguments swapped: compiles fine!

// Refactored: the type carries the rule
record Email(String value) {
    Email {                                          // compact constructor validates once
        if (value == null || !value.matches("[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid email: " + value);
        }
    }
}
record Money(long paise) {
    Money {
        if (paise < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative money");
    }
    Money plus(Money other) { return new Money(paise + other.paise); }
}
void register(Email email, Phone phone, Money deposit) { /* ... */ }

Swapping arguments is now a compile error, and validation lives in one place. (Phone would be another record.)

Example 2: feature envy → Move Method

// Smell: InvoicePrinter is more interested in Order's data than its own
class InvoicePrinter {
    long total(Order order) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (OrderItem i : order.items()) sum += i.unitPaise() * i.qty();
        return sum;
    }
}

// Fix: the method moves to the class that owns the data
record Order(String id, List<OrderItem> items) {
    long total() {
        return items.stream().mapToLong(i -> i.unitPaise() * i.qty()).sum();
    }
}

Example 3: switch on type → polymorphism

This one is covered in OCP. A quick cousin: if (employee.type == MANAGER) ... else if (type == ENGINEER) ... repeated in pay(), bonus() and title(). Replace the type code with an interface or an abstract class Employee with one subclass per type, or a Strategy/State object when the type changes at run time.

Example 4: data clumps → Extract Class

// Smell: street, city, state, pincode travel together in many signatures
void ship(String street, String city, String state, String pincode) { }
boolean deliverable(String street, String city, String state, String pincode) { }

// Fix
record Address(String street, String city, String state, String pincode) {
    boolean isMetro() { return List.of("Mumbai", "Delhi", "Chennai", "Kolkata").contains(city); }
}
void ship(Address to) { }
boolean deliverable(Address to) { }

Once the clump becomes a class, behaviour like isMetro() finds a natural home.

Shotgun surgery versus divergent change

They are opposites, and interviewers like to ask. Divergent change: one class changes for many reasons (too much in one place; split it). Shotgun surgery: one reason for change touches many classes (one concern scattered; gather it). Both come from wrong boundaries.

Safe refactoring workflow

  1. Make sure tests cover the code. If none, write characterization tests that record current behaviour.
  2. Change one small thing (rename, extract, move).
  3. Run the tests. If red, undo and try a smaller step.
  4. Commit often, so each step can be reverted alone.

Tip: let the IDE do it

IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse have automated, behaviour-preserving Extract Method, Extract Class, Move, Rename, Introduce Parameter Object and Inline. Static analysis tools such as SonarQube report long methods and duplication. Use them as hints, not as judges.

Interview: code smells

  • What is a code smell? A sign of a design problem, not a bug. Name three and the fix for each: long method (Extract Method), switch on type (polymorphism), data clumps (parameter object).
  • What is refactoring? Improving structure without changing behaviour, in small, tested steps.
  • Feature envy? A method uses another object's data more than its own; move it there.

UML class diagrams: boxes, relationships and how they map to Java

A UML class diagram shows classes (name, attributes, methods) and the relationships between them (association, aggregation, composition, inheritance, realization, dependency) so that you can discuss a design before and after you code it.

UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standard way of drawing software designs. You do not need all of it. In interviews and design discussions you mostly need two diagrams: the class diagram (the static structure: what exists and how it is connected) and the sequence diagram (the dynamic behaviour: who calls whom, in what order; see next article). In low-level design interviews (Module 3) a class diagram is usually the first thing you draw. Here we write diagrams in Mermaid text, which becomes a picture.

The class box

A class is a box with three compartments: the name, the attributes (fields) and the operations (methods). A visibility symbol precedes each member.

SymbolMeaningJava
+publicpublic
-privateprivate
#protectedprotected
~package-privateno modifier
 
public class BankAccount {
    private String accountNumber;
    private long balanceInPaise;
    protected AccountStatus status;

    public void deposit(long amount) { /* ... */ }
    public void withdraw(long amount) { /* ... */ }
    public long getBalance() { return balanceInPaise; }
    List<String> auditTrail() { /* ... */ return List.of(); }
}

In Mermaid, static members are marked with a $ suffix and abstract with *, but you rarely need them. Special kinds of types are shown with an annotation line such as <<interface>>, <<abstract>> or <<enumeration>>.

The six relationships

RelationshipMermaidMeaning
Inheritance (generalisation)Animal <|-- DogDog is a Animal (extends)
RealizationShape <|.. CircleCircle implements the interface Shape
AssociationCustomer --> OrderCustomer knows / uses Order (a field)
AggregationDepartment o-- EmployeeWhole has parts; parts live independently
CompositionHouse *-- RoomWhole owns parts; parts die with the whole
DependencyOrderService ..> MailerUses temporarily (parameter, local variable, return)

Each relationship as Java code

The diagram arrow tells you what to look for in the code:

// Inheritance:   Animal <|-- Dog
abstract class Animal { abstract void makeSound(); }
class Dog extends Animal { void makeSound() { System.out.println("Woof"); } }

// Realization:   Pet <|.. Dog   (a class can do both)
interface Pet { void play(); }
class Puppy extends Animal implements Pet {
    void makeSound() { }
    public void play() { }
}

// Association:   Customer --> Order     (a field holds a reference)
class Customer {
    private final List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();     // 1 to many
}

// Aggregation:   Department o-- Employee   (parts are passed in; they can outlive it)
class Department {
    private final List<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>();
    void add(Employee e) { staff.add(e); }
}

// Composition:   House *-- Room   (the whole creates and owns its parts)
class House {
    private final List<Room> rooms = new ArrayList<>();
    House() { rooms.add(new Room("Hall")); }
}

// Dependency:    OrderService ..> Mailer   (no field; used inside a method only)
class OrderService {
    void confirm(Order order, Mailer mailer) {       // Mailer arrives as a parameter
        mailer.send(order.customerEmail(), "Confirmed");
    }
}

Aggregation versus composition is the classic confusion: in code both are fields, so the difference is in lifetime and ownership (see Core Java · Module 2). Many professional diagrams use only plain association and composition. If you are unsure, an association arrow is rarely wrong.

Multiplicity and labels

Multiplicity says how many instances take part: 1 exactly one, 0..1 optional, * many, 1..* at least one. Put it in quotes beside each end, and add a label for the role.

Read it aloud: "A customer places zero or more orders. An order contains one or more items, and the items belong to that order alone (composition). Each item refers to one product. An order may have one payment." Mapping to Java: Customer has List<Order>; Order has List<OrderItem> created inside it; OrderItem has a Product field; Order has an optional Payment field.

How to draw a class diagram in an interview

  1. List the nouns in the requirement: these are candidate classes.
  2. List the verbs: these become methods, placed on the class that owns the data.
  3. Add relationships and multiplicity; use composition when the part cannot exist alone.
  4. Extract interfaces where behaviour varies (payment methods, pricing rules), and mark them <<interface>>.
  5. Show only what helps: skip getters and setters, trivial fields and every utility class.

Edge cases and conventions

  • Mermaid generics use tildes: List~Order~, not angle brackets. In this site's source you must also write < as &lt; in the arrows.
  • Arrow direction in association shows navigability: Order --> Customer means Order holds the reference. A plain line -- means no direction is stated.
  • The JPA @OneToMany and @ManyToOne pair is a bidirectional association drawn with two arrows or one plain line.
  • Dependency (..>) is weaker than association: no field, only a temporary use.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Using inheritance arrows for "has-a" ideas; confusing the filled diamond (composition) with the hollow one (aggregation).
  • Drawing every getter, every DTO and every utility. A diagram that shows everything shows nothing.
  • Pointing the realization arrow from the interface to the class. It points to the interface.

Interview: UML class diagram

  • Explain the difference between association, aggregation and composition using ownership and lifetime.
  • Explain inheritance versus realization: solid versus dashed line, both with a hollow triangle at the parent.
  • In LLD rounds, draw the classes with key methods and multiplicities, then say which design principle each interface supports.

UML sequence diagrams: lifelines, messages and alt/loop blocks

A sequence diagram shows objects as vertical lifelines and the messages between them as horizontal arrows in time order, so you can explain one scenario (such as placing an order or logging in) step by step.

A class diagram shows what exists; a sequence diagram shows what happens during one use case. Time runs from top to bottom. It is the best tool to explain request flows, to check that a design has the right collaborators, and to spot a class that does too much or too little.

The parts of a sequence diagram

Participant / lifeline
A box at the top (an object, service or actor such as the user) with a dashed vertical line below it that represents its life during the scenario. In Mermaid: participant or actor.
Synchronous message
A call where the caller waits for the answer: a solid line with a filled arrowhead (A->>B: message), like an ordinary Java method call.
Return message
The reply, drawn as a dashed line (B-->>A: result).
Asynchronous message
A call where the sender does not wait (a message put on a queue, @Async, an event). Drawn with an open arrowhead: A-)B: message in Mermaid.
Activation bar
A thin box on a lifeline showing when the object is busy. Mermaid uses activate/deactivate or the shortcut +/- on arrows.
Fragment (alt, opt, loop)
A labelled box around messages: alt (if / else), opt (if with no else), loop (repeat), par (parallel).

Example 1: place an order

What this diagram teaches you about the design:

  • OrderService is the coordinator; it talks to inventory, payment and repository. If this list grows past four or five collaborators, think about a Facade or events.
  • The confirmation email is asynchronous: failure to send it must not roll back the order.
  • The "declined" branch shows compensation (release the reserved stock). Missing branches in a diagram are missing code in the program.

The matching Java skeleton:

public OrderConfirmation placeOrder(Cart cart) {
    for (CartItem item : cart.items()) {
        inventory.reserve(item.sku(), item.qty());               // loop
    }
    PaymentResult result = payments.charge(cart.totalInPaise());
    if (result.approved()) {                                     // alt
        Order order = repository.save(Order.from(cart, result.receipt()));
        events.publish(new OrderPlaced(order.id()));             // async
        return OrderConfirmation.of(order);
    }
    inventory.release(cart.items());                             // else: compensate
    throw new PaymentFailedException(result.reason());
}

Example 2: login with a token

The same picture helps with the JWT flow you will meet in the Spring Security notes (Security).

Mermaid syntax cheat sheet

WriteMeaning
A->>B: textSynchronous call
B-->>A: textReturn (dashed)
A-)B: textAsynchronous message
A->>A: textA call to itself
participant X as Long nameShort alias for a long name
alt ... else ... endIf / else
opt ... endOptional (if without else)
loop ... endRepeat
Note over A,B: textA note spanning lifelines

Tips for good sequence diagrams

  • One diagram per scenario. Draw the happy path first, then add the failure branches.
  • Show five to seven participants at most; group the rest ("Database", "Payment provider").
  • Name messages after methods or HTTP calls so the code is easy to match.
  • Use the diagram to find design problems: a lifeline that talks to everyone is a god object; a lifeline with no messages is unnecessary.

Edge cases

  • Do not draw getters, logging and framework internals; show business collaborations.
  • In a microservices flow, show the network hop and timeouts: a synchronous call across services is a failure point (see distributed system patterns).

Interview: sequence diagrams

  • Class diagram vs sequence diagram? Static structure versus dynamic interaction over time.
  • Synchronous vs asynchronous message? The caller waits for the reply, or does not.
  • Be ready to sketch "place an order" or "login" on a whiteboard: actors, services, alt for success and failure.

Interview questions — Design principles

What do cohesion and coupling mean, and what should you aim for?

Cohesion is how strongly the members of one module belong together; coupling is how much one module depends on others. Aim for high cohesion and low coupling: each class has one focused job, and classes talk through small interfaces. This makes change cheap, because a change touches few places.

Explain each letter of SOLID in one line.

S: a class has one reason to change. O: add behaviour by adding new code, not by editing old code. L: a subtype can replace its parent without breaking callers. I: prefer small, role-specific interfaces to fat ones. D: depend on abstractions, not on concrete details; high-level code owns the abstraction.

Does SRP mean a class should have only one method?

No. SRP is about reasons to change (or actors), not about method count. A class with fifteen methods that all serve one concern is fine. A class with three methods that mix SQL, pricing and email is not. Ask: "who would ask me to change this class?" If the answer is several different groups, split it.

How do you apply OCP to a growing switch statement?

Introduce an interface (for example DiscountPolicy), write one class per branch, and let the caller loop over or look up the right implementation. A new case becomes a new class. In Spring you can inject List<DiscountPolicy> or Map<String, DiscountPolicy> so new @Component classes are found automatically. This is the Strategy pattern.

Why is a Square not a valid subclass of a mutable Rectangle?

A Rectangle promises that setting the width leaves the height unchanged. Square breaks this by changing both. Code like r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); expects area 20, but a Square gives 16. The child cannot be substituted for the parent, which violates LSP. Fix: use immutable types or a shared Shape interface, not inheritance between them.

Which SOLID principle does a method that throws UnsupportedOperationException usually break?

LSP, because callers of the parent type expect the method to work. The root cause is often ISP: the interface is too fat, so some implementers cannot honour all of it. Split the interface into smaller roles so that each class implements only what it supports.

What is the difference between DIP, DI and IoC?

DIP is a design principle: high-level code depends on an abstraction, not on a low-level detail. DI is a technique: objects receive their collaborators from outside (usually via the constructor) instead of creating them. IoC is the wider idea that a framework or container controls object creation and flow, calling your code. Spring's container is an IoC container that performs DI, and DI makes DIP practical. You can inject a concrete class and still violate DIP.

Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?

Dependencies are explicit and cannot be forgotten, fields can be final, the object is never half-built, and you can create it in a plain unit test with new without Spring. Field injection hides dependencies and needs reflection or a container to set them.

Is DRY the same as "never write similar code twice"?

No. DRY is about duplicated knowledge, such as one business rule in three places. Two blocks that look alike but change for different reasons should stay separate; merging them couples unrelated things, which is worse than the duplication. Use the rule of three: abstract when the third copy appears and the common shape is clear.

How do KISS and YAGNI stop over-engineering?

KISS prefers the simplest design that solves the problem. YAGNI says do not build features or flexibility "just in case", because the guess about the future is usually wrong and unused code still costs. Keep the code loosely coupled and well tested so that real changes are cheap, and add the abstraction when a second or third real case shows up.

Why favour composition over inheritance?

Inheritance couples a child to the parent's implementation (fragile base class), is fixed at compile time and allows one parent. Composition holds collaborators behind interfaces, so you can swap them at run time and test with fakes. It also avoids class explosion: channels × priorities needs N × M subclasses by inheritance but only N + M classes with composition.

What is the Law of Demeter? Give an example violation.

A method should talk only to itself, its parameters, its fields and objects it creates. order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity() makes the caller depend on three classes' structure. Fix: order.isShippedTo("Mumbai"), so only Order and Customer know the details. Fluent builders and streams are not violations because each call is on the same type.

Name five code smells and the refactoring for each.

Long method → Extract Method. Large class → Extract Class. Primitive obsession → value objects (Email, Money). Feature envy → Move Method. Switch on type → replace conditional with polymorphism. Others: data clumps → parameter object; shotgun surgery → gather the scattered concern into one class.

Why should you avoid boolean flag parameters?

The call send(user, text, true) does not say what true means, and a flag shows the method does two things. Split it into two well-named methods or pass an enum such as Priority.URGENT.

Aggregation versus composition: how do they differ in a class diagram and in code?

Both mean "whole has parts". In aggregation (hollow diamond) the parts exist independently and are passed in, like employees in a department. In composition (filled diamond) the whole creates and owns the parts and they die with it, like rooms in a house. In Java both are fields; the difference is who creates the parts and who controls their lifetime.

Cheat sheet — Design principles

  • Good design low cost of change: high cohesion, low coupling.
  • Cohesion things inside a module belong together; describe the class without "and".
  • Coupling how much modules know about each other; depend on interfaces, not classes.
  • Encapsulation hide data, expose behaviour; every public getter is a small leak.
  • Program to an interface declare List, not ArrayList; depend on roles.
  • SRP one reason to change (one actor); not "one method".
  • OCP extend by adding classes, not editing; replace growing switch with an interface (Strategy).
  • LSP a subtype must work wherever the parent works; no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions, no surprise exceptions.
  • ISP many small role interfaces beat one fat interface; no empty or throwing stubs.
  • DIP high-level code owns the abstraction; low-level details implement it.
  • DIP vs DI vs IoC principle vs technique (inject through constructor) vs container controls flow.
  • DRY one authoritative place for each piece of knowledge, not each line of text.
  • Rule of three copy twice, abstract on the third.
  • KISS simplest thing that works; YAGNI do not build it until needed.
  • Law of Demeter no a.getB().getC().doIt() chains (builders are fine).
  • Tell, Don't Ask account.withdraw(x), not read-decide-set from outside.
  • Separation of concerns controller → service → repository; cross-cutting through aspects.
  • Composition over inheritance N + M classes beat N × M; inherit only for true is-a.
  • Clean code intent-revealing names, short methods, ≤3 parameters, no flags, guard clauses, named constants, comments say why.
  • Code smells long method, large class, primitive obsession, feature envy, shotgun surgery, switch on type, duplication, data clumps.
  • Refactor safely tests first, tiny steps, run tests after each, commit often.
  • UML class + - # ~ visibility; inheritance <|--; realization <|..; association -->; aggregation o--; composition *--; dependency ..>.
  • Multiplicity 1, 0..1, *, 1..* in quotes at each end.
  • UML sequence lifelines, ->> sync, -->> return, -) async, alt/opt/loop blocks.

Practice — Design principles

  1. Spot the responsibilities (easy). Take a UserService that registers a user, hashes the password, saves to the database, sends a welcome email and writes an audit log. List its reasons to change. Done when you have a list of at least four concerns and a name for each class you would extract.
  2. Apply SRP (easy/medium). Refactor the class from exercise 1 into a coordinator plus collaborators (PasswordHasher, UserRepository, WelcomeMailer, AuditLog). Done when UserService.register is under ten lines and you can unit-test it with fakes and no database.
  3. Replace a switch with Strategy (medium). Write a ShippingCostCalculator with a switch on STANDARD, EXPRESS, SAME_DAY. Refactor to a ShippingPolicy interface with one class per mode. Done when adding INTERNATIONAL needs no edit to the calculator; then inject List<ShippingPolicy> with Spring.
  4. Fix an LSP violation (medium). Given abstract class Account { withdraw(); } with a FixedDepositAccount that throws UnsupportedOperationException in withdraw, redesign the hierarchy with Account, Withdrawable and Depositable interfaces. Done when no method throws UnsupportedOperationException and callers cannot pass an FD to withdrawAll.
  5. Segregate an interface (medium). Split a 6-method ProductRepository into reader, writer and search interfaces. Make a catalog page depend only on the reader. Done when a test for the catalog fakes one method, not six.
  6. Invert a dependency (medium). Take a class that calls new SmtpMailer() and new MySqlDao() inside its methods. Introduce interfaces, constructor injection and a Spring @Service. Done when you can swap both in a plain JUnit test and the service never imports a JDBC or SMTP class.
  7. Composition over inheritance (medium/hard). Model a coffee shop with EspressoWithMilk, EspressoWithSoy, LatteWithSugar and so on as subclasses. Replace it with a Drink composed of a base, a milk and toppings. Done when you can create ten combinations with six classes in total.
  8. Clean-code makeover (medium). Take any 60-line method from your own project. Apply: rename, extract three methods, replace magic numbers with constants or an enum, remove a boolean flag, add guard clauses. Done when each method does one thing and tests still pass.
  9. Find the smells (medium). Review a pull request or an open-source class and write down five smells from the table, each with the line numbers and the refactoring you would apply.
  10. Diagrams (hard). For a "library management" system, draw (a) a class diagram with at least six classes, using composition, an interface and multiplicity, and (b) a sequence diagram for "borrow a book" with an alt block for "book unavailable". Done when every arrow can be mapped to a field, parameter or method call in Java.

Module 2·LLD · week 2Must

Design patterns

18 topics · about 2.5 h of reading

A design pattern is a named, proven solution to a problem that keeps appearing in object-oriented design. "Use a Strategy here" lets a whole team understand a design in four words. Patterns also explain the frameworks you use every day: Spring is full of singletons, factories, proxies, templates and observers, and the JDK uses them too (Comparator, InputStream wrappers, Runnable).

This module teaches 13 patterns in detail, in three groups (creational, structural, behavioural), and then shows where Spring uses them. Each pattern follows the same shape: intent, the problem, structure, complete Java code on a realistic example, JDK and Spring usage, pros and cons, and when not to use it. It builds on Module 1: nearly every pattern is a way to apply SOLID, especially the Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion principles. The next module, LLD interview problems, uses these patterns in full designs.

  • Explain what a design pattern is and the three GoF categories.
  • Write Singleton (thread-safe, five ways), Factory, Builder, Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility and Template Method from memory.
  • Tell Adapter, Decorator, Proxy and Facade apart, and State from Strategy.
  • Point to the pattern behind a Spring feature (@Transactional, JdbcTemplate, application events, the filter chain).
  • Choose a pattern from the problem, and decide when not to use one.

What design patterns are, how to learn them and the danger of over-engineering

A design pattern is a reusable, named solution to a common design problem; the Gang of Four book groups 23 of them into creational, structural and behavioural patterns, and the right way to learn them is to start from the problem, not from the pattern.

In 1994 four authors (Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides, called the Gang of Four or GoF) published Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software. It describes 23 patterns they had seen in good code. A pattern is not a library you import or code you copy. It is a description of a problem, a solution structure and the trade-offs, which you adapt to your case. The value is in three things: a ready solution, a shared vocabulary ("wrap it in a Decorator"), and a reminder of the costs.

The three categories

CategoryConcernPatterns in these notes
CreationalHow objects are createdSingleton, Factory (Simple, Method, Abstract), Builder; also Prototype
StructuralHow classes and objects are combined into larger structuresAdapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy; also Composite, Flyweight
BehaviouralHow objects communicate and share responsibilityStrategy, Observer, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method; also Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor

How to read each pattern

  1. Intent: one line saying what the pattern is for.
  2. The problem: the pain, as a short story. If you do not feel the pain, you do not need the pattern.
  3. Structure: the classes and their relationships (a UML class diagram, see UML class diagrams).
  4. Code: a complete, realistic Java version.
  5. Where you have seen it: JDK and Spring examples.
  6. Pros, cons, and when not to use it.

How to learn patterns well

  • Problem first. Ask "what changes here, and what hurts?" and then "which pattern solves that?". Memorising names without problems gives you a hammer looking for nails.
  • Find them in code you know. new BufferedReader(new FileReader(...)) is Decorator. Collections.sort(list, comparator) is Strategy. Once you see them, they stay in memory.
  • Write each one once on a small example and then refactor a messy class into it.
  • Learn the trade-offs. Every pattern adds classes and indirection. A pattern is a purchase; know the price.

Patterns and the principles

Patterns are not new ideas on top of SOLID. They are SOLID applied to recurring situations: Strategy, State, Decorator and Template Method apply the Open/Closed Principle; Factory, Adapter and Facade apply Dependency Inversion; Strategy and Decorator use composition over inheritance.

The danger: over-engineering

Beginners who just learned patterns put them everywhere: a SingletonFactoryBuilder to create a class used once. This hurts: more classes, more files, harder reading, and flexibility nobody asked for (YAGNI). A language also reduces the need for some patterns. With lambdas and records, Java removes much of the ceremony: a Strategy can be a lambda, a Command can be a Runnable, a Builder is often not needed for a small record.

When to introduce a pattern

  • You have a real problem you can name (a growing switch, an unreadable 8-argument constructor, a third-party API you cannot change).
  • The simple solution has already hurt once or twice.
  • You can say in one sentence what the pattern buys you.

If not, write the simple code first. Refactor to a pattern when the need appears.

Anti-patterns to know

  • God object: one class that knows and does everything.
  • Spaghetti code: tangled control flow with no structure.
  • Golden hammer: using the one pattern you know for every problem.
  • Singleton abuse: global state in disguise (see Singleton).
  • Premature abstraction: an interface with one implementation and no plan for a second.

Interview: design patterns in general

  • What is a design pattern? A general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring design problem, with a name, structure and trade-offs. Not code to copy.
  • Name the three categories with two examples each. Creational: Singleton, Builder. Structural: Adapter, Proxy. Behavioural: Strategy, Observer.
  • Which patterns have you used? Pick three from your projects: Strategy for payment methods, Builder for request objects, Observer through Spring events. Explain the problem each solved.

Singleton: thread-safe implementations, breaking it, and Spring's singleton scope

Singleton guarantees that a class has exactly one instance and gives global access to it; in Java you write it with an eager field, a holder class or an enum, and you must understand how threads, reflection, serialization and cloning can break it.

Intent: ensure that a class has only one instance and provide a global point of access to it.

The problem

Some things must exist once in a process: an application configuration, a connection pool, a logger registry, a cache, a hardware device handle. If two ConnectionPool objects each opened 50 connections, the database would run out. You need a way to stop others from calling new. The answer is a private constructor plus a static method that returns the single instance.

1. Eager initialisation

Create the instance when the class loads. It is simple and thread-safe, because the JVM guarantees that class initialisation runs once and is visible to all threads.

public final class AppConfig {
    private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig();   // created at class load

    private final java.util.Properties props = new java.util.Properties();

    private AppConfig() {                  // nobody else can call new
        props.setProperty("currency", "INR");
    }

    public static AppConfig getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }

    public String get(String key) { return props.getProperty(key); }
}

Downside: the object is built even if it is never used, which matters when it is expensive. Also, an exception in the constructor happens at class-load time (ExceptionInInitializerError).

2. Lazy initialisation with synchronized

Create the instance on the first call. The naive version is not thread-safe: two threads may both see null and both create an object. Making the method synchronized fixes it:

public final class LazySingleton {
    private static LazySingleton instance;

    private LazySingleton() { }

    public static synchronized LazySingleton getInstance() {    // safe, but slow
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new LazySingleton();
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

Correct, but every call takes the lock, even long after the instance exists. That cost is small today but visible on a very hot path.

3. Double-checked locking with volatile

Check once without a lock (fast path); only if it is null, lock and check again.

public final class DclSingleton {
    private static volatile DclSingleton instance;     // volatile is REQUIRED

    private DclSingleton() { }

    public static DclSingleton getInstance() {
        DclSingleton local = instance;                 // 1st check, no lock
        if (local == null) {
            synchronized (DclSingleton.class) {
                local = instance;                      // 2nd check, with lock
                if (local == null) {
                    instance = local = new DclSingleton();
                }
            }
        }
        return local;
    }
}

Why volatile? The statement instance = new DclSingleton() is really three steps: (1) allocate memory, (2) run the constructor to set the fields, (3) write the reference into instance. The compiler and CPU may reorder 2 and 3. Then a second thread, doing the unlocked first check, can see a non-null instance that points to an object whose constructor has not finished, and use a half-built object. volatile forbids that reordering and guarantees that a thread seeing the reference also sees the finished fields (the Java memory model, Core Java · Module 6). Without volatile DCL is broken. Copying into a local variable avoids a second volatile read on the fast path.

4. The holder idiom (Bill Pugh)

Put the instance in a private static nested class. The JVM loads the nested class only when getInstance() first touches it, and class initialisation is thread-safe. You get laziness and thread safety with no locks and no volatile. This is the usual recommendation for a lazy singleton.

public final class ConnectionPool {
    private ConnectionPool() { /* open connections */ }

    private static class Holder {                       // loaded on first use
        private static final ConnectionPool INSTANCE = new ConnectionPool();
    }

    public static ConnectionPool getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;
    }
}

5. The enum singleton

Joshua Bloch (Effective Java) calls a single-element enum the best way to write a singleton. The JVM guarantees one instance per constant, thread-safe creation, and protection against reflection and serialization attacks.

public enum IdGenerator {
    INSTANCE;

    private final java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong next =
            new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong(1000);

    public long nextId() { return next.getAndIncrement(); }
}

// usage
long id = IdGenerator.INSTANCE.nextId();

Limits: an enum cannot extend another class (it can implement interfaces), and it is eager, in the sense of being created when the enum class loads.

VariantLazy?Thread-safe?Safe from reflection / serialization?
Eager fieldNoYesNo
synchronized methodYesYes (slower)No
Double-checked locking + volatileYesYesNo
Holder idiomYesYesNo
EnumOn class loadYesYes

Breaking a singleton, and the fixes

Reflection. setAccessible(true) on the private constructor lets any code create a second instance.

import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;

Constructor<AppConfig> c = AppConfig.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
c.setAccessible(true);
AppConfig second = c.newInstance();
System.out.println(second == AppConfig.getInstance());     // false: two instances!

Fix: throw from the constructor if an instance exists (if (INSTANCE != null) throw new IllegalStateException();), or use an enum. Reflection cannot instantiate enums: newInstance throws IllegalArgumentException("Cannot reflectively create enum objects"). Note that with Java modules and a security manager, access can also be restricted.

Serialization. If the singleton implements Serializable, each deserialization builds a new object. Fix: add readResolve() that returns the real instance, and mark fields transient or avoid serializing. Enums handle this automatically.

public final class Session implements java.io.Serializable {
    private static final Session INSTANCE = new Session();
    private Session() { }
    public static Session getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }

    private Object readResolve() {              // called after deserialization
        return INSTANCE;                        // discard the new copy
    }
}

Cloning. If the class (or a parent) implements Cloneable, clone() makes a second copy. Fix: do not implement Cloneable, or override clone() to throw CloneNotSupportedException or return the instance.

Multiple class loaders. A singleton is one per class loader, not per JVM. In application servers, two web apps (or a hot-reload tool) can each load their own copy. And in a cluster, every JVM has its own singleton, so it cannot guard a database-wide or cluster-wide resource.

Spring's singleton scope versus the GoF Singleton

By default, a Spring bean has singleton scope: the container creates one instance of the bean per container (per bean definition) and returns it every time. It sounds like Singleton, but the mechanism is different:

QuestionGoF SingletonSpring singleton bean
Who enforces "one"?The class itself (private constructor)The container
Scope of "one"Per class loaderPer container and bean definition (you can define two beans of one class)
Can you call new?NoYes (plain Java classes; Spring just does not)
How do users get it?getInstance() (global access)Dependency injection
TestingHard to replaceEasy: inject a fake
 
@Service                                  // singleton scope by default
class PricingService {
    private final TaxPolicy taxPolicy;
    PricingService(TaxPolicy taxPolicy) { this.taxPolicy = taxPolicy; }
}

@Service
@Scope("prototype")                       // a new instance every time it is requested
class ShoppingCart { }

Because a singleton bean is shared by all request threads, it must be stateless or thread-safe. Do not keep per-user data in fields of a @Service. This is the most common bug caused by the singleton scope. Prefer Spring beans over hand-written GoF singletons in application code. More on scopes: Spring fundamentals.

Singletons in the JDK

  • Runtime.getRuntime() returns the one runtime of the JVM.
  • Collections.emptyList() returns one shared immutable instance, and every enum constant is a singleton by definition.

Pros

  • One shared instance for a truly unique resource.
  • Lazy creation saves memory when the object is costly.
  • Controlled access to the instance.

Cons

  • It is global state: any code can touch it, which hides dependencies.
  • Hard to unit-test and to replace with a fake.
  • Violates SRP (it controls its own lifecycle and does its job).
  • Needs care with threads, serialization, reflection and class loaders.

When NOT to use a Singleton

  • When you only need "one in practice". Let the DI container manage one instance and inject it. That gives you the single instance without the global access.
  • For objects that carry per-user or per-request state.
  • When tests need to reset or replace the object. Static state leaks between tests.
  • In a cluster, when you need "one across all servers". You need a distributed lock or a database, not a singleton.

Common mistakes

  • Double-checked locking without volatile.
  • A lazy "check then create" without any synchronisation.
  • A singleton that is mutable and shared (a mutable HashMap field), updated from many threads.
  • A Spring @Component that also has a getInstance() method. Pick one mechanism.

Interview: Singleton

  • How do you write a thread-safe Singleton? Name three ways: holder idiom, enum, DCL with volatile. Say you prefer the holder or the enum.
  • Why volatile in double-checked locking? It stops the reordering of "assign reference" before "run constructor", so no thread sees a half-built object.
  • How can a singleton be broken? Reflection, serialization, cloning, multiple class loaders. Fixes: throw in the constructor, readResolve, do not implement Cloneable, or use an enum.
  • Spring singleton vs GoF Singleton? One per container and bean definition, enforced by the container, injected; GoF is one per class loader, enforced by the class itself.
  • Why is Singleton called an anti-pattern? Hidden global state and poor testability.

The Factory family: static factory, Simple Factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory

Factories move object creation out of the code that uses the object, so callers depend on an interface and not on a concrete class; the family has four members that differ in how much they let you vary: static factory methods, Simple Factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory.

Intent: create objects without exposing the creation logic, so that the caller works with an abstraction.

The problem

A notification feature starts simple. The code that sends a message also decides which class to build:

public void notifyUser(String channel, String to, String text) {
    Notifier notifier;
    if (channel.equals("EMAIL")) {
        notifier = new EmailNotifier(smtpHost);
    } else if (channel.equals("SMS")) {
        notifier = new SmsNotifier(apiKey);
    } else if (channel.equals("PUSH")) {
        notifier = new PushNotifier(fcmToken);
    } else {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(channel);
    }
    notifier.send(to, text);
}

Every caller that needs a notifier repeats this if chain. Adding WhatsApp edits many methods. The calling code knows concrete classes and their constructor arguments. Moving the creation into one place fixes it.

Level 0: static factory methods

A static factory method is a static method that returns an instance. It is not a GoF pattern, but it is the most used form in Java (Effective Java, Item 1). Advantages over constructors: it has a name (Money.ofRupees(5)), it need not create a new object each call (caching, as in Integer.valueOf), it can return a subtype, and it can hide the implementation class (List.of returns a private JDK class).

NameConventionExample
ofAggregate of parameters, conciseList.of(1, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 11)
valueOfVerbose alternative to of, often type conversionInteger.valueOf("5"), Status.valueOf("ACTIVE")
fromConvert one type to anotherDate.from(instant)
parseBuild from a stringLocalDate.parse("2026-11-11")
copyOfCopyList.copyOf(list)
getInstance / instanceReturns an instance, possibly sharedCalendar.getInstance()
create / newInstanceAlways a new instanceArray.newInstance(...)
newXxxFactory on another class returning a new XxxFiles.newBufferedReader(path)

Level 1: Simple Factory

A Simple Factory is one class (often with a static method) that holds the if/switch and returns the right product. It is not a GoF pattern, but it is the first step and enough for many programs.

public interface Notifier {
    void send(String to, String text);
}

class EmailNotifier implements Notifier {
    public void send(String to, String text) { System.out.println("EMAIL " + to + ": " + text); }
}
class SmsNotifier implements Notifier {
    public void send(String to, String text) { System.out.println("SMS " + to + ": " + text); }
}
class PushNotifier implements Notifier {
    public void send(String to, String text) { System.out.println("PUSH " + to + ": " + text); }
}

enum Channel { EMAIL, SMS, PUSH }

public final class NotifierFactory {
    private NotifierFactory() { }

    public static Notifier create(Channel channel) {
        return switch (channel) {                       // exhaustive for an enum
            case EMAIL -> new EmailNotifier();
            case SMS   -> new SmsNotifier();
            case PUSH  -> new PushNotifier();
        };
    }
}

// caller depends on Notifier and Channel only
NotifierFactory.create(Channel.SMS).send("98100", "OTP 4521");
SMS 98100: OTP 4521

The factory itself still has a switch, so adding a channel edits the factory (an OCP violation, but only in one place). To avoid it, register creators in a map or let Spring collect the implementations (see Spring below).

Level 2: Factory Method (GoF)

Factory Method: a base class defines an algorithm and declares an abstract method that creates the product; subclasses decide which concrete product to create. The creator uses the product only through the interface.

import java.util.List;

interface Exporter {
    String export(List<String> rows);
}
class CsvExporter implements Exporter {
    public String export(List<String> rows) { return String.join("\n", rows); }
}
class JsonExporter implements Exporter {
    public String export(List<String> rows) {
        return rows.stream().map(r -> "\"" + r + "\"")
                   .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.joining(",", "[", "]"));
    }
}

abstract class ReportJob {
    public final void run(List<String> rows) {
        Exporter exporter = createExporter();               // the factory method
        System.out.println(exporter.export(rows));
    }
    protected abstract Exporter createExporter();          // subclasses decide
}

class CsvReportJob extends ReportJob {
    protected Exporter createExporter() { return new CsvExporter(); }
}
class JsonReportJob extends ReportJob {
    protected Exporter createExporter() { return new JsonExporter(); }
}

public class FactoryMethodDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new CsvReportJob().run(List.of("a", "b"));
        new JsonReportJob().run(List.of("a", "b"));
    }
}
a
b
["a","b"]

Factory Method is the Template Method pattern (Template Method) applied to creation. Use it when a class cannot know in advance which objects it must create, and subclasses (or a framework user) should decide.

Level 3: Abstract Factory (GoF)

Abstract Factory creates a family of related products that must be used together, without naming their concrete classes. Think of a checkout that needs a tax calculator and an invoice formatter that match the country: Indian GST with a GSTIN invoice, or US sales tax with a different invoice. Mixing an Indian calculator with a US formatter would be a bug; the factory makes sure the family stays consistent.

interface TaxCalculator { long taxOn(long amountInPaise); }
interface InvoiceFormatter { String format(long totalInPaise); }

interface RegionFactory {                       // the abstract factory
    TaxCalculator taxCalculator();
    InvoiceFormatter invoiceFormatter();
}

class IndiaFactory implements RegionFactory {
    public TaxCalculator taxCalculator() { return amount -> amount * 18 / 100; }   // GST
    public InvoiceFormatter invoiceFormatter() {
        return total -> "Tax Invoice: Rs " + total / 100.0;
    }
}
class UsFactory implements RegionFactory {
    public TaxCalculator taxCalculator() { return amount -> amount * 7 / 100; }    // sales tax
    public InvoiceFormatter invoiceFormatter() {
        return total -> "Invoice: $" + total / 100.0;
    }
}

class Checkout {
    private final RegionFactory region;
    Checkout(RegionFactory region) { this.region = region; }

    String bill(long amount) {
        long total = amount + region.taxCalculator().taxOn(amount);
        return region.invoiceFormatter().format(total);
    }
}

// new Checkout(new IndiaFactory()).bill(100000)  -> "Tax Invoice: Rs 1180.0"
// new Checkout(new UsFactory()).bill(100000)     -> "Invoice: $1070.0"

Both interfaces here have one method, so lambdas implement them. Adding a new region is a new factory class; adding a new product (say, a ShippingRule) means changing the factory interface and all factories, which is the main weakness.

Comparison

Static factorySimple FactoryFactory MethodAbstract Factory
GoF pattern?NoNoYesYes
CreatesOne typeOne product family chosen by a parameterOne product, chosen by a subclassA family of related products
Uses inheritance?NoNoYes, subclasses overrideUsually composition (inject the factory)
Adding a variantEdit the methodEdit the switchAdd a subclassAdd a factory class
Typical exampleList.ofNotifierFactory.create(ch)Collection.iterator()DocumentBuilderFactory

In the JDK and Spring

  • Static factory methods: Integer.valueOf, List.of, LocalDate.of, Optional.of, Executors.newFixedThreadPool.
  • Factory Method: Collection.iterator() (each collection returns its own iterator type) and Iterable.iterator().
  • Abstract Factory: javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory, java.sql.Connection (creates Statements that match the driver).
  • Spring: the BeanFactory/ApplicationContext is a giant factory; a FactoryBean<T> lets a bean produce another object; @Bean methods are factory methods. Injecting Map<String, Notifier> or List<Notifier> replaces a hand-written factory switch:
@Component("EMAIL") class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { /* ... */ }
@Component("SMS")   class SmsNotifier   implements Notifier { /* ... */ }

@Service
class NotificationService {
    private final Map<String, Notifier> notifiers;      // key = bean name

    NotificationService(Map<String, Notifier> notifiers) { this.notifiers = notifiers; }

    void send(String channel, String to, String text) {
        Notifier n = notifiers.get(channel);
        if (n == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown channel " + channel);
        n.send(to, text);                                   // new channel = new @Component
    }
}

Pros

  • Callers depend on interfaces, not on concrete classes (DIP).
  • Creation logic lives in one place; construction details can change freely.
  • New products are added with little or no change to callers (OCP).
  • Abstract Factory keeps related products consistent.

Cons

  • More classes and indirection.
  • Factory Method needs a subclass per product.
  • Abstract Factory is hard to extend with a new product kind.

When NOT to use a factory

  • When there is only one implementation and no plan for another: just call the constructor.
  • When a DI container already chooses the implementation. Do not write a factory for what @Bean, profiles or @ConditionalOnProperty can do.
  • Do not build an Abstract Factory unless products truly must match as a family.

Interview: factories

  • Factory Method vs Abstract Factory? Factory Method: one product, subclass decides, uses inheritance. Abstract Factory: a family of products, object composition. Abstract Factory is often implemented with several factory methods.
  • Why prefer a static factory to a constructor? Names, caching, subtype return, hiding the class (Effective Java Item 1).
  • How would you remove the switch from a factory in Spring? Inject a Map<String, Interface>.

Builder: telescoping constructors, immutable objects and Lombok

Builder constructs a complex object step by step with named, readable calls and produces a finished (usually immutable) object, which avoids constructors with many parameters.

Intent: separate the construction of a complex object from its representation, so that you can build it step by step and get a valid, usually immutable, result.

The problem: telescoping constructors

An email message has two required values (recipient, subject) and many optional ones (cc, bcc, body, reply-to, attachments, priority). With constructors you end up with a "telescope":

public class EmailMessage {
    public EmailMessage(String to, String subject) { /* ... */ }
    public EmailMessage(String to, String subject, String body) { /* ... */ }
    public EmailMessage(String to, String subject, String body, String cc) { /* ... */ }
    public EmailMessage(String to, String subject, String body, String cc, String bcc,
                        String replyTo, boolean highPriority) { /* ... */ }
}

// What does this call mean? Which string is cc, which is bcc?
new EmailMessage("a@x.com", "Hi", "Body", null, "boss@x.com", null, true);

Problems: you cannot tell what each argument means, swapping two strings compiles fine, you pass null for the optional ones, and you need a constructor for every combination. The other common escape, a no-argument constructor plus setters (the JavaBeans style), leaves the object half-built and mutable between calls, so it cannot be immutable or thread-safe.

Structure

A hand-written builder for an immutable class

The product has a private constructor and only final fields. The nested Builder takes the required values in its constructor, offers one method per optional value (each returns this, so you can chain), and checks the rules in build().

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public final class EmailMessage {
    private final String to;
    private final String subject;
    private final String body;
    private final List<String> cc;
    private final boolean highPriority;

    private EmailMessage(Builder b) {
        this.to = b.to;
        this.subject = b.subject;
        this.body = b.body;
        this.cc = List.copyOf(b.cc);                   // immutable copy
        this.highPriority = b.highPriority;
    }

    public static Builder builder(String to, String subject) {   // required values
        return new Builder(to, subject);
    }

    public String to() { return to; }
    public String subject() { return subject; }
    public String body() { return body; }
    public List<String> cc() { return cc; }
    public boolean highPriority() { return highPriority; }

    @Override public String toString() {
        return "EmailMessage{to=" + to + ", subject=" + subject + ", cc=" + cc
             + ", highPriority=" + highPriority + "}";
    }

    public static final class Builder {
        private final String to;                       // required
        private final String subject;                  // required
        private String body = "";                      // optional, with a default
        private final List<String> cc = new ArrayList<>();
        private boolean highPriority;

        private Builder(String to, String subject) {
            this.to = to;
            this.subject = subject;
        }

        public Builder body(String body) { this.body = body; return this; }
        public Builder cc(String address) { this.cc.add(address); return this; }
        public Builder highPriority() { this.highPriority = true; return this; }

        public EmailMessage build() {
            if (to == null || !to.contains("@")) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("A valid recipient is required");
            }
            if (subject == null || subject.isBlank()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Subject is required");
            }
            return new EmailMessage(this);              // validated, then frozen
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EmailMessage m = EmailMessage.builder("asha@example.com", "Your invoice")
                .body("Please find it attached.")
                .cc("accounts@example.com")
                .highPriority()
                .build();
        System.out.println(m);
    }
}
EmailMessage{to=asha@example.com, subject=Your invoice, cc=[accounts@example.com], highPriority=true}

Each call reads like a sentence. Required values cannot be forgotten because they are in the factory method. The finished object is immutable and always valid, because validation runs once in build().

Lombok @Builder

Lombok (a code-generation library, annotation processor) writes the builder for you. You add it as a dependency and your IDE needs the plugin.

import lombok.Builder;
import lombok.Singular;
import lombok.Value;

@Value                     // all fields private final, getters, equals/hashCode/toString
@Builder(toBuilder = true) // generates CustomerBuilder, plus customer.toBuilder()
public class Customer {
    String name;
    String email;
    @Builder.Default String country = "IN";
    @Singular java.util.List<String> phones;     // generates phone("..") and phones(..)
}

// Customer c = Customer.builder().name("Asha").email("a@x.com").phone("98100").build();
// Customer moved = c.toBuilder().country("US").build();     // copy with one change

Lombok's builder does not make required fields mandatory: a forgotten field is just null, unless you add checks (for example @NonNull on a field, which generates a null check in the constructor). Hand-written builders force required values in the entry point.

Builders with records

A record with two or three components needs no builder; call the constructor. With many optional components, a record can still have a hand-written builder, or you can use "wither" methods that return a changed copy: p.withCity("Pune"). Libraries such as RecordBuilder and the IDE can generate builders for records.

Builders in the JDK and Spring

  • StringBuilder builds a string by appending; strictly a builder in the everyday sense, though without a separate product type.
  • HttpClient.newBuilder() and HttpRequest.newBuilder() (Java 11+) are textbook builders:
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.time.Duration;

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NORMAL)
        .build();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
        .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/orders/42"))
        .header("Accept", "application/json")
        .GET()
        .build();
  • Others: Stream.builder(), Locale.Builder, ProcessBuilder, java.util.stream.Collectors (not a builder), and in Spring UriComponentsBuilder, RestClient.builder(), WebClient.builder(), SpringApplicationBuilder and User.withUsername(...) in Spring Security.

Director (the classic GoF variant)

The GoF description adds a Director class that knows a recipe (the order of build steps), such as "build a standard welcome mail". In practice a static helper does that: EmailTemplates.welcome(user) returns a pre-configured builder. You do not need a separate Director class in everyday Java.

Pros

  • Readable call sites with named values.
  • Immutable objects without a huge constructor.
  • Validation in one place before the object exists.
  • Same builder can make different representations or presets.

Cons

  • More code (a second class), unless Lombok generates it.
  • Fields are duplicated in the builder and the product.
  • A builder can be used incorrectly: not calling a required method is only caught at run time (unless required values are in the entry point).

When NOT to use a Builder

  • For a class with two or three fields: a constructor, static factory or record is simpler (KISS).
  • When all fields are required and there are few of them.
  • Builders and JPA entities mix badly: entities need a no-argument constructor and frameworks set fields by reflection. Use builders for DTOs, commands and value objects.

Common mistakes

  • Reusing one builder after build() without copying its lists, so two products share a mutable list. Copy collections in the constructor (List.copyOf).
  • Putting validation in the builder methods only. Validate in build(), where all fields are known.
  • Building the object without the invariants (a "builder" that just calls setters on a mutable object).

Interview: Builder

  • What problem does Builder solve? Telescoping constructors and half-built mutable objects. You get readable, step-by-step construction and an immutable, valid result.
  • Builder vs Factory? Factory chooses which class to create in one call; Builder assembles one complex object over many calls.
  • Where have you seen Builder? StringBuilder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Lombok @Builder, UriComponentsBuilder.

Adapter: making incompatible interfaces work together

Adapter wraps an existing class with an incompatible interface and translates calls, so your code can use it through the interface it expects, without changing either side.

Intent: convert the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect, so classes with incompatible interfaces can work together.

The problem

Your shop code talks to a PaymentGateway interface that you designed. Now the business signs a contract with a provider whose SDK is a jar you cannot change. Its method names, parameter types and result codes are all different: it takes rupees as a double, a card number as a String, and returns an int status code. If you call the SDK directly from the order code, the vendor's API spreads across your system, and changing the vendor later hurts. Like a travel plug adapter, you wrap the foreign socket in a shape your plug fits.

Implementation

// --- Target: what our application expects ---
record PaymentRequest(String cardToken, long amountInPaise, String orderId) { }
record PaymentResult(boolean success, String reference, String message) { }

interface PaymentGateway {
    PaymentResult pay(PaymentRequest request);
}

// --- Adaptee: the third-party SDK, which we cannot change ---
class FastPaySdk {
    // returns 0 on success, 101 = declined, 500 = server error
    public int makePayment(String card, double rupees, String currency) {
        return rupees < 50_000 ? 0 : 101;
    }
    public String lastTransactionId() { return "FP-" + System.nanoTime(); }
}

// --- Adapter: translates our interface to the SDK ---
class FastPayAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final FastPaySdk sdk;

    FastPayAdapter(FastPaySdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }

    @Override
    public PaymentResult pay(PaymentRequest request) {
        double rupees = request.amountInPaise() / 100.0;                  // paise to rupees
        int code = sdk.makePayment(request.cardToken(), rupees, "INR");   // call the SDK
        return switch (code) {                                            // map the result
            case 0   -> new PaymentResult(true, sdk.lastTransactionId(), "Approved");
            case 101 -> new PaymentResult(false, null, "Declined by bank");
            default  -> new PaymentResult(false, null, "Gateway error " + code);
        };
    }
}

// --- Client: knows only the target interface ---
class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    CheckoutService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }

    String checkout(String orderId, long paise, String token) {
        PaymentResult r = gateway.pay(new PaymentRequest(token, paise, orderId));
        return r.success() ? "Paid, ref " + r.reference() : "Failed: " + r.message();
    }
}

public class AdapterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CheckoutService service = new CheckoutService(new FastPayAdapter(new FastPaySdk()));
        System.out.println(service.checkout("O-1", 129900, "tok_abc"));
        System.out.println(service.checkout("O-2", 9_000_000, "tok_abc"));
    }
}
Paid, ref FP-123456789
Failed: Declined by bank

The vendor's names, the double rupees and the integer codes stay inside FastPayAdapter. Switching to another provider is a new adapter class (say RazorpayAdapter) with no change to CheckoutService. In tests, use a fake PaymentGateway.

Object adapter vs class adapter

The version above is an object adapter: it holds the adaptee in a field (composition). A class adapter would inherit from the adaptee and implement the target interface at the same time. Java has single class inheritance, so class adapters are rare and need the target to be an interface. Prefer the object adapter: it works with any subclass of the adaptee and keeps the coupling loose (composition over inheritance).

Anti-corruption layer

In larger systems, an adapter that shields your domain from a foreign model (a legacy system, a partner API, another microservice) is called an anti-corruption layer. It translates not just method names but concepts and error handling, so the foreign model does not leak into yours.

Adapters in the JDK and Spring

  • Arrays.asList(array) adapts an array to the List interface (writes go through to the array).
  • InputStreamReader adapts a byte InputStream to a character Reader; OutputStreamWriter does the reverse.
  • Collections.enumeration(c) and Enumeration.asIterator() convert between old and new iteration styles.
  • Executors.callable(runnable) adapts a Runnable to a Callable.
  • Spring MVC: HandlerAdapter lets DispatcherServlet call any kind of handler (annotated controllers, HttpRequestHandlers, functional endpoints) in the same way. Spring has adapters such as MessageListenerAdapter in its messaging modules too.
  • Spring Data repositories and HttpMessageConverters also translate between your types and external representations.

Pros

  • Reuses existing code without changing it.
  • Keeps vendor-specific code in one class (SRP).
  • Easy to replace a vendor or fake it in tests (DIP, OCP).

Cons

  • An extra class and one more call per operation.
  • When the two interfaces are very different, the adapter becomes complicated.
  • Some features of the adaptee may not map to the target interface.

When NOT to use an Adapter

  • When you control both sides: change the interface instead of wrapping it.
  • When a method reference or lambda is enough, for example turning a Function into a Comparator with Comparator.comparing.
  • Do not let the adapter grow business logic. It only translates.

Why the pattern exists

Software rarely starts from a blank page. You integrate a payment SDK, a legacy billing module, a partner's SOAP service or an open-source library, and none of them was written against your interfaces. You cannot edit them (they are a jar, or owned by another team), and you do not want to edit your own clients either (they are many and stable). The only place left for the translation code is a new class in the middle. That class is the Adapter. It exists so that foreign ideas stop at the boundary: your domain keeps its own language, and the translation is written once and tested once.

The call flow

A second example: file storage

Your app stores invoices through a FileStore interface. In development you use the local disk; a legacy partner system only offers a client that works with (host, path, byte[]) and throws its own checked exception. Two adapters make both look the same.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

interface FileStore {
    void save(String name, byte[] content);
    byte[] load(String name);
}

// Adapter 1: java.nio.file.Files already does the job, we only change the shape
class LocalDiskStore implements FileStore {
    private final Path root;
    LocalDiskStore(Path root) { this.root = root; }
    public void save(String name, byte[] content) {
        try { Files.write(root.resolve(name), content); }
        catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
    }
    public byte[] load(String name) {
        try { return Files.readAllBytes(root.resolve(name)); }
        catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
    }
}

// The adaptee: a legacy client we cannot change (fragment, class assumed)
class LegacyArchiveClient {
    void put(String host, String path, byte[] data) throws ArchiveException { /* ... */ }
    byte[] get(String host, String path) throws ArchiveException { return new byte[0]; }
}
class ArchiveException extends Exception { }

// Adapter 2: translates names and exceptions
class ArchiveStore implements FileStore {
    private final LegacyArchiveClient client;
    private final String host;
    ArchiveStore(LegacyArchiveClient client, String host) {
        this.client = client;
        this.host = host;
    }
    public void save(String name, byte[] content) {
        try { client.put(host, "/invoices/" + name, content); }
        catch (ArchiveException e) { throw new IllegalStateException("Archive save failed", e); }
    }
    public byte[] load(String name) {
        try { return client.get(host, "/invoices/" + name); }
        catch (ArchiveException e) { throw new IllegalStateException("Archive load failed", e); }
    }
}

Note the two jobs an adapter really has: shape translation (names, units, argument order) and error translation (a vendor's checked exception becomes your own exception, so no vendor type leaks to callers).

Adapter in one line: lambdas and method references

When the target is a functional interface, a lambda is an adapter written inline. Comparator.comparing(Employee::name) adapts a "key extractor" to the comparison role, and executor.submit(() -> legacy.run()) adapts a call to Runnable. Write a full class only when the translation has state, several methods, or needs its own tests.

Adapter or something else?

PatternInterface changes?Purpose
AdapterYes: A to BMake an existing class fit the interface you need
DecoratorNo, sameAdd behaviour
FacadeYes: many classes to one simple APIHide a subsystem
ProxyNo, sameControl access (lazy, remote, security)

A quick test: "I have class X and need it to look like interface Y" is Adapter. "I want X plus logging" is Decorator. "I want one simple call over five classes" is Facade. The full table is in Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy vs Facade.

Wrong: vendor types leak through

class FastPayAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    // returns the SDK's int code to the caller
    public int pay(PaymentRequest r) throws FastPayException {
        return sdk.makePayment(r.cardToken(),
                               r.amountInPaise() / 100.0, "INR");
    }
}

Right: only domain types cross the boundary

class FastPayAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    public PaymentResult pay(PaymentRequest r) {
        try {
            int code = sdk.makePayment(r.cardToken(),
                                       r.amountInPaise() / 100.0, "INR");
            return map(code);                   // own result type
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            return new PaymentResult(false, null, "Gateway unavailable");
        }
    }
}

Rules

  • The adapter implements the interface the client owns. The target interface should not mention vendor concepts.
  • Convert units, ids and error types inside the adapter. Document the mapping (for example, which vendor code means "declined").
  • One adapter per adaptee. If you need two vendors, write two adapters and pick one by configuration.

Conventions

  • Name it after the adaptee: FastPayAdapter, ArchiveStore. Keep adapters in an infrastructure or adapter package, away from the domain (this is the "ports and adapters" style, also called hexagonal architecture).
  • Test the adapter with a fake adaptee, and test the client with a fake target.

Edge cases

  • Lossy mapping: a double rupee amount can lose precision (0.1 + 0.2). Compute from integer paise as late as possible, or use BigDecimal.
  • Unmappable features: if the target has refund and the adaptee cannot, do not throw silently; split the interface (ISP) so the adapter implements only what it can.
  • Timeouts and retries belong to the adapter or a decorator around it, not to the business code.
  • Two-way adapter: one class implementing both interfaces so two systems can call each other. It is rare; avoid it unless needed.

Interview: Adapter

  • What is Adapter? A wrapper that converts one interface to another so that incompatible classes can work together. Give the payment SDK example.
  • Name JDK examples. InputStreamReader, Arrays.asList.
  • Adapter vs Decorator? Adapter changes the interface; Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour. See the comparison table.

Interview: harder Adapter questions

  • Where would you use it in a real project? Wrapping each payment, SMS or email vendor behind your own interface, and as the anti-corruption layer towards legacy systems.
  • Class adapter vs object adapter in Java? Object adapter (composition); Java has single inheritance, so a class adapter is limited.
  • Is Spring's HandlerAdapter really an Adapter? Yes: DispatcherServlet works with the HandlerAdapter interface, and one implementation exists per handler type.
  • How does it support OCP? A new vendor is a new adapter; the client is not edited.

Decorator: adding behaviour by wrapping

Decorator wraps an object that has the same interface and adds behaviour before or after delegating to it, so you can stack features (caching, logging, retries) at run time without subclassing.

Intent: attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically, as a flexible alternative to subclassing.

The problem

A PriceService loads product prices from a database. You need logging, then caching, then retry on failure, and sometimes you want only some of these. If you use inheritance (CachedLoggingPriceService, LoggingRetryingPriceService, ...) the classes multiply, as in the inheritance explosion. A decorator is a class that implements the same interface, holds another object of that interface, and adds one concern. You stack them like layers.

Implementation

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

interface PriceService {
    long priceOf(String sku);
}

class DbPriceService implements PriceService {            // the real component
    public long priceOf(String sku) {
        System.out.println("  DB query for " + sku);
        return 49900;
    }
}

abstract class PriceServiceDecorator implements PriceService {
    protected final PriceService delegate;
    protected PriceServiceDecorator(PriceService delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; }
}

class LoggingPriceService extends PriceServiceDecorator {
    LoggingPriceService(PriceService delegate) { super(delegate); }

    public long priceOf(String sku) {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        long price = delegate.priceOf(sku);                       // call the wrapped object
        System.out.println("priceOf(" + sku + ") = " + price + " in "
                + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1000 + " us");
        return price;
    }
}

class CachingPriceService extends PriceServiceDecorator {
    private final Map<String, Long> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    CachingPriceService(PriceService delegate) { super(delegate); }

    public long priceOf(String sku) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(sku, delegate::priceOf);     // only calls on a miss
    }
}

public class DecoratorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PriceService service =
            new LoggingPriceService(new CachingPriceService(new DbPriceService()));
        service.priceOf("SKU-1");
        service.priceOf("SKU-1");
    }
}
  DB query for SKU-1
priceOf(SKU-1) = 49900 in 812 us
priceOf(SKU-1) = 49900 in 15 us

The second call did not hit the database, and the logging decorator on the outside saw both calls. The order of wrapping matters: logging outside caching logs every call; caching outside logging would log only the cache misses. The client holds a PriceService and cannot tell how many layers there are.

Note: computeIfAbsent on ConcurrentHashMap must not modify the map from inside the mapping function. A single database call is fine.

Decorator in Java I/O

The classic JDK example is the I/O stream family. InputStream is the component interface; FileInputStream is the concrete component; BufferedInputStream, GZIPInputStream and DataInputStream are decorators.

import java.io.*;
import java.util.zip.GZIPInputStream;

try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(          // adds line reading + buffering
        new InputStreamReader(                            // adapter: bytes to chars
            new GZIPInputStream(                          // adds decompression
