        "SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id = ?",
        (rs, rowNum) -> new Employee(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name"),
                                     rs.getLong("salary")),     // RowMapper callback
        10);

// TransactionTemplate: begin, run your code, commit or roll back
Long id = transactionTemplate.execute(status -> {
    repository.save(order);
    return order.id();
});

The callback version is a Strategy-like design (composition), but the structure "fixed skeleton plus a variable step" is Template Method. Compare: inheritance-based Template Method uses extends; callback-based uses a lambda passed in.

Template Method in the JDK and frameworks

  • AbstractList, AbstractMap, AbstractSet: you implement get(int) and size() (for an AbstractList) and the class gives you iterator(), indexOf, equals, hashCode and more, written in terms of those steps. This is a very common interview example.
  • InputStream.read(byte[]) is built on the single abstract read(); Reader and Writer likewise.
  • HttpServlet.service() inspects the HTTP method and calls doGet, doPost, etc., which you override.
  • AbstractApplicationContext.refresh() in Spring is a famous template method; JdbcTemplate, JmsTemplate, OncePerRequestFilter.doFilter (calls your doFilterInternal) and AbstractController do the same.
  • JUnit's @BeforeEach / test / @AfterEach life cycle is a template method run by the framework.

Pros

  • Removes duplicated skeleton code (DRY).
  • The framework controls the order; subclasses cannot break it.
  • Easy way to offer extension points (hooks).

Cons

  • Uses inheritance: subclasses are tied to the base class (fragile base class; Liskov must hold).
  • The more steps and hooks, the harder to know what to override.
  • One parent only; you cannot combine two templates.
  • Hard to read: the control flow jumps between base and subclass.

When NOT to use Template Method

  • When the variation can be a Strategy passed in (composition): it is more flexible and avoids inheritance. Many modern designs replace Template Method with Strategy or callbacks.
  • When there is only one implementation.
  • When the subclass would need to change the order of steps. The skeleton is then not really fixed.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting final on the template method, so a subclass overrides the whole algorithm.
  • Calling an overridable method from a base-class constructor: the subclass method runs before the subclass fields are initialised.
  • Too many abstract methods: the subclass becomes a form to fill in. Prefer a few steps plus hooks with defaults.

Interview: Template Method

  • What is it? A base class fixes the algorithm's steps; subclasses override some steps. Example: report exporter, AbstractList.
  • Template Method vs Strategy? Template Method varies steps through inheritance (compile time); Strategy varies the whole algorithm through composition (run time).
  • Which Spring classes use it? JdbcTemplate, TransactionTemplate, AbstractApplicationContext.refresh.
  • What is the Hollywood principle? "Don't call us, we'll call you": the framework calls your code.

Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy vs Facade

All four wrap other objects, but they differ in intent: Adapter changes an interface, Decorator adds behaviour, Proxy controls access, and Facade simplifies a whole subsystem.

These four structural patterns look alike in a class diagram: one class holds a reference to another and forwards calls. Interviewers ask for the difference because the structure is the same and only the intent separates them. The fastest way to decide is to ask what the wrapper does to the interface and to the behaviour.

AdapterDecoratorProxyFacade
IntentMake an incompatible interface fitAdd responsibilitiesControl accessSimplify a subsystem
Interface of the wrapperDifferent from the wrapped objectSameSameNew, simpler
WrapsOne objectOne object (can stack)One objectMany objects
Who creates the wrapped object?Passed inPassed inOften the proxy itself (lazy) or the frameworkUsually created or injected into the facade
Behaviour added?Translation onlyYes, new featuresAccess, caching, laziness, security, transactionsOrchestration
Client aware?Uses the target interfaceChooses the layersUsually unawareCalls the facade on purpose
ExampleInputStreamReader, payment SDK wrapperBufferedInputStream, caching service@Transactional bean, Hibernate lazy entityOrderFacade, SLF4J, JdbcTemplate

How to choose

  1. Do you need to call a class whose interface does not match what your code expects, and you cannot change it? Adapter.
  2. Do you want to add a feature (logging, caching, compression) to a class while keeping its interface, in combinations that the caller picks? Decorator.
  3. Do you want to control whether, when or how the real object is reached (lazy, permission, remote, transaction), without the caller knowing? Proxy.
  4. Do you have many classes and want one easy entry point for a common job? Facade.

The same problem, four ways

Imagine a payment library:

  • Adapter: the vendor's method is makePayment(card, rupees, currency); you wrap it as pay(PaymentRequest).
  • Decorator: a LoggingGateway and a RetryingGateway that implement PaymentGateway and wrap another gateway, stacked as you like.
  • Proxy: a FraudCheckingGatewayProxy that decides whether the call goes through at all, or a Spring proxy that opens a transaction around it.
  • Facade: a CheckoutFacade.checkout(cart) that calls inventory, payment and shipping.

Blurry borders

  • Decorator and Proxy have the same structure. A decorator is usually built by the client to add a feature; a proxy is often hidden from the client, and it often creates or finds the real object itself.
  • A caching wrapper can be called either a caching proxy or a caching decorator. Name it after the dominant reason: "adds a feature" or "controls access".
  • A Spring AOP proxy that adds behaviour around a call is a proxy in mechanism and a decorator in effect.
  • An adapter that also wraps several objects starts to look like a facade. Keep adapters one-to-one.

Interview: the four-way question

  • Answer in one line each: Adapter converts, Decorator enhances, Proxy controls, Facade simplifies.
  • Give one JDK or Spring example each: InputStreamReader, BufferedReader, @Transactional proxy, SLF4J or JdbcTemplate.
  • Add that Decorator and Proxy have the same structure and differ in intent.

Where Spring uses design patterns

Spring is built from patterns: singleton beans, factories (the container), proxies for @Transactional, template classes like JdbcTemplate, observer-style application events, the DispatcherServlet front controller, HandlerAdapter, filter chains and strategy-based resolvers.

When you can name the pattern behind a Spring feature, the feature stops being magic, and you can predict its limits (such as the self-invocation trap). The table below is the quick map. Each row names the pattern, the Spring feature, and what the pattern explains.

PatternWhere in SpringWhat it explains
Singleton (container-managed)Default bean scopeOne shared bean per container; keep beans stateless
Factory / Abstract FactoryBeanFactory, ApplicationContext, FactoryBean, @Bean methodsThe container creates objects, you ask it for them
Dependency Injection (IoC)Constructor injection, @AutowiredThe container wires collaborators (DIP)
Proxy@Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize, Spring Data repositoriesAdvice runs around your method; self-invocation bypasses it (Proxy)
Template Method (callbacks)JdbcTemplate, TransactionTemplate, RestTemplate, JmsTemplate, AbstractApplicationContext.refresh()Boilerplate in the template, your code in the callback (Template Method)
ObserverApplicationEventPublisher, @EventListener, ApplicationListenerDecoupled in-process events (Observer)
Front ControllerDispatcherServletOne servlet receives all requests and routes them to controllers
AdapterHandlerAdapter, HttpMessageConverter style translationDifferent kinds of handlers called the same way (Adapter)
Chain of ResponsibilityServlet Filter chain, SecurityFilterChain, HandlerInterceptorsOrdered handlers, any of which can stop the request (Chain)
StrategyViewResolver, HandlerMethodArgumentResolver, HttpMessageConverter, PasswordEncoder, ResourceLoaderPluggable algorithms (Strategy)
DecoratorBeanPostProcessor wrapping beans, ContentCachingRequestWrapper, TransactionAwareDataSourceProxyAdd features by wrapping (Decorator)
FacadeJdbcTemplate, JpaRepository, SLF4J, SpringApplication.runOne simple API over complex machinery (Facade)
BuilderUriComponentsBuilder, RestClient.builder(), SpringApplicationBuilder, User.withUsername(), MockMvcRequestBuildersFluent construction (Builder)
CompositeCompositePropertySource, composite validatorsTreat a group like one object (Composite)
Prototype@Scope("prototype")A new instance per request for the bean (Prototype)

Four examples in detail

1. Singleton beans

The container creates each singleton bean once and hands out the same instance. It is a different mechanism from the GoF class (see Singleton), but the same warning applies: shared state is shared by every thread.

2. Proxies for @Transactional

The proxy opens a transaction, calls your method and commits or rolls back (see the sequence diagram in Proxy). Because it is a proxy, three rules follow: the call must come through the proxy (no self-invocation), the method must be public in the usual setup, and the class must not be final. When something "mysteriously" does not run in a transaction, check these first.

3. JdbcTemplate

It is both a Template Method (the fixed skeleton of acquire connection, prepare, execute, map, release) and a Facade over JDBC. Your RowMapper lambda is the variable step. It also translates checked SQLException into the unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy.

4. Application events

One bean publishes a plain object, and other beans react. The order service does not know who listens. Add @Async for non-blocking listeners and @TransactionalEventListener for commit-aware ones (see Observer).

How a request flows: several patterns together

Version note

These patterns are stable across Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x. Details that moved: the servlet API package is jakarta.servlet since Boot 3, and RestTemplate is in maintenance mode in favour of RestClient (Spring Framework 6.1+), which uses the Builder pattern. The Template and Strategy ideas are the same in both.

Interview: patterns in Spring

  • Which design patterns does Spring use? Name at least five with the feature: Singleton (bean scope), Factory (ApplicationContext), Proxy (@Transactional), Template (JdbcTemplate), Observer (events), Front Controller (DispatcherServlet), Chain (filters), Strategy (resolvers).
  • How does Spring implement AOP? With proxies (JDK dynamic or CGLIB), created by a BeanPostProcessor.
  • Is the DispatcherServlet a pattern? Yes, Front Controller: a single entry point that delegates.

Other patterns in brief: Prototype, Composite, Flyweight, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor

Seven more GoF patterns are worth knowing by name and one-line idea: Prototype (copy an existing object), Composite (tree of parts treated like one), Flyweight (share small immutable objects), Iterator (traverse without exposing structure), Mediator (central coordinator), Memento (save and restore state) and Visitor (add operations to a class hierarchy from outside).

You will rarely write these from scratch, but interviewers ask about them, and you use several every day without knowing it. Learn the idea and one Java example for each.

Prototype (creational)
Create new objects by copying an existing one instead of building from scratch. Useful when construction is expensive or when you need many variations of a configured template (a default invoice, a game enemy). In Java: clone(), copy constructors or a copy()/toBuilder() method. See shallow vs deep copy in Core Java. Spring: @Scope("prototype") makes the container return a fresh instance for each request (it is "prototype scope", not exactly the GoF copy).
Composite (structural)
Compose objects into a tree, and treat single objects and groups through the same interface. A file system (file and folder both have size()), a menu with sub-menus, a UI component tree, an organisation chart, a product bundle containing products. A call on the root goes recursively to all children. 
interface FileNode { long size(); }
record FileLeaf(String name, long bytes) implements FileNode {
    public long size() { return bytes; }
}
record Folder(String name, java.util.List<FileNode> children) implements FileNode {
    public long size() { return children.stream().mapToLong(FileNode::size).sum(); }
}
JDK: Swing/AWT Container holds Components; Map.putAll style bulk operations on collections of collections. Spring Security has composite delegating classes.
Flyweight (structural)
Share many small, identical, immutable objects to save memory, by separating the shared intrinsic state from the per-use extrinsic state. In Java: the Integer cache (Integer.valueOf(100) returns a cached object for -128 to 127), the String pool, Boolean.TRUE, enum constants. Use it when you have millions of similar objects (characters in a text editor, tiles in a game map).
Iterator (behavioural)
Give sequential access to the elements of a collection without exposing its structure. Java built it in: Iterable and Iterator (hasNext, next, remove) power the enhanced for loop. To make your class loopable, implement Iterable<T>. Iterators of ArrayList are fail-fast: structural modification during iteration throws ConcurrentModificationException. See Collections.
Mediator (behavioural)
Replace many-to-many direct links between objects with one coordinator, so objects talk only to the mediator. Examples: a chat room (users send to the room, which relays), an air-traffic controller, a UI form where the dialog enables the Submit button when fields are valid. Java: java.util.Timer coordinates tasks; ExecutorService sits between submitters and threads; Spring's DispatcherServlet mediates between handlers and views; message brokers do the same between services. Risk: the mediator becomes a god object.
Memento (behavioural)
Capture and store an object's internal state in an opaque snapshot so it can be restored later, without breaking encapsulation. Used for undo, checkpoints and "save game". The object (originator) creates the memento; a caretaker keeps a stack of them; only the originator can read the contents. Java: serialization snapshots, record copies of immutable state. It complements Command undo: Command reverses an operation, Memento restores a saved state.
Visitor (behavioural)
Add new operations to a class hierarchy without changing the classes, by moving each operation into a visitor with one visit method per type. The elements have a single accept(visitor) method (double dispatch). Good when the types are stable but operations change often (a compiler walking a syntax tree, tax rules over different item types). Bad when new types appear often, because every visitor must change. JDK: java.nio.file.FileVisitor with Files.walkFileTree. In modern Java (17+), sealed interfaces plus a pattern-matching switch give a lighter alternative.

Quick example: Iterator for a custom class

import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;

public class Playlist implements Iterable<String> {
    private final List<String> songs;
    public Playlist(List<String> songs) { this.songs = List.copyOf(songs); }

    @Override
    public Iterator<String> iterator() {
        return new Iterator<>() {
            private int index = 0;
            public boolean hasNext() { return index < songs.size(); }
            public String next() { return songs.get(index++); }
        };
    }
}

// for (String s : new Playlist(List.of("A", "B"))) System.out.println(s);

Other patterns you may hear of

Interpreter (evaluate a small language), Bridge (separate abstraction from implementation so both vary: the notification-channel example in composition over inheritance is a Bridge in spirit), and Null Object (an object that does nothing, instead of null: Collections.emptyList(), a NoOpNotifier). Beyond GoF: Repository, Dependency Injection, Specification, Circuit Breaker and Saga appear in architecture (Module 6).

Interview: the "less common" patterns

  • Expect one-line definitions: Composite = tree treated uniformly; Flyweight = shared immutable objects; Visitor = new operation without changing the classes.
  • Give the JDK example each: Integer cache for Flyweight, Iterator for Iterator, FileVisitor for Visitor.
  • Admit when you have not used one, but show you know the problem it solves.

Pattern selection cheat sheet: if you need this, consider that

Start from the problem you feel in the code (a growing switch, a huge constructor, a foreign API, a repeated skeleton) and map it to the pattern that fixes it; if you cannot name the problem, you do not need the pattern yet.

If you need ...ConsiderQuick reason
Exactly one shared instance of a resourceSingleton (or a Spring singleton bean)Holder idiom or enum; prefer the DI container
To hide which class gets createdStatic factory / Simple Factory / Factory MethodCallers depend on the interface
A family of matching objectsAbstract FactoryKeeps products consistent
To build an object with many optional partsBuilderReadable, immutable result
To copy a configured objectPrototype / copy constructorAvoid expensive set-up
To use a class whose interface does not matchAdapterTranslate, keep vendor code in one class
To add features to an object at run time, in combinationsDecoratorWrap with the same interface
One easy entry point to many classesFacadeHide orchestration
To control or defer access to an object (lazy, secure, remote, transactional)ProxySame interface, gatekeeper
To treat a tree of parts like one objectCompositeUniform interface, recursion
To share millions of identical small objectsFlyweightSave memory
To swap algorithms or rules (replace a growing switch)StrategyOne class per rule
To change behaviour as status changesStateOne class per state
To notify many parties of a changeObserver / eventsSubject does not know listeners
To queue, schedule, log or undo operationsCommandRequest as an object
A pipeline where each step may stop the requestChain of ResponsibilityFilters, validators, approvals
The same algorithm order with different stepsTemplate MethodFixed skeleton, hooks
To traverse a structure without exposing itIteratorImplement Iterable
Many objects talking to many othersMediatorOne coordinator
Save and restore stateMementoSnapshots for undo
New operations over a stable class hierarchyVisitor (or sealed types and switch)Operation outside the classes
To avoid null checks for "nothing to do"Null ObjectDo-nothing implementation

Easily confused pairs

PairDifference in one line
Strategy vs StateStrategy: client picks an algorithm. State: the object changes its own behaviour as its state changes.
Strategy vs Template MethodComposition (swap whole algorithm) vs inheritance (fill in steps).
Factory vs BuilderFactory picks which class; Builder assembles one complex object in steps.
Decorator vs ProxyDecorator adds features chosen by the client; Proxy controls access.
Adapter vs FacadeAdapter converts one interface; Facade simplifies many classes.
Observer vs MediatorObserver: one subject, many listeners. Mediator: many peers talk through a coordinator.
Command vs StrategyCommand: one request as an object (with data, maybe undo). Strategy: a reusable algorithm.
Singleton vs static classA Singleton is a real object (implements interfaces, can be passed, lazily created); a static class cannot.

A 4-question test before you add a pattern

  1. What exact pain am I feeling in the code today?
  2. Is there a simpler fix (a method, a parameter, a lambda, a record)?
  3. Will a teammate understand it faster with the pattern than without it?
  4. Can I give it a name that the team already knows?

Tip: patterns in interviews

For a low-level design question (Module 3) you will usually need Strategy (pricing, payment, parking fees), State (vending machine, order, elevator), Observer (notifications), Factory (creating vehicles or notifiers), Singleton (a manager or logger) and Builder (complex requests). Name the pattern aloud and say which pain it removes.

Interview questions — Design patterns

What is a design pattern, and what are the three categories?

A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a common design problem, with structure and trade-offs; it is a description, not code to copy. The Gang of Four grouped 23 patterns into creational (how objects are created: Singleton, Factory, Builder), structural (how objects are composed: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy) and behavioural (how objects interact: Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method).

How do you write a thread-safe Singleton? Why does double-checked locking need volatile?

Best choices: the holder idiom (a private static nested class holding the instance) or a single-element enum. Double-checked locking also works if the field is volatile. Without it, the assignment instance = new X() can be reordered, so another thread might see a non-null reference to an object whose constructor has not finished. volatile forbids that reordering and gives safe publication.

How can a Singleton be broken, and how do you prevent each way?

Reflection (setAccessible(true) on the constructor): throw from the constructor if an instance exists, or use an enum. Serialization (each deserialization creates a new object): add readResolve() returning the instance. Cloning: do not implement Cloneable, or throw from clone(). Multiple class loaders also create one instance per loader. An enum singleton resists the first three.

What is the difference between a Spring singleton bean and the GoF Singleton?

A GoF Singleton is enforced by the class itself (private constructor) and is one per class loader, accessed globally with getInstance(). A Spring singleton is enforced by the container: one instance per bean definition per container, injected where needed, and the class itself can still be instantiated with new. Spring singletons are shared across threads, so they must be stateless or thread-safe.

Factory Method versus Abstract Factory?

Factory Method defines one creation method that subclasses override to decide the product (inheritance). Abstract Factory is an interface with several creation methods that produce a family of related products, such as TaxCalculator and InvoiceFormatter for one country, and you swap the whole factory. A Simple Factory is neither: one class with a switch that returns the right product.

When would you use Builder, and how does it compare with a telescoping constructor?

Use Builder when a class has many parameters, several optional, and you want immutability and readable code. Telescoping constructors (many overloads) are unreadable and easy to call with swapped arguments; setters leave a half-built, mutable object. A builder collects values by name, validates in build() and returns an immutable object. Examples: HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Lombok @Builder.

Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy vs Facade?

Adapter changes an interface so incompatible classes work together. Decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour, stackable at run time. Proxy keeps the interface and controls access (lazy loading, security, caching, transactions). Facade gives a new, simpler interface over many classes. Examples: InputStreamReader; BufferedReader; the Spring @Transactional proxy; SLF4J or an OrderFacade.

How does @Transactional work, and why does a call from another method of the same class not start a transaction?

Spring wraps the bean in a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy for interfaces, or a CGLIB subclass; Boot uses CGLIB by default). The proxy begins the transaction, calls your method, and commits or rolls back (rollback on runtime exceptions by default). A call using this inside the class goes directly to the target object and skips the proxy, so no transaction logic runs. Fix by moving the method to another bean, or by using AspectJ weaving.

How would you replace a long if/else on payment type with a pattern?

Use Strategy: define a PaymentStrategy interface and one class per method. In Spring, make each a @Component and inject a List or Map of them into the service, which picks by key. Adding a method means adding a class. If the choice depends on the order's lifecycle (not the client's pick), use State instead.

Strategy vs State?

The structure is the same: a context delegates to an interface. In Strategy, the client chooses an algorithm, and strategies are independent of each other. In State, the object changes its own state object as events happen, and the states usually know the transitions. Use State for order life cycles and vending machines; use Strategy for pricing and payment rules.

Explain Observer and its Spring implementation. What is the catch?

A subject notifies registered listeners about changes without knowing them. In Spring, publish an event with ApplicationEventPublisher and handle it with @EventListener. Catches: listeners run synchronously on the publisher's thread by default (and inside its transaction), so a slow or failing listener affects the publisher; use @Async or @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT). Also beware of forgotten listeners that leak memory. For cross-service events you need a message broker.

What is the Command pattern used for, and which Java type is a command?

Command turns a request into an object with execute() (and undo()). It lets you queue, schedule, log, retry or undo operations and decouples the sender from the receiver. Runnable and Callable are commands, and ExecutorService is the invoker. A text editor's undo stack of command objects is the standard example.

Where does Chain of Responsibility appear in Spring and servlets?

Servlet filters: each Filter receives a FilterChain and calls chain.doFilter to continue or returns to stop. Spring Security is a SecurityFilterChain of ordered filters (CORS, CSRF, authentication, authorization). HandlerInterceptors in Spring MVC are similar. A handler that does not call the next one ends the chain, for example to return 401.

What is Template Method, and how is it different from Strategy?

Template Method defines the fixed order of steps in a final method of a base class; subclasses implement some steps (abstract methods or hooks). Examples: AbstractList, HttpServlet.service, JdbcTemplate with callbacks. It varies steps by inheritance, decided at compile time. Strategy varies a whole algorithm by composition, decided at run time. Prefer Strategy when you need flexibility or want to avoid inheritance.

Which patterns would you name when designing a notification system?

Strategy or Factory for channels (email, SMS, push), Observer or events to trigger notifications from business actions, Decorator for retry, logging or rate limiting around a channel, Template Method for shared message-building steps, Builder for the message object, and Chain of Responsibility for fallback channels. Mention that you would start simple and add patterns only as the need appears.

Cheat sheet — Design patterns

  • Pattern named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem; learn the problem first.
  • Categories creational (creation), structural (composition), behavioural (interaction).
  • Singleton one instance; holder idiom or enum; DCL needs volatile; break by reflection, serialization, clone; prefer a Spring bean.
  • Spring singleton one per container per bean definition; must be stateless or thread-safe.
  • Static factory of, valueOf, from, getInstance, create, copyOf; named, can cache, can return subtypes.
  • Simple Factory one switch that returns products; not GoF.
  • Factory Method subclass decides which product; Abstract Factory family of related products.
  • Builder step-by-step construction, validate in build(), immutable result; Lombok @Builder; skip for 2-3 fields.
  • Adapter converts an interface (third-party SDK to your interface); object adapter over class adapter.
  • Decorator same interface, adds behaviour, stackable; BufferedReader; order matters.
  • Facade one simple API over a subsystem; SLF4J, JdbcTemplate, OrderFacade; keep it thin.
  • Proxy same interface, controls access: virtual, protection, remote, caching.
  • Spring AOP JDK proxy (interfaces) or CGLIB (subclass; Boot default); self-invocation bypasses the proxy.
  • Strategy interchangeable algorithms; replaces switch; Comparator; inject Map/List of beans.
  • Observer subject notifies listeners; Spring @EventListener; sync by default; Observable is deprecated.
  • Command request as object; undo/redo, queues; Runnable, Callable.
  • State one class per state, object swaps its state; order life cycle, vending machine.
  • State vs Strategy object changes state itself vs client picks algorithm.
  • Chain of Responsibility ordered handlers that may stop the request; servlet filters, Spring Security chain.
  • Template Method final skeleton plus abstract steps and hooks; AbstractList; Hollywood principle.
  • Template callbacks JdbcTemplate, TransactionTemplate: skeleton in the template, your lambda varies the step.
  • Adapter / Decorator / Proxy / Facade converts / enhances / controls / simplifies.
  • Others Prototype (copy), Composite (tree), Flyweight (share), Iterator, Mediator, Memento (snapshot), Visitor.
  • Do not over-engineer no pattern without a pain; lambdas and records replace much ceremony.

Practice — Design patterns

  1. Singleton five ways (easy). Write an AppConfig singleton using eager init, synchronized, double-checked locking, the holder idiom and an enum. Write a test with 100 threads calling getInstance() and assert that all references are the same. Done when all five variants pass.
  2. Break and fix a singleton (medium). Break your class-based singleton with reflection, serialization and clone, then fix each. Done when the enum version cannot be broken by the same code and the others fail loudly or return the original.
  3. Replace a switch with Strategy (easy/medium). Take a PriceCalculator with a switch on REGULAR, PREMIUM, STUDENT. Refactor it into a PricingStrategy interface, then with Spring inject a Map<String, PricingStrategy>. Done when a new customer type is a new class only.
  4. Factory and Builder (medium). Build a NotifierFactory that returns email, SMS or push senders, and a NotificationRequest with a builder (required: recipient, message; optional: subject, priority, scheduled time). Done when invalid requests fail in build().
  5. Add logging with a Decorator (medium). Take a UserRepository interface and add LoggingUserRepository (log each call and its time) and CachingUserRepository as decorators. Done when you can stack them in either order and explain the difference in the log.
  6. Adapter for a payment SDK (medium). Define PaymentGateway, then adapt two fake vendor SDKs with different method names, units and error codes. Done when the checkout code compiles without importing either vendor class.
  7. Observer with Spring events (medium). Publish an OrderPlacedEvent; write three listeners (email, loyalty, analytics). Make one listener @Async and one @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT). Done when a rolled-back order sends no email.
  8. State machine (medium/hard). Implement an order (NEW → PAID → SHIPPED → DELIVERED, cancel from NEW or PAID) with the State pattern and write a test for every illegal transition. Then redo it as an enum with abstract methods and compare the code size.
  9. Chain and Template Method (medium/hard). Build an order-validation chain (five checks, ordered cheap-first) and a servlet-style filter chain that logs timing. Then write a ReportExporter template with CSV and HTML subclasses. Done when adding a check or a format needs no change to existing classes.
  10. Proxy and the self-invocation trap (hard). Write a JDK dynamic proxy that logs the duration of any interface method. Then, in a Spring Boot app, reproduce a @Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW) method called from the same class, show in the logs that no new transaction starts, and fix it by moving the method to another bean. Done when you can explain the fix with a sequence diagram.
3

Module 3·LLD · week 3Must

LLD interview problems

13 topics · about 2 h of reading

Low-level design (LLD) interviews ask you to turn a vague real-world idea ("design a parking lot") into classes, relationships and working Java code in about an hour. There is no single right answer. The interviewer watches how you ask questions, pick entities, apply the design principles and patterns where they help, handle two users clicking at the same time, and explain your choices.

This module first teaches how these interviews are scored and a repeatable method for them. It then covers the one topic that separates average from strong answers: concurrency, especially double booking. After that come ten classic problems, each with requirements, a class diagram, core code, edge cases and the follow-up questions interviewers love. Every problem reuses the same few ideas, so the tenth feels much easier than the first.

Background you may want open in another tab: Core Java · Module 6 (multithreading) and SQL · Module 5 (how databases work inside).

  • Run a 45–60 minute LLD interview from clarifying questions to final code, using a script.
  • Model any problem as entities, relationships, enums and a few well-placed patterns.
  • Explain and prevent double booking with locks, database constraints, versions and seat holds.
  • Write compilable core Java for ten standard problems: parking lot, tic-tac-toe, library, vending machine, elevator, LRU cache, Splitwise, BookMyShow, rate limiter and food delivery.
  • Answer the usual follow-ups ("make it thread safe", "add a new vehicle type", "support undo") without redesigning from scratch.

How LLD interviews work and how they are scored

An LLD round is a 45–60 minute conversation where you gather requirements, model entities, draw a class diagram and write core code; interviewers score communication and design judgement at least as much as the final code.

What the round looks like

You get one sentence: "Design a parking lot" or "Design BookMyShow". The interviewer is deliberately vague. A whiteboard, a shared document or an IDE is open. You are expected to talk the whole time. At product companies and startups the round often ends with runnable code and a small main that proves it works. At service companies the round may stop at the class diagram and a few key methods. Either way the same skills are checked.

This is different from a high-level design (HLD) round. HLD is about servers, databases, caches and scale across machines. LLD is about classes, interfaces and methods inside one service. The LLD interviewer cares whether your code is easy to extend, test and read.

The scoring rubric

AreaWhat a strong candidate showsWeak signal
Requirement gatheringAsks 5–8 sharp questions, states assumptions, sets scopeStarts drawing at once
Object modellingNouns become classes with one clear job; sensible enums; correct relationshipsOne god class, or 30 tiny classes
Patterns used sensiblyStrategy, State, Observer only where a real variation exists, and says whyPattern name-dropping, Singleton everywhere
Code qualityClean names, small methods, interfaces, validation, no copy-pastePublic fields, giant if/else chains
ExtensibilityAdding a vehicle type or pricing rule needs a new class, not edits in five placesEvery change touches existing code
ConcurrencySpots shared state, protects the critical section, knows DB-level optionsNever mentions threads
CommunicationThinks aloud, checks in, accepts hints, explains trade-offsSilent coding, defensive about feedback

A 45–60 minute plan

  1. Clarify (5–8 min). Ask questions, write the agreed requirements as bullets, mark what is out of scope.
  2. Entities and public API (5 min). List nouns, then the 3–5 methods the outside world calls, such as park(vehicle) and unpark(ticket).
  3. Class diagram (8–10 min). Boxes, relationships, enums, where patterns plug in.
  4. Core code (20–25 min). Write the model, then the main flow. Skip getters and trivial classes; say "assume getters".
  5. Edge cases and concurrency (5 min). Walk the failure paths; name the shared state and how you protect it.
  6. Extensions (5 min). Answer "what if we add X". A good design absorbs it with one new class.

A script: what to say at each step

Opening
"Before I design, I would like to confirm the scope. Let me ask a few questions, then I will state my assumptions."
After requirements
"So the core use cases are A, B and C. I will leave payments and notifications out unless you want them. Is that fine?"
Modelling
"I see these entities: ... The relationship between X and Y is one-to-many, so X holds a list of Y."
Choosing a pattern
"Pricing can change independently of parking, so I will put it behind a PricingStrategy interface. That keeps ParkingLot closed for modification."
Before coding
"I will code the model first, then the main flow, and leave getters and tests for the end."
Concurrency
"Two users can reach this method together. The shared state is X, so I protect this critical section with Y."
Closing
"Known limits: in-memory only, single JVM. For persistence I would add a repository interface and a DB constraint on Z."

Clarifying questions that work for almost any problem

  • Who are the users or actors (customer, admin, system)? Which of them do we support first?
  • What are the three or four main use cases? What is explicitly out of scope (payments, UI, notifications)?
  • What are the variations (vehicle types, payment modes, split types)? Will new ones be added later?
  • What are the limits and sizes (capacity, number of floors, users)? This decides data structures.
  • Is it a single process or several servers? Do we need thread safety? Do we need persistence?
  • What happens on failure (lot full, item out of stock, payment declined)? Exception, error code or retry?
  • Do we need history, audit or reports?

Common mistakes that cost the offer

  • Jumping to code with no requirements or diagram. You will rewrite it half-way.
  • God classes: one ParkingLot that parks, prices, prints tickets and talks to the database. See SRP.
  • Overusing patterns: a Factory for a class with one constructor, or Singleton for everything. Use a pattern when you can name the variation it protects.
  • Ignoring concurrency in booking, inventory or counter problems.
  • Using strings and ints where an enum or a small class is clearer.
  • Silent coding: 15 minutes without a word. The interviewer cannot score what they cannot hear.
  • Gold-plating: designing a payment gateway when the question was a vending machine.

If the interviewer interrupts with a hint

Take it. Say "good point, that changes X" and adjust. Interviewers give hints when they want to see how you collaborate. Arguing, or ignoring the hint, scores worse than a flawed first design.

The LLD method: requirements to code, with a worked example

Follow five steps every time: requirements, entities, class diagram, core code, edge cases; here the method is applied to a small shopping cart with discounts.

The five steps

  1. Requirements. Split into functional (what the system does) and non-functional (thread safety, extensibility, performance). Write assumptions down.
  2. Entities. Underline the nouns in the requirements: they are candidate classes. Verbs become methods. Things with a fixed set of values become enums. Things that vary by behaviour become interfaces.
  3. Class diagram. Decide relationships: has-a (composition/aggregation), is-a (inheritance, used sparingly), uses (dependency). See Module 1 on UML.
  4. Core code. Model classes first (immutable where possible), then the one service class that runs the main use case. Depend on interfaces, inject them through the constructor.
  5. Edge cases. Null and empty input, limits, duplicates, failure paths, concurrent callers.

Noun-verb trick

Not every noun is a class. "Customer name" is a field of Customer, not a class. Make a class only if it has its own data and behaviour, or its own identity and lifecycle. Not every verb is a method on the first noun you thought of: ask "who has the data needed to do this?" and put the method there.

Worked example: shopping cart with discounts

1. Requirements (and assumptions)
  • A customer adds items with quantity to a cart and sees the total.
  • Discounts: a percentage off the whole cart, and "flat amount off if total is above a threshold". More rules will come later.
  • Assumptions: single currency, money kept in paise (long) to avoid floating point errors, one discount at a time, single user per cart (no concurrency).
2. Entities

Nouns: cart, item, product, discount. Items have a price and quantity. Discount rules vary, so DiscountRule is an interface (the Strategy pattern). Cart is the class that owns items and applies a rule.

3. Core code
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

record Product(String name, long pricePaise) { }

record CartItem(Product product, int quantity) {
    CartItem {
        if (quantity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
    }
    long lineTotal() { return product.pricePaise() * quantity; }
}

interface DiscountRule {
    long discount(long subtotalPaise);          // how much to subtract
}

class PercentOff implements DiscountRule {
    private final int percent;
    PercentOff(int percent) { this.percent = percent; }
    public long discount(long subtotal) { return subtotal * percent / 100; }
}

class FlatOffAboveThreshold implements DiscountRule {
    private final long threshold, flat;
    FlatOffAboveThreshold(long threshold, long flat) {
        this.threshold = threshold;
        this.flat = flat;
    }
    public long discount(long subtotal) { return subtotal >= threshold ? flat : 0; }
}
class Cart {
    private final List<CartItem> items = new ArrayList<>();

    void add(Product product, int quantity) {
        items.add(new CartItem(product, quantity));
    }

    long subtotal() {
        return items.stream().mapToLong(CartItem::lineTotal).sum();
    }

    long total(DiscountRule rule) {
        long sub = subtotal();
        long off = Math.min(rule.discount(sub), sub);   // never go below zero
        return sub - off;
    }
}

public class CartDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Cart cart = new Cart();
        cart.add(new Product("Keyboard", 150_000), 1);
        cart.add(new Product("Mouse", 50_000), 2);
        System.out.println(cart.total(new PercentOff(10)));
        System.out.println(cart.total(new FlatOffAboveThreshold(200_000, 30_000)));
    }
}
225000
220000
4. Edge cases and extensions
  • Quantity zero or negative: rejected in the record's compact constructor.
  • A discount larger than the subtotal: capped with Math.min.
  • Empty cart: subtotal 0, total 0, no exception.
  • "Add coupon codes": a new DiscountRule class. Cart does not change (open/closed principle).
  • "Combine two discounts": a CompositeRule that holds a list of rules (the Composite idea from Module 2).

Rule: keep money in integers

Store paise or cents in a long, or use BigDecimal. double cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so totals drift by a paisa and tests fail in surprising ways.

Convention: depend on interfaces, build in main

Pass collaborators (rules, repositories, clocks) into constructors. In an interview this single habit shows dependency inversion, makes the code testable, and costs nothing.

Why you need a method

Most candidates fail an LLD round not because they do not know patterns, but because they start typing classes in the first minute. Halfway through they discover a requirement they never asked about, the design has no room for it, and the clock is running. A fixed method makes your thinking visible, keeps you from forgetting steps under stress, and gives the interviewer easy places to steer you. How the round is scored is explained in How LLD interviews work; this article is the step-by-step routine you follow inside that round.

The interview flow with a time budget

Step 1 in detail: clarifying questions and what to say

Never accept the one-line problem as the full problem. Ask short, specific questions, and say your assumption aloud so that the interviewer can correct you. A good set:

  • Scope: "Which features are in scope for today? I will cover X and Y, and leave Z as an extension. Is that fine?"
  • Actors: "Who uses it: only customers, or admins too?"
  • Rules: "Is there a limit, a time window, a priority order?" (for example, how many items, how long a loan lasts).
  • Scale and concurrency: "Is it one process or many? Can two users act on the same item at the same time?"
  • Persistence and interface: "Can I keep data in memory and skip the UI and database for now?"
  • Extensibility: "Which part do you expect to change most? Pricing rules? Payment types?" This tells you where to put an interface.

A sentence to say: "I will state my assumptions, then list entities, then draw the classes, then code the main flow. Stop me if you want a different order." It shows structure and invites guidance.

Steps 2 and 3 in detail: from nouns to a diagram

Write the requirement sentences on the board, underline nouns and circle verbs, then fill a small table. This is easy to explain aloud and hard to get wrong.

In the requirementBecomesExample (cart)
A noun with data and behaviourClassCart, CartItem
A noun with only dataField or recordprice, quantity
A fixed set of valuesenumOrderStatus
"Different kinds of ..." / "rules will change"Interface plus implementationsDiscountRule
A verb that belongs to one thingMethod on that classcart.add()
A verb across several thingsService classCheckoutService

Say why each relationship is what it is: "A cart owns its items, so composition. A cart only uses a discount rule for one call, so a dependency." Pick a pattern only when a requirement points at it: "rules will change" suggests Strategy; "status changes the behaviour" suggests State; "notify several parties" suggests Observer. See the selection cheat sheet.

Step 4 in detail: how to write the code

  1. Start with enums and records (they are fast and show good habits).
  2. Write the interfaces next, then one or two implementations, not all.
  3. Write the service class with the main use case; inject collaborators through the constructor.
  4. Add a short main that proves it works, with the expected output.
  5. Say "I will skip getters and the remaining implementations; the pattern is the same." Interviewers prefer a clean core to a long dump.

Step 5 in detail: edge cases, concurrency and extensions

Leave the last minutes for this; it is where senior candidates stand out. Walk through three lists out loud:

  • Bad input: null, empty, zero or negative values, unknown ids, duplicates.
  • Concurrency: "Two users could check out the last item. The check and the update must be one atomic step. I would use synchronized on the item, or a database constraint if the data is persistent." The full toolbox is in Concurrency in LLD.
  • Extensions: name two changes and show where they go. "A coupon code is a new DiscountRule. A new payment method is a new class. Neither edits Cart."

Applying the method to a different problem

"Design a notification service that sends email and SMS, and lets users choose channels." Nouns: user, notification, channel, preference. Channel varies, so it is an interface (Channel with EmailChannel and SmsChannel). Preferences are data held by the user. A NotificationService.notify(user, message) loops over the user's channels. Edge cases: a user with no channel, a failing channel (should the others still send?), retry, rate limit. Extension: push notification is one new class. The same five steps, five minutes of thinking, and the code writes itself.

Wrong: jump into code and a pattern

// minute 1: "I will use a Factory and a Singleton"
class NotificationFactory { /* ... */ }
class NotificationManager { static NotificationManager instance; }

Right: requirements decide the design

// minute 12: channels vary, so one small interface
interface Channel { void send(String to, String text); }
class NotificationService {
    private final java.util.List<Channel> channels;
    NotificationService(java.util.List<Channel> channels) { this.channels = channels; }
}

Rules

  • Do not code before you have stated requirements and assumptions.
  • Every class must justify itself: data plus behaviour, or identity and lifecycle.
  • Money in integer units or BigDecimal; time through an injected Clock so tests can control it.

Conventions

  • Keep one use case end to end instead of five half-written ones.
  • Keep the model free of I/O (no printing, no database calls inside entities).
  • Return results or throw clear exceptions; avoid returning null for failure.

Edge cases about the method itself

  • If the interviewer says "just the class diagram", spend the saved time on relationships, multiplicity and extension points.
  • If the problem is a known one (parking lot, elevator), do not recite a memorised answer. Still ask your questions; the assumptions differ between interviewers.
  • If you get stuck, say what you would try next. Silence costs more than a wrong first guess.

Interview: using the method as an answer

  • "How do you approach an LLD problem?" Requirements and assumptions, entities from nouns, relationships and a class diagram, the core flow in code, then edge cases, concurrency and extensions. Mention that you ask questions first.
  • "What do you do when requirements are vague?" Ask, state a default, and record it so you can change it later.
  • "How do you decide on an interface?" Where the requirement says behaviour varies or will change.
  • "What would you improve with more time?" Persistence, validation, tests, events and metrics.

Concurrency in LLD: preventing double booking

Double booking is a check-then-act race: two requests both see a seat free, then both book it; fix it by making the check and the write one atomic step using a lock, a database constraint, a row lock or a version column, and use holds with expiry for seats that are chosen but not yet paid.

The race condition

Booking code often reads: "if seat is free, mark it booked". The two steps (check, then act) are separate. If two threads interleave between them, both pass the check.

class Seat {
    private String bookedBy;                        // null means free

    boolean book(String user) {
        if (bookedBy == null) {                    // check
            // another thread can run here
            bookedBy = user;                       // act
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}

The cure is always the same idea: make check and act atomic, so nobody can slip in between. How you do that depends on where the truth lives: in memory of one JVM, or in a database shared by many servers.

Solution 1: in-memory locks (single JVM)

See Core Java · Module 6 for the basics of synchronized, ReentrantLock and the memory model.

import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentMap;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

class SafeSeat {
    private String bookedBy;

    synchronized boolean book(String user) {       // lock on this seat object
        if (bookedBy != null) return false;
        bookedBy = user;
        return true;
    }

    synchronized boolean isFreeUnsafe() { return bookedBy == null; }
}

class SeatMap {
    // Lock-free style: putIfAbsent is atomic for ConcurrentHashMap
    private final ConcurrentMap<String, String> owner = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    boolean book(String seatId, String user) {
        return owner.putIfAbsent(seatId, user) == null;   // null means we won
    }
}

class MultiSeatBooking {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();   // one lock per show

    boolean bookAll(java.util.List<SafeSeat> seats, String user) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            // check all first, then book all; needs to be one critical section
            for (SafeSeat s : seats) if (!s.isFreeUnsafe()) return false;
            seats.forEach(s -> s.book(user));
            return true;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();                          // always unlock in finally
        }
    }
}

Look at the shape of the last class: when a booking touches several seats, one lock per seat is risky (deadlock if two users lock seats in opposite order). Two safe options: one lock per show (simple, less parallelism), or per-seat locks always taken in sorted seat-id order.

Why per-seat locks can deadlock

User A locks seat 5 then waits for seat 6. User B locks seat 6 then waits for seat 5. Neither moves. Fix: sort the seat ids and always lock in that order, or use tryLock with a timeout and roll back.

In-memory locks stop at the JVM boundary

If you run two copies of your Spring Boot app behind a load balancer, synchronized in copy 1 knows nothing about copy 2. For a real booking system the database must be the referee.

Solution 2: database constraints

Make the invalid state impossible to store. A unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) in a bookings table lets exactly one insert win; the loser gets a constraint violation, which you turn into "seat already taken".

CREATE TABLE booking (
    id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    show_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
    seat_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
    user_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
    created   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    CONSTRAINT uq_show_seat UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id)
);

-- Second insert for the same show and seat fails with a unique violation
INSERT INTO booking (show_id, seat_id, user_id) VALUES (10, 12, 1);
INSERT INTO booking (show_id, seat_id, user_id) VALUES (10, 12, 2);  -- error

This is the strongest and simplest guard. In Spring you catch DataIntegrityViolationException and return a clean "seat taken" message. It works across any number of servers.

Solution 3: pessimistic lock with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

Lock the rows you are about to change so others wait. Inside a transaction:

BEGIN;
SELECT status FROM show_seat
 WHERE show_id = 10 AND seat_id IN (12, 13)
 ORDER BY seat_id            -- same order for everyone avoids deadlocks
 FOR UPDATE;                  -- other transactions block here until we commit
-- application checks every status = 'AVAILABLE'
UPDATE show_seat SET status = 'BOOKED', user_id = 1
 WHERE show_id = 10 AND seat_id IN (12, 13);
COMMIT;

Use it when conflicts are common (a hot show) and you want a guaranteed result without retries. The cost: waiting transactions hold connections. Keep the transaction short, never wait for the user inside it. Details are in SQL · Module 5.

Solution 4: optimistic locking with a version column

Do not lock. Read the row with its version; update only if the version is unchanged; if no row was updated, someone else won, so retry or fail.

-- read: status = 'AVAILABLE', version = 7
UPDATE show_seat
   SET status = 'BOOKED', user_id = 1, version = version + 1
 WHERE show_id = 10 AND seat_id = 12
   AND status = 'AVAILABLE' AND version = 7;
-- rows affected = 1 -> we won;  rows affected = 0 -> someone else changed it

In JPA you add a @Version field and Hibernate does this for you, throwing OptimisticLockException on conflict. Optimistic locking is best when conflicts are rare.

Solution 5: temporary holds with expiry

Real users pick seats, then spend two minutes typing card details. You cannot keep a database lock for that long. Instead, introduce a middle state: AVAILABLE → HELD → BOOKED. A hold records held_by and hold_expires_at. Payment success turns it to BOOKED; timeout or failure turns it back.

-- try to hold: succeeds if free, or if an old hold has expired
UPDATE show_seat
   SET status = 'HELD', held_by = 1, hold_expires_at = now() + interval '5 minutes'
 WHERE show_id = 10 AND seat_id = 12
   AND (status = 'AVAILABLE'
        OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now()));
-- rows affected = 1 -> hold granted

A background job (or lazy check on read, as above) releases expired holds. The single conditional UPDATE is atomic, so two users cannot both get the hold.

Solution 6: distributed locks (Redis), with caveats

A distributed lock is a lock shared by many servers, often kept in Redis with SET key value NX PX 30000 (set only if absent, auto-expire in 30 seconds). Only the holder who set the key may delete it, so the value is a unique token and the release checks it.

Caveats of distributed locks

  • The lock expires on a timer. If the holder pauses (long GC, slow network) past the expiry, a second holder enters while the first still thinks it holds the lock.
  • A fencing token (a number that grows with each lock grant, checked by the database on write) protects against that stale holder.
  • A Redis failover can lose the key, so two clients may hold the lock. Multi-node schemes such as Redlock are debated for safety-critical use.
  • It adds a moving part. If a database constraint can do the job, prefer the constraint.

Comparison

TechniqueWorks across serversBest whenMain drawback
synchronized / ReentrantLockNoSingle JVM, in-memory model, interviewsUseless with multiple instances
putIfAbsent / atomic map opsNoSingle seat or key claimsDoes not cover multi-seat bookings alone
Unique constraintYesAlways; the last line of defenceNeeds error handling for the loser
SELECT ... FOR UPDATEYesHigh contention, must succeedBlocking, long transactions hurt
Optimistic versionYesLow contentionRetries under heavy contention
Hold with expiryYes (stored in DB or cache)Human checkout stepsNeeds expiry cleanup
Redis distributed lockYesCoordinating non-DB workTiming and failover caveats

How to answer "how do you avoid double booking?"

  1. Name the race: check-then-act on shared state.
  2. In the code you write: lock the critical section (per show or sorted per-seat locks).
  3. In production: a unique constraint as the final guard, a conditional update or row lock for the claim, a hold state with expiry for checkout.
  4. Mention what you would not do: keep a DB transaction open while the user pays.

Common mistakes

  • Locking a new object each call (synchronized (new Object())): nobody else shares it, so it protects nothing.
  • Using a ConcurrentHashMap but still doing if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v). That is check-then-act again; use putIfAbsent or compute.
  • Forgetting to release the hold or lock on the failure path.

Design a parking lot

Model vehicles, spots, floors, tickets and a pricing Strategy; park a vehicle by finding a free spot of the right type, and make the spot claim atomic so two cars never get the same spot.

Requirements and assumptions

Functional:

  • A lot has several floors; each floor has spots of types BIKE, CAR and TRUCK.
  • On entry the system finds a free spot for the vehicle type and issues a ticket.
  • On exit the system computes the fee from the parking duration and frees the spot.
  • The lot reports free spots per type.

Non-functional: thread-safe (several gates run at once), easy to add new pricing rules and vehicle types.

Assumptions: one lot, in-memory, a vehicle uses exactly one spot of its own type, fee is hourly and any started hour is charged, payment is out of scope, one entry gate chooses the spot (no reservation in advance).

Entities

ClassResponsibility
VehicleType (enum)BIKE, CAR, TRUCK; also the spot size class
VehiclePlate number and type
ParkingSpotOne spot: id, type, and whether it is taken
ParkingFloorOwns spots; finds and claims a free one
TicketVehicle, spot, entry time
PricingStrategyInterface: duration and type to fee
ParkingLotFacade: park and unpark; tracks active tickets

Key design decisions

  • Strategy for pricing (Module 2): hourly today, flat-rate or weekend-rate tomorrow. ParkingLot never changes (open/closed principle, Module 1).
  • Enum for types instead of a Vehicle subclass per type: the types differ only by data (the rate and the spot size), not behaviour. Subclasses would be inheritance for its own sake.
  • The spot owns its own occupancy and uses an atomic compare-and-set, so claiming a spot is one indivisible step.
  • Inject a Clock so tests can move time instead of sleeping.
  • A spot-allocation strategy (nearest to entrance, lowest floor first) can be a second Strategy if asked; here floors are scanned in order.

Core code: model

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK }

record Vehicle(String plate, VehicleType type) { }

class ParkingSpot {
    private final String id;
    private final VehicleType type;
    private final AtomicReference<Vehicle> parked = new AtomicReference<>();

    ParkingSpot(String id, VehicleType type) {
        this.id = id;
        this.type = type;
    }

    String id() { return id; }
    VehicleType type() { return type; }
    boolean isFree() { return parked.get() == null; }

    /** Atomic: only one thread can move the spot from empty to occupied. */
    boolean tryPark(Vehicle v) {
        return v.type() == type && parked.compareAndSet(null, v);
    }

    void free() { parked.set(null); }
}

record Ticket(String id, Vehicle vehicle, ParkingSpot spot, Instant entry) { }

Core code: pricing and floor

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

interface PricingStrategy {
    long fee(VehicleType type, Duration parkedFor);   // result in paise
}

class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    private final Map<VehicleType, Long> ratePerHour = new EnumMap<>(VehicleType.class);

    HourlyPricing() {
        ratePerHour.put(VehicleType.BIKE, 1_000L);
        ratePerHour.put(VehicleType.CAR, 3_000L);
        ratePerHour.put(VehicleType.TRUCK, 6_000L);
    }

    public long fee(VehicleType type, Duration parkedFor) {
        long minutes = Math.max(1, parkedFor.toMinutes());
        long hours = (minutes + 59) / 60;               // any started hour counts
        return hours * ratePerHour.get(type);
    }
}

class ParkingFloor {
    private final List<ParkingSpot> spots;

    ParkingFloor(List<ParkingSpot> spots) { this.spots = List.copyOf(spots); }

    Optional<ParkingSpot> claimSpot(Vehicle v) {
        for (ParkingSpot s : spots) {
            if (s.isFree() && s.tryPark(v)) return Optional.of(s);  // CAS decides the winner
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }

    long freeCount(VehicleType t) {
        return spots.stream().filter(s -> s.type() == t && s.isFree()).count();
    }
}

Core code: the lot (facade)

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.UUID;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

class ParkingLot {
    private final List<ParkingFloor> floors;
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Set<String> platesInside = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();

    ParkingLot(List<ParkingFloor> floors, PricingStrategy pricing, Clock clock) {
        this.floors = List.copyOf(floors);
        this.pricing = pricing;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    Ticket park(Vehicle v) {
        if (!platesInside.add(v.plate())) {                  // atomic duplicate check
            throw new IllegalStateException("Vehicle already inside: " + v.plate());
        }
        for (ParkingFloor f : floors) {
            var spot = f.claimSpot(v);
            if (spot.isPresent()) {
                Ticket t = new Ticket(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), v,
                                      spot.get(), Instant.now(clock));
                active.put(t.id(), t);
                return t;
            }
        }
        platesInside.remove(v.plate());                      // undo on failure
        throw new IllegalStateException("Lot full for " + v.type());
    }

    long unpark(String ticketId) {
        Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId);                  // atomic: one exit per ticket
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown ticket " + ticketId);
        Duration d = Duration.between(t.entry(), Instant.now(clock));
        long fee = pricing.fee(t.vehicle().type(), d);
        t.spot().free();
        platesInside.remove(t.vehicle().plate());
        return fee;
    }
}
import java.time.Clock;
import java.util.List;

public class ParkingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var floor = new ParkingFloor(List.of(
                new ParkingSpot("F0-1", VehicleType.CAR),
                new ParkingSpot("F0-2", VehicleType.BIKE)));
        var lot = new ParkingLot(List.of(floor), new HourlyPricing(), Clock.systemUTC());

        Ticket t = lot.park(new Vehicle("KA01AB1234", VehicleType.CAR));
        System.out.println("Spot: " + t.spot().id());
        System.out.println("Fee: " + lot.unpark(t.id()));
        System.out.println("Free cars: " + floor.freeCount(VehicleType.CAR));
    }
}
Spot: F0-1
Fee: 3000
Free cars: 1

Concurrency

  • Two gates can reach the same free spot. compareAndSet(null, v) lets only one succeed; the loser moves to the next spot.
  • active.remove(ticketId) is atomic, so a ticket cannot be used for two exits (no double refund or double free).
  • platesInside.add returns false for a duplicate, an atomic "is this car already in?" check.

Use atomics for one flag, locks for several fields

An AtomicReference is perfect when one value changes. If a spot also tracked "reserved until" and "owner", you would use a lock or an immutable state object swapped with CAS.

Edge cases

  • Lot full for one type but free for another: message names the type.
  • Lost or unknown ticket: IllegalArgumentException; a real system has a lost-ticket fee and manual lookup.
  • Same ticket scanned twice at exit: the second call finds nothing and fails cleanly.
  • Parked less than a minute: charged one hour (minimum rule is a pricing concern, so it is in the strategy).
  • Day boundary and long stays: use Duration, not clock hours.

Extensions interviewers ask

  • EV charging spots: add EV_CAR to the enum or a SpotFeature set on ParkingSpot; add a charging fee in a decorator over PricingStrategy.
  • Bigger vehicle in a bigger spot: replace the type equality in tryPark with a canFit method and try the smallest fitting spot first.
  • Spot allocation policy: a SpotAllocationStrategy interface (nearest to the lift, fill floor by floor).
  • Display board: an Observer on spot changes (Module 2).
  • Multiple entry and exit gates: already safe because state lives in the lot, not in gates.
  • Persistence: a TicketRepository interface; the DB gets a unique constraint on active (spot) so two tickets cannot share a spot.

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 5 min: ask about types, floors, pricing, concurrency; state assumptions.
  2. 8 min: draw the diagram; say "pricing is a Strategy, spots own their occupancy".
  3. 20 min: code ParkingSpot, PricingStrategy, ParkingLot.park/unpark.
  4. 7 min: explain the CAS claim, edge cases, then the EV extension.

Design tic-tac-toe (and how Snake and Ladder differs)

Keep game state (board, players, current turn, status) in one Game class, validate every move, and detect a win in O(1) with row, column and diagonal counters instead of scanning the board.

Requirements and assumptions

  • Two players, X and O, alternate turns on an N×N board (default 3×3); X starts.
  • A move is rejected if it is out of range, on an occupied cell, by the wrong player, or after the game ended.
  • The game ends when a player fills a whole row, column or diagonal (win), or the board is full (draw).
  • Assumptions: console or API driven, no AI opponent, no undo for now, single-threaded game (one game object per match, moves arrive one at a time).

Entities

  • Mark (enum X, O) and GameStatus (enum IN_PROGRESS, WON, DRAW).
  • Player (name, mark).
  • Board: the grid and the win detection. It knows nothing about players' names or turns.
  • Game: owns the board and players, enforces turn order, exposes makeMove.

Key design decisions

  • Separate Board from Game (single responsibility, Module 1): the board validates geometry; the game validates turn order. Either can change alone.
  • O(1) win check. Give X the value +1 and O the value −1. Keep a running sum per row, per column and for both diagonals. After a move only the sums touched by that cell change; if any reaches N or −N, that player wins. Scanning the board is O(N) per move, which is also fine in an interview, but counters impress.
  • Return the status from makeMove, so the caller prints or reacts; the game has no console code inside (keeps it testable and reusable in a REST controller).
  • Patterns: none are needed, and saying so is a good sign. If asked for different board sizes or win rules, a WinRule Strategy fits; for undo, the Command pattern (Module 2).

Core code

enum Mark { X, O }

enum GameStatus { IN_PROGRESS, WON, DRAW }

record Player(String name, Mark mark) { }

class Board {
    private final int n;
    private final Mark[][] cells;
    private final int[] rowSum, colSum;
    private int diagSum, antiSum, filled;

    Board(int n) {
        this.n = n;
        this.cells = new Mark[n][n];
        this.rowSum = new int[n];
        this.colSum = new int[n];
    }

    /** Places a mark and returns true if this move completes a line. */
    boolean place(int r, int c, Mark m) {
        if (r < 0 || r >= n || c < 0 || c >= n) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cell out of range: " + r + "," + c);
        }
        if (cells[r][c] != null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Cell already taken: " + r + "," + c);
        }
        cells[r][c] = m;
        filled++;
        int v = (m == Mark.X) ? 1 : -1;
        rowSum[r] += v;
        colSum[c] += v;
        if (r == c) diagSum += v;
        if (r + c == n - 1) antiSum += v;
        return Math.abs(rowSum[r]) == n || Math.abs(colSum[c]) == n
            || Math.abs(diagSum) == n || Math.abs(antiSum) == n;
    }

    boolean isFull() { return filled == n * n; }
}
import java.util.List;

class Game {
    private final Board board;
    private final List<Player> players;
    private int turn = 0;
    private GameStatus status = GameStatus.IN_PROGRESS;
    private Player winner;

    Game(int size, Player first, Player second) {
        this.board = new Board(size);
        this.players = List.of(first, second);
    }

    GameStatus makeMove(Player p, int row, int col) {
        if (status != GameStatus.IN_PROGRESS) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Game is over");
        }
        if (!players.get(turn).equals(p)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Not " + p.name() + "'s turn");
        }
        boolean won = board.place(row, col, p.mark());   // may throw; turn does not change
        if (won) {
            status = GameStatus.WON;
            winner = p;
        } else if (board.isFull()) {
            status = GameStatus.DRAW;
        } else {
            turn = 1 - turn;                              // switch only after a valid move
        }
        return status;
    }

    Player winner() { return winner; }
}

public class TicTacToeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Player a = new Player("Asha", Mark.X), b = new Player("Ravi", Mark.O);
        Game g = new Game(3, a, b);
        g.makeMove(a, 0, 0); g.makeMove(b, 1, 0);
        g.makeMove(a, 0, 1); g.makeMove(b, 1, 1);
        System.out.println(g.makeMove(a, 0, 2));
        System.out.println(g.winner().name());
    }
}
WON
Asha

Edge cases

  • Invalid move (taken cell, out of range): exception thrown before the turn switches, so the same player retries.
  • Move after the game ended: rejected.
  • The winning move that also fills the board: win is checked first, so it is a win, not a draw.
  • Both diagonals on odd boards share the centre cell; the counters handle that naturally.

Concurrency

One game is a turn-based conversation, so moves are naturally serial. If two clients can call makeMove on the same game (a web service), make the method synchronized; the turn check then rejects the stale caller. Games are independent, so different games never contend.

Snake and Ladder: what changes

The same split works: Board (size, snakes and ladders as a Map<Integer, Integer> from start cell to end cell), Dice, Player (name, position) and Game (turn queue, status). A turn is: roll the dice, compute pos + roll; if it exceeds the last cell the player stays; otherwise follow a snake or ladder if one starts there. The first to land exactly on the last cell wins.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Random;

class SnakeBoard {
    private final int last;
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> jumps = new HashMap<>();  // snakes and ladders

    SnakeBoard(int last) { this.last = last; }

    void addJump(int from, int to) {
        if (from == to || from < 1 || to < 1 || from >= last) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Bad jump " + from + "->" + to);
        }
        jumps.put(from, to);
    }

    int move(int position, int roll) {
        int next = position + roll;
        if (next > last) return position;              // needs an exact roll
        return jumps.getOrDefault(next, next);          // follow snake or ladder once
    }
}

class Dice {
    private final Random random = new Random();
    int roll() { return random.nextInt(6) + 1; }
}

Make Dice an interface if you want deterministic tests (inject a fixed sequence). Validate that jumps do not form a loop (a ladder ending on a snake head that leads back to the ladder start).

Extensions interviewers ask

  • N players or bigger boards: the players list and the board size are already parameters. For N×N with a win length K < N (Gomoku style), counters no longer work; scan around the last move in four directions.
  • Undo: keep a stack of Move commands; undo reverses counters (subtract the same value) and steps the turn back.
  • Computer player: a MoveStrategy interface (random, minimax).
  • Replay and history: store moves in a list; replay is a fold over the list.

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 5 min: board size, players, win rule, undo yes or no.
  2. 5 min: draw Game, Board, Player, enums; say why Board and Game are separate.
  3. 20 min: code Board.place with the counters, then Game.makeMove.
  4. 10 min: show a run, discuss invalid moves, then undo with Command and the AI Strategy.

Design a library management system

Separate the idea of a book (title, author) from a physical copy that can be loaned; model members, loans with due dates and a fine Strategy, and make check-out of one copy atomic.

Requirements and assumptions

Functional:

  • The library holds books; each book can have several physical copies, each with a barcode.
  • Members search books by title or author, borrow a copy and return it.
  • A member may hold at most 5 loans; a loan lasts 14 days.
  • Late returns cost a fine per overdue day.

Non-functional: two members cannot borrow the same copy; fine rules must be easy to change.

Assumptions: one library branch, in-memory, reservations and notifications are extensions, librarians are not modelled as separate roles in the core code.

Entities and relationships

The key insight: Book and BookCopy are two classes. "Clean Code" is a book (one title, one ISBN); the three shelf copies are BookCopy objects. Status belongs to the copy, not the book.

Key design decisions

  • Book vs copy split avoids a "copies available" integer that must be kept in sync with who holds what.
  • Loan as an entity (not just a field) gives you due date, history and the fine calculation a home. Many-to-many "member borrows book" almost always needs a link class with its own data.
  • Strategy for fines (Module 2): per-day today, capped or category-based tomorrow.
  • Search sits behind a method on Library; if asked for many criteria, extract a SearchCriteria interface or use predicates.
  • A Clock is injected so due dates are testable.

Core code: model

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

enum CopyStatus { AVAILABLE, LOANED }

record Book(String isbn, String title, String author) { }

class BookCopy {
    private final String barcode;
    private final Book book;
    private CopyStatus status = CopyStatus.AVAILABLE;

    BookCopy(String barcode, Book book) {
        this.barcode = barcode;
        this.book = book;
    }

    String barcode() { return barcode; }
    Book book() { return book; }

    synchronized boolean tryCheckout() {            // check and set in one step
        if (status != CopyStatus.AVAILABLE) return false;
        status = CopyStatus.LOANED;
        return true;
    }

    synchronized void release() { status = CopyStatus.AVAILABLE; }
}

class Member {
    static final int MAX_LOANS = 5;
    private final String id, name;
    private final Set<String> borrowed = new HashSet<>();

    Member(String id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }

    String id() { return id; }

    synchronized boolean tryAddLoan(String barcode) {
        if (borrowed.size() >= MAX_LOANS) return false;
        return borrowed.add(barcode);
    }

    synchronized void removeLoan(String barcode) { borrowed.remove(barcode); }
}

record Loan(BookCopy copy, Member member, LocalDate issued, LocalDate due) { }

interface FineStrategy {
    long fine(long overdueDays);                    // paise
}

class PerDayFine implements FineStrategy {
    public long fine(long overdueDays) { return Math.max(0, overdueDays) * 200; }
}

Core code: the library service

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

class Library {
    private static final int LOAN_DAYS = 14;

    private final Map<String, Book> books = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, List<BookCopy>> copies = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Member> members = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Loan> loansByBarcode = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final FineStrategy fines;
    private final Clock clock;

    Library(FineStrategy fines, Clock clock) {
        this.fines = fines;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    void addMember(Member m) { members.put(m.id(), m); }

    void addBook(Book b, int copyCount) {
        books.put(b.isbn(), b);
        List<BookCopy> list = copies.computeIfAbsent(b.isbn(), k -> new ArrayList<>());
        synchronized (list) {
            for (int i = 0; i < copyCount; i++) {
                list.add(new BookCopy(b.isbn() + "-" + (list.size() + 1), b));
            }
        }
    }

    List<Book> search(String text) {
        String q = text.toLowerCase();
        return books.values().stream()
                .filter(b -> b.title().toLowerCase().contains(q)
                          || b.author().toLowerCase().contains(q))
                .toList();
    }

    Loan checkout(String memberId, String isbn) {
