        Member m = members.get(memberId);
        List<BookCopy> list = copies.get(isbn);
        if (m == null || list == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown member or book");

        for (BookCopy c : List.copyOf(list)) {
            if (!c.tryCheckout()) continue;               // someone else holds this copy
            if (!m.tryAddLoan(c.barcode())) {              // limit reached: undo
                c.release();
                throw new IllegalStateException("Loan limit reached");
            }
            LocalDate today = LocalDate.now(clock);
            Loan loan = new Loan(c, m, today, today.plusDays(LOAN_DAYS));
            loansByBarcode.put(c.barcode(), loan);
            return loan;
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("No copy available");
    }

    long returnCopy(String barcode) {
        Loan loan = loansByBarcode.remove(barcode);
        if (loan == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Copy is not on loan");
        long overdue = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(loan.due(), LocalDate.now(clock));
        loan.member().removeLoan(barcode);
        loan.copy().release();
        return fines.fine(overdue);
    }
}
import java.time.Clock;

public class LibraryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Library lib = new Library(new PerDayFine(), Clock.systemDefaultZone());
        lib.addMember(new Member("M1", "Asha"));
        lib.addBook(new Book("978-0132350884", "Clean Code", "Robert C. Martin"), 2);

        Loan loan = lib.checkout("M1", "978-0132350884");
        System.out.println("Due: " + loan.due().isAfter(loan.issued()));
        System.out.println("Fine: " + lib.returnCopy(loan.copy().barcode()));
        System.out.println(lib.search("clean").size());
    }
}
Due: true
Fine: 0
1

Concurrency

  • BookCopy.tryCheckout is synchronized on the copy: two members racing for the last copy cannot both win.
  • The member's limit is checked inside the member's own lock; if the limit fails we undo the copy checkout. That is a compensating step, simpler than holding two locks.
  • loansByBarcode.remove is atomic, so a double return does not double-charge a fine.

Mistake: a counter on Book

Keeping availableCopies++/-- on Book tempts you into an unsynchronized read-modify-write and loses updates under load. Derive availability from the copies themselves.

Edge cases

  • Same member borrows two copies of the same title: policy question; add a check on the member's loans by ISBN if not allowed.
  • Return of a copy that is not on loan, or an unknown barcode: clean error.
  • Overdue by zero or negative days (early return): Math.max(0, ...) gives no fine.
  • Member with unpaid fines: block new loans (add a check in checkout).
  • Lost copy: a third status LOST and a replacement-cost fee.

Extensions interviewers ask

  • Reservations: a queue of waiting members per ISBN; on return, notify the first one (Observer, Module 2) and hold the copy for 2 days.
  • Different member types (student 3 loans, staff 10): a MembershipPolicy Strategy holding the limit and loan days.
  • Renewals: extend due once if nobody reserved the book; make Loan hold a mutable due date or create a new Loan.
  • Multiple branches: add Branch; copies belong to a branch.
  • Search by many fields: an index map (author to books) or a database full-text index.

What the interviewer is testing

Library management is a favourite "warm-up" LLD problem because it looks easy and hides several design questions. The interviewer wants to see whether you (1) separate the idea of a book from a physical copy, (2) model the link between member and copy as its own thing with dates (a loan), (3) keep rules such as fines and limits out of the entities so they can change, and (4) notice that two members can race for the last copy. Candidates who put an int availableCopies on Book and a borrow() method on Member usually get stuck on all four. The general routine is in The LLD method; here it is applied with the talking points.

Clarifying questions to ask, and the answers to assume

You askWhy it mattersAssume if not told
One branch or many?Decides if copies belong to a branchOne branch
Same loan rules for all members?Strategy for limits and daysSame rules; extension later
Reservations when all copies are out?Adds a queue and notificationsOut of scope, discuss at the end
Can a book be renewed?Mutable due date or new loanNot in scope
Digital catalogue search by what?Index or a simple filterTitle and author
Is it multi-threaded or persistent?Locks vs database constraintsIn-memory, thread-safe

Say: "I will build checkout, return, search and fines. Reservations and renewals I will mention as extensions." That one sentence protects your time.

The lifecycle of one copy

The checkout flow, step by step

Extension in code: membership types and reservations

import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedDeque;

// Strategy: limits and days depend on the membership type
enum Membership {
    STUDENT(3, 14), STAFF(10, 30);

    private final int maxLoans;
    private final int loanDays;
    Membership(int maxLoans, int loanDays) {
        this.maxLoans = maxLoans;
        this.loanDays = loanDays;
    }
    int maxLoans() { return maxLoans; }
    int loanDays() { return loanDays; }
}

// Reservation queue: first come, first served, per ISBN
class ReservationQueue {
    private final Map<String, Deque<String>> waiting = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    void reserve(String isbn, String memberId) {
        waiting.computeIfAbsent(isbn, k -> new ConcurrentLinkedDeque<>())
               .addLast(memberId);
    }

    Optional<String> nextFor(String isbn) {
        Deque<String> q = waiting.get(isbn);
        return q == null ? Optional.empty() : Optional.ofNullable(q.pollFirst());
    }
}

// Observer: told when a copy comes back, so it can notify the next member
interface ReturnListener {
    void onCopyReturned(String isbn, String nextMemberId);
}

In returnCopy you would call reservations.nextFor(isbn) and, if a member id is present, notify the listener and keep the copy in a RESERVED state until a deadline. Replacing the fixed MAX_LOANS and LOAN_DAYS constants with a field of type Membership on Member touches only those two places; Library asks the member for its limits.

Concurrency: from JVM locks to database constraints

  • In memory: the check-and-set on BookCopy is atomic because both steps are inside one synchronized method. Never hold two locks at once (copy and member) unless you always take them in the same order, or you invite a deadlock.
  • In a database: the same rule becomes a constraint. In PostgreSQL, a partial unique index guarantees that a copy has at most one open loan, even with many application servers:
CREATE TABLE loan (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    copy_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES book_copy(id),
    member_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES member(id),
    issued_on   DATE   NOT NULL,
    due_on      DATE   NOT NULL,
    returned_on DATE
);

-- at most one active loan per copy: the second insert fails
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_loan_per_copy
    ON loan (copy_id) WHERE returned_on IS NULL;

The application catches the unique-violation error, treats it as "someone else took this copy" and tries the next copy. This is the same idea as in Concurrency in LLD: make the database the final referee.

Wrong: availability as a counter

class Book {
    int available = 3;
    boolean borrow() {
        if (available > 0) { available--; return true; }   // race
        return false;
    }
}

Right: state lives on each copy

for (BookCopy c : copies) {
    if (c.tryCheckout()) {          // atomic check-and-set on one copy
        return new Loan(c, member, today, today.plusDays(14));
    }
}
throw new IllegalStateException("No copy available");

Rules

  • A Book is a title; a BookCopy is a physical item with its own barcode and status.
  • Limits, loan days and fines are policies, not constants buried in the entities.
  • Check-and-update of a copy's status must be one atomic step.

Conventions

  • Give Loan the dates and let it answer "is it overdue on this day?" rather than computing in the service.
  • Inject a Clock; in tests use Clock.fixed(...) to test fines without waiting.
  • Keep search in its own method or class (CatalogSearch) so you can later swap the in-memory filter for a database query.

Edge cases and exceptions

  • Returning a copy twice: loansByBarcode.remove returns null the second time, so you throw IllegalArgumentException and charge no second fine.
  • Crash between "copy marked loaned" and "loan saved": in a database use one transaction; in memory the compensating release() covers the limit failure but not a JVM crash, which is why real systems persist.
  • A member returns a book after the library's closing time: the policy (count that day or not) is a requirement; ask the interviewer.

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 5 min: ask about member types, limits, fines, reservations, branches.
  2. 7 min: diagram; stress Book vs BookCopy and Loan as a link entity.
  3. 20 min: code BookCopy, Loan, Library.checkout/returnCopy.
  4. 8 min: concurrency on the last copy, edge cases, then reservations with Observer.

Interview: sentences that score points

  • "I separate Book from BookCopy so availability is derived, not a counter I must keep in sync."
  • "Loan is an association class: it carries the due date, so fines and history have a home."
  • "Fines are a Strategy; membership limits are another small policy. Neither is hard-coded."
  • "Two members racing for the last copy are handled by an atomic check-and-set on the copy; in a database I would add a unique partial index."
  • "For reservations I would add a queue per ISBN and an Observer to notify the next member."

Design a vending machine with the State pattern

A vending machine behaves differently depending on whether it is idle, holds money or is out of service, so give each situation its own State class and let the machine delegate every action to its current state instead of using nested if statements.

Requirements and assumptions

  • The machine sells products identified by a code (A1, B2) with a price and a stock count.
  • Flow: insert money, choose a product, receive the product and change.
  • The user may cancel before choosing and gets a refund.
  • Reject: choosing without money, not enough money, sold-out product, unknown code.
  • An admin can refill stock (separate API, not covered by user states).
  • Assumptions: money is accepted as a total amount in paise (no coin hardware), change is always available, one user at a time, the machine object is shared by the keypad, so its methods are synchronized.

The state machine first

Draw this before the class diagram: states are the nodes, user actions are the arrows. Each state decides what every action means. In Idle, "select product" is an error; in HasMoney, "select product" tries to sell.

Key design decisions

  • State pattern (Module 2): the alternative is a switch (state) inside every method. Adding an OutOfServiceState then means editing every switch; with State it is one new class.
  • Default methods throw IllegalStateException, so each concrete state overrides only what is valid for it.
  • The machine owns data (balance, inventory); states own transitions. States are stateless, so they could be shared, but creating them keeps the code simple.
  • Inventory is a separate class (single responsibility): stock changes do not touch the state logic.

Core code: inventory and state interface

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

record Product(String code, String name, long pricePaise) { }

record Dispense(Product product, long changePaise) { }

class Inventory {
    private final Map<String, Product> products = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();

    void add(Product p, int quantity) {
        products.put(p.code(), p);
        stock.merge(p.code(), quantity, Integer::sum);
    }

    Product find(String code) {
        Product p = products.get(code);
        if (p == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown product " + code);
        return p;
    }

    boolean inStock(String code) { return stock.getOrDefault(code, 0) > 0; }

    void take(String code) { stock.merge(code, -1, Integer::sum); }
}

interface VendingState {
    default void insertMoney(VendingMachine m, long paise) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot insert money now");
    }
    default Dispense select(VendingMachine m, String code) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot select now");
    }
    default long cancel(VendingMachine m) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Nothing to cancel");
    }
}

Core code: the two states and the machine

class IdleState implements VendingState {
    @Override
    public void insertMoney(VendingMachine m, long paise) {
        if (paise <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        m.addBalance(paise);
        m.setState(new HasMoneyState());
    }
    // select and cancel inherit the default: they throw
}

class HasMoneyState implements VendingState {
    @Override
    public void insertMoney(VendingMachine m, long paise) {
        if (paise <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        m.addBalance(paise);
    }

    @Override
    public Dispense select(VendingMachine m, String code) {
        Product p = m.inventory().find(code);
        if (!m.inventory().inStock(code)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Sold out: " + p.name());
        }
        if (m.balance() < p.pricePaise()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(
                "Insert " + (p.pricePaise() - m.balance()) + " more paise");
        }
        m.inventory().take(code);
        long change = m.balance() - p.pricePaise();
        m.clearBalance();
        m.setState(new IdleState());
        return new Dispense(p, change);
    }

    @Override
    public long cancel(VendingMachine m) {
        long refund = m.balance();
        m.clearBalance();
        m.setState(new IdleState());
        return refund;
    }
}

class VendingMachine {
    private VendingState state = new IdleState();
    private final Inventory inventory;
    private long balance;

    VendingMachine(Inventory inventory) { this.inventory = inventory; }

    synchronized void insertMoney(long paise) { state.insertMoney(this, paise); }
    synchronized Dispense select(String code) { return state.select(this, code); }
    synchronized long cancel() { return state.cancel(this); }

    // used by states
    Inventory inventory() { return inventory; }
    long balance() { return balance; }
    void addBalance(long p) { balance += p; }
    void clearBalance() { balance = 0; }
    void setState(VendingState s) { state = s; }
}

public class VendingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Inventory inv = new Inventory();
        inv.add(new Product("A1", "Cola", 4_000), 2);
        VendingMachine vm = new VendingMachine(inv);

        vm.insertMoney(5_000);
        Dispense d = vm.select("A1");
        System.out.println(d.product().name() + ", change " + d.changePaise());
        try {
            vm.select("A1");                      // back to Idle: not allowed
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Cola, change 1000
Error: Cannot select now

Concurrency

The public methods of VendingMachine are synchronized, which makes each action (check state, change balance, move state) atomic. A physical machine has one keypad, so this is enough. For a networked fleet, each machine is still one object per JVM; the server-side stock count becomes a database row updated with UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0.

Edge cases

  • Money inserted, product sold out: stay in HasMoney so the user can pick another item or cancel.
  • Exact payment: change is 0.
  • Unknown code: IllegalArgumentException before touching stock.
  • Machine cannot make change: add a coin float to the machine and check it before selling (a real constraint; ask about it).
  • Power loss mid-transaction: persist balance, or refund on restart.

Where State differs from Strategy

Both swap an object behind an interface. In Strategy the client chooses the algorithm and it rarely changes during use. In State the object changes itself from one state to the next as events happen, so states know about each other.

Extensions interviewers ask

  • Out-of-service state: add OutOfServiceState where everything throws except cancel; the machine enters it when a sensor fails. No existing state changes.
  • Dispensing as its own state when the motor takes seconds: Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing, then Idle.
  • Coin and note handling: a CoinChanger class with denominations and a greedy change algorithm.
  • Several payment methods: a PaymentMethod Strategy (cash, UPI QR).
  • Sales report and low-stock alerts: an Observer on Inventory.

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 5 min: flow, error cases, cash or UPI, admin refill.
  2. 8 min: draw the state diagram on the board first, then the classes.
  3. 20 min: code the interface with default methods, two states, the machine.
  4. 7 min: run the demo, discuss State vs switch, add out-of-service.

Design an elevator system

Each elevator keeps its own direction and sorted sets of stops and serves them with a LOOK-style sweep (go one way serving stops, then reverse); a controller assigns each new request to the best elevator through a swappable selection Strategy.

Requirements and assumptions

Functional:

  • A building has N floors and M elevators.
  • Hall call: a person on a floor presses UP or DOWN; the system sends one elevator.
  • Cabin request: a person inside presses a destination floor.
  • Each elevator moves one floor at a time, stops at requested floors and idles when nothing is pending.

Non-functional: requests arrive from many threads at once; the selection rule must be replaceable; no starvation of far floors.

Assumptions: no weight limit, no door timing (doors open instantly), no emergency mode, time is simulated by calling step(), and a hall call is served as "go to that floor" (direction-aware pickup is an extension).

The scheduling idea

A naive elevator serves requests in arrival order (FCFS) and zig-zags. Disk schedulers solved the same problem with SCAN: keep going in one direction serving every request on the way, then reverse. LOOK is SCAN that reverses at the last pending request instead of the building's end. It is simple and avoids starvation.

Entities

  • Direction (enum UP, DOWN, IDLE).
  • Elevator: id, current floor, direction, two TreeSets of stops (up and down). Owns its movement.
  • ElevatorSelector (interface): picks the elevator for a hall call. A Strategy.
  • ElevatorController: receives requests, asks the selector, forwards. Facade.

Key design decisions

  • Two sorted sets per elevator: TreeSet gives ordered stops and O(log n) add and remove. Going up, the next stop is simply the next floor reached; going down likewise.
  • Strategy for dispatch (Module 2): nearest idle, nearest moving toward the caller, least loaded, zoned. Swap without touching the controller.
  • State per elevator: the direction enum is the minimum. If doors, maintenance and overload matter, turn it into the State pattern (same idea as the vending machine).
  • Simulated time: step() moves one floor. A real scheduler thread calls stepAll() every second. Tests call it directly, no sleeping.

Core code: the elevator

import java.util.TreeSet;

enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }

class Elevator {
    private final int id;
    private int floor = 0;
    private Direction direction = Direction.IDLE;
    private final TreeSet<Integer> upStops = new TreeSet<>();
    private final TreeSet<Integer> downStops = new TreeSet<>();

    Elevator(int id) { this.id = id; }

    synchronized int floor() { return floor; }
    synchronized Direction direction() { return direction; }
    int id() { return id; }

    synchronized void addStop(int target) {
        if (target == floor) { arrive(); return; }          // already here
        if (target > floor) upStops.add(target); else downStops.add(target);
        if (direction == Direction.IDLE) {
            direction = (target > floor) ? Direction.UP : Direction.DOWN;
        }
    }

    /** Move one floor in the current direction (one tick of time). */
    synchronized void step() {
        switch (direction) {
            case UP -> {
                floor++;
                if (upStops.remove(floor)) arrive();
                if (upStops.isEmpty()) {
                    direction = downStops.isEmpty() ? Direction.IDLE : Direction.DOWN;
                }
            }
            case DOWN -> {
                floor--;
                if (downStops.remove(floor)) arrive();
                if (downStops.isEmpty()) {
                    direction = upStops.isEmpty() ? Direction.IDLE : Direction.UP;
                }
            }
            case IDLE -> { }
        }
    }

    private void arrive() {
        System.out.println("Elevator " + id + " stops at " + floor);
    }
}

Core code: selector and controller

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

interface ElevatorSelector {
    Elevator select(List<Elevator> all, int floor);
}

class NearestSelector implements ElevatorSelector {
    private static final int AWAY_PENALTY = 100;

    public Elevator select(List<Elevator> all, int floor) {
        return all.stream()
                .min(Comparator.comparingInt((Elevator e) -> cost(e, floor)))
                .orElseThrow();
    }

    private int cost(Elevator e, int floor) {
        int distance = Math.abs(e.floor() - floor);
        Direction d = e.direction();
        boolean toward = (d == Direction.UP && floor >= e.floor())
                      || (d == Direction.DOWN && floor <= e.floor());
        return (d == Direction.IDLE || toward) ? distance : distance + AWAY_PENALTY;
    }
}

class ElevatorController {
    private final List<Elevator> elevators;
    private final ElevatorSelector selector;
    private final int floors;

    ElevatorController(List<Elevator> elevators, ElevatorSelector selector, int floors) {
        this.elevators = List.copyOf(elevators);
        this.selector = selector;
        this.floors = floors;
    }

    void requestElevator(int floor, Direction wanted) {
        checkFloor(floor);
        selector.select(elevators, floor).addStop(floor);   // hall call
    }

    void selectFloor(int elevatorId, int floor) {
        checkFloor(floor);
        elevators.get(elevatorId).addStop(floor);          // cabin request
    }

    void stepAll() { elevators.forEach(Elevator::step); }

    private void checkFloor(int floor) {
        if (floor < 0 || floor >= floors) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("No such floor: " + floor);
        }
    }
}

public class ElevatorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var ctl = new ElevatorController(
                List.of(new Elevator(0), new Elevator(1)), new NearestSelector(), 10);
        ctl.requestElevator(5, Direction.UP);     // elevator 0 is chosen (tie, first wins)
        ctl.selectFloor(0, 8);
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) ctl.stepAll();
    }
}
Elevator 0 stops at 5
Elevator 0 stops at 8

Concurrency

  • All mutable state of an elevator is touched only inside synchronized methods, so a cabin press and the scheduler tick cannot corrupt the sets.
  • The selector reads floor and direction from several elevators without a global lock. The picture may be slightly stale, which is acceptable for a heuristic: the worst case is a slightly worse choice, never a wrong state.
  • One scheduler thread (ScheduledExecutorService) drives stepAll(); request threads only add stops.

Edge case: never hold two elevator locks together

The controller never locks two elevators at once, so there is no deadlock. If a feature needs to move a stop from one elevator to another, lock in id order.

Edge cases

  • Request for the current floor: open the door, no movement.
  • Duplicate requests for the same floor: sets ignore duplicates.
  • Invalid floor: rejected by the controller.
  • Request behind the current direction: parked in the other set; served after the sweep, so a far floor waits at most one sweep (no starvation).
  • Hall call direction: a person going DOWN at floor 6 should only be picked by an elevator that will continue down. The simple version ignores the direction; the direction-aware version keeps hall calls separate from cabin stops.

Extensions interviewers ask

  • Multiple elevators: already modelled; discuss other selectors (zones, least busy).
  • Peak-hour logic (morning rush to floor 0): a selector that parks idle elevators on the ground floor.
  • Weight and capacity: a load field; skip hall calls if full.
  • Express and VIP elevators: a flag per elevator and a filtering selector.
  • Maintenance mode: a State that rejects new stops and finishes current ones.
  • Display panel: an Observer on elevator movement.

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 5 min: hall vs cabin requests, number of elevators, how time is simulated.
  2. 5 min: explain SCAN/LOOK in two sentences with the floor drawing.
  3. 8 min: diagram: controller, elevator, selector Strategy.
  4. 20 min: code Elevator.addStop/step, then selector and controller.
  5. 7 min: thread safety, direction-aware hall calls, maintenance State.

Design an LRU cache (HashMap + doubly linked list)

An LRU cache evicts the least recently used entry when full; combine a HashMap for O(1) lookup with a doubly linked list that keeps entries in recency order, so both get and put run in O(1).

Requirements and assumptions

  • get(key) returns the value or null, and marks the entry most recently used.
  • put(key, value) inserts or updates, marks it most recently used, and if the size exceeds capacity removes the least recently used entry.
  • Both operations O(1) average time.
  • Generic in key and value; capacity fixed at construction (must be positive).
  • Then: thread safety.

Why two structures

Structure aloneLookupMove to frontEvict oldest
HashMapO(1)no orderno order
Doubly linked listO(n)O(1) if you hold the nodeO(1) at the tail
Both togetherO(1)O(1)O(1)

The map gives you the node for a key in O(1). Because the list is doubly linked, you can unlink that node without scanning (you know its prev and next). The head side holds the most recently used; the tail side holds the eviction candidate.

Key design decisions

  • Sentinel head and tail nodes mean insert and remove never check for null neighbours.
  • The node stores its key so eviction can remove the entry from the map: you find the tail node, then need its key to call map.remove.
  • Private helper methods unlink(node) and addFirst(node); get and put compose them.
  • A generic class, and no pattern needed. An eviction policy Strategy (LRU, LFU, FIFO) is the extension that earns one (Module 2).

Core code

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class LRUCache<K, V> {
    private static final class Node<K, V> {
        final K key;
        V value;
        Node<K, V> prev, next;
        Node(K key, V value) {
            this.key = key;
            this.value = value;
        }
    }

    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, Node<K, V>> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node<K, V> head = new Node<>(null, null);   // most recent side
    private final Node<K, V> tail = new Node<>(null, null);   // least recent side

    public LRUCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be > 0");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail;
        tail.prev = head;
    }

    public synchronized V get(K key) {
        Node<K, V> n = map.get(key);
        if (n == null) return null;
        unlink(n);
        addFirst(n);                       // now most recently used
        return n.value;
    }

    public synchronized void put(K key, V value) {
        Node<K, V> n = map.get(key);
        if (n != null) {                   // update existing
            n.value = value;
            unlink(n);
            addFirst(n);
            return;
        }
        if (map.size() == capacity) {      // evict least recently used
            Node<K, V> lru = tail.prev;
            unlink(lru);
            map.remove(lru.key);
        }
        n = new Node<>(key, value);
        map.put(key, n);
        addFirst(n);
    }

    public synchronized int size() { return map.size(); }

    private void unlink(Node<K, V> n) {
        n.prev.next = n.next;
        n.next.prev = n.prev;
    }

    private void addFirst(Node<K, V> n) {
        n.next = head.next;
        n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n;
        head.next = n;
    }
}
public class LRUDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LRUCache<String, Integer> cache = new LRUCache<>(2);
        cache.put("a", 1);
        cache.put("b", 2);
        System.out.println(cache.get("a"));   // a becomes most recent
        cache.put("c", 3);                    // evicts b
        System.out.println(cache.get("b"));
        System.out.println(cache.get("c"));
    }
}
1
null
3

The LinkedHashMap shortcut

Java already has this structure. A LinkedHashMap built with accessOrder = true moves an entry to the end on every access, and removeEldestEntry lets you evict automatically.

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

class LruMap<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;

    LruMap(int capacity) {
        super(16, 0.75f, true);                  // true = access order
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
        return size() > capacity;                // called after each put
    }
}

Which should you write in the interview?

Say the shortcut first ("in production I would use LinkedHashMap with access order, or Caffeine"), then offer to build it by hand, which is what the question usually wants. Writing only the shortcut can look like dodging the data structure.

Thread safety

The simplest correct version is what the code above does: synchronized on every method. Note that even get must be synchronized, because it writes (it reorders the list). A ConcurrentHashMap alone does not help, since map and list must change together as one step.

  • One lock: simple, correct, becomes a bottleneck under heavy reads.
  • Read-write lock: does not help, because every read is a write.
  • Segmented (striped) caches: N independent LRU caches chosen by hash(key) % N; each has its own lock, so threads rarely collide. Eviction becomes approximate per segment.
  • Library route: Caffeine records accesses in buffers and applies reordering lazily, so reads barely block. In a Spring app you would use it through the cache abstraction rather than writing your own.

Edge cases

  • Capacity 1: every new key evicts the previous one. The code handles it because eviction happens before the insert.
  • Updating an existing key never evicts anything.
  • Null keys: HashMap allows them but the sentinel nodes also hold null keys; reject null keys explicitly if you want a clean contract.
  • get of a stored null value is indistinguishable from a miss; use Optional or disallow null values.

Extensions interviewers ask

  • TTL (expiry): store expiresAt in the node; check it in get and treat expired as a miss; optionally a cleaner thread.
  • LFU instead of LRU: map from frequency to a linked list of keys, plus a minFrequency counter, for O(1).
  • Pluggable eviction: an EvictionPolicy interface with onAccess and evict (Strategy).
  • Write-through or load on miss: a loader function passed to the constructor, used by get.
  • Distributed cache: consistent hashing across nodes (HLD topic, later modules).

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 3 min: clarify get/put semantics, capacity, generics, thread safety.
  2. 5 min: explain why a map alone or a list alone fails; draw map plus list.
  3. 20 min: write Node, unlink, addFirst, then get and put.
  4. 10 min: run the example, mention the LinkedHashMap version.
  5. 7 min: thread safety options and TTL or LFU follow-ups.

Design Splitwise (expenses, balances and settling debts)

Record each expense as "who paid, how much, split how among whom" using a SplitStrategy (equal, exact, percentage), keep a pairwise balance sheet, and simplify debts by computing each person's net balance and matching the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor.

Requirements and assumptions

Functional:

  • Users add expenses: one person pays; the amount is split among participants.
  • Split types: equal, exact (each person's amount given), percentage.
  • Show who owes whom: per user, and for the whole group.
  • Settle up: record a payment from one user to another.
  • Simplify debts: the fewest transfers that clear everything.

Assumptions: one currency, amounts in paise as long, one group (extension: many groups), the payer may or may not be in the split, rounding leftovers go to the first participants one paisa at a time so the parts always add up to the total.

Entities

  • Split: a user id and the amount that user owes for one expense.
  • SplitStrategy: interface that turns (total, participants, values) into a list of Splits; implementations for equal, exact and percentage. Strategy pattern.
  • Expense: payer, total, list of splits. Kept for history.
  • BalanceSheet (inside the service here): owes[debtor][creditor] in paise.
  • Transfer: from, to, amount, the output of simplification.

Key design decisions

  • Strategy per split type so a new type (by shares, by item) is a new class. A small EnumMap from SplitType to strategy plays the role of a factory (Module 2).
  • Validate in the strategy: exact amounts must sum to the total; percentages must sum to 100.
  • Net out opposite debts immediately: if B owes A 100 and A now owes B 30, store "B owes A 70". The sheet never has both directions for one pair.
  • Simplify on demand from the sheet, without mutating it. It produces a plan; actually settling is a separate call.
  • Money is long paise. Splitting Rs 10.00 three ways is 334, 333, 333 paise, not 333.33 each.

Core code: split strategies

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

enum SplitType { EQUAL, EXACT, PERCENT }

record Split(String userId, long amountPaise) { }

interface SplitStrategy {
    /** values is null for EQUAL; amounts for EXACT; percentages for PERCENT. */
    List<Split> split(long total, List<String> users, List<Long> values);
}

class EqualSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public List<Split> split(long total, List<String> users, List<Long> values) {
        int n = users.size();
        long base = total / n, extra = total % n;
        List<Split> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            out.add(new Split(users.get(i), base + (i < extra ? 1 : 0)));  // spread leftovers
        }
        return out;
    }
}

class ExactSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public List<Split> split(long total, List<String> users, List<Long> values) {
        long sum = values.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
        if (sum != total) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amounts must add up to total");
        List<Split> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++) out.add(new Split(users.get(i), values.get(i)));
        return out;
    }
}

class PercentSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public List<Split> split(long total, List<String> users, List<Long> values) {
        long pct = values.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
        if (pct != 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Percentages must add up to 100");
        List<Split> out = new ArrayList<>();
        long assigned = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++) {
            long amount = total * values.get(i) / 100;
            out.add(new Split(users.get(i), amount));
            assigned += amount;
        }
        long left = total - assigned;                       // rounding leftover
        out.set(0, new Split(out.get(0).userId(), out.get(0).amountPaise() + left));
        return out;
    }
}

Core code: the service and debt simplification

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

record Transfer(String from, String to, long amountPaise) { }

class SplitwiseService {
    private final Map<SplitType, SplitStrategy> strategies = new EnumMap<>(SplitType.class);
    // owes.get(debtor).get(creditor) = amount in paise
    private final Map<String, Map<String, Long>> owes = new HashMap<>();

    SplitwiseService() {
        strategies.put(SplitType.EQUAL, new EqualSplit());
        strategies.put(SplitType.EXACT, new ExactSplit());
        strategies.put(SplitType.PERCENT, new PercentSplit());
    }

    synchronized void addExpense(String payer, long total, SplitType type,
                                 List<String> users, List<Long> values) {
        if (total <= 0 || users.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Bad expense");
        for (Split s : strategies.get(type).split(total, users, values)) {
            if (!s.userId().equals(payer) && s.amountPaise() > 0) {
                addDebt(s.userId(), payer, s.amountPaise());
            }
        }
    }

    synchronized void settle(String from, String to, long amount) {
        addDebt(to, from, amount);              // paying reduces what 'from' owes 'to'
    }

    private void addDebt(String debtor, String creditor, long amount) {
        Map<String, Long> reverse = owes.computeIfAbsent(creditor, k -> new HashMap<>());
        long back = reverse.getOrDefault(debtor, 0L);       // does creditor owe debtor?
        if (back >= amount) {
            if (back == amount) reverse.remove(debtor); else reverse.put(debtor, back - amount);
        } else {
            reverse.remove(debtor);
            owes.computeIfAbsent(debtor, k -> new HashMap<>()).merge(creditor, amount - back, Long::sum);
        }
    }

    synchronized long owed(String debtor, String creditor) {
        return owes.getOrDefault(debtor, Map.of()).getOrDefault(creditor, 0L);
    }

    private record Bal(String user, long amount) { }

    /** Greedy min cash flow: biggest debtor pays biggest creditor. */
    synchronized List<Transfer> simplify() {
        Map<String, Long> net = new HashMap<>();            // + means is owed, - means owes
        owes.forEach((d, m) -> m.forEach((c, amt) -> {
            net.merge(d, -amt, Long::sum);
            net.merge(c, amt, Long::sum);
        }));
        PriorityQueue<Bal> creditors = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.amount(), a.amount()));
        PriorityQueue<Bal> debtors = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.amount(), a.amount()));
        net.forEach((u, v) -> {
            if (v > 0) creditors.add(new Bal(u, v));
            else if (v < 0) debtors.add(new Bal(u, -v));    // store debt as positive
        });
        List<Transfer> plan = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!creditors.isEmpty() && !debtors.isEmpty()) {
            Bal c = creditors.poll(), d = debtors.poll();
            long pay = Math.min(c.amount(), d.amount());
            plan.add(new Transfer(d.user(), c.user(), pay));
            if (c.amount() > pay) creditors.add(new Bal(c.user(), c.amount() - pay));
            if (d.amount() > pay) debtors.add(new Bal(d.user(), d.amount() - pay));
        }
        return plan;
    }
}
import java.util.List;

public class SplitwiseDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var sw = new SplitwiseService();
        sw.addExpense("A", 300_000, SplitType.EQUAL, List.of("A", "B", "C"), null);
        sw.addExpense("B", 60_000, SplitType.EQUAL, List.of("B", "C"), null);
        System.out.println("B owes A: " + sw.owed("B", "A"));
        sw.simplify().forEach(t ->
            System.out.println(t.from() + " pays " + t.to() + " " + t.amountPaise()));
    }
}
B owes A: 100000
C pays A 120000
B pays A 80000

Why the greedy simplification works

Only each person's net balance matters: what they are owed minus what they owe. Net balances always sum to zero. Repeatedly settling the largest debtor against the largest creditor clears at least one person per transfer, so with N people with non-zero balance you need at most N-1 transfers. Finding the true minimum is NP-hard (it is a subset-sum style problem); the greedy result is the standard interview answer and is optimal in most practical cases. Say that sentence aloud; interviewers like it.

Concurrency

Group members add expenses at the same time. The service methods are synchronized, so each expense (several balance updates) applies atomically and simplify sees a consistent sheet. For many independent groups, keep one service (or lock) per group so groups never block each other. In a database, an expense and its balance changes go in one transaction; balances are derived or updated with UPDATE ... SET amount = amount + ?.

Edge cases

  • Payer not in the split: they paid for others; every split row creates a debt to the payer.
  • Payer is the only participant: no debt created.
  • Exact amounts do not add up, or percentages are not 100: reject before changing anything (validation happens before the loop).
  • Rounding: leftover paise are assigned deterministically, so totals always match.
  • Settling more than owed: here it flips the direction (the other person now owes); a stricter version rejects it.
  • Unknown user ids: validate against a user registry.

Extensions interviewers ask

  • Groups and friends: a Group entity with its own balance sheet.
  • Split by shares or by item: new strategies; no change to the service.
  • Multiple currencies: a Money type and an exchange-rate service.
  • Edit or delete an expense: keep expenses as an event log; reverse the old effect, apply the new one.
  • Notifications: Observer on expense added.
  • Activity feed and history: read from the history list.

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 5 min: split types, groups, simplification, currency, rounding.
  2. 7 min: diagram with SplitStrategy; explain pairwise sheet and netting.
  3. 20 min: code the three strategies, addExpense, addDebt.
  4. 8 min: explain and code the greedy simplify; walk the example numbers.
  5. 5 min: concurrency and the group extension.

Design BookMyShow (seat booking without double booking)

Model movies, shows and per-show seats; let a user hold seats for a few minutes under a per-show lock (all or nothing), pay, then confirm, so two people can never get the same seat and abandoned checkouts free their seats automatically.

Requirements and assumptions

Functional:

  • Cities have theatres; theatres have screens; screens have seats. A show is a movie on a screen at a time.
  • Users browse shows and see seat availability for a show.
  • A user selects seats (up to 6), pays, and receives a booking.
  • Seat prices vary by seat category (for example regular and premium).
  • Unpaid selections expire after 5 minutes.

Non-functional: no seat is ever sold twice, even with thousands of users on one popular show; booking is all-or-nothing for multiple seats.

Assumptions: payment is an external call that may succeed or fail, no cancellations or refunds in the core code, in-memory model first; the database version is discussed afterwards.

Entities

A very common mistake is to put "booked" on the physical Seat. A physical seat exists once; its availability is different for each show. So the booking state lives on ShowSeat, one object per seat per show.

ClassResponsibility
Movie, Theatre, Screen, SeatMostly static data: titles, locations, layout
ShowMovie, screen, start time; owns its ShowSeats and the lock
ShowSeatSeat id, price, status AVAILABLE, HELD or BOOKED, hold owner and expiry
HoldTemporary claim on seats: id, user, seat ids, expiry, total
BookingConfirmed purchase
BookingServiceOrchestrates hold, payment, confirm, release
PaymentGatewayInterface; the external payment service

Key design decisions

  • Per-show lock, not per-seat: a booking touches several seats, and one lock per show makes all-or-nothing trivial and deadlock-free. Different shows never block each other. (The reasoning and alternatives are in Concurrency in LLD.)
  • Hold, pay, confirm: the lock is held for microseconds (to mark seats HELD), never during payment. Payment takes seconds and must not block other users.
  • Lazy expiry: a HELD seat whose time passed counts as available. No timer threads are needed for correctness; a cleaner job only tidies memory.
  • Confirm re-checks the hold owner and the expiry before marking BOOKED.
  • Patterns: a thin Facade (BookingService), a Strategy for seat pricing if rules grow, an Observer to notify users (Module 2).

Core code: seats, holds and the show

import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.UUID;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

enum SeatStatus { AVAILABLE, HELD, BOOKED }

class SeatUnavailableException extends RuntimeException {
    SeatUnavailableException(String seatId) { super("Seat " + seatId + " unavailable"); }
}

record Hold(String id, String userId, List<String> seatIds, Instant expiresAt, long total) { }

record Booking(String id, String userId, String showId, List<String> seatIds, long total) { }

class ShowSeat {
    final String seatId;
    final long price;
    SeatStatus status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE;
    String heldBy;                          // hold id
    Instant holdUntil;

    ShowSeat(String seatId, long price) {
        this.seatId = seatId;
        this.price = price;
    }

    boolean isAvailable(Instant now) {
        return status == SeatStatus.AVAILABLE
            || (status == SeatStatus.HELD && !now.isBefore(holdUntil));   // expired hold
    }
}

class Show {
    static final int MAX_SEATS = 6;
    private final String id;
    private final Map<String, ShowSeat> seats = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Hold> holds = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    Show(String id, List<ShowSeat> layout) {
        this.id = id;
        layout.forEach(s -> seats.put(s.seatId, s));
    }

    String id() { return id; }

    Hold hold(String userId, List<String> seatIds, Instant now, Duration ttl) {
        List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(seatIds));   // drop duplicates
        if (ids.isEmpty() || ids.size() > MAX_SEATS) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Choose 1 to " + MAX_SEATS + " seats");
        }
        lock.lock();
        try {
            long total = 0;
            for (String sid : ids) {                              // check ALL first
                ShowSeat s = seats.get(sid);
                if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("No seat " + sid);
                if (!s.isAvailable(now)) throw new SeatUnavailableException(sid);
                total += s.price;
            }
            Hold h = new Hold(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), userId, ids, now.plus(ttl), total);
            for (String sid : ids) {                              // then mark ALL
                ShowSeat s = seats.get(sid);
                s.status = SeatStatus.HELD;
                s.heldBy = h.id();
                s.holdUntil = h.expiresAt();
            }
            holds.put(h.id(), h);
            return h;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

Core code: confirm, release and the service

These two methods belong in the same Show class; they are shown separately to keep the blocks short.

// inside class Show

Booking confirm(String holdId, String userId, Instant now) {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        Hold h = holds.get(holdId);
        if (h == null || !h.userId().equals(userId)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("No such hold");
        }
        if (!now.isBefore(h.expiresAt())) {
            releaseLocked(h);
            throw new IllegalStateException("Hold expired, please select seats again");
        }
        for (String sid : h.seatIds()) {
            ShowSeat s = seats.get(sid);
            if (!holdId.equals(s.heldBy)) throw new SeatUnavailableException(sid);
        }
        for (String sid : h.seatIds()) seats.get(sid).status = SeatStatus.BOOKED;
        holds.remove(holdId);
        return new Booking(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), userId, id, h.seatIds(), h.total());
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

void release(String holdId) {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        Hold h = holds.get(holdId);
        if (h != null) releaseLocked(h);
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

private void releaseLocked(Hold h) {
    for (String sid : h.seatIds()) {
        ShowSeat s = seats.get(sid);
        if (h.id().equals(s.heldBy) && s.status == SeatStatus.HELD) {   // only our own hold
            s.status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE;
            s.heldBy = null;
            s.holdUntil = null;
        }
    }
    holds.remove(h.id());
}
import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

interface PaymentGateway {
    boolean charge(String userId, long amountPaise);
}

class BookingService {
    private static final Duration HOLD_TTL = Duration.ofMinutes(5);
    private final Map<String, Show> shows;
    private final PaymentGateway payment;
    private final Clock clock;

    BookingService(Map<String, Show> shows, PaymentGateway payment, Clock clock) {
        this.shows = shows;
        this.payment = payment;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    Booking checkout(String showId, String userId, List<String> seatIds) {
        Show show = shows.get(showId);
        if (show == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("No show " + showId);

        Hold hold = show.hold(userId, seatIds, Instant.now(clock), HOLD_TTL);  // fast, locked
        try {
            if (!payment.charge(userId, hold.total())) {                       // slow, unlocked
                throw new IllegalStateException("Payment failed");
            }
            return show.confirm(hold.id(), userId, Instant.now(clock));
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            show.release(hold.id());                                           // free the seats
            throw e;
        }
    }
}
import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class BookMyShowDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Show show = new Show("S1", List.of(new ShowSeat("A1", 25_000), new ShowSeat("A2", 25_000)));
        Instant now = Instant.now();

        Hold h = show.hold("u1", List.of("A1", "A2"), now, Duration.ofMinutes(5));
        try {
            show.hold("u2", List.of("A2"), now, Duration.ofMinutes(5));
        } catch (SeatUnavailableException e) {
            System.out.println("u2: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        Booking b = show.confirm(h.id(), "u1", now.plusSeconds(60));
        System.out.println("Booked " + b.seatIds() + " total " + b.total());

        var service = new BookingService(Map.of("S1", show), (u, amt) -> true, Clock.systemUTC());
        try {
            service.checkout("S1", "u3", List.of("A1"));
        } catch (SeatUnavailableException e) {
            System.out.println("u3: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
u2: Seat A2 unavailable
Booked [A1, A2] total 50000
u3: Seat A1 unavailable

Concurrency: from this code to production

The in-memory ReentrantLock works for one JVM. With several app servers, move the truth into the database (see Concurrency in LLD and SQL · Module 5):

-- hold N seats atomically: succeeds only if ALL rows were updated
UPDATE show_seat
   SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :holdId, hold_expires_at = now() + interval '5 minutes'
 WHERE show_id = :show AND seat_id IN (:seats)
   AND (status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now()));
-- if rows updated <> number of seats: ROLLBACK (someone else got one)

-- final guard on the bookings table
ALTER TABLE booking_seat ADD CONSTRAINT uq_show_seat UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id);

Keep that transaction to the one statement above. Never keep it open while the user pays.

Edge cases

  • Payment succeeds but the hold expired meanwhile: confirm fails; you must refund. Use a longer hold than the payment timeout, and make the refund path explicit.
  • Payment fails or the user closes the tab: release (explicit, or lazily by expiry).
  • Same user clicks twice: duplicate seat ids are removed; the second hold on the same seats fails unless you allow re-hold by the same user.
  • Two users want overlapping seat sets: one wins entirely, the other gets none (no partial holds).
  • Show already started or cancelled: check startTime in hold.
  • Idempotent payment callbacks: confirm by hold id so a repeated callback does not create two bookings (the hold is removed on first confirm).

Extensions interviewers ask

  • Cancellation and refund: a CANCELLED booking state; seats go back to AVAILABLE; refund through the gateway.
  • Dynamic pricing: a PricingStrategy deciding each ShowSeat price by demand or time.
  • Seat recommendations ("seats together"): scan a row for a contiguous free block.
  • Search shows by city and movie: indexes by city and movie id.
  • Waiting list: Observer: notify when a held seat is released.
  • Coupons and offers: decorator over the price (Module 2).

How to present this in 60 minutes

  1. 6 min: requirements; ask about holds, payment, cancellation, scale.
  2. 8 min: entities; point out Seat vs ShowSeat; diagram.
  3. 8 min: draw the double-booking timeline and name the fix (lock the check and the mark together).
  4. 25 min: code Show.hold, confirm, release, checkout.
  5. 13 min: expiry, payment failure, database version with conditional update and unique constraint.

Design a rate limiter (token bucket)

A rate limiter decides per client whether a request is allowed; the token bucket gives each client a bucket that refills at a steady rate and spends one token per request, which allows short bursts while enforcing a long-run average, and it needs a lock per bucket to be thread safe.

Requirements and assumptions

  • allow(key) returns true if the client (user id, API key or IP) may proceed, false if it must be rejected (an API would answer HTTP 429 Too Many Requests).
  • Limit example: 100 requests per minute per user, with bursts up to 20.
  • Constant-time check; thousands of threads; many keys.
  • Algorithms must be swappable: token bucket, fixed window, sliding window.
  • Assumptions: single JVM first (distributed version at the end), limits are the same for all keys (per-key rules are an extension), time comes from an injectable clock.

The algorithms compared

AlgorithmIdeaProsCons
Token bucketTokens refill steadily up to capacity; each request takes oneAllows bursts; O(1); tiny stateBurst can be large if capacity is big
Leaky bucketRequests queue and leave at a fixed rateVery smooth outputBursts are delayed or dropped
Fixed window counterCount per minute; reset at minute boundarySimplestBoundary spike: up to 2x limit around a reset
Sliding window logKeep timestamps of recent requestsExactMemory grows with the limit
Sliding window counterWeighted blend of the current and previous window countsCheap and smoothApproximate

How the token bucket works

The bucket holds up to capacity tokens and refills at refillPerSecond. You do not need a timer thread. On each call compute how many tokens have accrued since the last call: elapsed × rate, add them, cap at capacity, then try to take one. This is lazy refill.

Key design decisions

  • Interface RateLimiter (Strategy, Module 2): callers (a servlet filter or Spring interceptor) never know which algorithm runs.
  • One TokenBucket per key held in a ConcurrentHashMap with computeIfAbsent, which creates the bucket atomically.
  • Lock per bucket, not a global lock: different users never wait for each other.
  • Monotonic clock: use System.nanoTime() (via a supplier) for elapsed time. Wall-clock time can jump backwards.
  • Doubles for tokens allow fractional refill (0.5 token after half a second at 1 per second).

Core code

import java.util.function.LongSupplier;

interface RateLimiter {
    boolean allow(String key);
}

class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerNano;
    private final LongSupplier nanoClock;
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefill;

    TokenBucket(long capacity, double refillPerSecond, LongSupplier nanoClock) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerNano = refillPerSecond / 1_000_000_000.0;
        this.nanoClock = nanoClock;
        this.tokens = capacity;                         // start full
        this.lastRefill = nanoClock.getAsLong();
    }

    synchronized boolean tryConsume() {
        refill();
        if (tokens >= 1) {
            tokens -= 1;
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    private void refill() {
        long now = nanoClock.getAsLong();
        double added = (now - lastRefill) * refillPerNano;
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + added);    // never exceed capacity
        lastRefill = now;
    }
}
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.LongSupplier;

class TokenBucketLimiter implements RateLimiter {
    private final Map<String, TokenBucket> buckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerSecond;
    private final LongSupplier clock;

    TokenBucketLimiter(long capacity, double refillPerSecond, LongSupplier clock) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerSecond = refillPerSecond;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public boolean allow(String key) {
        return buckets
                .computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new TokenBucket(capacity, refillPerSecond, clock))
                .tryConsume();
    }
}

/** Alternative: exact sliding window using a log of timestamps. */
class SlidingWindowLogLimiter implements RateLimiter {
    private final Map<String, Deque<Long>> logs = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final int limit;
    private final long windowNanos;
    private final LongSupplier clock;

    SlidingWindowLogLimiter(int limit, long windowMillis, LongSupplier clock) {
        this.limit = limit;
        this.windowNanos = windowMillis * 1_000_000L;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public boolean allow(String key) {
        Deque<Long> log = logs.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayDeque<>());
        synchronized (log) {
            long now = clock.getAsLong();
            while (!log.isEmpty() && now - log.peekFirst() >= windowNanos) {
                log.pollFirst();                         // drop requests outside the window
            }
            if (log.size() >= limit) return false;
            log.addLast(now);
            return true;
        }
    }
}
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

public class RateLimiterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AtomicLong now = new AtomicLong();               // fake clock in nanoseconds
        RateLimiter limiter = new TokenBucketLimiter(3, 1.0, now::get);

        List<Boolean> first = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) first.add(limiter.allow("user-1"));
        System.out.println(first);

        now.addAndGet(2_000_000_000L);                   // two seconds pass
        List<Boolean> second = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) second.add(limiter.allow("user-1"));
        System.out.println(second);
        System.out.println(limiter.allow("user-2"));      // other users have their own bucket
    }
}
[true, true, true, false]
[true, true, false]
true

Concurrency

  • Refill and consume must be one step: tryConsume is synchronized, so two threads cannot both spend the last token.
  • computeIfAbsent on ConcurrentHashMap creates exactly one bucket per key even under races.
  • Lock-free option: keep (tokens, lastRefill) in an immutable object inside an AtomicReference and loop with compareAndSet. Good to mention, rarely required.

Fixed window boundary problem

With a limit of 100 per minute, a client can send 100 requests at 10:00:59 and 100 more at 10:01:00: 200 requests in two seconds, all allowed. Sliding windows and token buckets avoid this.

Edge cases

  • Long idle period: tokens are capped at capacity, so an idle client does not bank unlimited credit.
  • Clock going backwards: nanoTime does not; with wall-clock time guard against negative elapsed values.
  • Memory: millions of keys create millions of buckets. Evict idle ones (a bucket full for a while can be dropped and recreated full) with a scheduled cleanup or a bounded cache (like the LRU cache).
  • Cost-based requests: tryConsume(n) for expensive calls.
  • What to return: the HTTP layer sends 429 and a Retry-After header; the limiter can expose "seconds until next token".

Distributed rate limiting

Several app servers need one shared count, usually in Redis. A check-then-update must be atomic, so people use a Lua script (Redis runs a script without interleaving other commands) or simple INCR plus EXPIRE for a fixed window. Trade-offs: an extra network hop per request, the limiter itself can become a bottleneck or point of failure (decide: fail open or fail closed), and strict global accuracy costs latency. Many teams accept small errors by letting each node keep a local bucket and sync periodically, or put the limit in an API gateway. This leads into the HLD module.

Extensions interviewers ask

  • Different limits per user tier or per endpoint: a rule lookup (key, route) -> config; build the bucket from the rule.
  • Multiple limits together (10 per second and 1000 per hour): a composite limiter that must satisfy all.
  • Metrics: count rejected requests per key.
  • Queue instead of reject: leaky bucket with a bounded queue.
  • Dynamic config reload: volatile reference to the rule table.

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 5 min: key, limit, burst, single node or distributed, reject or queue.
  2. 5 min: compare the five algorithms in one table; pick token bucket and say why.
  3. 20 min: code TokenBucket with lazy refill, the limiter map, the demo with a fake clock.
  4. 10 min: thread safety, memory cleanup of idle keys.
  5. 5 min: distributed version with Redis and Lua, fail-open or fail-closed.

Design a food delivery order flow (Observer for status updates)

An order moves through a fixed set of statuses (placed, accepted, preparing, ready, picked up, delivered or cancelled); validate each transition with a table, and notify the customer, restaurant, delivery dispatcher and analytics through the Observer pattern so the order class does not know who is listening.

Requirements and assumptions

  • A customer places an order from one restaurant with items and quantities.
  • Status flow: PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, READY, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED. Cancellation is allowed before PICKED_UP.
  • Different parties react to each change: the customer gets a notification, the restaurant sees new orders, a delivery partner is assigned when food is READY, analytics records everything.
  • Invalid transitions (DELIVERED to PREPARING) are rejected.
  • Assumptions: money in paise; payment, maps and routing are out of scope; notifications are printed to the console; observers run synchronously in the core code (asynchronous delivery is discussed below).

The state diagram

Entities

Key design decisions

  • Observer (Module 2): when the status changes, the order loops over its observers. Adding SMS, email, a loyalty-points service or analytics means a new observer class and one subscribe call; Order never changes (open/closed, Module 1).
  • Transition table inside the enum instead of if chains: the legal moves are data, easy to read and test. If each status also had different behaviour, you would use the State pattern as in the vending machine. Here statuses carry no behaviour, only rules, so an enum plus table is lighter.
  • Notify outside the lock and isolate observers: one failing observer must not stop the others or roll back the order.
  • Snapshot of observers (CopyOnWriteArrayList) so subscribing during a notification does not throw ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Delivery partner assignment is a Strategy (nearest, least busy) used inside DeliveryDispatcher.

Core code: status rules and the order

import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;

enum OrderStatus {
    PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, READY, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, CANCELLED;

    private static final Map<OrderStatus, Set<OrderStatus>> NEXT = new EnumMap<>(OrderStatus.class);
    static {
        NEXT.put(PLACED, EnumSet.of(ACCEPTED, CANCELLED));
        NEXT.put(ACCEPTED, EnumSet.of(PREPARING, CANCELLED));
        NEXT.put(PREPARING, EnumSet.of(READY, CANCELLED));
        NEXT.put(READY, EnumSet.of(PICKED_UP, CANCELLED));
        NEXT.put(PICKED_UP, EnumSet.of(DELIVERED));
        NEXT.put(DELIVERED, EnumSet.noneOf(OrderStatus.class));
        NEXT.put(CANCELLED, EnumSet.noneOf(OrderStatus.class));
    }

    boolean canMoveTo(OrderStatus target) { return NEXT.get(this).contains(target); }
}

record OrderItem(String name, int quantity, long pricePaise) { }

interface OrderObserver {
    void onStatusChanged(Order order, OrderStatus from, OrderStatus to);
}

class Order {
    private final String id, customerId, restaurantId;
    private final List<OrderItem> items;
    private OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.PLACED;
    private final List<OrderObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    Order(String id, String customerId, String restaurantId, List<OrderItem> items) {
        if (items.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Order has no items");
        this.id = id;
        this.customerId = customerId;
        this.restaurantId = restaurantId;
        this.items = List.copyOf(items);
    }

    String id() { return id; }
    String customerId() { return customerId; }
    String restaurantId() { return restaurantId; }
    synchronized OrderStatus status() { return status; }

    long total() {
        return items.stream().mapToLong(i -> i.pricePaise() * i.quantity()).sum();
    }

    void subscribe(OrderObserver o) { observers.add(o); }

    void moveTo(OrderStatus next) {
        OrderStatus old;
        synchronized (this) {                                  // validate and change atomically
            if (!status.canMoveTo(next)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Illegal move " + status + " -> " + next);
            }
            old = status;
            status = next;
        }
        for (OrderObserver o : observers) {                    // notify outside the lock
            try {
                o.onStatusChanged(this, old, next);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                System.err.println("Observer failed: " + e.getMessage());   // isolate failures
            }
        }
    }
}

Core code: observers and a demo

class CustomerNotifier implements OrderObserver {
    public void onStatusChanged(Order o, OrderStatus from, OrderStatus to) {
        System.out.println("Customer " + o.customerId() + ": order " + o.id() + " is " + to);
    }
}

class RestaurantNotifier implements OrderObserver {
    public void onStatusChanged(Order o, OrderStatus from, OrderStatus to) {
        if (to == OrderStatus.PLACED || to == OrderStatus.CANCELLED) {
            System.out.println("Restaurant " + o.restaurantId() + ": order " + o.id() + " " + to);
        }
    }
}

class DeliveryDispatcher implements OrderObserver {
    public void onStatusChanged(Order o, OrderStatus from, OrderStatus to) {
        if (to == OrderStatus.READY) {
            System.out.println("Dispatcher: finding a delivery partner for " + o.id());
        }
    }
}
import java.util.List;

public class FoodDeliveryDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Order order = new Order("O1", "C1", "R1",
                List.of(new OrderItem("Biryani", 2, 25_000), new OrderItem("Raita", 1, 4_000)));
        order.subscribe(new CustomerNotifier());
        order.subscribe(new DeliveryDispatcher());

        order.moveTo(OrderStatus.ACCEPTED);
        order.moveTo(OrderStatus.PREPARING);
        order.moveTo(OrderStatus.READY);
        order.moveTo(OrderStatus.PICKED_UP);
        order.moveTo(OrderStatus.DELIVERED);
        System.out.println("Total: " + order.total());
        try {
            order.moveTo(OrderStatus.PREPARING);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Customer C1: order O1 is ACCEPTED
Customer C1: order O1 is PREPARING
Customer C1: order O1 is READY
Dispatcher: finding a delivery partner for O1
Customer C1: order O1 is PICKED_UP
Customer C1: order O1 is DELIVERED
Total: 54000
Error: Illegal move DELIVERED -> PREPARING

Concurrency

  • The restaurant presses "accepted" while the customer presses "cancel" at the same instant. Both call moveTo. The synchronized block validates and changes the status as one step, so one wins and the other gets IllegalStateException (or a valid transition from the new state). Nobody sees a half-updated order.
  • With a database: UPDATE orders SET status = 'ACCEPTED' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'PLACED' and check that one row changed. That is the same compare-and-set idea (Concurrency in LLD).
  • Notifying outside the lock means two quick updates might notify out of order. If order matters to observers, include a sequence number or deliver through a single-threaded queue per order.

Edge cases

  • Illegal transition or a repeated one: rejected with a clear message.
  • Cancel after pickup: not allowed by the table; real systems add a "refund request" flow instead.
  • An observer throws (SMS provider down): logged, others still run; consider retries.
  • Restaurant never accepts: a timeout job moves PLACED to CANCELLED after N minutes.
  • Observers that are slow: do not call a slow network API inside the loop; hand the event to a queue.
  • Memory: unsubscribe observers of finished orders, or let the order go out of scope.

Extensions interviewers ask

  • Asynchronous notifications: publish an event to an executor or a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ). Observers become consumers. This is the same Observer idea scaled across services (Spring Boot · Module 7).
  • Delivery partner assignment: a Strategy (nearest, least loaded, rating), plus a partner state (available, busy).
  • Order undo or edit: allow item edits only in PLACED.
  • Payment: add PAYMENT_PENDING before PLACED, and a refund observer on CANCELLED.
  • Different order types (pickup, dine-in): different transition tables chosen by a factory.
  • Live tracking: a location stream from the partner app, separate from status.

How to present this in 45 minutes

  1. 5 min: statuses, who needs to know what, cancellation rules.
  2. 7 min: draw the state diagram, then Order plus observers.
  3. 20 min: code the enum with the transition table, Order.moveTo, two observers.
  4. 8 min: run the demo; discuss the race of accept vs cancel and failing observers.
  5. 5 min: async events and partner assignment Strategy.

Interview questions — LLD interview problems

How do you start an LLD interview question?

I do not start with code. First I ask clarifying questions about users, main use cases, variations, limits and whether thread safety or persistence is needed. I write the agreed scope and my assumptions down. Next I list entities and the public methods, draw a class diagram, and only then write code, model first and main flow second. I keep talking so the interviewer can follow my reasoning.

How do you find the classes in a problem?

I underline nouns in the requirements, keep those that have their own data and behaviour or identity, and turn plain attributes into fields. Fixed sets of values become enums. Verbs become methods on the class that owns the data needed. I look for things that vary (pricing, split rules, selection rules) and put them behind an interface. I also ask what changes together and what changes separately, which shows where one class should become two (for example Book and BookCopy, Seat and ShowSeat).

When do you use a design pattern in an LLD answer, and when not?

Only when I can name the variation or the problem it solves: Strategy for pricing or split rules, State for a machine whose behaviour depends on its mode, Observer when many parties react to one change, Factory when object creation depends on a type. Using a pattern with nothing varying (Singleton for everything, a Factory for one class) is a negative sign. I say "no pattern needed here" when that is true, as in tic-tac-toe.

Explain the double-booking problem and how you prevent it.

It is a check-then-act race: two requests both see a seat as free and both book it. The fix is to make the check and the write one atomic step. In memory I use a lock around the critical section (one lock per show so multi-seat booking is all-or-nothing). In a real system with several servers the database decides: a unique constraint on (show, seat), a conditional update such as WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE', SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for high contention, or an optimistic version column. For checkout I add a HELD state with expiry.

Why not keep a database transaction open while the user pays?

Payment takes seconds or minutes. An open transaction holds locks and a connection, so other users queue up and the pool runs dry. Instead I use a short transaction to mark the seats HELD with an expiry time, release the lock, take the payment, then another short transaction to confirm. If the user leaves, the hold expires.

Why is a per-show lock a good choice for BookMyShow?

A booking changes several seats at once, and it must succeed for all or none. One lock per show makes that trivial and avoids deadlocks that per-seat locks cause when two users lock seats in opposite order. Different shows use different locks, so they do not slow each other. The lock is held only while flipping seat states, never during payment. If one show becomes extremely hot, I would go to per-seat locks in sorted order or to database-level conditional updates.

Implement an LRU cache with O(1) operations. Which structures and why?

A HashMap from key to node gives O(1) lookup. A doubly linked list ordered by recency gives O(1) move-to-front and O(1) removal of the tail, because a node knows its neighbours. get moves the node to the front; put inserts at the front and, if over capacity, removes the tail node and its map entry (the node stores its key for that). Sentinel head and tail nodes avoid null checks. In Java, LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true and removeEldestEntry does the same.

Is a ConcurrentHashMap enough to make an LRU cache thread safe?

No. Each map operation is safe, but the cache must update the map and the recency list together, and even get writes (it reorders). Those compound steps need one lock, so the simple answer is synchronized methods. For more throughput: segment the cache into several independent LRUs by key hash, or use a library such as Caffeine that buffers recency updates.

Compare the token bucket and the fixed window rate limiter.

A fixed window counts requests per time slot and resets at the boundary. It is simple but allows up to double the limit across a boundary (100 at 10:00:59 and 100 at 10:01:00). A token bucket refills continuously, allows a bounded burst equal to capacity, and enforces the average rate over time, with O(1) time and memory per key. Refill is computed lazily from timestamps, no timer thread. Both need atomic updates per key.

How do you make a rate limiter work across many servers?

Keep the counters or buckets in a shared store such as Redis and make each check atomic, for example with a Lua script, because separate GET and SET calls would race. Costs: an extra network call per request and a new failure point, so decide whether the limiter fails open or closed. Alternatives are enforcing at the API gateway or using local buckets with periodic sync when small inaccuracy is acceptable.

How does the State pattern help the vending machine, compared with a switch statement?

With a switch, every method (insert, select, cancel) contains a branch per state, so adding OutOfService means editing all of them and it is easy to miss one. With State, each state class implements what each action means in that state, and the machine delegates. A new state is a new class. Invalid actions fall back to default methods that throw. The cost is more classes, which is worth it when states and actions both multiply.

How do you schedule an elevator? Explain the idea behind your algorithm.

Each elevator keeps its direction and two sorted sets of stops, one above and one below. It moves toward the next stop in its direction, serves everything on the way, and reverses when no stops remain in that direction (LOOK, a variant of SCAN from disk scheduling). This avoids zig-zagging and starvation. A dispatcher Strategy assigns a hall call to the best elevator, for example the idle one or the one moving toward the caller that is nearest. Each elevator's state changes under its own lock.

How does Splitwise simplify debts?

Compute each person's net balance (owed to them minus what they owe); the sum is zero. Put creditors and debtors into two priority queues. Repeatedly take the largest debtor and the largest creditor, transfer the smaller of the two amounts, and push back whatever remains. Each transfer clears at least one person, so there are at most N-1 transfers. The true minimum number of transfers is NP-hard in general, so the greedy method is the practical answer.

Why store money as a long of paise and not a double?

Binary floating point cannot represent values like 0.1 exactly, so sums drift and equality checks fail. A long of the smallest unit (paise) is exact and fast. When dividing, decide where the leftover paise go (for example the first participants get one extra), so the parts always add up to the total. BigDecimal is the alternative when you need fractional units or currencies with different scales.

The interviewer says "make it thread safe" at the end. What do you do?

I name the shared mutable state and the compound operations on it (check-then-act, read-modify-write). For each I choose the smallest tool: an atomic or putIfAbsent for a single value, a lock per object (per show, per bucket, per account) for multi-step updates, never a global lock if objects are independent. I keep slow work (payment, network) outside the lock, lock in a fixed order if two locks are needed, and mention the database constraint as the real guard for multiple servers.
