Cheat sheet — LLD interview problems

  • Method requirements, entities, class diagram, core code, edge cases, extensions.
  • Time plan 5-8 clarify, 5 API, 8-10 diagram, 20-25 code, 5 edge/concurrency, 5 extensions.
  • Clarify actors, use cases, variations, limits, threads, persistence, failure behaviour.
  • Entity test own data and behaviour or identity; else it is a field; fixed values are enums.
  • Money long paise or BigDecimal, never double; decide where rounding leftovers go.
  • Double booking check-then-act race; fix with atomic check and write.
  • In-memory fixes synchronized, ReentrantLock (finally unlock), putIfAbsent, per-show lock, sorted multi-lock order.
  • Database fixes unique constraint, conditional UPDATE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, version column.
  • Seat hold AVAILABLE, HELD with expiry, BOOKED; lazy expiry; no lock during payment.
  • Distributed lock Redis SET NX PX with token; caveats: expiry during pauses, failover; use fencing tokens.
  • Parking lot enum types, Spot with atomic claim, PricingStrategy, ticket map, injected Clock.
  • Tic-tac-toe Board vs Game; row, column, diagonal counters give O(1) win check.
  • Library Book vs BookCopy, Loan as link entity, FineStrategy, limits per member.
  • Vending machine State pattern, default methods throw, machine holds data, states hold transitions.
  • Elevator two TreeSets per elevator, LOOK sweep, selector Strategy, step() simulates time.
  • LRU HashMap plus doubly linked list with sentinels; node stores key; get also writes, so lock it.
  • LinkedHashMap LRU accessOrder true plus removeEldestEntry.
  • Splitwise SplitStrategy (equal, exact, percent), pairwise sheet with netting, greedy min cash flow with two heaps.
  • BookMyShow Seat vs ShowSeat, per-show lock, hold, pay, confirm, release.
  • Rate limiter token bucket with lazy refill, lock per bucket, nanoTime, 429 and Retry-After.
  • Fixed window flaw boundary spike up to double the limit.
  • Food delivery transition table in the enum, Observer for notifications, notify outside the lock, isolate failures.
  • Patterns seen Strategy (pricing, fines, split, selector, limiter), State, Observer, Facade, Command for undo.
  • Mistakes jumping to code, god class, pattern overuse, silent coding, ignoring concurrency.

Practice — LLD interview problems

  1. Warm-up: shopping cart. Rebuild the cart from the LLD method article from memory, then add a coupon-code rule and a combined rule. Done when adding a rule needs no change to Cart and you have a test for each rule.
  2. Race it. Write the broken Seat.book from the concurrency article, run it with 200 threads on one seat in a loop and count winners. Then fix it with synchronized and with putIfAbsent. Done when the count is always exactly 1.
  3. Parking lot. Implement it with the Strategy for pricing. Add EV spots and a "nearest free spot" allocation policy. Done when a unit test with a fake Clock checks the fee for 59 minutes, 61 minutes and 5 hours.
  4. Tic-tac-toe, then Snake and Ladder. Code both with an injected dice. Add undo to tic-tac-toe using a stack of moves. Done when a scripted game ends in a win, a draw and an invalid move.
  5. Library and vending machine. Code the library with reservations (a waiting queue notified on return) and the vending machine with an OutOfServiceState. Done when every invalid action throws a clear exception.
  6. Elevator. Run three elevators with random requests from several threads and a scheduler calling stepAll() every 100 ms. Print the stops. Done when no request waits longer than two full sweeps.
  7. LRU cache. Write the hand-made version, the LinkedHashMap version, then add a TTL. Done when the same test suite passes on both and a 16-thread stress test never throws.
  8. Splitwise. Add all three split types, history and simplify. Done when the sum of all net balances is zero in every test and a group of 5 people with 8 expenses needs at most 4 transfers.
  9. BookMyShow in 60 minutes. Set a timer and code the hold, pay, confirm flow. Then write the SQL conditional update and unique constraint for the same flow. Done when 100 threads fighting for 10 seats produce exactly 10 bookings and no seat is booked twice.
  10. Rate limiter and food delivery. Build the token bucket with a fake clock and a sliding window alternative, then the order flow with an asynchronous observer using an executor. Done when both pass tests, including a failing observer that does not stop the others.
4

Module 4·HLD · week 4Must (concepts)

HLD fundamentals

8 topics · about 58 min of reading

High-level design (HLD) is the view from far above the code. In the earlier modules you designed classes and objects (low-level design). Here you design a whole system: which services exist, where the data lives, how requests travel, and what happens when a machine, a network link or a whole data centre fails. This module gives you the vocabulary and the arithmetic that every later design is built from.

You already build Spring Boot services. HLD asks the next question: what if one million people call your service at the same time, and one of the three servers behind it dies in the middle? The answers use a small set of ideas: estimate the load, scale out, stay available, and choose how consistent your data must be. Module 5 then gives you the building blocks (load balancers, caches, queues, shards) that put these ideas into practice.

  • Walk through one request from the browser to the database and back, naming every hop.
  • Choose between REST, gRPC, WebSockets, SSE, long polling and webhooks for a given feature.
  • Explain latency, throughput and percentiles, and say why an average hides the pain.
  • Do a back-of-the-envelope estimate of requests per second, storage and bandwidth.
  • Explain stateless services and where session state goes when you scale out.
  • Calculate availability for components in series and in parallel, and read a nines table.
  • Explain CAP with a partition scenario, PACELC, quorums and consistency models, and pick the right consistency for each feature.

What system design interviews test, and the path of one request

A system design interview tests whether you can turn vague requirements into a sensible architecture, justify trade-offs with numbers, and follow one request through every layer: client, DNS, CDN, load balancer, app servers, cache, database, queue and workers.

What the interviewer is really checking

There is no single correct answer. The interviewer watches how you think. A good candidate clarifies the problem first, states assumptions, sketches a simple design, estimates the load, and then improves the design where the numbers say it will hurt. Weak candidates jump to "Kafka and microservices" in the first minute without knowing how many users there are.

The signals they look for are the same in nearly every interview:

  • Requirements: you separate functional requirements (what the system does: "shorten a URL", "post a photo") from non-functional requirements (how well it does it: latency, availability, consistency, durability, scale).
  • Estimation: you size the problem before choosing tools.
  • Trade-offs: every choice costs something. You say what you gain and what you pay. "I use a cache here; the price is stale data for up to 60 seconds, which is fine for a product page."
  • Depth on demand: when asked "how does that work inside?", you can go one level down (how replication works, what a partition key is).
  • Failure thinking: you ask "what if this node dies?" before the interviewer does.

How HLD connects to your Spring Boot work

A Spring Boot application is one box in an HLD diagram. The controller, service and repository layers you write live inside that box. Almost every HLD concept has a place where you already touch it:

HLD ideaWhere you meet it in Spring Boot
Stateless serviceNo data in HttpSession; JWT or a Redis session
Cache@Cacheable with Redis (Spring Boot · Module 6)
QueueKafka or RabbitMQ listeners (Spring Boot · Module 7)
Database scalingRead replicas, connection pools, indexes (SQL · Module 6)
Load balancingSeveral instances behind Nginx or an ALB (DevOps · Module 2)
Health checksActuator /actuator/health

A repeatable framework for any design question

  1. Clarify the scope and the users. Ask: who uses it, how many, read-heavy or write-heavy, which features are in scope.
  2. List requirements: functional first, then non-functional with numbers (for example "99.9% available, p99 read latency under 200 ms").
  3. Estimate requests per second, storage and bandwidth (the estimation article).
  4. Draw the API and the data model (a few endpoints, a few tables).
  5. Draw the high-level design: client, load balancer, services, database.
  6. Deep dive into one or two hard parts (the hot path, the bottleneck).
  7. Handle failures and scale: replication, caching, sharding, monitoring.

The path of one request

Take a user opening a shopping page on Flipkart-style site. Here is the journey a typical large web system makes. Not every system has every box, and a small one has only a few of them. The skill is knowing when each box earns its place.

  1. Client. The browser or mobile app builds an HTTPS request. It may first check its own cache (the browser cache) and skip the network.
  2. DNS. The client turns shop.example.com into an IP address. The answer is often cached and may point to the nearest region (DNS).
  3. CDN. Static files (images, JavaScript, CSS) come from an edge server near the user. A hit ends the journey here (CDN).
  4. Load balancer. Dynamic requests (API calls) arrive at one public address. The load balancer picks a healthy app server and often terminates TLS (Load balancers).
  5. App server. Your Spring Boot instance authenticates the request and runs the business logic. It should hold no user state, so any instance can serve any request.
  6. Cache. Before touching the database, the app asks Redis. A hit returns in about a millisecond (Caching).
  7. Database. On a miss, the app queries the database, usually a read replica for reads and the primary for writes (Replication).
  8. Queue and workers. Slow or non-urgent work (send email, resize image, update the search index) is put on a queue and the response returns at once. Workers consume the queue later (Queues).

Tip: start with the simplest design that meets the numbers

Begin with one app server and one database on the whiteboard. Add a box only when a number or a failure case demands it: "At 5,000 reads per second one database will struggle, so I add a cache." This shows judgement, not buzzwords.

Interview angle: what to say in the first five minutes

  • "Let me clarify scope and non-functional requirements before I draw anything."
  • "Let me estimate the scale so I know which parts need to be distributed."
  • "I will start simple and then evolve the design where the numbers hurt."
  • Always state assumptions aloud; the interviewer can correct them cheaply.

Common mistake: designing for Google scale on day one

A system with 10,000 users does not need sharding, Kafka and five microservices. Over-engineering costs money and makes failures harder to find. Say what the design looks like now and how it grows at 10x and 100x. That is exactly what a senior engineer does at work.

Words you will hear in every design talk

Scalability
The ability to handle more load by adding resources, without a redesign.
Availability
The fraction of time the system answers correctly (see Availability).
Consistency
Whether all readers see the same, latest data (see CAP).
Durability
Once the system says "saved", the data survives crashes.
Bottleneck
The one part that limits the whole system's speed. Find it, fix it, find the next one.

Client–server and communication styles: REST, gRPC, WebSockets and more

Use REST over HTTP+JSON as the default for public APIs, gRPC for fast internal service-to-service calls, WebSockets for two-way real-time traffic, SSE for server-to-browser streams, long polling as a fallback, and webhooks to let another system call you when something happens.

Client–server in one paragraph

In the client–server model a client starts a conversation and a server answers. The browser asks, your Spring Boot app replies. The client opens a connection (TCP, usually with TLS on top), sends a request, and waits for a response. HTTP is the request–response protocol of the web. Every style below is a different way to use this connection. The key questions are: who starts the message, how long the connection stays open, and how the data is encoded (text like JSON, or binary like Protocol Buffers).

REST over HTTP and JSON

REST models your system as resources (/orders/42) and uses HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) and status codes. Bodies are usually JSON. It is stateless: each request carries everything the server needs.

  • Strengths: universal (every language, browser and tool understands it), easy to debug with curl, easy to cache (GET responses, CDN, ETag), mature tooling (Spring MVC, OpenAPI).
  • Costs: JSON is text, so payloads are larger and parsing is slower than binary. You may need several round trips to build one screen (over-fetching or under-fetching). There is no built-in streaming or schema enforcement.
  • Use it for: public APIs, browser-to-backend calls, CRUD-style services.

For the design details of REST (status codes, idempotency, versioning, pagination), see Spring Boot · Module 2.

gRPC

gRPC is a remote procedure call framework from Google. You describe your service in a .proto file; tools generate client and server code in many languages. Messages are encoded with Protocol Buffers (a compact binary format), and calls travel over HTTP/2, which multiplexes many calls on one connection.

syntax = "proto3";

service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder (OrderRequest) returns (OrderReply);            // unary
  rpc WatchOrders (OrderRequest) returns (stream OrderReply);  // server streaming
  rpc Upload (stream Chunk) returns (UploadSummary);           // client streaming
  rpc Chat (stream Msg) returns (stream Msg);                  // bidirectional
}

message OrderRequest { int64 id = 1; }
message OrderReply   { int64 id = 1; string status = 2; }
  • Strengths: small and fast messages, strict typed contract, generated code, four call types including streaming, deadlines and cancellation built in.
  • Costs: not human-readable on the wire, browsers cannot call it directly (they need gRPC-Web and a proxy), harder to debug, and load balancers must understand HTTP/2.
  • Use it for: internal service-to-service calls in a microservice system where latency and bandwidth matter.

WebSockets

A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request that is "upgraded" to a long-lived, full-duplex TCP connection: either side can send a message at any time without a new request. Messages are small frames with very little overhead.

  • Strengths: real-time two-way traffic with low latency: chat, multiplayer games, live collaboration, trading screens.
  • Costs: the server must hold one open connection per user. That is memory and file descriptors, so a node serves tens of thousands, not millions. The connection is stateful, which makes load balancing, deploys and reconnects harder. You must write your own heartbeat, reconnect and message-ordering logic. Proxies and firewalls sometimes interfere.
  • Use it for: chat, live notifications with replies, collaborative editing.

Server-Sent Events, long polling and short polling

  • Short polling: the client asks "anything new?" every few seconds. Simple, but wasteful: most answers are empty, and updates are delayed up to one interval.
  • Long polling: the client asks, and the server holds the request open until it has data (or a timeout), then replies; the client immediately asks again. Works everywhere over plain HTTP, with less waste than short polling, but each message costs a full request cycle.
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE): one HTTP response that stays open and the server pushes text events through it. One direction only (server to client), built-in auto-reconnect in browsers, plain HTTP. Ideal for live scores, progress bars and notifications.

GraphQL (brief) and webhooks

GraphQL exposes a single endpoint where the client sends a query that names exactly the fields it wants. This removes over-fetching and lets a mobile screen get everything in one round trip. The costs: caching is harder (every query is a POST with a different body), a naive resolver design causes the N+1 query problem, and expensive queries must be limited. It fits client-driven apps with many different screens.

A webhook reverses the direction: you give another system a URL, and it sends an HTTP POST to you when something happens (Razorpay telling you a payment succeeded, GitHub telling you about a push). You avoid polling, but you must handle retries, duplicates (make the handler idempotent), verify a signature so nobody can fake events, and respond fast (accept, then process asynchronously).

Comparison table

StyleDirectionFormatBest forMain cost
RESTClient asksJSON (text)Public APIs, CRUDChatty, no streaming
gRPCBoth, with streamingProtobuf (binary)Internal service callsNot browser-native
WebSocketFull duplexAny framesChat, gamesStateful, many open sockets
SSEServer to clientText eventsLive feeds, progressOne-way only
Long pollingClient asks, server holdsAnyFallback, simple pushRequest per message
GraphQLClient asksJSONVaried client screensCaching, N+1, query cost
WebhookOther system calls youJSONEvent notifications between companiesRetries, duplicates, security

Rule: every network call can fail, so set timeouts and make writes idempotent

A call may time out after the server already did the work. The client then retries and the work runs twice. Give writes an idempotency key (for example a payment request id) so the retry is safe. Never call another service without a timeout.

Real projects usually mix styles

A typical product uses REST between the mobile app and the API gateway, gRPC or REST between internal services, a WebSocket or SSE channel for live notifications, Kafka for events between services, and webhooks from the payment provider. You pick per interaction, not once for the whole system.

Interview angle

  • "Chat needs both sides to push, so I use WebSockets. Notifications are one-way, so SSE is lighter. For service-to-service I use gRPC for speed, and REST at the edge for compatibility."
  • Mention the cost of WebSockets: sticky connections and one socket per user, so the gateway layer for sockets is scaled and deployed separately.
  • Say that you pick the simplest style that meets the latency need; polling every 30 seconds is fine for a dashboard.

Latency, throughput and percentiles

Latency is how long one request takes, throughput is how many requests finish per second; measure latency with percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not averages, and remember the rough cost of memory, disk and network operations.

Two different questions

Latency is the time for one request, from sending to getting the answer, in milliseconds. Throughput is how much work the system finishes per unit of time: requests per second (RPS or QPS), messages per second, or megabytes per second.

Analogy: a motorway. Latency is how long one car takes from Mumbai to Pune. Throughput is how many cars reach Pune per hour. Adding lanes raises throughput but does not make any single car faster. A faster speed limit lowers latency. The two are linked but not the same: a system can have high throughput and poor latency (a batch job that handles millions of rows but each takes minutes), or low latency and low throughput (a fast server that handles only one request at a time).

LatencyThroughput
QuestionHow long does one request take?How many requests per second?
UnitmsRPS, MB/s
Improved byCaching, closer servers (CDN), faster queries, less network hopsMore servers, parallelism, batching, async work
Trade-offBatching raises latency per itemHigher load at saturation raises latency

Why averages lie: percentiles

Suppose 99 requests take 100 ms and one takes 10 seconds. The average is about 199 ms and looks healthy, but one in every hundred users waited ten seconds. Latency has a long tail, so we use percentiles:

  • p50 (median): half of the requests are faster than this. The "typical" user.
  • p95: 95% are faster; 1 in 20 is slower.
  • p99: 1 in 100 is slower. Heavy users see it often.
  • p99.9: the extreme tail, often GC pauses, cold caches or retries.

The tail matters more than it looks. A page that makes 20 backend calls is slow if any call is slow. If each call has a 1% chance of being slow, the page is slow with probability 1 − 0.9920 ≈ 18%. This is called tail latency amplification. That is why SLOs are written as "p99 under 300 ms", never "average under 100 ms".

Latency numbers worth remembering

These are rough orders of magnitude (hardware changes them, but the ratios hold). Their value is telling you what to avoid in a hot path: every step down the table is roughly ten to a hundred times slower.

OperationApproximate timeFeels like
CPU register / L1 cacheabout 1 nsinstant
Main memory (RAM) readabout 100 nsfast
Compress 1 KBa few microsecondsfast
SSD random readabout 100 µs1,000x RAM
Round trip inside one data centreabout 0.5 msnetwork is not free
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSDabout 1 msfine for bulk
Spinning disk seekabout 10 msavoid for random IO
Round trip across a continentabout 50–100 msphysics (speed of light)
Round trip India to US or Europeabout 150–250 mswhy CDNs and regions exist

The lessons: memory is fast, so cache in memory; disk is slower, so prefer sequential access and indexes; each network hop costs real time, so avoid chatty calls; and distance cannot be tuned away, so put data near users.

Little's law

Little's law links three numbers in any stable system:

L = λ × W

L = average number of requests inside the system at once
λ = arrival rate (requests per second)
W = average time each request spends in the system (seconds)

Example: your service gets 2,000 requests per second and each takes 50 ms (0.05 s). Then L = 2,000 × 0.05 = 100 requests in flight at once. If a Tomcat instance has 200 worker threads, one instance handles it with room to spare. If a database call slows down to 500 ms, L becomes 1,000, the threads run out, requests queue, and latency climbs further. This is how a slow dependency takes down a healthy service. It also shows how to size connection pools and thread pools: concurrency needed = rate × time.

What happens near saturation

A server at 50% load answers quickly. As utilisation approaches 100%, queues build and latency rises sharply, not smoothly. Plan to run services at 60–70% of peak capacity, keep the rest as headroom for spikes and failures, and use load shedding (reject some requests early with 503 or 429) rather than letting every request time out.

Common mistake: reporting the average and the maximum only

The average hides the tail; the maximum is one unlucky request. Report p50, p95 and p99, and measure at the client or load balancer so queueing time is included. Also avoid averaging percentiles across servers; merge the raw histograms instead.

Tip: ways to cut latency, in the order you try them

  1. Do less: remove unneeded calls and use indexes.
  2. Do it nearby: CDN for static content, regional deployments, a cache close to the app.
  3. Do it in parallel: call independent services at the same time, not one after the other.
  4. Do it later: return now and finish slow work through a queue.

Interview angle

  • "I would track p99 latency, because averages hide the slow tail that real users feel."
  • Quote ratios, not exact figures: memory is about 1,000x faster than SSD, and a cross-region call is about 1,000x slower than a local memory read.
  • Use Little's law to justify thread-pool or connection-pool sizes.

Back-of-the-envelope estimation

Estimation means turning "10 million users" into requests per second, storage per year and bandwidth using round numbers (a day is about 105 seconds), so you can decide how many servers, how much disk and which components the design needs.

Why estimate at all

The numbers decide the design. A system with 50 requests per second runs on one small server and one database. A system with 50,000 requests per second needs caching, replicas and probably sharding. Interviewers do not want exact answers; they want to see a calm, structured calculation that lands within the right power of ten. A back-of-the-envelope estimate is exactly that: quick arithmetic on the back of an envelope.

The method

  1. State assumptions clearly (users, actions per user, size of each item). Ask the interviewer or pick sensible numbers and say them aloud.
  2. Round hard. Use 86,400 ≈ 100,000 seconds per day, 1 month ≈ 2.5 million seconds, 1 year ≈ 30 million seconds (about 3 × 107).
  3. Compute average RPS = requests per day ÷ 86,400.
  4. Compute peak RPS = average × a peak factor (2x to 5x; use 3x if unsure).
  5. Compute storage = items per day × size per item × days kept × replication factor.
  6. Compute bandwidth = RPS × size per request (in and out separately).
  7. Sanity-check and convert to servers, disks and cache size. Write units on every line.

Numbers to memorise

PowerValueNameHandy meaning
2101,0241 KBabout a thousand
220about 1 million1 MBa photo thumbnail
230about 1 billion1 GBa movie, or RAM on a phone
240about 1 trillion1 TBone cheap disk
250about 1 quadrillion1 PBa large company's data
  • Seconds: 1 day ≈ 86,400 ≈ 105; 1 year ≈ 3 × 107.
  • Rule of thumb: 1 million requests per day ≈ 12 requests per second (1,000,000 ÷ 86,400).
  • Typical sizes: a character is 1 byte in ASCII (1–4 in UTF-8); a tweet-like post is a few hundred bytes; a row of metadata is about 1 KB; a compressed photo is 200 KB–2 MB; a minute of video is tens of MB at standard quality.
  • Network: 1 Gbps ≈ 125 MB per second. A bit is one eighth of a byte; do not mix up Mbps and MB/s.
  • Availability and capacity heuristics: one typical Spring Boot instance serves a few hundred to a couple of thousand simple requests per second; a single well-tuned relational database handles a few thousand to some tens of thousands of simple queries per second; Redis handles on the order of 100,000 simple operations per second per node. Treat all of these as rough, and say so.

A fully worked example: a photo-sharing app

Assumptions (stated aloud): 10 million daily active users (DAU). Each user makes about 20 requests per day (opening the feed, scrolling, liking, posting). Read-heavy: 90% reads, 10% writes. On average each user uploads 0.1 photos per day, so 1 million photos per day. Average stored photo: 500 KB. Metadata per photo and per other write: about 1 KB. Photos are kept for 5 years. Replication factor 3. Peak traffic is 3x the average.

Step 1: requests per second
Requests per day  = 10,000,000 users × 20 = 200,000,000
Average RPS       = 200,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 2,315  → about 2,300 RPS
Peak RPS (3x)     ≈ 7,000 RPS
Reads  (90%)      ≈ 6,300 RPS at peak
Writes (10%)      ≈ 700 RPS at peak

Using 105 seconds the average is 2,000 RPS; it is fine to round either way. What the number tells you: 7,000 RPS is far above one database's comfort for complex queries, but a handful of app servers and a cache can handle it.

Step 2: how many app servers
Assume one instance handles ~700 RPS comfortably (it does real work: DB + cache).
Peak 7,000 / 700 = 10 instances
Keep headroom for failures and spikes (run at ~50% of capacity): ~20 instances
Spread across 2–3 availability zones so one zone loss still leaves capacity.
Step 3: storage
Photos per day    = 1,000,000 × 500 KB = 500 GB/day
Photos per year   = 500 GB × 365 ≈ 182 TB  → about 180 TB/year
Five years        ≈ 0.9 PB, ×3 replicas ≈ 2.7 PB (object storage, e.g. S3)

Writes per day    = 10% × 200M = 20M rows (photos, likes, comments)
Metadata per day  = 20M × 1 KB = 20 GB/day
Metadata per year = 20 GB × 365 ≈ 7.3 TB/year
Five years        ≈ 36 TB, ×3 replicas ≈ 110 TB (database cluster)

Insight: the photos dominate storage by far (about 25x the metadata), so photos go to object storage and only a URL goes into the database. And 36 TB of metadata in five years does not fit one database server comfortably, which is a signal to plan for sharding (Sharding).

Step 4: bandwidth
Ingress (uploads): 500 GB/day / 86,400 s ≈ 5.8 MB/s ≈ 46 Mbps average
Egress (reads): assume an average response (JSON + media via CDN) of 100 KB
  Average: 2,300 RPS × 100 KB ≈ 230 MB/s ≈ 1.8 Gbps
  Peak (3x): ≈ 5.5 Gbps
Most egress bytes are images and should be served by a CDN, not your servers.

Egress is about 40x ingress, so this is a read-heavy system and a CDN pays for itself.

Step 5: cache size
Rule of thumb (80/20): 20% of the data serves 80% of reads.
Hot metadata read per day: 180M reads, assume 1 KB each = 180 GB/day of reads
Cache the hot 20% of daily reads: ≈ 36 GB
→ A few Redis nodes with 16–32 GB each, or one large node plus a replica.

Reading the result

Average 2,300 RPS and peak 7,000 RPS means: a stateless app tier of about 20 instances behind a load balancer, a cache tier of a few tens of GB, a primary database with read replicas now and a sharding plan for later, object storage in the petabyte range, and a CDN for images. You designed the shape of the system before drawing a single box.

More estimates you will be asked

  • URL shortener: 100 million new URLs per month ≈ 40 writes per second; with a 10:1 read ratio ≈ 400 reads per second. A record is about 500 bytes, so 100 million × 500 B = 50 GB per month, about 3 TB over 5 years. Tiny. A single database plus a cache is enough; the real interview content is the key generation.
  • Chat app: 50 million DAU, 40 messages per user per day = 2 billion messages per day ≈ 23,000 per second; at 100 bytes each ≈ 200 GB per day. Concurrent WebSocket connections might be 10 million, so at 50,000 connections per server you need about 200 gateway servers.
  • Video streaming: 1 million concurrent viewers × 3 Mbps = 3 Tbps of egress. That is only possible with a CDN and edge caches; it shows how bandwidth, not CPU, drives the cost.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing bits and bytes (Mbps vs MB/s) and being off by 8x.
  • Using the average as the design target and forgetting the peak.
  • Forgetting replication, indexes and growth when sizing storage.
  • Spending ten minutes on exact arithmetic. Round and move on; the order of magnitude is the answer.
  • Not saying what the number means for the design.

Tip: keep a tidy block on the whiteboard

Write DAU, requests per user, size per item and retention at the top, then derive RPS, storage and bandwidth below. If the interviewer changes an assumption, you change one line and redo the chain.

Interview angle

  • "Let me assume 10 million DAU with 20 requests each; that is 200 million per day, roughly 2,300 per second on average and about 7,000 at peak."
  • Always finish with "so the design needs X", for example "so a single database will not hold the write load and I plan for sharding".
  • Practice prompts: Twitter timeline reads, WhatsApp messages per second, YouTube storage per day, Zomato peak orders at 8 pm, UPI transactions per second at festival peak.

Vertical vs horizontal scaling, and stateless services

Scaling up (vertical) means a bigger machine and is simple but capped and a single point of failure; scaling out (horizontal) means more machines behind a load balancer and needs stateless services, so keep session state in a shared store or in a token, not in server memory.

Two ways to add capacity

Vertical scaling (scale up) means giving one machine more CPU, RAM, disk or faster hardware. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more machines and sharing the work between them.

AspectScale up (vertical)Scale out (horizontal)
HowBigger server or instance typeMore servers behind a load balancer
Code changesNoneService must be stateless; data must be shared or partitioned
Upper limitHard: biggest machine you can buyPractically very high
Cost curveGets steeply expensive at the top endRoughly linear with commodity machines
FailureOne machine is a single point of failureSurvives losing a node
Downtime to scaleOften a restartNone: add nodes live
ComplexityLowHigher: load balancing, consistency, deployment
Best forEarly stage, databases (first step)Stateless app tiers, caches, queues, shards

A sensible path: start vertical because it is cheap in engineering time, then scale out the stateless tiers first, and treat the database last because it is the hardest to scale out (Database scaling ladder).

What makes a service stateless

A stateless service keeps no information about a client between requests inside its own memory or disk. Each request carries what is needed (a token, parameters), or the service fetches it from a shared store. The result: any instance can handle any request, so you can add, remove, restart or replace instances freely, and a crashed instance loses nothing important.

A stateful service remembers things locally: a logged-in user in an HttpSession, an uploaded file on local disk, a counter in a static field, a local in-memory cache that must match other instances. Those are the typical blockers to scaling out.

Hidden stateWhy it breaks scale-outMove it to
HTTP session in memoryNext request may reach another instanceRedis session store, or a JWT
Files on local diskOther instances cannot see themObject storage (S3)
Scheduled job in each instanceRuns N timesOne scheduler with a lock (ShedLock) or a queue
In-memory counters / locksEach instance has its own valueRedis or the database
Local cacheInstances disagree on stale valuesDistributed cache, or short TTL on local ones

Where does session state go?

Users log in once and expect to stay logged in. There are three common answers.

1. Sticky sessions

The load balancer remembers which instance served a user (via a cookie or the client IP) and keeps sending them there, so the in-memory session works. It is easy but weak: load becomes uneven, a crash logs out everyone on that instance, and scaling in or rolling deploys drop sessions. Use it only as a temporary fix.

2. A shared session store (Redis)

The session lives in Redis, and every instance reads it by session id (cookie). With Spring, add spring-session-data-redis and the framework replaces the servlet session with a Redis-backed one; your controllers do not change. Cost: one extra network hop (about a millisecond) per request and Redis becomes a dependency that must itself be highly available. Benefit: sessions can be revoked instantly (delete the key).

3. Stateless tokens (JWT)

The server puts the identity and claims into a signed JSON Web Token and gives it to the client; the client sends it on every request; any instance verifies the signature with a key, with no lookup. Best for scale and for service-to-service calls. Cost: you cannot easily revoke a token before it expires (use short lifetimes, refresh tokens or a deny-list), tokens are larger than a session id, and you must never put secrets in the payload (it is only encoded, not encrypted). See Spring Boot · Module 4 for the JWT flow.

OptionServer lookupRevocationWeak point
Sticky sessionsNone (in memory)EasyUneven load, lost on crash
Redis session storeOne Redis readInstantRedis must be highly available
JWTNone (signature check)Hard until expiryToken theft, size, revocation

Stateless is for the app tier; state has to live somewhere

State does not disappear; you push it to specialised systems that are built to hold it: the database (durable data), Redis (sessions, cache), object storage (files), the queue (pending work). Those systems scale by their own rules (replication, sharding), which module 5 covers. After this change a load balancer in front of N identical instances is enough to scale the app tier. See Load balancers.

Auto-scaling and the limits of scale-out

Cloud platforms can add and remove instances automatically based on CPU, request count or queue length (DevOps · Module 5). Stateless instances start in seconds and are disposable. But scale-out is not magic: the shared pieces behind it (one database, one Redis) can become the new bottleneck, and adding app instances then increases pressure on them (more connections, more queries). Always ask what is the next bottleneck after scaling the app tier.

Rule: design every app instance to be disposable

If killing any instance at any moment causes data loss or logged-out users, the service is not ready to scale out. Write data to a shared store before replying, and keep nothing important in memory or on local disk.

Common mistake: a static HashMap as a "database"

A static Map of carts or tokens works on your laptop and fails the moment two instances run: each has its own map. This is the number one reason a monolith cannot be scaled out without a rewrite.

Interview angle

  • "I keep the app tier stateless so I can add instances behind the load balancer. Session data goes to Redis, or we use JWTs for stateless auth."
  • Explain the sticky-session downside in one line: uneven load and sessions lost on a crash.
  • Mention that databases usually scale up first and out later, because scaling them out brings consistency problems.

Availability, reliability and what "99.9% uptime" means

Availability is the fraction of time a system works; each extra "nine" cuts the allowed downtime ten times, components in series multiply their availabilities (worse), components in parallel multiply their failure chances (better), and you reach high availability by removing single points of failure with redundancy and failover.

Availability as a percentage

Availability = uptime ÷ (uptime + downtime), usually written as a percentage and described by its "nines". "Three nines" means 99.9%. The allowed downtime shrinks very fast:

AvailabilityNinesDowntime per yearPer month (30 days)
99%twoabout 3.65 daysabout 7.2 hours
99.9%threeabout 8.77 hoursabout 43 minutes
99.99%fourabout 52.6 minutesabout 4.3 minutes
99.999%fiveabout 5.26 minutesabout 26 seconds

The formula is downtime = (1 − availability) × period. For 99.9% over a year: 0.001 × 365 days × 24 h = 8.76 hours. The jump from 99.9% to 99.99% looks small but means going from "a bad afternoon per year" to "less than an hour per year", which usually needs automatic failover, because no human can react in minutes. Each nine costs much more than the last, so choose the number from the business need. A college timetable app does not need five nines; a payments switch does.

SLI, SLO and SLA

SLI (Service Level Indicator)
A measured number: "the fraction of requests that returned non-5xx", "the share of requests under 300 ms".
SLO (Service Level Objective)
The internal target for an SLI: "99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days". Teams use it to decide when to stop shipping features and fix reliability.
SLA (Service Level Agreement)
A contract with customers, often with refunds or credits when broken: "99.95% monthly uptime or you get a credit". The SLA is looser than the SLO so the team has a safety margin.

The gap between 100% and your SLO is the error budget. With a 99.9% SLO you may fail 0.1% of requests; if the budget is spent, you pause risky releases. This turns "be reliable" into a number that engineers and product managers can argue about calmly.

Availability in series and in parallel

A request usually passes through many components. How they are connected decides the total.

In series (every part is required)

Multiply the availabilities. The chain is weaker than its weakest link:

Total = A1 × A2 × A3
Load balancer 99.9% × app 99.9% × database 99.9%
  = 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.997  →  99.7%
Downtime ≈ 0.003 × 8,760 h ≈ 26 hours per year (not 8.77 hours!)

Ten dependencies at 99.9% each give about 99%. This is why a microservice call chain of ten services is dangerous: the more hard dependencies a request needs, the lower the total availability.

In parallel (any one part is enough)

Multiply the failure chances. The system is down only if all copies are down:

Total = 1 − (1 − A1) × (1 − A2)
Two servers at 99.9% each
  = 1 − (0.001 × 0.001) = 1 − 0.000001 = 0.999999  →  99.9999%
Three servers: 1 − 0.001^3 = 99.9999999%

These are theoretical best cases. They assume failures are independent. If both servers share one power supply, one rack, one bug or one bad deploy, they fail together and the calculation is wrong. This is why real redundancy spreads copies over racks, availability zones and regions, and why code bugs (identical on every copy) are not fixed by adding replicas.

Combining both

Compute parallel groups first, then multiply the groups in series. Example: load balancer (99.99%) → two app servers (99.9% each, parallel) → one database (99.9%): app group = 99.9999%, total = 0.9999 × 0.999999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.89%. The single database is now the weak point. You improve the system by making that part redundant, not by buying more app servers.

Single points of failure and redundancy

A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure takes the whole system down. Walk the request path and ask of every box: "if this dies, what happens?" Typical SPOFs: one load balancer, one database primary, one DNS provider, one availability zone, one shared config service, one person who knows the password. The cure is redundancy: run more than one copy and make the switch between them automatic.

Failover: active-passive vs active-active

Active-passive (standby)Active-active
HowOne node serves; a standby waits and takes over on failureAll nodes serve traffic at once
Failover timeSeconds to minutes (detect, promote, redirect)Near zero; others already serving
Capacity useStandby idle: wasted moneyAll capacity used
ComplexitySimpler; one writerHigher: shared state, conflicts, split-brain risk
ExampleDatabase primary with a hot standbyStateless app servers behind a load balancer

Failover steps in a typical active-passive pair: a health check or heartbeat detects the primary is down, a coordinator promotes the standby, traffic is redirected (virtual IP, DNS or the load balancer), and the old primary is fenced off so it cannot keep accepting writes. Split-brain is the danger case: both nodes believe they are primary and accept different writes. Quorum-based election (an odd number of voters, majority wins) and fencing prevent it. Also note that async replication may lose the last few writes at failover (Replication).

Redundancy can go beyond servers: multiple availability zones (separate buildings in a city) survive a data centre fire; multiple regions survive a regional outage and also reduce latency, at the cost of complexity and money.

Reliability, availability, durability, fault tolerance

These four words are often mixed up.

TermMeaningExample
ReliabilityThe system does the correct thing, consistently, over timeA transfer debits and credits the right amounts
AvailabilityThe system is up and answers when askedThe app responds 99.95% of the time
DurabilitySaved data is not lostS3 advertises extremely high durability (eleven nines); a single disk has far less
Fault toleranceThe system keeps working while parts failOne of three replicas dies, users notice nothing

They are different: a system can be available but unreliable (it answers quickly with wrong data), or durable but unavailable (data is safe, but the site is down for an hour). A fault is a component misbehaving; a failure is when users see the effect. Fault tolerance means faults do not become failures.

Techniques to raise availability

  • Redundancy at every layer, spread across zones.
  • Health checks and automatic failover, so recovery is in seconds.
  • Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, and circuit breakers so one slow dependency does not drag down the caller (Module 6).
  • Graceful degradation: when recommendations are down, show the page without them rather than an error.
  • Safe deployments: rolling, blue-green or canary releases and quick rollback; many outages come from changes, not hardware.
  • Backups and tested restore; monitoring and alerts on the SLIs.

Exception: "available" does not mean "correct"

A server that is up but answers with stale or wrong data counts as available in the simple formula. That is why SLIs should measure successful responses (right status, within the latency target), not just whether the process is alive.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a second app server but keeping one database and calling it highly available.
  • Ignoring that serial dependencies multiply: five hard dependencies at 99.9% is about 99.5%.
  • Promising 99.999% in an SLA without automatic failover or an on-call process.
  • Counting planned maintenance as "not downtime" without telling users.

Interview angle

  • "99.9% is about 8.8 hours of downtime per year, 43 minutes per month. Four nines is about 52 minutes per year, which needs automatic failover."
  • Show the arithmetic: serial 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.8%; parallel 1 − 0.0012 = 99.9999%.
  • Say "no single point of failure" and then name each layer's redundancy: multi-AZ load balancer, N app instances, database with a standby, replicated cache.

CAP theorem and PACELC

CAP says that when a network partition happens, a distributed data system must choose between consistency (reject or delay requests) and availability (answer, maybe with stale data); since partitions cannot be avoided, the real choice is CP or AP, and PACELC adds that even without a partition you trade latency for consistency.

The three letters

  • Consistency (C): every read sees the most recent write, as if there were one copy of the data. (This is the "linearizable" meaning, not the same as the "C" in ACID.)
  • Availability (A): every request to a working node gets a non-error answer, without a guarantee it is the latest data.
  • Partition tolerance (P): the system keeps operating even when the network drops or delays messages between nodes, so the cluster splits into groups that cannot talk.

The partition scenario

Two data centres, Mumbai and Chennai, each hold a copy of a user's balance: ₹1,000. The link between them breaks. Both sides are still running and still receiving requests. A user in Mumbai withdraws ₹800. Mumbai cannot tell Chennai. Now a request for the balance arrives in Chennai. What should Chennai do?

  • CP (consistency over availability): Chennai refuses to answer (returns an error or waits) because it cannot be sure it has the latest value. The data stays correct; some users see errors until the partition heals.
  • AP (availability over consistency): Chennai answers ₹1,000 from its own copy. Everyone gets an answer, but it is stale, and if both sides accept writes the copies diverge and must be merged later.

When the partition heals, an AP system has to reconcile conflicting writes (last-write-wins by timestamp, version vectors, application-level merge, CRDTs); a CP system simply resumes.

Why "CA" is not a real choice

The folk version says "pick any two of three". That is misleading. In a distributed system over a network, partitions will happen (cables, switches, GC pauses, misconfigured firewalls look like partitions). You cannot choose to not have them. So P is not optional, and the real choice, during a partition, is between C and A. A "CA" system only exists on a single node (or one that is never partitioned), which is not distributed in the interesting sense. When nothing is partitioned, a system can offer both C and A; CAP only forces the trade-off during the partition.

CP and AP examples

LeansExamples (typical behaviour)When you want it
CPZooKeeper, etcd, Consul (consensus-based); HBase; MongoDB with majority write and read concerns; single-primary relational databasesMoney, inventory counts, leader election, locks, configuration
APCassandra and DynamoDB (by default, tunable); Riak; DNS; CouchDBShopping carts, likes, feeds, sessions, telemetry

Many systems are tunable

Cassandra and DynamoDB let each request choose how many replicas must agree (see quorums), so the same database can behave CP-like for one query and AP-like for another. Treat the labels as tendencies, not permanent tags. Behaviour also depends on configuration, so say "by default" or "when configured with…" in interviews.

PACELC: the full picture

CAP only talks about the rare partition. PACELC (Daniel Abadi) says: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. The second half matters every day: to keep replicas consistent, a write must wait for acknowledgements from other nodes (more latency); to be fast, it returns early and lets replicas catch up (weaker consistency).

System typeIf partitionElseExample
PA / ELAvailabilityLatencyCassandra and DynamoDB at default settings
PC / ECConsistencyConsistencyTraditional single-primary RDBMS with sync replication, Google Spanner-style systems
PC / ELConsistencyLatencySome designs that are strict only when partitioned

Cross-region replication shows the ELC trade-off clearly: a synchronous write to Singapore from Mumbai pays about 60 ms or more per write; asynchronous replication is fast but a regional failure can lose the last writes.

Choosing per feature, not per system

One product has different needs in different places. A strong design says so:

  • Payments, wallet balance, seat booking, inventory at checkout: choose consistency. An error is better than selling the same seat twice or losing money.
  • Likes, view counts, follower counts, feed ordering: choose availability and latency. Showing 1,203 instead of 1,205 hurts nobody.
  • Shopping cart: classic AP (Amazon's Dynamo paper): never refuse an "add to cart"; merge carts later.
  • User profile read right after update: needs at least read-your-writes, even in an otherwise eventual system.

Common mistakes

  • Saying "we pick CA". Distributed systems cannot opt out of partitions.
  • Treating CAP's "consistency" as ACID's "consistency". They are different ideas.
  • Calling a whole database "CP" or "AP" forever, instead of saying it depends on configuration.
  • Forgetting that partial failures (slow nodes, packet loss) behave like partitions.

Interview angle

  • Start from the partition: "When the network splits, I must either reject some requests (CP) or serve possibly stale data (AP)."
  • Add PACELC: "Even without a partition, stronger consistency costs latency."
  • Give a feature-level answer: "Payments are CP; the like counter is AP."
  • Link to SQL · Module 6 for CAP basics, then go beyond them with the partition story and tunable consistency.

Strong vs eventual consistency, consistency models and quorums

Strong (linearizable) consistency makes a distributed store look like one copy, eventual consistency lets replicas catch up later, and in between sit useful guarantees such as read-your-writes, monotonic reads and causal consistency; quorums (R + W > N) let you tune the trade-off per request.

Why replicas disagree

To survive failures and serve more reads, data is copied to several nodes. A write reaches the copies at slightly different times: network delay, a slow node, an asynchronous replication stream. In the gap, two readers can ask two nodes and get two different answers. A consistency model is the promise a system makes about which answers are allowed. Stronger promises are easier for application programmers but cost latency and availability.

The models, strongest to weakest

ModelPromise (one line)Example
Strong / linearizableEvery read returns the latest completed write; the system behaves like a single copy with one global orderBank balance, seat lock, etcd, Spanner
SequentialAll clients see the operations in the same order, though not necessarily real-time orderSome coordination services
CausalIf B happened because of A (a reply to a comment), everyone sees A before B; unrelated writes may appear in any orderComment threads, chat replies
Read-your-writesAfter you write, your own later reads see that writeEdit profile, then refresh and see the change
Monotonic readsOnce you have seen a value, you never see an older one later (time does not go backwards)Scrolling a feed without items vanishing
EventualIf writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value eventually; no promise whenDNS, like counts, Cassandra at low consistency levels

Strong consistency is the simplest to reason about, but it needs coordination (a leader or consensus such as Raft or Paxos) on every write and often on reads, so it costs latency, and during a partition the minority side cannot proceed. Eventual consistency is fast and always available, but the application must tolerate stale reads and conflicting writes.

A stale read, step by step

Ways to give users read-your-writes without making everything strongly consistent:

  • Read from the primary for a short window (for example 5 seconds) after the user writes.
  • Route a user's reads to the primary for data they own, and to replicas for other people's data.
  • Remember the log position or version of the user's last write and read only from a replica that has caught up to it.
  • Sticky routing of a user to one replica also gives monotonic reads.

Quorums: N, R and W in simple words

In leaderless stores such as Cassandra, DynamoDB-style systems and Riak, data is stored on N replicas. A write is reported successful when W replicas have acknowledged it. A read asks R replicas and returns the newest version among them.

If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica,
so a read always includes at least one node that has the latest write.

N = 3 (three copies)
W = 2, R = 2  → R + W = 4 > 3  → reads see the latest write (strong-ish)
W = 1, R = 1  → R + W = 2 ≤ 3  → fast, but reads may be stale (eventual)
W = 3, R = 1  → R + W = 4 > 3  → fast reads, slow writes, writes fail if any node is down
W = 1, R = 3  → R + W = 4 > 3  → fast writes, slow reads

A quorum is not a full guarantee of linearizability: sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, clock skew and nodes that join or leave can still produce surprises. Systems add read repair (fix stale replicas when a read notices a difference), hinted handoff (hold a write for a down node) and anti-entropy (background sync) to converge.

Common settings are N = 3 with quorum reads and writes (R = W = 2). That tolerates one failed replica and still reads fresh data. In Cassandra you choose per query: ONE, QUORUM, ALL, or a local variant per data centre.

Conflict resolution when writes diverge

  • Last write wins (LWW): keep the highest timestamp. Simple, but clocks drift and silently drops a concurrent update.
  • Version vectors: detect that two writes were concurrent and keep both versions for the application to merge (the Dynamo shopping-cart approach).
  • CRDTs: data types designed so concurrent updates merge automatically (counters, sets). Good for likes and collaborative editing.

Choosing consistency per feature

FeatureMinimum consistencyWhy
Payment, wallet debitStrong (single leader, transaction)Double spend is unacceptable
Seat or stock reservationStrong on the final claimOverselling is costly
Own profile after editRead-your-writesUsers think the save failed otherwise
Comment threadCausalA reply must not appear before its parent
Like and view countersEventualSlight errors are invisible
Search results, recommendationsEventualIndex updates seconds later are fine

The expensive part of a system (payments) can be strongly consistent in a small, well-protected database, while the high-volume parts (feed, counters) are eventually consistent. Mixing models in one product is normal.

Exception: eventual consistency is not "no consistency"

Eventual consistency promises convergence once writes stop. Production systems usually converge in milliseconds to seconds. The danger is not that data is wrong forever, but that the application logic (for example "check balance, then debit") assumes freshness it does not have.

Common mistake: reading the balance from a replica before debiting

A check-then-act sequence on stale data lets two requests both pass the check. Do the check and the update on the primary in one transaction, or use a conditional update such as UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 800 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 800.

Interview angle

  • "With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2 the read and write sets overlap, so reads see the latest write while tolerating one node down."
  • Name the model you need instead of just saying "eventual": read-your-writes for profile edits, causal for comments.
  • Explain how you would fix a stale read after a write (read from primary briefly, or track the replica position).

Interview questions — HLD fundamentals

What do system design interviews test, and how do you structure your answer?

They test whether you can handle an open problem: clarify requirements, estimate scale, propose a simple design, find the bottleneck, and justify trade-offs. A structure that works: clarify scope, list functional and non-functional requirements, estimate load, define the API and data model, draw the high-level design, deep-dive into the hard part, then cover failures and scaling.

When would you choose gRPC over REST?

For internal service-to-service calls where latency, payload size and a strict contract matter. gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers, giving smaller binary messages, multiplexing, generated clients and streaming. REST is better at the public edge: browsers call it natively, it is easy to debug and cache, and any partner can use it.

WebSockets, SSE or long polling for live notifications?

If only the server pushes (notifications, scores), SSE is the lightest: plain HTTP with auto-reconnect. If both sides send frequently (chat, games, collaboration), use WebSockets, and accept the cost of one open connection per user. Long polling is a fallback when proxies block the others. For infrequent updates, plain polling every 30 seconds may be enough.

What is the difference between latency and throughput?

Latency is the time one request takes; throughput is how many requests complete per second. A motorway analogy: latency is one car's journey time, throughput is cars per hour. More servers raise throughput but do not make one request faster. Caching and nearby servers cut latency. Batching raises throughput but can raise per-item latency.

Why use p99 instead of the average latency?

Latency distributions have a long tail. An average of 200 ms can hide 1% of requests taking ten seconds. Those users are real, and a page with many backend calls hits the slow tail often: with 20 calls and a 1% slow chance each, about 18% of page loads are slow. SLOs are therefore stated as percentiles, for example "p99 under 300 ms".

Estimate the requests per second for 10 million daily users making 20 requests each.

10 million × 20 = 200 million requests per day. Divide by about 86,400 seconds: roughly 2,300 requests per second on average. With a peak factor of 3, plan for about 7,000 RPS. At about 700 RPS per instance that is 10 instances at peak, and about 20 with headroom and zone redundancy.

What is Little's law and how do you use it?

L = λ × W: requests in flight equals arrival rate times time in system. At 2,000 RPS with 50 ms per request, 100 requests are in flight. It sizes thread and connection pools, and shows why a slow dependency is dangerous: if a call goes from 50 ms to 500 ms, concurrency needed grows tenfold, pools run out and the service stalls.

Vertical vs horizontal scaling: which first, and why?

Vertical is simplest (a bigger machine, no code changes) so it is a good first step, especially for databases. But it has a ceiling, costs rise steeply and it is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds machines behind a load balancer and has no hard ceiling, but needs stateless services and shared or partitioned data. Typically you scale the stateless app tier out and the database up first, then add replicas and shards.

What makes a service stateless, and where do sessions go?

A stateless service keeps no per-client data in its own memory or disk between requests, so any instance can handle any request. Sessions move to Redis (shared store, instant revocation) or to a signed JWT (no lookup, but harder to revoke). Sticky sessions work but cause uneven load and lose sessions when an instance dies. Files go to object storage, scheduled jobs use a lock.

What does 99.9% availability mean in downtime?

(1 − 0.999) × one year = about 8.77 hours per year, or about 43 minutes per month. 99.99% is about 52 minutes a year, and 99.999% about 5 minutes a year. Each extra nine costs far more and usually requires automatic failover because humans cannot respond in minutes.

Three components each have 99.9% availability. What is the total in series and what if two are in parallel?

In series you multiply: 0.9993 ≈ 0.997, so 99.7% (about 26 hours of downtime a year). Two in parallel: 1 − (0.001 × 0.001) = 99.9999%, assuming failures are independent. In practice shared racks, zones, deploys and bugs break that assumption, so redundancy must be spread across failure domains.

Explain the CAP theorem with an example. Why is "CA" not a real choice?

When a network partition separates replicas, a system must choose: refuse some requests to stay consistent (CP) or answer with possibly stale data to stay available (AP). Example: Mumbai and Chennai lose their link; Mumbai accepts a withdrawal; Chennai cannot know. Partitions cannot be prevented in a real network, so P is forced, and the only choice is C or A during the partition. "CA" only describes a system that is not distributed.

What does PACELC add to CAP?

If there is a Partition choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the daily cost of strong consistency: waiting for replicas to acknowledge. Cassandra defaults to PA/EL (fast and available), while a single-primary database with synchronous replication is PC/EC.

What is a quorum and when does R + W > N matter?

With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read queries R replicas. If R + W > N the read and write sets must share at least one replica, so a read includes a node with the latest write. N = 3, R = W = 2 is the common setting: one node can be down and reads stay fresh. Lower R and W give speed and availability but allow stale reads.

How would you pick consistency for payments vs likes?

Payments use strong consistency: one leader, transactions, conditional updates; an error is better than a double spend. Likes use eventual consistency: availability and latency matter more, and small count errors do not matter. Profile edits need read-your-writes. Consistency is chosen per feature, not once per product.

Cheat sheet — HLD fundamentals

  • Interview flow clarify, requirements, estimate, API and data, high-level design, deep dive, failures.
  • Request path client, DNS, CDN, load balancer, app servers, cache, database, queue, workers.
  • REST default for public APIs, JSON, easy caching, no streaming.
  • gRPC HTTP/2 plus Protobuf, fast internal calls, streaming, not browser-native.
  • WebSocket full duplex, one open connection per user, stateful.
  • SSE server-to-client push over HTTP with auto-reconnect.
  • Polling short polling wastes requests; long polling holds the request open.
  • Webhook the other system calls you; verify signature, be idempotent, reply fast.
  • Latency vs throughput time per request vs requests per second.
  • Percentiles use p50, p95, p99; averages hide the tail.
  • Latency ladder RAM about 100 ns, SSD about 100 µs, same-DC hop about 0.5 ms, cross-continent about 100 ms.
  • Little's law L = λ × W (in flight = rate × time).
  • Time constants a day is about 105 s; 1 million per day is about 12 per second.
  • Estimation average RPS = per day / 86,400; peak = 2–5x average; storage = items × size × days × replicas.
  • Scale up vs out up is simple but capped; out needs stateless services and a load balancer.
  • Stateless no per-client memory or disk; sessions in Redis or JWT, files in S3.
  • Nines 99.9% about 8.77 h/year; 99.99% about 52.6 min/year; 99.999% about 5.26 min/year.
  • Series multiply availabilities (worse); parallel 1 − product of failure chances (better).
  • SLI / SLO / SLA measurement, internal target, customer contract; the gap is the error budget.
  • SPOF any single component whose failure stops the system; remove with redundancy.
  • Failover active-passive (standby, slower) vs active-active (all serve, more complex); beware split-brain.
  • CAP during a partition choose consistency (CP) or availability (AP); "CA" is not a distributed option.
  • PACELC partition: A or C; else: latency or consistency.
  • Quorum R + W > N makes read and write sets overlap; N = 3, R = W = 2 is typical.
  • Models strong, causal, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, eventual; choose per feature.

Practice — HLD fundamentals

  1. Draw the request path for opening your favourite shopping app's home page. Name every hop and say what could be cached at each one. Done when your diagram has at least six boxes and each has a one-line purpose.
  2. For each case choose REST, gRPC, WebSocket, SSE, long polling or webhook, and give one reason: live cricket score, food delivery map tracking, order service calling inventory service, payment confirmation from Razorpay, collaborative document editing.
  3. A service handles 3,000 requests per second with an average of 80 ms per request. Use Little's law to find the requests in flight. How many Tomcat threads per instance if you run 4 instances and want 50% headroom? Done when you show the calculation.
  4. Estimate for a URL shortener with 100 million new URLs per month and a 10:1 read to write ratio: writes per second, reads per second, storage for 5 years at 500 bytes per record. Done when each line has units and a one-line conclusion about the design.
  5. Estimate storage and bandwidth for a video app: 5 million daily users each upload 0.02 videos of 50 MB and watch 20 minutes at 2 Mbps. State your assumptions and the peak egress in Gbps.
  6. Calculate availability: a load balancer (99.99%), 3 app servers in parallel (99.9% each), and one database (99.95%). Then add a hot standby database (99.95%) in parallel and recalculate. Done when you show both numbers and say which component was the weak point.
  7. Convert your Spring Boot demo to be stateless: move HttpSession data to Redis with Spring Session, start two instances on ports 8081 and 8082, and show that logging in on one keeps you logged in on the other.
  8. Write the partition scenario for a seat-booking system in your own words: which side does what if it chooses CP, and what if it chooses AP? Which would you choose for seats, and for a "viewing now" counter?
  9. With N = 5, list three (R, W) pairs: one that guarantees fresh reads, one fast-write setting, one fast-read setting. Say how many node failures each tolerates for reads and for writes.
  10. Roadmap check: explain to a friend, in two minutes and without notes, the difference between latency and throughput, why we need percentiles, and what 99.99% uptime allows per year.
5

Module 5·HLD · weeks 5–6Must (concepts)

Building blocks

16 topics · about 1.5 h of reading

Every large system is assembled from a small set of reusable parts: DNS and a CDN at the edge, load balancers and gateways at the front door, caches next to the app, replicated and sharded databases, queues between services, and object storage and search engines for special kinds of data. This module explains each block the same way: the problem it solves, how it works, the options, the cost, how it fails, and how to talk about it in an interview.

Module 4 gave you the numbers and the vocabulary (latency, availability, consistency). Here you use them to choose blocks. Many blocks you have already met from the Spring Boot side: caching with @Cacheable, Kafka listeners, replication in SQL. This module takes the system-design view: why the block exists, what breaks at scale, and which trade-off you accept.

  • Explain DNS resolution, TTL trade-offs, GeoDNS, and what a CDN caches and how to invalidate it.
  • Pick a load balancer layer (L4 or L7), an algorithm and a health-check strategy.
  • Design an API gateway and choose a rate-limiting algorithm, with a Redis implementation.
  • Choose a caching pattern and eviction policy, and fix stampede, penetration and avalanche.
  • Climb the database scaling ladder: replicas, partitioning, sharding and consistent hashing.
  • Choose between SQL and the NoSQL families, and between Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS.
  • Design file storage with S3 and presigned URLs, and keep a search index in sync.

DNS in system design

DNS translates names to IP addresses through a cached hierarchy of resolvers; in system design you use it to point users to the nearest or a healthy region (GeoDNS, latency-based routing, failover), and you pick a TTL that balances speed against how fast you can change the answer.

What problem it solves

Humans use names (api.shop.example) and machines use IP addresses. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the distributed phone book that maps one to the other. It is the very first step of almost every request, and it is also a design tool: because you control the answer, you can decide which IP a user receives.

How resolution works

  1. The browser checks its own cache and the operating system cache (and the hosts file).
  2. If missing, it asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the ISP or a public service. The resolver does the legwork.
  3. The resolver asks a root server, then the TLD server (for .com, .in), then the domain's authoritative server, which holds the real records.
  4. The answer comes back with a TTL (time to live): how many seconds every cache may reuse it. Each cache along the way stores it.

Because of caching, most lookups never reach your authoritative server, so DNS is fast and cheap, and also slow to change.

Record types you should know

RecordMapsUse
A / AAAAName to IPv4 / IPv6 addressPoint a site at a server or load balancer
CNAMEName to another namewww to a CDN or load-balancer hostname
NSDomain to its name serversDelegation
MXDomain to mail serversEmail routing
TXTName to textDomain verification, SPF/DKIM

A CNAME cannot sit at the bare domain (zone apex) in standard DNS; cloud providers offer "alias" records for that case.

TTL: the main trade-off

Long TTL (hours)Short TTL (30–60 s)
Load on DNS serversLowHigh
Lookup latency for usersMostly cached, fastMore cold lookups
Speed of change or failoverSlow: stale answers lingerFast
Good forStable recordsFailover records, planned migrations

Before a migration, lower the TTL a day ahead so the cutover takes minutes. Even then, some resolvers and clients ignore TTL and keep old answers longer, so never rely on DNS for instant failover.

DNS as a traffic-steering tool

  • Round-robin DNS: several A records for one name; resolvers rotate them. Crude load spreading with no health awareness.
  • Weighted routing: send 10% of users to the new version (a canary) and 90% to the old.
  • GeoDNS / geolocation routing: answer depends on where the resolver is: Indian users get the Mumbai IP, European users the Frankfurt IP. Good for data-residency rules.
  • Latency-based routing: the provider answers with the region that measured lowest latency to the user.
  • DNS failover: the DNS service runs health checks against each endpoint and stops returning an unhealthy one. Combined with a short TTL this gives regional failover in a minute or two.
  • Anycast: many servers around the world announce the same IP and the network routes each user to the nearest. Used by public DNS and CDNs.

Managed services such as Amazon Route 53 and Cloudflare provide these policies. In the multi-region design from earlier, DNS is the first and coarsest load balancer: it picks the region, then a regional load balancer picks the server.

Failure modes and costs

  • DNS is a SPOF unless you use multiple name servers, ideally from more than one provider. A DNS outage makes a healthy site unreachable.
  • Stale caches keep sending users to a dead IP until TTL expires.
  • JVM caching: Java can cache DNS lookups for a long time in some configurations (see the networkaddress.cache.ttl security property). A service that calls a hostname whose IP changes (a load balancer or a managed database endpoint) can keep using an old IP, so set a modest TTL for long-running JVMs.
  • Cache poisoning and spoofing are attacks on resolvers; DNSSEC adds signatures.

Interview angle

  • "DNS is the first hop. I use latency-based or geo routing to send users to the nearest region and health checks for failover, with a short TTL on those records."
  • State the limit: DNS failover is minutes, not seconds, because clients cache; use a load balancer or anycast for fast failover inside a region.

CDN: content delivery networks

A CDN keeps copies of your content on edge servers close to users so most requests never reach your origin; it cuts latency, bandwidth cost and origin load, and you control it with cache-control headers and versioned URLs.

The problem

Physics sets a floor for latency: a round trip from Bengaluru to a US server is around 200 ms, and a web page needs many round trips. Serving the same 2 MB image from your origin to a million users also burns your bandwidth and CPU. A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a global fleet of edge servers (points of presence, PoPs) that cache your files near users. Examples: Cloudflare, Amazon CloudFront, Akamai, Fastly.

How it works

DNS or anycast sends the user to a nearby edge. On a hit the edge answers at once. On a miss it fetches from the origin, stores the response according to the cache headers, and returns it. Many CDNs add a shield (a middle cache tier) so that a miss in many edges becomes one request to the origin.

Pull vs push CDN

Pull (origin pull)Push
HowEdge fetches from origin on the first missYou upload files to the CDN storage ahead of time
EffortLow: just point the CDN at your originHigher: your build or app uploads and removes files
First requestSlow (miss)Fast (already there)
Storage costOnly what is requestedEverything you push, even if unused
Best forMost sites, frequently changing contentLarge, rarely changing files (game patches, video)

What to put on a CDN: static vs dynamic

Static content (images, CSS, JavaScript bundles, fonts, videos, downloads) is the classic fit: identical for everyone, rarely changing. Dynamic content (a user's cart, a personalised feed) usually cannot be cached shared across users. Modern CDNs still help with dynamic traffic: they keep connections to the origin warm, terminate TLS near the user, compress, can cache API responses that are the same for everybody (a product catalogue for 30 seconds) and can run small code at the edge. Never cache per-user responses under a shared key.

Controlling the cache: HTTP headers

Header / directiveMeaning
Cache-Control: max-age=NBrowsers and CDNs may reuse for N seconds
s-maxage=NLike max-age but only for shared caches such as CDNs
public / privateShared caches may store / only the user's browser may store
no-storeNever store (bank statements, tokens)
no-cacheStore, but revalidate with the origin before each reuse
immutableContent at this URL never changes; skip revalidation
stale-while-revalidate=NServe stale content while fetching a fresh copy in the background
ETag / If-None-MatchValidator: the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body if unchanged
Vary: Accept-EncodingCache separate variants (for example gzip vs plain)
 
@GetMapping("/products/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Product> get(@PathVariable long id) {
    Product p = service.find(id);
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofMinutes(5)).cachePublic())
        .eTag("v" + p.version())
        .body(p);
}

Invalidation: how to change what is cached

  1. Versioned (fingerprinted) URLs: name files by content, app.3f9c2a.js. A new build means a new URL, so the old cache entry is simply never asked for again. Cache these for a year with immutable. This is the best strategy for static assets (Vite and webpack do it by default).
  2. Short TTL for things that change but can be a little stale (a home page for 60 s).
  3. Explicit purge or invalidation: call the CDN API to remove a path. It works but is slower, may cost money per request, and propagates in seconds to minutes. Keep it for emergencies (a wrong price, a legal takedown).
  4. Never cache the HTML shell for long; it points to the fingerprinted files.

Benefits, costs, failure modes

Pros

  • Much lower latency for far-away users.
  • Offloads most bandwidth and requests from the origin.
  • Absorbs traffic spikes and some DDoS attacks.
  • Gives TLS and compression close to the user.

Cons

  • Stale content if headers are wrong; invalidation is slow.
  • Cost per GB and per request; some CDNs charge for purges.
  • Cache-key mistakes can leak private data between users.
  • An extra dependency: a CDN outage can take down the whole site's assets.

Common mistake: caching a response that varies per user

If an API returns data tied to a cookie or Authorization header and the CDN caches it as public, the next user gets someone else's data. Mark such responses private or no-store, and keep cookies out of the cache key for static paths.

Real projects

A typical setup: the React build from Vite goes to S3, CloudFront sits in front, assets are fingerprinted with a one-year cache, index.html has a short TTL, user uploads are served from the same CDN through object-storage URLs (Object storage), and the API is not cached at the edge except for a few public endpoints.

Interview angle

  • "Static assets and media go through a CDN with long-lived, fingerprinted URLs, so deploys do not need purges."
  • Name the trade-off: stale content and invalidation delay in return for latency and offload.
  • For video streaming, say that the CDN carries almost all bytes; the origin only serves misses.

Load balancers: L4 vs L7, algorithms and health checks

A load balancer spreads incoming traffic over several healthy servers behind one address; L4 balancers route by IP and port (fast, simple), L7 balancers read HTTP (smart routing, TLS, headers), and you choose an algorithm and health checks to avoid sending traffic to a sick or overloaded node.

What problem it solves

One server has a limit and is a single point of failure. A load balancer (LB) gives clients one stable address and distributes requests over a pool of servers. It makes horizontal scaling work (Scaling), removes dead servers from rotation, and lets you deploy without downtime by draining one server at a time. For the Nginx basics see DevOps · Module 2.

L4 vs L7

The layers refer to the OSI model. An L4 (transport-layer) balancer sees only IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports; it forwards connections without understanding the content. An L7 (application-layer) balancer terminates the connection, reads the HTTP request (path, host, headers, cookies) and makes a routing decision per request.

L4 load balancerL7 load balancer
SeesIP, port, TCP/UDPURL, headers, cookies, body
SpeedVery fast, millions of connections, low CPUSlower: parses and often decrypts
RoutingBy address and port onlyBy path (/api vs /img), host, header, cookie
TLSPasses through or terminatesUsually terminates; can re-encrypt to backends
Extra featuresFewSticky cookies, compression, rate limits, retries, WAF, redirects
