ProtocolsAny TCP/UDP (databases, gaming, MQTT)HTTP, HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSocket
ExamplesAWS NLB, HAProxy in TCP mode, LVSAWS ALB, Nginx, HAProxy in HTTP mode, Envoy

Common pattern: an L4 balancer or anycast at the very front for raw speed and DDoS absorption, then L7 balancers that route by path to different services.

Balancing algorithms

AlgorithmHow it picksGood for / watch out
Round robin1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 …Equal servers, similar requests. Ignores load.
Weighted round robinBigger servers get more turnsMixed machine sizes, canary releases
Least connectionsServer with the fewest open connectionsUneven or long requests; better than round robin when durations vary
Least response timeFastest recent responses, fewest connectionsAdapts to slow nodes. Needs measurement.
IP hashHash of client IP chooses the serverCheap stickiness. Breaks when pool changes; NAT groups many users on one IP.
Consistent hashingHash of a key (user id, URL) onto a ringCache servers and shards: few keys move when nodes change (details)
Random / power of two choicesPick two at random, take the less loadedScales well with many balancers; near-optimal

Health checks

The balancer must know who is alive.

  • Active checks: the balancer probes each server every few seconds (a TCP connect or an HTTP GET to /actuator/health). After N failures the server is removed; after M successes it returns.
  • Passive checks: the balancer watches real traffic; too many errors or timeouts from a server mark it down. No extra probe traffic, but real users hit the failure first.

Design the health endpoint carefully. A liveness check says the process runs. A readiness check says it can take traffic (database connected, warmed up). Do not make the check depend on every downstream service: if the shared database slows down and every health check fails, the balancer pulls all servers out and you cause a total outage. Also use connection draining (finish in-flight requests before removing a server) and slow start for new servers.

upstream api_servers {
    least_conn;
    server 10.0.1.11:8080 weight=2 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    server 10.0.1.12:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    server 10.0.1.13:8080 backup;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name api.shop.example;
    # ssl_certificate and key directives here: TLS ends at the balancer

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://api_servers;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;
    }
}

Sticky sessions, TLS termination and routing

  • Sticky sessions (session affinity) pin a client to one server using a cookie or IP hash. Downsides: uneven load, lost sessions when the server dies, harder deploys. Prefer stateless apps with a shared session store.
  • TLS termination: the balancer holds the certificate, decrypts, and talks plain HTTP (or re-encrypts) to backends. This centralises certificates and saves CPU on app servers. Inside a trusted network plain HTTP is common; stricter setups re-encrypt (end-to-end TLS) or use mutual TLS.
  • Path and host routing: /api/* to the API pool, /ws/* to the WebSocket pool, admin.shop.example to a locked-down pool. Also blue-green and canary rollouts by weights.
  • Client IP: behind an L7 balancer the app sees the balancer's IP; read X-Forwarded-For (and configure Spring Boot's forwarded-headers support).

Making the load balancer itself highly available

A single balancer is a new single point of failure. Options: run two in active-passive with a floating virtual IP that moves on failure (keepalived and VRRP for self-managed), or active-active behind DNS or anycast. Cloud load balancers (ALB, NLB, Google Cloud Load Balancing) are already distributed across zones and managed for you. In Kubernetes the Service, Ingress and the cloud load balancer play these roles (DevOps · Module 5). There is also client-side load balancing (the client library such as Spring Cloud LoadBalancer picks an instance from a service registry) and a service mesh sidecar, both common between internal services.

Failure modes

  • All servers fail health checks together (a bad check) and traffic goes nowhere.
  • Retry storms: the balancer retries failed requests on other servers and doubles the load on an already struggling pool. Limit retries and use backoff.
  • Uneven load from sticky sessions or from a few very heavy clients.
  • Thundering herd on a recovering server; slow start helps.
  • Idle timeouts: the balancer closes long-lived connections (WebSockets, long polls) unless timeouts are raised and heartbeats sent.

Interview angle

  • "An L7 balancer routes by path and terminates TLS; an L4 balancer is faster and good for raw TCP. I use least connections when request durations vary, and active health checks on a readiness endpoint."
  • "The balancer is redundant: two across zones, or a managed cloud balancer."
  • Mention connection draining for zero-downtime deployments, and that sticky sessions are a smell rather than a design.

API gateway and BFF

An API gateway is the single front door for clients of a microservice system: it routes requests and handles the cross-cutting work (authentication, rate limiting, TLS, logging, aggregation, protocol translation) so each service does not repeat it; a BFF is a gateway tailored to one kind of client.

The problem

With ten microservices, a mobile app would need ten addresses, ten authentication checks, and ten round trips to draw one screen. Every service would also re-implement rate limits, logging and CORS. An API gateway is a server that sits between clients and your services and presents one uniform entry point. A gateway differs from a plain load balancer: the load balancer spreads traffic over identical servers; the gateway understands your APIs and decides which service gets each call.

Responsibilities

JobWhat it does
RoutingMaps /orders/** to the order service, by path, host, header or version
Authentication / authorisationValidates the JWT or API key once at the edge, passes identity downstream
Rate limiting and quotasProtects services and enforces plans (next article)
TLS terminationHandles certificates; internal traffic can be simpler
Request aggregationOne client call fans out to several services and merges the result
Protocol translationPublic REST/JSON to internal gRPC; WebSocket upgrades
ResilienceTimeouts, retries, circuit breaker, fallback responses
ObservabilityAccess logs, metrics, a correlation id on every request
Caching, compression, CORS, request validationCommon web concerns, handled in one place

Common products: Spring Cloud Gateway (a natural fit for a Java team), Kong, NGINX, Envoy-based gateways, AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management. See Spring Boot · Module 7 for Spring Cloud Gateway.

Backend for Frontend (BFF)

One generic gateway tends to grow a lot of client-specific code. A Backend for Frontend gives each client type its own thin gateway service: a mobile BFF that returns compact payloads for slow networks, a web BFF that returns what the React app needs, a partner BFF with a stable versioned API. The BFF belongs to the front-end team, aggregates calls, and shapes responses, while the core services stay generic. The cost is more services to run and some duplicated code.

Trade-offs and failure modes

  • Single point of failure and bottleneck: run many gateway instances behind a load balancer; keep the gateway stateless and fast.
  • Extra hop: adds a few milliseconds. Keep logic in the gateway thin.
  • The "god gateway": if business logic creeps in, the gateway becomes a monolith that every team must change. Keep it to cross-cutting work and routing.
  • Gateway security is not enough: services should still verify identity (zero trust) in case something bypasses the gateway.

What a request goes through

Seeing the order of work makes the gateway concrete. A call to GET /orders/42 from a mobile app passes through a chain of steps. Each step can reject the request early, which is why the cheap checks (TLS, rate limit, token) come before the expensive one (calling a service).

Two details matter. First, the gateway must remove any identity header sent by the client (such as X-User-Id) before it adds its own, or a user could pretend to be someone else. Second, it must add a correlation id (for example X-Request-Id) so one request can be followed through every service log.

Gateway vs load balancer vs reverse proxy vs service mesh

These four are often mixed up, and interviewers like the question. They overlap in technology (Envoy and NGINX appear in several roles) but differ in purpose.

ComponentSitsMain jobUnderstands your API?
Load balancerIn front of copies of one serviceSpread traffic, health checksNo (L4) or a little (L7)
Reverse proxyIn front of serversForward requests, TLS, caching, compressionOnly paths and headers
API gatewayAt the edge, for external clientsRouting between services, auth, quotas, aggregationYes: routes, plans, API keys
Service meshBeside every service (sidecar), for internal callsmTLS, retries, timeouts, telemetry between servicesTraffic level, not business meaning

A short way to remember: the gateway handles north-south traffic (clients to your system); a service mesh handles east-west traffic (service to service). Most systems use a load balancer in front of the gateway instances, a gateway at the edge, and optionally a mesh inside. See DNS and CDN for what sits even further out.

A configuration example: Spring Cloud Gateway

For a Java team, Spring Cloud Gateway is the natural pick: it is a Spring Boot application, so routes, filters and security use the tools you already know. A route has an id, a target uri, predicates (when the route matches) and filters (what to change on the way). The setup, the starter and the filter catalogue are covered in Spring Boot · Module 7.

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: orders
          uri: http://order-service:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1          # /api/orders/42 becomes /orders/42
        - id: catalog
          uri: http://catalog-service:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/products/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1

Property names changed in newer Spring Cloud releases

Newer Spring Cloud Gateway releases split the project into a WebFlux server and a WebMVC server, and the route properties moved under a longer prefix (for example spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.routes). The same route can also be written in Java with RouteLocatorBuilder. Check the reference of the version in your project before copying YAML.

BFF in practice: one call, three services

A mobile home screen needs the user's name, the open orders and a few recommendations. Without a BFF, the phone makes three calls over a slow network. A BFF makes the three calls on the fast data-centre network, in parallel, and returns one small JSON:

import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.client.WebClient;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

record Home(String userName, String openOrders, String picks) { }

class HomeBff {
    private final WebClient users;
    private final WebClient orders;
    private final WebClient recs;

    HomeBff(WebClient users, WebClient orders, WebClient recs) {
        this.users = users;
        this.orders = orders;
        this.recs = recs;
    }

    Mono<Home> home(String userId) {
        Mono<String> u = users.get().uri("/users/{id}", userId)
                .retrieve().bodyToMono(String.class);
        Mono<String> o = orders.get().uri("/orders?user={id}&status=open", userId)
                .retrieve().bodyToMono(String.class);
        Mono<String> r = recs.get().uri("/picks/{id}", userId)
                .retrieve().bodyToMono(String.class)
                .onErrorReturn("[]");                 // recommendations are optional
        return Mono.zip(u, o, r, Home::new);           // three calls run in parallel
    }
}

Note the last design choice: recommendations are optional, so if that service fails the screen still loads with an empty list. Decide for each downstream call whether it is required or optional; that is graceful degradation. (The code assumes Spring WebFlux is on the classpath.)

More failure modes and how to handle them

  • Slow service drags the gateway down: without timeouts, threads or connections pile up on the slow backend and the gateway stops answering everyone. Set a timeout per route and a limit on concurrent calls.
  • Retry storms: if the gateway retries failed calls and every instance does the same, a struggling service receives double or triple the load. Retry only safe (idempotent) requests, a small number of times, with back-off.
  • Circuit breaker: after repeated failures, stop calling the service for a while and return a fallback or a fast 503.
  • Bad config deploy: a wrong route takes the whole site down. Keep route config in version control, roll out gradually and keep the last good version.
  • Large uploads and long connections: proxying big files or WebSockets through the gateway consumes its memory and connections. Use presigned URLs to object storage for uploads (see Object storage).

Pros

  • One public address and one place for TLS, auth, quotas and logs.
  • Clients are shielded from internal service moves and splits.
  • Aggregation cuts mobile round trips.

Cons

  • One more hop and one more component to run, scale and secure.
  • A shared gateway team can become a bottleneck for releases.
  • Risk of business logic creeping in.

Rules

  • Keep the gateway stateless so any instance can handle any request, and run at least two instances.
  • Strip client-supplied identity headers; add trusted ones after authentication.
  • Every route needs a timeout. No exceptions.

Conventions

  • Version the public API in the path (/v1/orders) and route versions to different services if needed.
  • Return consistent error bodies and use 429 for rate limits and 503 for an unavailable backend.
  • Log request id, route, status and latency; alert on latency percentiles and 5xx rate (Latency, throughput and percentiles).

When NOT to use a gateway (or a BFF)

  • A monolith or two services: a reverse proxy and a load balancer are enough.
  • One client type with similar needs: a shared gateway is enough; a BFF per client is extra cost.
  • Service-to-service calls inside the cluster should not detour through the public gateway; use direct calls, or a mesh.

Interview angle

  • "Clients talk only to the gateway; it authenticates, rate limits and routes. Services behind it stay private."
  • Contrast it with a load balancer in one line: the balancer spreads load over copies of one service, the gateway routes between different services and applies policies.
  • Mention BFF when a mobile and a web client have very different needs.

Interview: follow-ups on the gateway

  • Gateway vs load balancer? The balancer picks among identical servers; the gateway chooses between different services and applies API policies.
  • Gateway vs service mesh? Gateway: edge, north-south. Mesh: inside, east-west.
  • Is the gateway a single point of failure? Not if you run several stateless instances behind a load balancer and across zones.
  • When BFF? When clients (mobile, web, partners) need different payloads and release at different speeds.
  • Where does authorisation happen? Coarse checks (token valid, scope) at the gateway; fine-grained business rules in the service.

Rate limiting: algorithms, Redis and responses

Rate limiting caps how many requests a client may make in a time window to protect the system from abuse and overload; the main algorithms are token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, sliding window log and sliding window counter, and a distributed limiter keeps its counters in Redis with atomic operations.

Why limit, and who to limit

A rate limiter rejects or delays requests above an allowed rate. It protects against accidental overload (a client bug in a retry loop), abuse and scraping, brute-force logins, and noisy neighbours in a shared system. It also enforces paid plans (100 calls per minute on the free tier) and keeps costs predictable. You choose the key to limit by: user id, API key, IP address, tenant, or an endpoint (login is limited more strictly than reads).

Where to rate limit

  • CDN / edge / WAF: blocks floods early and cheaply, mostly by IP.
  • API gateway or load balancer: the usual place; one policy for all services, before expensive work happens.
  • In the service: fine-grained limits that need business knowledge (per-tenant quotas, expensive endpoints), using a library such as Bucket4j or Resilience4j.
  • Client side: well-behaved clients also limit themselves, but never trust that.

The five algorithms

1. Token bucket

A bucket holds up to capacity tokens. Tokens are added at a fixed refill rate. Each request takes one token; with none left, the request is rejected. Because the bucket can fill while a client is idle, short bursts are allowed (up to the capacity) but the long-term average stays at the refill rate. Memory is tiny: two numbers per key (tokens and last refill time). This is the most widely used algorithm (used by API gateways and cloud providers). A Java implementation is in Module 3.

2. Leaky bucket

Requests enter a queue of fixed size (the bucket) and leave at a constant rate (the leak). If the queue is full, new requests are dropped. The output is perfectly smooth, which is good when the downstream system needs steady traffic (a payment partner that accepts exactly 50 per second). Cost: bursts are queued and delayed rather than served at once, and old requests may wait behind new ones.

3. Fixed window counter

Count requests per fixed time slot (for example per minute). If the count exceeds the limit, reject until the next slot. Very simple and cheap (one counter per key per window). The flaw is the boundary burst: with a limit of 100 per minute, a client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00, so 200 requests in two seconds.

4. Sliding window log

Keep a timestamp of every request in the last window (a sorted set). On each request remove old timestamps, count the rest, allow if under the limit. This is exact, with no boundary burst. Cost: memory proportional to the limit per key (storing 10,000 timestamps for a 10,000-per-hour key), so it suits low limits.

5. Sliding window counter

A cheap approximation of the log. Keep counters for the current and previous fixed windows, and weight the previous one by how much of it still overlaps the sliding window:

estimate = current_count + previous_count × (1 − elapsed_fraction_of_current_window)

Limit 100 per minute. Previous minute: 80. Now 15 s into this minute: 30 so far.
estimate = 30 + 80 × (1 − 15/60) = 30 + 60 = 90  → allow (under 100)

Memory is two counters per key, and the smoothing is good enough in practice (the error is small when traffic is fairly even). It is a popular balanced choice.

Comparison

AlgorithmBurstsAccuracyMemory per keyWeak point
Token bucketAllowed up to capacityGood2 numbersBurst can stress downstream
Leaky bucketSmoothed into a steady flowGoodA queueAdds delay; queue management
Fixed windowDouble burst at boundariesPoor1 counterBoundary burst
Sliding window logNoExactOne entry per requestMemory heavy
Sliding window counterSmoothedApproximate2 countersAssumes even traffic

A distributed implementation with Redis

With many gateway instances, counters cannot live in each instance's memory (a client could get N times the limit). Keep them in Redis, shared by all instances. The operations must be atomic or two requests can both read "99" and both be allowed.

Fixed window with INCR and EXPIRE
import java.time.Duration;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;

public class FixedWindowLimiter {
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final int limit;
    private final Duration window;

    public FixedWindowLimiter(StringRedisTemplate redis, int limit, Duration window) {
        this.redis = redis;
        this.limit = limit;
        this.window = window;
    }

    public boolean allow(String clientId) {
        long slot = System.currentTimeMillis() / window.toMillis();
        String key = "rl:" + clientId + ":" + slot;
        Long count = redis.opsForValue().increment(key);   // atomic INCR
        if (count != null && count == 1) {
            redis.expire(key, window);                     // first hit sets the TTL
        }
        return count != null && count <= limit;
    }
}

Watch the gap between INCR and EXPIRE: if the process dies in between, the key never expires. Including the window slot in the key makes stale keys harmless, and a Lua script removes the gap entirely.

Token bucket as a Lua script

Redis runs a Lua script atomically, so read-modify-write is safe. This script keeps tokens and the last refill time in a hash. (Check your Redis version's rules for using time inside scripts; passing now from the caller is the simplest portable way, at the price of clock differences between app servers.)

-- KEYS[1] = bucket key
-- ARGV[1] = capacity, ARGV[2] = refill tokens per second, ARGV[3] = now in ms
local data = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local tokens = tonumber(data[1])
local ts = tonumber(data[2])
if tokens == nil then
  tokens = capacity
  ts = now
end
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= 1 then
  tokens = tokens - 1
  allowed = 1
end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / rate * 1000) * 2)
return allowed

From Java, run it with Spring Data Redis's DefaultRedisScript and redis.execute(script, keys, args...). Sliding window log in Redis uses a sorted set: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE (drop old), ZCARD (count), ZADD (record), wrapped in a script or a transaction.

What to return to the client

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 12
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1731312000
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"rate_limit_exceeded","message":"Try again in 12 seconds"}
  • Use status 429 Too Many Requests, not 403 or 500.
  • Retry-After tells well-behaved clients how many seconds to wait.
  • The X-RateLimit-* headers (a widespread convention; an IETF draft standardises similar RateLimit-* names) let clients slow down before they are rejected.
  • Clients should respond with exponential backoff with jitter.

Design decisions and failure modes

  • Fail open or closed? If Redis is down, should the limiter let all traffic through (risking overload) or block all (risking an outage)? Most systems fail open for ordinary APIs and fail closed for security-critical ones such as login. Keep a small local fallback limiter.
  • Race conditions: use atomic commands or Lua, never read-then-write from the app.
  • Latency: a Redis round trip per request adds about a millisecond; limit locally in batches or use sticky routing if that matters.
  • Hot keys and sharding: one very popular client key sits on one Redis node; shard keys by client id.
  • Rule hierarchy: per-IP, per-user and global limits together; return the strictest.
  • Distinguish rate limiting from load shedding: limits are per client; load shedding drops requests when the whole system is overloaded.

Common mistake: limiting by IP only

Many users share one IP behind a company or mobile carrier NAT, and attackers rotate IPs. Limit by authenticated identity when you can, and use IP limits as a coarse outer layer.

Interview angle

  • "I use a token bucket in the gateway: it allows short bursts and enforces a steady average, and it needs only two values per client in Redis."
  • Explain why fixed windows allow double bursts at the boundary, and how the sliding window counter fixes it cheaply.
  • Return 429 with Retry-After; decide fail-open vs fail-closed out loud.

Caching: layers, patterns, eviction and invalidation

A cache keeps copies of expensive-to-get data in a faster place; you choose where to cache (browser, CDN, proxy, app, Redis), a read/write pattern (cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind, write-around), an eviction policy (LRU, LFU, TTL) and an invalidation strategy, accepting some staleness in return for speed and lower load.

What problem it solves

Reading from memory is about 1,000 times faster than from SSD and far faster than a cross-network database query (latency numbers). Most workloads read a small hot set of data again and again (the same products, the same profiles). A cache stores that hot data in fast storage so most reads skip the slow source. Benefits: lower latency, higher throughput, fewer database queries (and a smaller database bill). The price: stale data, extra moving parts, and the famous hard problem of knowing when to invalidate.

For Spring's @Cacheable and Redis integration see Spring Boot · Module 6, and for Redis itself SQL · Module 6. This article is the system-design view.

Where to cache: the layers

LayerCachesStrengthWeakness
Browser / clientStatic files, API responses with headersZero network costYou cannot purge a user's browser
CDNStatic assets, public pagesNear the user, huge offloadSlow invalidation (CDN)
Reverse proxy (Nginx, Varnish)Whole HTTP responsesNo app code changeCoarse; keys by URL
Application local (Caffeine, in-heap map)Hot objects, config, lookupsNanoseconds, no networkEach instance has its own copy; may disagree
Distributed (Redis, Memcached)Sessions, objects, query results, countersShared by all instances, largeNetwork hop; an extra system to run
Database (buffer pool, query cache)Pages and index blocks in memoryAutomaticOutside your control; still a DB call

A common combo is a tiny local cache (Caffeine) in front of Redis: a "two-level" cache. It is fastest but doubles the staleness problem, so keep local TTLs very short (seconds).

The caching patterns

PatternRead pathWrite pathConsistencyMain risk
Cache-asideApp checks cache, on a miss loads from DB and fills the cacheApp writes to DB, then deletes (or updates) the cache keyEventual; stale until TTL or deleteRaces between a delete and a concurrent read-fill
Read-throughCache itself loads from DB on a missSame as cache-asideEventualNeeds a cache layer with loader support
Write-throughReads hit a warm cacheWrite goes to cache and DB together, returns after bothStrong between cache and DBSlower writes; caches data never read
Write-behind (write-back)Reads hit the cacheWrite to cache, DB updated later in batchesDB lags behindData loss if the cache dies before flushing
Write-aroundMisses go to DB then cacheWrites go to DB only, bypass cacheCache stale until TTLFirst read after write is slow
  • Cache-aside is the default for web apps: simple, resilient (if the cache dies, the app still works from the database), and caches only what is requested. Spring's @Cacheable implements it.
  • Read-through is the same idea with the loading logic inside the cache library or service (Caffeine LoadingCache, many managed caches).
  • Write-through keeps the cache always fresh for written data; good for read-heavy data that is updated rarely and must not be stale (profile settings). Write latency is the cost.
  • Write-behind gives very fast writes and batching (counters, analytics), but you can lose acknowledged writes. Use it only where loss is tolerable or the cache is durable.
  • Write-around avoids filling the cache with data that is written once and rarely read (logs, uploads).
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Optional;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

public class ProductService {
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final ProductRepository repo;
    private final ObjectMapper json = new ObjectMapper();

    public ProductService(StringRedisTemplate redis, ProductRepository repo) {
        this.redis = redis;
        this.repo = repo;
    }

    public Optional<Product> find(long id) throws Exception {
        String key = "product:" + id;
        String cached = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
        if (cached != null) {                                   // hit
            return Optional.of(json.readValue(cached, Product.class));
        }
        Optional<Product> fromDb = repo.findById(id);           // miss
        if (fromDb.isPresent()) {
            redis.opsForValue().set(key, json.writeValueAsString(fromDb.get()),
                                    Duration.ofMinutes(5));
        }
        return fromDb;
    }

    public void update(Product p) {
        repo.save(p);                                           // 1. write the source of truth
        redis.delete("product:" + p.id());                      // 2. then invalidate the cache
    }
}

Note the order in update: write the database first, then delete the cache entry. Deleting first lets a concurrent reader refill the cache with the old value before your write lands. Even in the right order a tiny race window remains; a TTL bounds the damage.

Eviction policies

Memory is limited, so when the cache is full it must evict something.

PolicyEvictsGood forWeakness
LRU (least recently used)The entry untouched the longestGeneral use; recent items are likely reusedOne big scan can flush the hot set
LFU (least frequently used)The entry used the fewest timesStable popularity (top products)Old popular items linger; needs counters
FIFOThe oldest insertedSimpleIgnores usage entirely
TTL (time to live)Entries after a fixed lifetimeBounding stalenessNot an eviction by memory pressure by itself
RandomA random entryCheap, surprisingly decentUnpredictable

Redis configures this with maxmemory and maxmemory-policy (for example allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-ttl; Redis uses sampled approximations rather than an exact LRU). Caffeine uses a modern frequency-aware policy (W-TinyLFU).

LRU is a classic interview coding task. A hash map plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) get and put. In Java, LinkedHashMap in access order does it in a few lines:

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;

    public LruCache(int capacity) {
        super(16, 0.75f, true);              // true = access order (LRU)
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
        return size() > capacity;            // evict the least recently used
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LruCache<String, Integer> c = new LruCache<>(2);
        c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2);
        c.get("a");                          // a is now most recent
        c.put("c", 3);                       // evicts b
        System.out.println(c.keySet());
    }
}
[a, c]

This class is not thread-safe; production code uses Caffeine or Redis.

Invalidation strategies

  • TTL only: accept staleness up to N seconds. Simple and robust; always set one, even when you also invalidate explicitly, as a safety net.
  • Explicit invalidation on write: delete the key (or tag) after updating the database. Fresh, but every writer must know every cached view of the data.
  • Event-driven invalidation: publish a "product changed" event (Kafka, Redis pub/sub, or CDC from the database log); consumers evict. Decouples writers from caches.
  • Versioned keys: include a version in the key (product:42:v7); a new version makes the old entry unreachable, and eviction cleans it up.
  • Write-through or refresh-ahead: update or reload the entry instead of deleting it.

"There are only two hard things in computer science"

Cache invalidation is on the famous list because the cache and the source can disagree in many ways: races, failed deletes, multiple writers, derived data. The robust answer is: short TTL for safety, delete on write for freshness, and a design where occasional staleness is acceptable.

What to cache, and what not to

Cache this

  • Read-heavy, rarely changing data: catalogues, configuration, reference data.
  • Expensive results: aggregates, rendered fragments, results of slow joins.
  • Hot objects: popular profiles, trending lists, session data.
  • Data where slight staleness is fine.

Avoid or be careful

  • Frequently changing data with strict freshness needs (account balance, stock count at checkout).
  • Write-heavy data that is rarely re-read.
  • Per-user private data in a shared cache without the user id in the key.
  • Huge objects, or anything that is cheaper to compute than to fetch.

Interview angle

  • "I use cache-aside with Redis, a TTL of a few minutes, and delete the key after writing the database."
  • Be ready to compare write-through (fresh, slower writes) with write-behind (fast, can lose data).
  • For eviction, say LRU by default; LFU when popularity is stable; mention O(1) with a hash map and a doubly linked list.

Classic cache problems: stampede, penetration, avalanche, hot keys

Caches fail in a few well-known ways: stale data, a stampede when a hot key expires, penetration by requests for keys that do not exist, an avalanche when many keys expire together, and hot keys that overload one node; each has a standard fix, and the hit ratio tells you if the cache works.

1. Stale data

The cache holds an old value after the source changed. Causes: a TTL that is too long, a missed invalidation, a race between a read-fill and a write. Fixes: delete on write after the database commit, a short TTL as a safety net, versioned keys, and event-based invalidation. Decide per data type how much staleness the business accepts: a product description may be 10 minutes old, a stock count at checkout may not.

2. Cache stampede (thundering herd)

A very popular key expires. In the same instant, thousands of requests miss, and all of them run the same expensive database query to rebuild it. The database spikes or collapses.

Fixes:

  • Locking (mutex per key): only the first requester rebuilds; the others wait or get the old value. Distributed version: SET lock:key token NX PX 5000 in Redis; always set an expiry on the lock and release it only if you still own it.
  • Request coalescing (single flight): inside one instance, concurrent requests for the same key share one in-flight load. In Java use a ConcurrentHashMap of CompletableFuture, or Caffeine's LoadingCache, which already does this.
  • Early (probabilistic) refresh: refresh a key shortly before it expires, in the background, or let the cache serve slightly stale data while one request refreshes (stale-while-revalidate).
  • Never-expire hot keys and refresh them with a scheduled job.
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public class SingleFlight<V> {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<V>> inFlight =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public V load(String key, Supplier<V> loader) {
        CompletableFuture<V> mine = new CompletableFuture<>();
        CompletableFuture<V> existing = inFlight.putIfAbsent(key, mine);
        if (existing != null) {
            return existing.join();               // someone else is loading: wait for them
        }
        try {
            V value = loader.get();               // only one thread runs the expensive load
            mine.complete(value);
            return value;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            mine.completeExceptionally(e);
            throw e;
        } finally {
            inFlight.remove(key);
        }
    }
}

3. Cache penetration

Requests ask for keys that do not exist (a random product id, or an attacker's flood). The cache never has them, so every request goes through to the database, and the cache gives no protection.

  • Cache the empty result (a "null" marker) with a short TTL, such as 30–60 seconds.
  • Bloom filter in front: a compact probabilistic set of all valid ids. If the filter says "definitely not present", reject at once. It can have false positives (rare, a harmless extra DB check) but never false negatives. Libraries: Guava BloomFilter; Redis has Bloom filter support through its modules. You must add new ids to the filter when records are created.
  • Validate input (id ranges, formats) and apply rate limiting per client.

4. Cache avalanche

Many keys expire at the same moment (you loaded them together with the same TTL), or the whole cache restarts empty. Suddenly the database gets the load of everything. Fixes:

  • TTL jitter: add a random amount, for example 5 minutes plus a random 0–60 seconds.
  • Warm the cache before taking traffic after a restart.
  • High availability for the cache (Redis replicas or cluster) so one failure does not empty it.
  • Protect the database: rate limiting, circuit breaker, request queues, and degraded responses if the cache is down.
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;

static Duration ttlWithJitter(Duration base, Duration maxJitter) {
    long extra = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(maxJitter.toSeconds() + 1);
    return base.plusSeconds(extra);       // 5 min + 0..60 s
}

5. Hot keys

One key gets a huge share of traffic (a celebrity's profile, a flash-sale product). In a sharded cache that key lives on one node, which becomes the bottleneck even though the cluster is idle. Fixes: a short local (in-process) cache in front of Redis for those keys; replicate the hot key under several names (product:42#1 … #8) and read a random one; detect hot keys by monitoring and promote them automatically.

Summary table

ProblemWhat happensMain fixes
Stale dataOld value servedDelete on write, short TTL, versioned keys
StampedeMany rebuilds of one expired keyLock, single flight, early refresh
PenetrationMisses for non-existent keys hit the DBCache null, Bloom filter, validation
AvalancheMany keys expire togetherTTL jitter, warm-up, HA cache
Hot keyOne node overloadedLocal cache, key replication

Measuring: the hit ratio

Hit ratio = hits ÷ (hits + misses). A healthy read cache is often above 90%, but the right target depends on the workload. A cache with a 60% hit ratio and an expensive miss path may not be worth its complexity. In Redis, INFO stats reports keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses. Also watch evictions (a high count means the cache is too small), memory use, latency, and the miss-path latency. Spring Boot Actuator and Micrometer expose cache metrics (Spring Boot · Module 6).

The value of a hit ratio is easy to compute: if a hit costs 1 ms and a miss costs 51 ms (1 ms cache check plus 50 ms database), a 90% ratio gives an average of 0.9 × 1 + 0.1 × 51 = 6 ms; at 99% it is 1.5 ms. Small ratio gains matter a lot when misses are expensive.

Common mistakes

  • Caching without a TTL: stale entries live forever after one missed invalidation.
  • One shared TTL for everything loaded together (avalanche).
  • Not caching "not found", so misses are never absorbed.
  • Storing mutable objects shared across threads in a local cache, then changing them.
  • Treating the cache as the source of truth. It can disappear at any time; the app must work without it, only slower.

Interview angle

  • Name all three: stampede (hot key expires; fix with locking or early refresh), penetration (non-existent keys; fix with null caching and Bloom filters), avalanche (mass expiry; fix with TTL jitter).
  • Explain the cache-aside write order: database first, then delete the key.
  • Close with the metric: "I would track the hit ratio, evictions and miss latency."

The database scaling ladder

Scale a database in order of cost and risk: tune queries and indexes, scale up the machine, add caching, add read replicas, partition big tables, and only then shard; denormalization and federation are side tools along the way.

Why a ladder

The database is usually the first real bottleneck, because it holds shared state and cannot simply be cloned like a stateless app server. Each step up the ladder buys more capacity but costs more complexity. A strong answer climbs one rung at a time and says what number forces the next rung. Jumping straight to sharding for 500 requests per second is a classic over-engineering mistake.

Rung by rung

  1. Query and index tuning. Find slow queries (EXPLAIN, slow-query log), add the right indexes, remove N+1 queries, fix missing pagination, use connection pooling (HikariCP) and proper pool sizes. One missing index can cost 100x. This is free capacity and always comes first (SQL · Module 5).
  2. Scale up (vertical). More CPU, RAM and faster NVMe disks. RAM matters most: if the working set (the hot data and indexes) fits in memory, reads are fast. Needs no code change, but has a ceiling and a single point of failure.
  3. Caching. Move repeated reads to Redis or a local cache (Caching). Often removes 80–95% of read load for read-heavy products. Does nothing for writes.
  4. Read replicas. Copy the data to followers and send reads to them (Replication). Scales reads almost linearly; writes still go to one primary; adds replication lag.
  5. Partitioning. Split one huge table into smaller pieces inside the same database (by date or id range). Queries touching one partition scan far less data, old partitions can be dropped or archived cheaply. Still one server.
  6. Sharding. Split data across several independent database servers so writes and storage scale out (Sharding). The biggest step: queries, transactions and operations all become harder.

Partitioning vs sharding

PartitioningSharding
WhereInside one database serverAcross many servers
GoalFaster queries, easier maintenanceScale writes and storage beyond one machine
Transactions and joinsWork normallyHard across shards
Application impactMostly noneLarge: routing, shard key, resharding

The word "partition" is also used loosely for "a shard" (Kafka partitions, DynamoDB partitions), so ask which one is meant.

Side tools

  • Denormalization: store redundant data to avoid joins (copy the user's name into each comment row, keep a precomputed like_count). Reads get faster; writes get more complex and the copies can drift apart, so update them from one place or an event.
  • Federation (functional partitioning): split the database by feature, not by row: a users database, an orders database, a products database. Each is smaller and can be scaled and tuned separately. The price is that joins across them move into application code, and it fits naturally with microservices owning their data.
  • CQRS-style read models: write to the main store, project data into a separate store optimised for reading (a search index, a denormalised table).
  • Archival: move old rows to cheap storage; smaller hot tables are faster.
  • Choose a different database when the access pattern fits one better (SQL vs NoSQL).

Worked reasoning

Suppose the estimate says 7,000 peak requests per second, 90% reads (the estimation example). Reads would be 6,300 per second. With a 90% cache hit ratio only about 630 reads per second reach the database. A single primary with a couple of replicas handles that and the 700 writes per second easily. So the design needs cache plus replicas, not sharding, today. Sharding enters only when the dataset grows beyond one server's disk (the estimate showed about 36 TB of metadata in five years) or writes exceed what one primary can do (many thousands per second).

Common mistake: sharding to fix a slow query

If one query is slow, spreading the table across servers will not fix a missing index; it will only make the problem 10 times larger and harder to debug. Measure first, then pick the rung that addresses the measured limit: CPU, memory, disk IO, connections, or storage size.

Interview angle

  • "I would start with indexes and query tuning, then a cache and read replicas. Sharding is the last resort because it breaks joins and transactions."
  • Say which limit you are hitting: read throughput (cache and replicas), write throughput or storage size (sharding).

Replication: leader–follower, multi-leader, leaderless

Replication keeps copies of the data on several nodes for availability and read scale; the usual setup is one leader with followers, synchronous replication is safer but slower than asynchronous, and asynchronous replication causes lag, which you handle with read-your-writes tricks.

Why replicate

Three reasons: availability (if the primary dies, a copy can take over), read scalability (many followers serve reads), and latency (a copy near the users). Replication does not scale writes (every copy must apply every write) and it does not replace backups (a bad DELETE replicates too). For SQL basics see SQL · Module 6.

Leader–follower (primary–replica)

One node, the leader, accepts writes and records them in a log (the WAL in PostgreSQL, the binlog in MySQL). Followers stream and replay the log. Reads can go to any follower. It is simple, has no write conflicts (one writer), and is the default in PostgreSQL, MySQL and most managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL). If the leader fails, a follower is promoted (failover).

Synchronous vs asynchronous

SynchronousAsynchronousSemi-synchronous
Leader waits forAll followers to confirmNobodyAt least one follower
Write latencyHigher; slowest followerLowestMedium
Data loss on leader crashNonePossible: recent writes not copiedVery unlikely
If a follower is downWrites can stallNo effectSwitch to another follower

Fully synchronous replication to all followers is rarely used because one slow node blocks writes. Most systems use async, or semi-sync with one synchronous follower so a committed write exists on at least two machines. This is the PACELC latency vs consistency choice in action (CAP and PACELC).

Replication lag and its anomalies

With async replication a follower may be milliseconds to seconds (sometimes minutes under load) behind. Readers see odd things:

  • Read-your-writes violation: you post a comment, the page reloads from a follower and your comment is missing.
  • Non-monotonic reads: one read hits a fresh follower, the next hits a stale one and data seems to go back in time.
  • Causality violation: a reply is visible but the question is not yet.

Mitigations: read from the leader for the user's own data or for a few seconds after a write; route critical reads (balances, checkout) to the leader; track the log position of the user's last write and read only from a follower that has reached it; pin a user to one follower (monotonic reads); monitor lag and take a lagging follower out of rotation. In Spring, a routing DataSource chooses leader or follower by whether a transaction is read-only (@Transactional(readOnly = true)).

import org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.lookup.AbstractRoutingDataSource;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionSynchronizationManager;

public class ReadWriteRoutingDataSource extends AbstractRoutingDataSource {
    @Override
    protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() {
        return TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly()
            ? "replica" : "primary";      // keys registered as target data sources
    }
}

Wrap the target sources in a LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the routing decision is made after the transaction's read-only flag is set; this is a common gotcha.

Failover details

Promoting a follower means: detect the failure (heartbeats and timeouts), choose the most up-to-date follower, reconfigure the others and the clients, and fence the old leader. Risks: with async replication the promoted follower may lack the last few writes (lost or conflicting writes), the old leader may return and believe it is still leader (split-brain), and a too-short timeout causes needless failovers during a load spike. Tools: Patroni (PostgreSQL), MySQL group replication or orchestrators, managed Multi-AZ setups.

Multi-leader replication

Several nodes accept writes, usually one leader per data centre, and replicate to each other. Benefits: low write latency in each region, and each region keeps working if the link between them fails. Cost: write conflicts (two users edit the same row in different regions). You need conflict resolution: last-write-wins, per-field merge, application-level merge, or CRDTs. It also has tricky corner cases with auto-incrementing keys, triggers and constraints. Use it only for real multi-region writes, or offline-capable clients (a calendar app syncing a phone), and prefer to avoid it otherwise.

Leaderless replication

No leader: the client (or a coordinator node) sends each write to several replicas and reads from several, using quorums (N, R, W). Used by Cassandra, Riak and DynamoDB-style stores. Strengths: no failover event, writes continue as long as a quorum is reachable, good for multi-region and high availability. Costs: weaker consistency, conflict handling (vector clocks or last-write-wins), read repair and anti-entropy to heal replicas, and no multi-row transactions in general.

ModelWrites accepted byConflictsExamplesBest for
Leader–followerOne leaderNonePostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB replica setMost applications
Multi-leaderOne per regionYes: must resolveMySQL group replication in multi-primary mode, CouchDB, Active DirectoryMulti-region writes, offline sync
LeaderlessAny replica (quorum)Yes: versions, LWWCassandra, Riak, DynamoDB-styleAlways-on, huge scale

Common mistakes

  • Sending a "read after write" to a follower and showing the user stale data.
  • Treating replicas as backups; deletions and corruption replicate too. Keep point-in-time backups.
  • Ignoring lag until a follower is minutes behind; alert on it.
  • Promoting an out-of-date follower without checking, and losing committed writes.

Interview angle

  • "One leader takes writes, followers serve reads asynchronously. Replication lag means I read my own writes from the leader."
  • Explain sync vs async as a durability vs latency trade-off, and semi-sync as the compromise.
  • Say that replication scales reads and availability, not writes; for writes you shard.

Sharding: strategies, shard keys, hot spots and resharding

Sharding splits one logical database into independent shards on different servers so writes and storage scale out; the shard key decides how well it works, and the costs are cross-shard queries, cross-shard transactions, hot spots and painful resharding.

The idea

When one primary cannot hold the data or handle the writes, you split the rows by a rule. Each shard is a complete database (usually with its own replicas) holding a subset of the rows. A router (in the application, a library, or a proxy such as Vitess or a MongoDB mongos) maps each request to the right shard.

Sharding strategies

StrategyRuleStrengthsWeaknesses
RangeKey ranges: A–H, I–P, Q–Z, or ids 1–1MRange queries stay on few shards; easy to understandHot spots (new ids all land on the last shard); uneven sizes
Hashhash(key) mod N (or consistent hashing)Even spread, few hot spotsRange queries scatter to all shards; mod N moves most keys when N changes
Directory / lookupA table maps each key (or range) to a shardFully flexible; move one tenant at a timeThe directory is a bottleneck and SPOF; extra lookup
GeographicBy region: India users on the Mumbai shardLow latency, data residency lawsUneven regions; cross-region users and queries
Tenant-basedBy customer or tenant idIsolation; a big tenant gets its own shardOne huge tenant is a hot spot

Choosing the shard key

This is the most important decision, and it is hard to change later. A good shard key:

  • Has high cardinality (many distinct values): user_id is good, country or status is bad.
  • Spreads load evenly: no single value attracts most of the traffic.
  • Matches the main access pattern, so common queries touch one shard: shard orders by customer_id if you mostly fetch "my orders".
  • Is stable: a key that changes means moving the row between shards.
  • Avoids monotonic values in range sharding (timestamps, auto-increment ids send all new writes to the newest shard).

Hot spots

A hot shard gets disproportionate load: a celebrity account, one giant tenant, today's date when sharding by date, or a flash-sale product. Fixes: hash-based keys; add a random suffix or salt to spread one hot key (and merge on read); give the heavy tenant a dedicated shard (directory-based); cache the hot data; split the hot shard further.

Resharding

Data grows, so shards fill up and you must add more. With hash mod N, going from 3 shards to 4 moves about 75% of keys, a huge migration. Better approaches:

  • Many logical shards on few servers: create, say, 256 logical shards up front and map them to 4 servers. To grow, move whole logical shards to new servers; the key-to-shard mapping never changes. This is the most common pragmatic design.
  • Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of the keys when a node joins (next article).
  • Directory-based mapping lets you move one range or tenant at a time.
  • Do the move online: copy data in the background, keep it in sync (dual writes or change-data capture), verify, switch traffic, delete the old copy.

What sharding breaks

  • Cross-shard queries: "all orders over ₹10,000 today" must go to every shard and be merged (scatter–gather): slow and fragile. Mitigate with a secondary index or search store, or by designing queries around the shard key.
  • Joins: across shards they happen in application code, or are avoided by denormalizing, or by co-locating related data (shard orders and order items by the same customer id).
  • Transactions: an ACID transaction across shards needs two-phase commit (slow and blocking) or a saga with compensating actions (Module 6). Prefer designs where one business operation touches one shard.
  • Unique ids: auto-increment ids collide across shards. Use UUIDs, a Snowflake-style id (timestamp + machine id + sequence), or an id service.
  • Operations: schema migrations, backups, monitoring and rebalancing now multiply by the number of shards.

Tools that provide sharding: Vitess (MySQL), Citus (PostgreSQL), MongoDB's built-in sharding, Cassandra and DynamoDB (shard by design with a partition key), CockroachDB and Spanner (distributed SQL that shards automatically and keeps transactions).

public class ShardRouter {
    private final int logicalShards = 256;              // fixed, never changes
    private final java.util.List<String> shardUrls;     // logical shard -> server

    public ShardRouter(java.util.List<String> shardUrls) {
        this.shardUrls = shardUrls;                     // size = 256, many point to one server
    }

    public String urlFor(long userId) {
        int logical = (int) Math.floorMod(Long.hashCode(userId), logicalShards);
        return shardUrls.get(logical);                  // moving a logical shard = edit the list
    }
}

Common mistakes

  • Sharding by a low-cardinality key such as country, status or boolean.
  • Starting with hash mod N and no plan for adding nodes.
  • Designing queries that always need all shards.
  • Sharding early, before replicas, caching and indexing are used up.

Interview angle

  • "I would shard by user id with a hash, using many logical shards so I can rebalance by moving whole shards. Single-user queries touch one shard."
  • Always name the cost: cross-shard joins, transactions and resharding. Offer co-location or sagas.
  • Say what you would watch: shard size, per-shard QPS, and skew.

Consistent hashing and virtual nodes

Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring so that adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys instead of nearly all of them; virtual nodes give each server many points on the ring for an even spread.

The problem with hash mod N

To pick a cache server for a key, the obvious rule is server = hash(key) mod N. It works until N changes. With 3 servers going to 4, a key stays only if hash mod 3 == hash mod 4, which is true for about 25% of keys. The other 75% now map to a different server: cache misses everywhere (a stampede on the database), or in a sharded database, a huge data migration. Servers join and leave constantly (autoscaling, failures), so we need a rule that moves few keys.

The ring

Map the hash space (for example 0 to 232 − 1) onto a circle. Hash each server to a position on the ring. To find the server for a key, hash the key to a position and walk clockwise to the first server you meet.

  • Remove a server: only its keys move, all to the next server clockwise. Everyone else is untouched.
  • Add a server: it takes over only the keys between itself and the previous server.
  • On average only K/N keys move (K keys, N servers), instead of almost all.

The unevenness problem and virtual nodes

With only a few servers placed by hash, the arcs between them differ in size, so one server may own 50% of the ring while another owns 10%. When a server fails, all its load falls on a single neighbour, which may then fail too.

The fix is virtual nodes (vnodes): each physical server gets many positions on the ring (100–200 is typical), by hashing "serverA#0", "serverA#1", and so on. The arcs average out, so each server owns roughly 1/N of the ring. When a server leaves, its many small arcs go to many different neighbours, spreading the extra load evenly. A bigger machine can simply be given more vnodes (weighting). The cost is a larger ring to store and search, and more metadata to keep in sync.

A Java sketch with TreeMap

A TreeMap keeps keys sorted, and ceilingEntry finds the first position at or after a hash in O(log n). If there is none, wrap around to the first entry.

import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class ConsistentHashRing {
    private final TreeMap<Long, String> ring = new TreeMap<>();
    private final int vnodes;

    public ConsistentHashRing(int vnodes) {
        this.vnodes = vnodes;
    }

    public void addNode(String node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < vnodes; i++) {
            ring.put(hash(node + "#" + i), node);        // many points per server
        }
    }

    public void removeNode(String node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < vnodes; i++) {
            ring.remove(hash(node + "#" + i));
        }
    }

    public String nodeFor(String key) {
        if (ring.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("no nodes");
        }
        Map.Entry<Long, String> e = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(key));   // next clockwise
        if (e == null) {
            e = ring.firstEntry();                                   // wrap around
        }
        return e.getValue();
    }

    private static long hash(String s) {
        try {
            byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")
                .digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return ByteBuffer.wrap(d).getLong();           // first 8 bytes as a long
        } catch (java.security.NoSuchAlgorithmException ex) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(ex);
        }
    }
}

Usage: create new ConsistentHashRing(150), call addNode("cache-1") for each server, and route with nodeFor("user:42"). If you add cache-4 later and compare the routing for a large set of keys, only about a quarter of them change, whereas with mod N about three quarters would. (MD5 is used here only as a well-spread hash, not for security; the sketch is not thread-safe and ignores replication.)

For replication on the ring, store each key on the next R distinct physical servers clockwise (the preference list in Dynamo-style systems).

Where it is used

  • Distributed caches (client libraries for Memcached use it; Redis Cluster uses a related fixed scheme of 16,384 hash slots, which also moves only slots when nodes change).
  • Databases: Cassandra and DynamoDB-style stores partition data on a ring with vnodes.
  • Load balancing with affinity: send the same key (user, URL) to the same backend so local caches stay warm.
  • CDNs and object stores to decide which node stores which object.

Edge cases

  • A single very hot key still lands on one server; consistent hashing balances keys, not traffic.
  • Hash collisions between nodes are rare but must be handled (add a salt).
  • After adding a node, the new node's cache is cold; the keys it takes over miss once.

Interview angle

  • "With mod N, adding a server remaps most keys. With consistent hashing only about 1/N move."
  • "Virtual nodes smooth the distribution and spread a failed node's load across many peers."
  • Be ready to code the TreeMap version: ceilingEntry with wrap-around.

SQL vs NoSQL and the NoSQL families

Choose SQL when you need relations, transactions and flexible queries (the default), and a NoSQL family when one access pattern or scale dominates: key-value for lookups and caches, document for flexible records, wide-column for massive writes, graph for relationships, plus time-series and search stores for special data.

What changes between the two

Relational (SQL) databases store rows in tables with a fixed schema, relate tables with keys, query them with SQL (joins, aggregates), and give ACID transactions. NoSQL ("not only SQL") is a family of databases that give up some of that (a fixed schema, joins, or multi-row transactions) in exchange for something else: easier horizontal scaling, flexible data shape, or speed for one access pattern. Do not choose by fashion; choose by access pattern, consistency need and scale. Fundamentals are in SQL · Module 6; this is the design view.

Decision table

QuestionSQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL)NoSQL (typical)
Data shapeStructured, related, stable schemaVaried, nested or evolving
QueriesAd-hoc: joins, filters, aggregatesKnown access patterns; designed around queries
TransactionsMulti-row ACID, strong consistencyOften per-item/partition; some support more
Scaling writesVertical, then replicas, then painful shardingBuilt-in horizontal partitioning
ConsistencyStrong by defaultTunable; often eventual
Schema changeMigrationsFlexible, but the app must handle old shapes
Maturity and toolingDecades, huge ecosystemVaries by product
Good first choice when…Money, orders, inventory, users, almost any business appHuge scale in one pattern, flexible documents, caching, graph traversals

Convention: start with PostgreSQL

A well-run relational database handles far more than most products ever need, supports JSON columns for flexible fields, and keeps your options open. Add specialised stores when a measured need appears (cache, search, analytics), and keep the relational database as the source of truth. This is called polyglot persistence: each data type in the store that fits it.

The NoSQL families

FamilyModelExamplesUse casesWeak at
Key-valueKey to opaque value; get/put by keyRedis, DynamoDB, MemcachedCaches, sessions, counters, leaderboards, shopping cartsQueries by anything but the key
DocumentKey to JSON-like document with nested fields; queryableMongoDB, Couchbase, FirestoreProduct catalogues, user profiles, content, evolving schemasMany-to-many relations, multi-document joins
Wide-columnRows with many sparse columns, grouped by partition key and sorted by clustering keyCassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB, BigtableHuge write rates: messages, events, IoT, activity feeds, time-ordered dataAd-hoc queries, joins; needs query-first modelling
GraphNodes and edges with propertiesNeo4j, Amazon NeptuneSocial graphs, recommendations, fraud rings, knowledge graphsBulk analytics; scaling out is harder
Time-seriesTimestamped measurementsInfluxDB, TimescaleDB, PrometheusMetrics, monitoring, sensor dataGeneral-purpose queries
SearchInverted index over textElasticsearch, OpenSearch, SolrFull-text search, log analyticsNot a primary store (Search)

How each one is used in a design

  • Key-value: Redis for the session store and cache; DynamoDB for a serverless primary store with single-digit-millisecond lookups at any scale when you know the key. Model the partition key with care.
  • Document: a product with different attributes per category (a phone has a screen size, a shirt has a fabric) fits a document better than a table with 80 nullable columns. Store data that is read together, together (embedding). Cost: duplicated data and no strong join story.
  • Wide-column: Cassandra models one table per query: for "latest 50 messages in chat X" use partition key chat_id and clustering key sent_at DESC. Writes are fast because they are append-style (LSM trees), and data spreads across a ring automatically (consistent hashing). You pay with limited query flexibility and eventual consistency.
  • Graph: "friends of friends who like X" is a few hops in a graph database but a painful self-join in SQL. Choose it when relationship traversal is the core feature.

Consistency, joins and the "NoSQL means no schema" myth

Many NoSQL systems favour availability and partition tolerance and offer tunable or eventual consistency (CAP), but this varies: MongoDB can be strongly consistent on a single primary, and DynamoDB offers strongly consistent reads when asked. "Schemaless" really means the schema lives in your application code, which then has to handle old and new document shapes. Joins are not available or are costly, so you denormalize and model data around the queries, not around the entities.

Common mistakes

  • Picking MongoDB because "it scales" when the data is relational and the load is small.
  • Using a document store for financial data that needs multi-row transactions.
  • Modelling a wide-column table like a SQL table and then needing ad-hoc queries.
  • Treating Elasticsearch or Redis as the only copy of important data.

Interview angle

  • "I choose by access pattern: orders and payments in PostgreSQL for transactions, sessions in Redis, product search in Elasticsearch, activity feed in Cassandra."
  • Do not say "NoSQL is faster" or "SQL does not scale"; say what each gives up.
  • For a chat or feed system, justify wide-column by write rate and the query pattern.

Message queues and streams: Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS and async processing

A queue or log sits between a producer and consumers so work happens asynchronously: it decouples services, absorbs spikes and enables retries; Kafka is a partitioned replayable log for high-throughput streams, RabbitMQ is a flexible broker with exchanges and acks, SQS is a managed queue, and consumers must be idempotent because delivery is at least once.

The problem: synchronous chains are fragile

If placing an order synchronously calls payment, inventory, email, invoice PDF and analytics, the user waits for all of them, and one slow or failing service breaks the order. With a message queue the order service saves the order, puts an "OrderPlaced" message on a queue and replies at once. Other services consume the message in their own time.

Benefits of asynchronous processing:

  • Decoupling: producer and consumer can be deployed, scaled and fail separately; you can add a new consumer without touching the producer.
  • Buffering spikes (load leveling): a flash sale produces 50,000 orders per second for a minute; the queue stores them and workers drain at their own steady rate.
  • Retries and resilience: if the email provider is down, the message waits and is retried.
  • Faster responses: slow work moves out of the request path.
  • Scaling workers independently by queue length.

Costs: eventual consistency (the invoice appears a few seconds later), harder debugging and tracing, duplicate and out-of-order messages, and one more system to run.

Two models: point-to-point and publish/subscribe

Point-to-point (work queue)Publish/subscribe
DeliveryEach message goes to exactly one of the competing consumersEach message goes to every subscriber (or every subscriber group)
UseDistribute jobs: resize images, send emailsBroadcast events: OrderPlaced for billing, search, analytics
ScalingAdd workers on the same queueEach subscriber group scales on its own
ExamplesSQS queue, RabbitMQ queueKafka topic with groups, SNS, RabbitMQ fanout exchange

Kafka: a distributed log

Kafka stores messages in a durable, append-only log. A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an ordered sequence, and each message has an offset (its position). Consumers do not delete messages; they track their offset. Messages stay until the retention time or size is reached, so consumers can replay history.

  • Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. Messages with the same key (for example orderId) hash to the same partition, so one order's events stay in order.
  • Consumer groups: consumers in one group split the partitions between them (scale out up to the number of partitions); a different group gets its own full copy of the stream. This gives both work-queue and pub/sub in one model.
  • Replication: each partition is copied to several brokers; a leader serves reads and writes. Producers choose the acknowledgement level (acks=all for durability).
  • Throughput is very high, as it uses sequential disk writes and batching; it fits event streaming, log and metric pipelines, CDC, event sourcing.
  • Costs: more operational weight (cluster management; modern versions use KRaft instead of ZooKeeper), partition count is hard to change later, no per-message priority, and consumer rebalancing pauses.

RabbitMQ: a smart broker

RabbitMQ implements AMQP. Producers publish to an exchange, which routes messages to queues by bindings and a routing rule (direct: exact key; topic: patterns like order.*; fanout: all queues; headers). Consumers read from a queue and acknowledge (ack) each message after processing; unacknowledged messages are redelivered. Once acked, the message is gone. It supports per-message TTL, priorities, dead-letter exchanges and flexible routing, and it is excellent for task queues with complex routing and moderate volume. It is not built for replay or for the throughput of Kafka. See Spring Boot · Module 7 for Spring AMQP and Spring Kafka.

Amazon SQS (and SNS)

SQS is a fully managed queue: no servers to run, scales automatically, pay per request. A consumer receives a message, which becomes invisible for the visibility timeout; if the consumer deletes it in time the work is done, otherwise it reappears and is retried. Standard queues give at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering and very high throughput; FIFO queues give ordering per message group and de-duplication, with lower throughput limits. Built-in dead-letter queues and retention up to 14 days. For pub/sub, SNS fans a message out to many SQS queues. Cost: vendor lock-in, no replay once deleted, polling latency.

Comparison

KafkaRabbitMQSQS
ModelPartitioned replicated logBroker: exchanges and queuesManaged queue
Message after readingStays until retention; replayableRemoved after ackRemoved on delete
OrderingPer partitionPer queue (with one consumer)FIFO queues per message group
ThroughputVery highModerate to highHigh, auto-scaling
RoutingTopic and key onlyRich (exchanges, patterns)Simple
Consumer modelPull, consumer groups, offsetsPush or pull, acks, prefetchPull, visibility timeout
OperationsHeavy (or managed MSK, Confluent)MediumNone
Best forEvent streaming, big data, event sourcing, replayTask queues, complex routing, RPCSimple cloud jobs, decoupling on AWS

Reliability: delivery semantics and idempotent consumers

  • At-most-once: the message may be lost, never duplicated (ack before processing).
  • At-least-once: never lost, but duplicates happen (ack after processing; a crash between processing and ack causes redelivery). This is the usual default.
  • Exactly-once: hard in general. Kafka offers idempotent producers and transactions inside Kafka; end to end across a database you get effectively once by combining at-least-once delivery with an idempotent consumer.

An idempotent consumer produces the same result if it sees a message twice. Common ways: record processed message ids in a table with a unique constraint; use natural idempotency (an upsert keyed by order id instead of an insert); version numbers. See the saga and outbox patterns in Module 6.

@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "invoice-service")
@Transactional
public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlaced event) {
    // processed_events has a UNIQUE constraint on event_id
    boolean firstTime = processedEvents.insertIfAbsent(event.eventId());
    if (!firstTime) {
        return;                              // duplicate delivery: do nothing
    }
    invoiceService.createInvoice(event.orderId());   // same transaction as the insert
}

Backpressure, retries and dead-letter queues

  • Backpressure: if producers outrun consumers, the queue grows without bound. Watch queue depth and consumer lag, scale consumers, limit producers (rate limits, bounded queues), or shed low-priority work. A queue hides overload; it does not remove it.
  • Retries: retry transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter; cap the number of attempts.
  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ): after N failed attempts a message moves to a DLQ so it does not block the others (a poison message otherwise retries forever). Alert on DLQ size, inspect, fix, and replay.
  • Ordering vs parallelism: strict ordering limits parallel consumption; order only what needs it, by key.

Typical event-driven uses

  • Send email or SMS after sign-up or order, with retries.
  • Generate thumbnails and video transcodes after an upload event.
  • Update the search index when a product changes (Search).
  • Keep caches and read models fresh; fan out a post to followers' feeds.
  • Collect logs, clickstream and metrics into analytics.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming exactly-once delivery and writing consumers that break on duplicates.
  • Publishing to the queue and writing to the database as two separate steps; one can fail (use the outbox pattern).
  • No DLQ, so one bad message blocks a partition or loops forever.
  • Putting large payloads in messages; send an id or an S3 link instead.

Interview angle

  • "I decouple the slow parts with a queue: the API returns 202 Accepted, workers do the rest, and consumers are idempotent because delivery is at least once."
  • Choose Kafka for high-volume streams, replay and multiple independent consumers; RabbitMQ for task routing; SQS when on AWS and you want zero operations.
  • Explain partitions: ordering per key, parallelism across partitions, consumers up to the number of partitions.

Object storage (S3) for files, presigned URLs and multipart uploads

Store files (images, videos, documents) in object storage such as S3, which is cheap, extremely durable and scales without limit, and keep only the metadata and the object key in your database; let clients upload and download directly with presigned URLs, and put a CDN in front.

Why not store files in the database or on the app server

Large binary files in a relational database bloat it, slow backups and replication, and waste expensive storage. Files on an app server's disk break statelessness (the next instance cannot see them) and die with the machine. Object storage is built for exactly this: a flat store of immutable blobs addressed by key over HTTP. Examples: Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and self-hosted MinIO.

S3 concepts

Bucket
A top-level container with a globally unique name; holds objects. Settings such as access policy, versioning and lifecycle rules apply per bucket.
Object
The file's bytes plus metadata. An object is written or replaced as a whole; you cannot edit part of it in place.
Key
The object's name inside the bucket, for example users/42/avatar/2026-11.jpg. The namespace is flat; the slashes only look like folders (a "prefix").
Metadata
System metadata (size, content type, ETag, last-modified) and your own key-value tags.
Storage class
Hot (frequent access), infrequent access, and archive tiers with lower price and slower or paid retrieval. Lifecycle rules move or delete objects by age automatically.
Versioning
Keeps old versions of an object, so an overwrite or delete can be undone.
  • Durability: S3 advertises eleven nines (99.999999999%) of durability for standard storage, achieved by storing data redundantly across multiple facilities. That is about durability (not losing objects), not availability (always reachable), which is lower.
  • Consistency: S3 now gives strong read-after-write consistency for object writes, overwrites and deletes, so a read after a successful PUT sees the new data.
  • Limits: a single object can be up to 5 TB; one PUT request up to 5 GB; larger uploads use multipart.
  • Not a file system: no append, no rename (it is copy and delete), no locking, and each request has network latency of tens of milliseconds. Do not use it for databases or for tiny frequent random writes.

The standard pattern: blob in S3, metadata in the database

The database row holds the object_key, owner, content type, size and status, and the bytes live in S3. Queries, permissions and joins stay in SQL, and storage scales separately.

Presigned URLs

A presigned URL is a normal S3 URL with a signature and expiry in its query string, created by your server with its credentials. Whoever holds it can perform that one operation (upload this key, or download this object) until it expires, with no AWS credentials of their own. Benefits: the file bytes skip your servers (saving bandwidth, CPU and memory), the bucket can stay private, and access is time-limited.

import java.time.Duration;
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.PutObjectRequest;
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.presigner.S3Presigner;
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.presigner.model.PutObjectPresignRequest;

public class PresignService {
    private final S3Presigner presigner;                    // built once, reused

    public PresignService(S3Presigner presigner) {
        this.presigner = presigner;
    }

    public String uploadUrl(String bucket, String key, String contentType) {
        PutObjectRequest put = PutObjectRequest.builder()
            .bucket(bucket).key(key).contentType(contentType).build();
        PutObjectPresignRequest req = PutObjectPresignRequest.builder()
            .signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(10))      // short-lived
            .putObjectRequest(put).build();
        return presigner.presignPutObject(req).url().toString();
    }
}

Generate keys on the server (for example a UUID under the user's prefix) so clients cannot overwrite other people's files, check the file type and size limits, and verify the upload before marking it complete. Downloads work the same way with a presigned GET for private files.

Multipart upload

For large files (videos, backups) S3 supports multipart upload: start an upload, send the file as numbered parts (5 MB to 5 GB each, up to 10,000 parts) in parallel, then complete the upload and S3 assembles them. Benefits: parallel speed, resume by re-sending only failed parts (important on mobile networks), and uploads beyond 5 GB. AWS recommends it for objects above about 100 MB. Add a lifecycle rule to abort unfinished uploads, or the abandoned parts keep costing money.

CDN in front, and other practices

  • Serve public media through a CDN (CDN) with the bucket private and the CDN allowed to read it. This cuts latency and S3 request cost.
  • Use fingerprinted or unique keys so objects never change and caches stay valid.
