  • Name the three pillars and what question each answers.
  • Mention correlation ids, RED/USE, percentiles over averages, and trace propagation.
  • In every HLD answer, finish with "I would add metrics, alerts on the SLO, and tracing".

Coordination basics: leader election, locks, consensus, heartbeats

Some tasks need exactly one node in charge or exclusive access; distributed systems do this with leader election and locks built on consensus services, but locks need leases and fencing tokens because processes pause and clocks lie.

Why coordination is needed

Many designs have jobs that must run on only one node at a time: a scheduler that sends the daily report, a primary database that accepts writes, a cleanup task, the single consumer of a partition. If two nodes both think they are in charge (split brain), you get double reports or corrupted data. This article is intuition only; the full theory is a university course.

Heartbeats and failure detection

How do you know a node is dead? You cannot, exactly: a silent node may be dead, slow or cut off by the network. Systems use heartbeats: each node sends a small "I am alive" message every second or so. If the others see nothing for a timeout (say 10 seconds), they suspect the node has failed. Short timeout: fast failover but false alarms during a pause. Long timeout: fewer false alarms but a long outage. Gossip spreads this knowledge without a central watcher: each node regularly tells a few random peers what it knows about the others, and news reaches the whole cluster in about log(N) rounds. Cassandra and many membership systems use gossip.

Leader election

A leader (primary, master) makes decisions or accepts writes; the followers copy it and wait. When the leader dies, the followers hold an election to pick a new one. The rules must guarantee at most one leader at a time. Practical ways:

  • Use a coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul): nodes try to create the same key; the one that succeeds is the leader and keeps it alive with a lease; if it stops renewing, the key expires and others compete again.
  • Use the database: UPDATE leader SET owner = ?, expires = ? WHERE expires < now(), and check the row count. Fine for small systems.
  • Use the consensus built into the product (Kafka's controller, Redis Sentinel, PostgreSQL managers such as Patroni).

Distributed locks

A distributed lock gives exclusive access to a resource across processes. A simple Redis version: SET lock:report token NX PX 30000 (set only if missing, expire in 30 s). Release only if the stored token is yours. The expiry is the lease: it exists so a crashed holder does not block everyone forever.

Why distributed locks are hard

A process can freeze (garbage collection, a stalled VM, a slow network) after it acquired the lock and wake up after the lease expired, still believing it is the owner. Clocks across machines are not perfectly in sync either, so "my lease is still valid" cannot be trusted.

The fix is a fencing token: the lock service gives a number that increases with each grant (A gets 33, later B gets 34). Every write to the storage includes the token, and the storage rejects any write with a token lower than one it has already seen. When A wakes up and writes with token 33 after B wrote with 34, the storage refuses. The protection lives in the resource, not in the lock.

  • If the work is idempotent, you may not need a lock at all.
  • Prefer database row locks or unique constraints when the data is already in one database.
  • For efficiency-only locks (avoid duplicate work), a simple Redis lock is acceptable. For correctness-critical locks, use a consensus-backed service with fencing.

Consensus and Raft in one paragraph

Consensus is getting several nodes to agree on one value even when some nodes crash and messages are delayed. Raft (used by etcd, Consul and others) does it by electing one leader per term. Clients send writes to the leader; the leader appends the entry to its log and copies it to followers; once a majority (quorum) has stored it, the entry is committed and applied. If the leader fails, a follower whose timer expires asks for votes; a candidate needs a majority, and only a node with an up-to-date log can win. With 3 nodes the cluster survives 1 failure, with 5 nodes 2 failures (a majority of N is ⌊N/2⌋ + 1). Paxos is the older, harder-to-explain cousin; ZooKeeper uses a similar protocol called ZAB. Use these systems as tools; you almost never implement them yourself.

Common mistakes

  • A lock with no expiry (a crash blocks everyone) or with expiry but no fencing (two holders).
  • Releasing a lock without checking the token, so you free someone else's lock.
  • Using a single Redis node as a "correct" lock; if it fails over, the lock state can be lost.
  • Running a cluster of 2 or 4 consensus nodes: no extra fault tolerance over 1 or 3 respectively.

Interview angle

  • Explain the pause-after-lease story and the fencing token fix.
  • Say "majority quorum" and "odd number of nodes" when Raft or ZooKeeper comes up.
  • Prefer not to need a lock: idempotency or a database constraint is often simpler.

Interview questions — Distributed system patterns

When would you choose microservices over a monolith?

Only when a real pain exists: independent scaling of one part, many teams blocked by one release train, different reliability or technology needs, or fault isolation. Otherwise start with a modular monolith. Microservices add network failures, distributed data, versioned contracts and operational cost. Splitting too early or along technical layers gives a distributed monolith.

What is a bounded context, and why does it matter for service boundaries?

A part of the business where terms have one clear meaning and one team owns the rules. "Product" means title and images to the catalogue, stock to inventory and price to billing. Cut services along these contexts so that things which change together stay together and the services need few calls to each other.

Sync vs async communication: how do you choose?

Sync (REST, gRPC) when the caller needs the answer to continue, such as a price lookup. Async (queue, events) for side effects, fan-out, spikes and long work. Sync couples availability and adds up latency; async decouples in time and smooths load but is eventually consistent and harder to debug. Real systems mix both: a fast sync call at the edge triggers async processing behind it.

Choreography or orchestration for a multi-service workflow?

Choreography: services react to each other's events; loose coupling but the flow is hidden. Orchestration: a coordinator sends commands and tracks state; the flow is visible and failure handling is in one place, but the orchestrator knows all participants. Use choreography for two to four simple steps and orchestration (or a workflow engine) for longer flows with compensation.

What is idempotency and how do you make a payment API idempotent?

Repeating an operation has the same effect as doing it once. For POST /payments the client sends an Idempotency-Key header, reused on every retry. The server inserts the key into a dedupe table with a primary key, does the work, and stores the response. A repeat returns the stored response. Also store a request hash to reject the same key with a different body, and handle the in-progress state.

How do you retry correctly?

Retry only transient failures on idempotent operations. Use exponential backoff with a cap, add jitter so clients do not retry in sync, limit attempts, and add a retry budget (for example retries at most 10% of traffic). Retry at one layer only; three layers with three attempts each can turn one request into 27 calls. Add a timeout and a circuit breaker.

At-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once: what is the difference?

At-most-once may lose messages (ack before processing). At-least-once may duplicate them (ack after processing, retry until acked). Exactly-once delivery is not possible over an unreliable network, so we combine at-least-once with idempotent consumers to get exactly-once effects. Kafka's idempotent producer and transactions help only inside Kafka.

Why is two-phase commit avoided in microservices?

It blocks: after voting yes, participants hold locks until the coordinator decides, and a coordinator crash leaves them in doubt. It also lowers availability because all participants must be up, adds latency, and many brokers and external APIs cannot take part. Sagas give up atomic isolation in return for availability.

Explain the saga pattern with an order example.

Order → payment → inventory → shipping, each a local transaction. If inventory fails after payment succeeded, run the compensations in reverse: refund the payment, cancel the order. Steps and compensations are idempotent, saga state is persisted, and hard-to-undo steps go last. It can be orchestrated (one coordinator) or choreographed (events). The UI shows PENDING until the end.

What is the dual-write problem and how does the outbox pattern solve it?

Writing to the database and publishing to a broker are two separate writes; a crash between them loses the event or announces something that never committed. With an outbox, the event row is saved in the same database transaction as the business data. A polling relay or CDC (for example Debezium) publishes it later, at least once, and consumers dedupe by event id.

Explain the circuit breaker and bulkhead patterns.

A circuit breaker counts failures and slow calls; above a threshold it opens and fails fast, then half-opens to test recovery, then closes. It protects threads and the sick dependency. A bulkhead limits resources per dependency (separate thread pools or concurrency caps) so one slow service cannot consume everything. Together with timeouts, fallbacks and load shedding they stop cascading failures.

Design a unique ID generator. Explain Snowflake.

64 bits: 1 sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch (241 ms ≈ 69.7 years), 10 bits machine id (1,024 generators), 12 bits sequence (4,096 IDs per ms per machine, about 4.1 million per second). IDs are unique, sortable by time and need no per-ID coordination. Risks: clock moving backwards and duplicate machine ids. Alternatives: UUID v7 and range-based ticket servers.

UUID v4 vs UUID v7 as a primary key?

v4 is fully random, so inserts scatter across the B-tree index, causing page splits and cache misses. v7 begins with a 48-bit millisecond timestamp, so new keys are mostly appended and indexes stay compact, while still needing no coordination. Both are 16 bytes, twice a BIGINT.

What are logs, metrics and traces, and what do RED and USE mean?

Logs say what happened, metrics say how much and how fast, traces show where one request spent time across services, linked by a trace id. RED (rate, errors, duration) is for request-driven services; USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) is for resources. Alert on symptoms such as error rate and p99 latency, not on raw CPU.

Why are distributed locks hard? What is a fencing token?

A lock holder can pause (garbage collection) past its lease, wake up and write while a new holder is also writing. A fencing token is a number that grows with each lock grant; the storage rejects writes with a token older than one it has seen. So correctness is enforced at the resource. Better still, avoid the lock with idempotency or a unique constraint.

Cheat sheet — Distributed system patterns

  • Monolith first split for independent scaling, team size, fault isolation
  • Distributed monolith services that must deploy together; the anti-pattern
  • Bounded context area where one team owns the meaning of the words
  • Database per service no shared tables, no joins across services, eventual consistency
  • Sync caller waits, simple, couples availability; async broker, decoupled, eventual
  • Choreography events and reactions; orchestration a coordinator with state
  • Idempotent N times equals once; GET, PUT, DELETE yes; POST no
  • Idempotency-Key client UUID per intent, dedupe table with PK, store response and request hash
  • Backoff wait = min(cap, base × 2^attempt); add full jitter
  • Retry storm 3 layers × 3 attempts = 27 calls; retry at one layer, use a budget
  • At-most-once ack first, may lose; at-least-once ack after work, may duplicate
  • Effectively once at-least-once + idempotent consumer (processed-message table)
  • DLQ parking place for messages that keep failing
  • 2PC prepare then commit; blocks, coordinator is a single point of failure
  • Saga local transactions + compensations in reverse; persist state; idempotent steps
  • Outbox event row in the same DB transaction; relay by polling or CDC (Debezium)
  • Timeouts connect short, read from p99; pass deadlines down the chain
  • Circuit breaker closed → open → half-open; counts slow calls too
  • Bulkhead separate pools per dependency; fallback degrade optional features
  • Load shedding reject early with 503/429 when over capacity; bounded queues
  • Snowflake 1 + 41 + 10 + 12 bits; 69.7 years; 1,024 machines; 4,096 per ms
  • UUID v4 random, bad for index locality; v7 time-ordered; JS needs 64-bit ids as strings
  • Observability structured logs + correlation id, metrics (counter, gauge, histogram), traces
  • RED rate, errors, duration; USE utilisation, saturation, errors; use p99 not average
  • Locks need a lease and a fencing token; Raft leader + majority quorum, odd node count

Practice — Distributed system patterns

  1. Take a small monolith you know (for example a shop with users, products, orders) and list its modules and their tables. Mark which tables each module reads and writes. Done when you can say where the service boundaries would go and which cross-module joins would have to become API calls.
  2. Write the idempotent payment endpoint from the notes in Spring Boot with a PostgreSQL dedupe table. Fire the same request 10 times in parallel (a script or a test with an executor). Done when exactly one payment row exists and all 10 responses are identical.
  3. Implement the Retry.withBackoff helper with full jitter and a max attempt count. Write a test with a fake call that fails twice and then succeeds; record the sleep times. Done when the delays are random but never above the backoff cap.
  4. Draw by hand the order → payment → inventory → shipping saga as a sequence diagram for both the happy path and a shipping failure. List every compensation in order. Done when each step has a named compensation and a status in the order table.
  5. Add a transactional outbox to a small Spring Boot service: an outbox table, a polling relay with SKIP LOCKED, and a consumer with a processed-message table. Kill the app between send and mark-published. Done when the consumer handles the duplicate without a double effect.
  6. Wrap a slow HTTP dependency with a timeout, a circuit breaker and a bounded concurrency limit (see Spring Boot · Module 7). Make the dependency sleep 30 seconds. Done when your service answers other endpoints normally and the breaker state changes to open.
  7. Fill in the Snowflake arithmetic yourself: years for 41 bits, machines for 10 bits, IDs per second per machine for 12 bits, and the Java shifts. Then run the generator from the notes with two threads. Done when 1 million IDs are generated with zero duplicates and the IDs increase over time.
  8. Add correlation ids: generate one in a servlet filter, put it in the logging MDC, return it in a response header, and send it on every outbound call. Done when one id finds the log lines from two services.
  9. Explain out loud, in under three minutes, the pause-after-lease story and the fencing token. Done when a friend can say why a Redis lock alone is not enough for correctness.
7

Module 7·HLD · week 8Good to know

HLD interview practice

11 topics · about 2 h of reading

A high-level design (HLD) interview gives you one vague sentence, such as "Design a URL shortener", and 45 minutes. Nobody expects a perfect answer. They want to see how you think: do you ask questions, do the arithmetic, pick sensible components, explain trade-offs and notice what can fail? This module gives you a repeatable method and ten fully worked problems, so that you have both the process and the building blocks ready.

Every problem uses tools from earlier modules. Estimation and trade-offs come from Module 4, the components (cache, queue, sharding, CDN, object storage) from Module 5, and idempotency, sagas, outbox and IDs from Module 6. Where a problem needs a pattern, it links back instead of re-explaining. The low-level class-design cousins of some of these problems are in Module 3.

All numbers in the capacity estimates are assumptions made for practice. They are round and approximate on purpose; in an interview you state your assumptions aloud and the interviewer adjusts them. They are not statistics about any real company.

After this module you will be able to:

  • Run a 45-minute HLD interview with a clear time plan and know how you will be scored.
  • Turn a vague prompt into requirements, estimates, APIs, a data model and a diagram.
  • Design the ten classic systems: URL shortener, Pastebin, rate limiter, notification system, chat, news feed, food delivery, ride sharing, video streaming and payments.
  • Discuss two to four deep dives per problem with options and trade-offs.
  • Answer "what if traffic grows 10 times?" and other follow-ups calmly.

The HLD interview method: a script, a checklist and a rubric

Spend 45 minutes in six phases (requirements, estimates, high-level design, data model, deep dive, trade-offs), say your reasoning out loud, drive the conversation yourself, and always cover numbers, bottlenecks and failure.

What an HLD interview tests

There is no single right answer. The interviewer checks whether you can: handle ambiguity by asking questions, size a system with simple arithmetic, assemble known building blocks into a coherent whole, justify choices by trade-offs, go deep on one or two hard parts, and communicate clearly. Seniority shows in depth and judgement, not in the number of boxes on the board.

The six phases and the clock

PhaseMinutesOutput on the board
1. Requirements and scope5Functional list, non-functional list, out-of-scope list
2. Capacity estimates5QPS, storage, bandwidth, read/write ratio
3. High-level design10–15API list and a box-and-arrow diagram
4. Data model5Tables or collections, keys, SQL vs NoSQL choice
5. Deep dive10–15One or two hard components, in detail with options
6. Trade-offs, bottlenecks, wrap-up5Failures, scaling, monitoring, what you would do next

Total: 40–50 minutes. For a 60-minute slot, give the deep dive more time. Wear a watch; the most common time mistake is spending 20 minutes on requirements and drawing, then rushing the part that scores most.

The script: what to say in each phase

Phase 1: requirements (5 min)

Say: "Before I design anything, I want to clarify scope. I will ask a few questions, then write down what is in and out." Then ask from this checklist, choosing the questions that matter:

  • Users and use cases: who uses it, and what are the two or three core actions?
  • Scale: how many users or requests per day? Read-heavy or write-heavy?
  • Features: what is in scope for 45 minutes, and what is a later extension?
  • Consistency and freshness: must users always see the latest data, or is a few seconds of delay fine?
  • Availability and latency: any target, such as 99.9% uptime or under 200 ms?
  • Durability: can we ever lose data? (A chat message: no. A view counter: maybe.)
  • Geography: one region or global? Mobile, web, or both?
  • Constraints: abuse and security, privacy, compliance, retention time.

Write two lists: functional (what the system does) and non-functional (how well: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability). End with "Out of scope: ...". Confirm: "Does this match what you have in mind?"

Phase 2: estimates (5 min)

Say: "I will do rough numbers to see which parts are hard. All approximate." Convert users to requests per second: daily requests ÷ 86,400 ≈ per second, and round 86,400 to about 100,000 when you are in a hurry. Peak is typically 2–3 times the average. Then storage (items × size × retention) and bandwidth (QPS × size). Use powers of ten and write the units. See Module 4 for the cheat numbers. State what the numbers imply: "4,000 reads per second is easy for one cache node, so the real problem is storage over 5 years" is the kind of conclusion that earns credit.

Phase 3: high-level design (10–15 min)

Say: "First the API, then a simple end-to-end design, then I will improve it." Define the 3–5 endpoints with request and response shapes. Draw the minimum working path: client → load balancer → app servers → database. Walk one write and one read through it. Then add components only when a requirement or number demands them: cache for read-heavy load, queue for slow or bursty work, CDN for static content, search index for text search. Name each addition and why.

Phase 4: data model (5 min)

List the main entities, their key fields, primary keys and the main access patterns ("lookup by short code", "latest posts of user X"). Choose SQL or NoSQL based on those patterns, scale and consistency needs, and say why. Mention indexes and the shard key if you will shard.

Phase 5: deep dive (10–15 min)

Say: "The hardest part here is X. Let me go deeper." Often the interviewer picks. Present options, compare them in a table or sentences, choose one, and state the cost of the choice. Two good deep dives beat five shallow ones.

Phase 6: trade-offs and wrap-up (5 min)

Cover: single points of failure and what happens when each box dies; bottlenecks; how it scales 10×; data loss and duplicates; monitoring and alerting; security and abuse; cost. Finish with a 20-second summary of the design and what you would build next.

How to drive the conversation

  • Narrate: "I am choosing X over Y because...". Silence worries interviewers.
  • Propose a plan at the start ("I will cover requirements, numbers, design, data, then a deep dive") and tick it off.
  • Check in at phase ends: "Shall I go deeper here, or move on?" Follow the interviewer's hints; a question usually points at what they want to see.
  • When you do not know, reason aloud from principles. Do not bluff about product internals.
  • Use the board: one diagram, labelled arrows, numbers beside components.
  • Say the trade-off every time you pick: "Fan-out on write makes reads fast but writes expensive."

How you are evaluated: a rubric

AreaWeakStrong
RequirementsJumps straight to boxesClarifies scope, writes functional and non-functional lists
EstimationNo numbers, or wild numbersClear assumptions, correct arithmetic, draws conclusions
DesignBuzzword list of technologiesWorks end to end; every component has a reason
Data"Use MongoDB" with no reasonEntities, keys and access patterns drive the choice
DepthStays at the surfaceGoes deep on the hard part with options and trade-offs
Failure thinkingAssumes everything worksHandles crashes, duplicates, hot spots, overload
CommunicationSilent or ramblingStructured, checks in, takes hints

Common mistakes

What loses points

  • No requirements: designing the wrong system.
  • No numbers: you cannot justify sharding or caching without them.
  • Over-engineering: Kafka, Kubernetes, microservices and a service mesh for 40 requests per second. Start simple, scale when numbers demand it.
  • Name-dropping: saying "Cassandra" without saying why.
  • Ignoring failure: never saying what happens when a node, a network link or a dependency fails.
  • Single point of failure left on the diagram.
  • Not listening: ignoring a hint to move to the part the interviewer cares about.
  • Defensive tone: treat challenges as new requirements, not attacks.

"What if traffic grows 10×?"

Answer with a method, not panic. First re-do the numbers: which resource hits its limit first? Then walk the path from the user inwards:

  1. Edge: CDN and caching for anything static or cacheable.
  2. App tier: stateless servers behind a load balancer scale horizontally; add instances and autoscaling.
  3. Cache: raise the hit ratio, add nodes, protect against hot keys.
  4. Database reads: add read replicas; accept replication lag where allowed.
  5. Database writes and storage: shard by a good key, or move the hot table to a store built for writes.
  6. Async the slow stuff: move non-urgent work to queues; add back-pressure.
  7. Protect the system: rate limits, load shedding, graceful degradation.

Then say what would break next at 100×. That shows you know scaling is a sequence of bottlenecks.

A skeleton to memorise

1. Requirements  functional | non-functional | out of scope
2. Numbers       QPS (avg, peak) | storage/year | bandwidth | R:W ratio
3. API           3-5 endpoints, request and response
4. Design        client - LB - app - cache - DB (+ queue, CDN, search)
5. Data          entities, keys, SQL or NoSQL and why, shard key
6. Deep dive     hardest part: options, choice, cost
7. Wrap-up       failures, scaling 10x, monitoring, security

Interview angle

  • Open with the plan and the clarifying questions. That alone separates you from most candidates.
  • Always give at least one number, one trade-off and one failure scenario per component you add.
  • Practise out loud with a timer. Saying it is a different skill from knowing it.

Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly)

A URL shortener maps a short code to a long URL; it is read-heavy, so the design is a key-value lookup with a cache in front, a collision-free way to create 7-character codes (counter plus base62, hash, or pre-generated keys), and a choice between 301 and 302 redirects that trades speed for analytics.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Given a long URL, create a short URL (for example https://sho.rt/aZ3k9Q1).
  • Opening the short URL redirects to the original URL.
  • Optional: custom alias, expiry time, click analytics, user accounts.

Non-functional: very low redirect latency (under about 50 ms server time), high availability (a dead short link breaks every page it was posted on), short codes that are hard to guess or enumerate, durable links (never lose a mapping), and eventual consistency is fine for analytics but not for the mapping itself. Out of scope: link-preview pages, malware scanning (mention it).

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • New URLs: 100 million per month. A month is about 30 × 86,400 = 2,592,000 seconds. Writes ≈ 100,000,000 ÷ 2,592,000 ≈ 39 per second, call it 40. Peak at 3× ≈ 120 per second.
  • Read:write ratio 100:1. Reads ≈ 40 × 100 = 4,000 per second on average, about 12,000 per second at peak.
  • Retention 5 years: 100M × 12 × 5 = 6 billion URLs.
  • Row size: code 7 B + long URL ~200 B + timestamps and user ~50 B, say 500 B with index overhead. Storage = 6 × 109 × 500 B = 3 × 1012 B = 3 TB. One modern database cluster handles that; sharding is for write throughput and availability more than raw size.
  • Code length: base62 has 62 characters (a–z, A–Z, 0–9). 626 ≈ 56.8 billion and 627 ≈ 3.52 trillion. For 6 billion URLs, 6 characters would fit, but 7 gives about 590 times headroom. Use 7.
  • Cache: 4,000 reads/s × 86,400 ≈ 345 million reads/day. If the hottest 20% of URLs get most traffic, caching 20% of one day's distinct URLs ≈ 0.2 × 345M × 500 B ≈ 35 GB. That fits a small Redis cluster.
  • Bandwidth: 4,000 × 500 B = 2 MB/s of response data. Tiny.

Conclusion: this is not a big-data problem. The interesting parts are generating unique codes, caching, and keeping redirects fast and available.

3. API design

POST /api/v1/urls
Authorization: Bearer ...
{"longUrl": "https://example.com/very/long/path?x=1",
 "customAlias": "diwali-sale",     // optional
 "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z"}   // optional

201 Created
{"shortCode": "aZ3k9Q1", "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/aZ3k9Q1",
 "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z"}

GET /aZ3k9Q1
302 Found
Location: https://example.com/very/long/path?x=1

GET /api/v1/urls/aZ3k9Q1/stats   -> {"clicks": 1532, "byDay": [...]}
DELETE /api/v1/urls/aZ3k9Q1      -> 204 No Content

Creation should accept an Idempotency-Key header so a retry does not create two codes (Idempotency). Unknown or expired codes return 404 (or 410 Gone for expired).

4. Data model

CREATE TABLE url_mapping (
    short_code  VARCHAR(10)   PRIMARY KEY,
    long_url    VARCHAR(2048) NOT NULL,
    user_id     BIGINT,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP     NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    expires_at  TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX idx_mapping_user ON url_mapping (user_id);

The main access pattern is a single-key lookup by short_code, with no joins and no transactions across rows. That fits a key-value or wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) very well, and also a sharded SQL database. PostgreSQL or MySQL is fine up to this scale with replicas; choose NoSQL if you expect much higher write rates or want built-in horizontal scaling. The shard key is short_code (even spread because codes are random-looking). Analytics are stored separately (see below).

5. High-level architecture

The read path (99% of traffic) and the write path have very different load, so deploy them as separate services or at least separate scaling groups. Redirect servers are stateless; any instance can serve any code.

6. Deep dive A: generating the short code

OptionHow it worksProsCons
Counter + base62Get next unique number, encode in base62No collisions, shortest codesCounter is a dependency; codes are guessable and sequential
Hash of the URLMD5 or SHA-256, take first 7 base62 charactersNo coordination; same URL gives same codeCollisions to handle; two users cannot have separate codes for one URL
Pre-generated keys (KGS)A key service creates random unused codes in advance; app takes oneFast, no collision check at request time, unguessableOne more service; must avoid giving a key twice

Counter + base62. Take a number such as 125 and convert it to base 62: repeatedly divide by 62 and map remainders to characters. A 64-bit counter from a ticket server with ranges or a Snowflake generator (Unique IDs) removes the single-database bottleneck: each app server leases a range of, say, 1,000 numbers and encodes them locally. To stop people enumerating links (aZ3k9Q1, aZ3k9Q2), apply a reversible shuffle to the number first, or use a random permutation.

public final class Base62 {
    private static final String ALPHABET =
        "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

    public static String encode(long n) {
        if (n == 0) return "0";
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        while (n > 0) {
            sb.append(ALPHABET.charAt((int) (n % 62)));
            n /= 62;
        }
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(encode(125));            // 125 = 2*62 + 1
        System.out.println(encode(3_521_614_606_207L)); // 62^7 - 1, the largest 7-char value
    }
}
21
ZZZZZZZ

Hash + collision handling. Compute base62(md5(longUrl)) and keep 7 characters. Seven characters is about 42 bits of the hash, so with billions of URLs collisions do happen (birthday effect). On insert, if the code exists with a different long URL, append a counter or salt to the input and hash again. This makes the write path a read-then-write loop; rely on the primary key constraint to catch the race between two writers.

Pre-generated keys. A separate key generation service fills a table of unused 7-char random codes. App servers take a batch of keys (for example 1,000) and mark them used atomically. Keys given to a server that crashes are simply lost, which is fine with 3.5 trillion possible codes. Pick this when unguessability matters.

7. Deep dive B: redirects, 301 vs 302 and analytics

StatusMeaningEffect
301 Moved PermanentlyCache this redirectBrowsers and proxies remember it; later clicks may never reach you, so no analytics and the link cannot be changed
302 Found (or 307)Temporary redirectEvery click hits your server: you can count it, change the target or expire the link; slightly more load

If you need analytics, expiry or editing, use 302 and accept the extra load (the numbers above are small). If you only want minimal cost and fixed links, 301. The click must not slow the redirect: the redirect service sends the user to the target first and writes a small event (code, time, country, user agent) to a queue; consumers aggregate into an analytics store (ClickHouse or similar, or counters in a time-series table). Losing a few click events is acceptable (at-most-once is fine, see Delivery semantics).

8. Deep dive C: caching hot links

Link popularity is highly skewed: a few viral links get most clicks. Use cache-aside in Redis: look up code; on a miss read the database and store with a TTL of hours; an LRU or LFU policy handles memory (Module 5). With a 90%+ hit ratio the database sees under 400 reads per second at the 4,000/s average. Add a tiny in-process cache for the top few thousand codes to protect Redis from hot keys. Cache "not found" for a short time so scanners guessing random codes do not reach the database (penetration), and a Bloom filter of all existing codes can reject most guesses outright. Expired links: store expires_at in the cache value and check it on every read; the database cleans up with a background job.

9. Bottlenecks and scaling

  • Database: add read replicas first; shard by short_code when storage or writes outgrow one cluster. Use consistent hashing so adding shards moves little data.
  • Availability: multiple app instances across zones; Redis with replicas; database with replicas and automatic failover. Serve cached redirects even if the database is briefly down.
  • Multi-region: replicate the mapping to each region and route users to the nearest one with DNS (Module 5). Writes can go to a home region.
  • Abuse: rate limit creation per user and IP; scan target URLs for malware and phishing; block known bad domains.
  • Monitoring: redirect p99 latency, cache hit ratio, error rate, counter or key pool remaining, queue lag.

Follow-up questions

  • Same long URL submitted twice: return the same code or a new one? (Per-user dedupe by hashing userId + url.)
  • How do you delete expired links at scale? (TTL in a key-value store, or a nightly batch by partition.)
  • How do you stop one user's custom alias clashing with generated codes? (Reserve a different namespace or length.)
  • What if the counter service dies? (Servers hold leased ranges; run two counter nodes with odd and even steps.)
  • How would you count unique visitors? (Approximate with HyperLogLog.)

Interview angle

  • Do the 627 arithmetic out loud; it shows you size the code length from the numbers.
  • Compare the three code-generation options in a sentence each and pick one with a reason.
  • Know 301 vs 302 and its analytics consequence.

Design Pastebin (text sharing with expiry)

Pastebin stores blocks of text under a short link; because pastes can be large and are rarely changed, keep small metadata in a database and the text itself in object storage behind a CDN, generate keys like a URL shortener, and expire pastes with a TTL plus a background cleaner.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • A user (logged in or anonymous) pastes text and gets a unique link.
  • Anyone with the link can read the paste. Options: public, unlisted or private.
  • Optional expiry (10 minutes, 1 day, 1 month, never), optional syntax highlighting language, optional custom alias.
  • Pastes are immutable once created (editing creates a new paste); users can delete their own.

Non-functional: high availability for reads, low read latency (a few hundred milliseconds), durability (a paste must not be lost before it expires), a size limit (say 10 MB), unguessable links for unlisted pastes, and abuse control (spam, malware, illegal content). Strong consistency for the "create then open" flow is nice: the creator opens the link immediately, so reads right after writes must work. Out of scope: collaborative editing, full-text search across all pastes.

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • Writes: 1 million new pastes per day → 1,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 12 per second; peak about 3× = 36 per second.
  • Reads: 5 reads per paste → 5 million reads per day → 5,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 58 per second; peak ~175 per second. Many pastes are read once or twice, a few go viral.
  • Average paste size 10 KB. Daily text = 1,000,000 × 10 KB = 10 GB. Per year = 10 GB × 365 ≈ 3.65 TB. Over 5 years ≈ 18 TB, before compression (text often compresses 3–5×) and before expiry removes many pastes.
  • Metadata: about 200 B per paste (key, owner, size, times, storage path) → 1M × 200 B = 200 MB per day, about 73 GB per year. Small enough for one database with replicas.
  • Read bandwidth: 58/s × 10 KB ≈ 580 KB/s average. Trivial. Even the 10 MB worst case at a few requests per second is manageable via a CDN.
  • Keys: 1M per day × 365 × 5 ≈ 1.8 billion keys. Base62 with 8 characters (628 ≈ 2.18 × 1014) leaves a huge margin and makes random guessing impractical.

Conclusion: request rates are low; the interesting problems are storing large blobs cheaply, expiry, and unguessable keys.

3. API design

POST /api/v1/pastes
{"content": "public class Hello { ... }",
 "language": "java",
 "visibility": "UNLISTED",
 "expiresInSeconds": 86400}

201 Created
{"key": "k3Fq9XaB", "url": "https://paste.example/k3Fq9XaB",
 "expiresAt": "2026-11-12T09:30:00Z"}

GET /api/v1/pastes/k3Fq9XaB
200 OK
{"key": "k3Fq9XaB", "language": "java", "createdAt": "...",
 "content": "public class Hello { ... }"}

DELETE /api/v1/pastes/k3Fq9XaB   (owner only)   -> 204 No Content

For large pastes, a good variant is to return metadata only and let the client fetch the raw text from a CDN URL (/raw/k3Fq9XaB), so big payloads never pass through the app servers.

4. Data model

Split metadata from content. Metadata is small, structured and queried by key or by user; content is a large blob read as a whole.

CREATE TABLE paste (
    paste_key    VARCHAR(12)  PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id     BIGINT,                          -- null for anonymous
    visibility   VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL,           -- PUBLIC, UNLISTED, PRIVATE
    language     VARCHAR(20),
    size_bytes   INT          NOT NULL,
    blob_path    VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,           -- e.g. pastes/2026/11/11/k3Fq9XaB
    created_at   TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    expires_at   TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX idx_paste_owner   ON paste (owner_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_paste_expires ON paste (expires_at);

The content lives in object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, MinIO; see Module 5). Why not keep 10 KB–10 MB text in the database? Large rows bloat the buffer cache and backups, slow replication, and cost far more per GB than object storage, which is cheap, durable (designed for many nines of durability) and scales to petabytes. Tiny pastes (under a few KB) could be stored inline in the row as an optimisation; do not start there.

Database choice: a relational database is fine for this volume (73 GB per year of metadata). A key-value store also works since the main lookup is by key. Choose what the team knows; mention the alternative.

5. High-level architecture

Write path: validate size and rate → get a unique key → upload the text to object storage at blob_path → insert the metadata row → return the link. Do the blob upload first; if the insert fails you have an orphan blob (cleaned up by a periodic scan), which is better than a metadata row pointing to a missing blob. Read path: check cache → on a miss read the metadata row, check expires_at and visibility → fetch the blob → fill the cache → return.

6. Deep dive A: key generation

The same options as the URL shortener apply: counter + base62, random pre-generated keys, or hashing. For Pastebin, unguessable keys matter more because "unlisted" means "anyone with the link", so a sequential key would let people walk through all pastes. Use a random 8-character base62 key from a key service, or encode a random 48-bit number (8 base62 characters). On insert, rely on the primary key: if a random key already exists (very unlikely), generate another and retry. For private pastes, also check ownership on read; the key alone is not authorisation.

7. Deep dive B: object storage and the read path

  • Immutability helps. A paste never changes, so it can be cached for a long time. The CDN and the browser can cache /raw/<key> with a long Cache-Control max-age, which removes most read load. When a paste is deleted or expires, purge it from the CDN (or accept bounded staleness for public pastes).
  • Signed URLs. For private pastes the app can hand out a short-lived signed URL to the object store, so the bytes flow storage → client directly. This keeps big traffic off the app servers and still enforces authorisation.
  • Compression. Compress text (gzip) before storing, typically cutting size 3–5×; the 18 TB five-year figure becomes roughly 4–6 TB.
  • Hot pastes. A viral paste is served by the CDN; the origin sees only misses. Cache metadata for hot keys in Redis with a TTL, using the patterns in Module 5.
  • Large uploads. For the 10 MB limit, either accept through the API with a body size cap or issue a pre-signed upload URL so the client uploads straight to storage, then calls the API to commit.

8. Deep dive C: expiry

Expired pastes must stop being served immediately, and their storage must eventually be reclaimed. Separate these two goals.

ApproachHowTrade-off
Lazy expiryOn every read, compare expires_at with now; if past, return 404 (and optionally delete)Always correct for reads; storage is not freed for pastes nobody reads
Background cleanerA scheduled job selects rows with expires_at < now() in batches, deletes the blob and then the rowFrees storage; needs the index on expires_at and batching to avoid load spikes
Native TTLUse a store with TTL (Redis, DynamoDB TTL, object-store lifecycle rules)No custom code; deletion time is approximate (often within hours or days)
Time-bucketed partitionsPartition metadata (and blob prefixes) by expiry date and drop whole partitionsVery cheap deletion; more design effort

A solid answer combines lazy expiry for correctness with a background cleaner (or lifecycle rule) for storage. Delete the row first and the blob second, or mark first and sweep later, so a failure leaves an orphan blob rather than a dangling pointer. Cache entries get a TTL no longer than the paste's remaining life.

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 60_000)
public void cleanExpired() {
    List<PasteMeta> batch = repo.findExpired(Instant.now(), 500);   // uses idx_paste_expires
    for (PasteMeta p : batch) {
        blobStore.delete(p.blobPath());      // idempotent: deleting a missing blob is fine
        repo.deleteByKey(p.key());
        cache.evict(p.key());
    }
}

9. Bottlenecks, scaling and abuse

  • Scaling is easy here. Stateless API servers behind a load balancer; metadata DB with read replicas; blobs in object storage that scales by itself. If metadata outgrows one DB, shard by paste_key.
  • Availability: cached and CDN content survive a database blip; run across zones.
  • Abuse: rate limit anonymous creation per IP; reject over-size content; scan for malware, credentials leaks and illegal material; provide a report button and takedown flow; add X-Content-Type-Options and serve raw text as text/plain so a paste cannot run as a web page (stored XSS).
  • Privacy: never put private paste content in logs; encrypt blobs at rest.
  • Monitoring: cache hit ratio, p99 latency, storage growth, orphan count, cleaner lag.

Follow-up questions

  • How would you add search over paste content? (A search index, fed by CDC or a queue; public pastes only.)
  • How do you stop the same spam paste being posted millions of times? (Content hash dedupe and rate limits.)
  • What if the object store is down? (Serve from cache/CDN; fail creates with a clear error or queue them.)
  • How would you support editing or versions? (New immutable version with a parent id.)
  • How do you make "burn after reading" pastes work? (Atomic delete on first read, with a conditional update to avoid two readers.)

Interview angle

  • The key insight to say early: "metadata in a database, content in object storage".
  • Treat expiry as two problems: correctness on read, reclamation in the background.
  • Mention immutability, CDN caching and unguessable keys.

Design a distributed rate limiter (with Redis)

A distributed rate limiter decides, in about a millisecond, whether a client may make a request now; the usual design keeps per-client counters or token buckets in Redis, updates them atomically with a Lua script, and decides what to do when Redis itself is slow or down.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Limit requests per client (user id, API key or IP) per rule, such as 100 requests per minute, or 10 per second on login.
  • Different limits per endpoint and per plan (free vs paid).
  • Reject excess requests with 429 Too Many Requests and tell the client when to retry.
  • Rules can be changed without redeploying.

Non-functional: very low added latency (a few milliseconds at most, since it sits on every request), accurate enough across many servers (not 10× over the limit), highly available (it must not become the outage), and scalable to the whole API's traffic. Decide the failure policy: when the limiter is down, do we fail open (allow traffic) or fail closed (block)? For most APIs fail open; for expensive or security-critical endpoints (login, SMS) fail closed or fall back to local limits. Out of scope: DDoS protection at network level (a CDN/WAF job).

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • Total API traffic: 50,000 requests per second at peak. Every request needs one limiter check → 50,000 checks per second.
  • One Redis node handles very roughly on the order of 100,000 simple operations per second (an approximation that depends on hardware and commands). A Lua script costs more than one GET, so budget a node for perhaps 30,000–50,000 checks per second. We need a cluster of 3–5 shards with headroom, sharded by client key.
  • Memory: 10 million active clients, each with a token bucket of about 100 bytes (key + two fields + overhead) → 10,000,000 × 100 B = 1 GB. Memory is not the problem; operations per second are.
  • Latency: a Redis round trip inside a data centre is roughly 0.5–1 ms. With a budget of 5 ms this is fine; with 100 rules per request it would not be (so check only the few rules that apply).

3. Choosing the algorithm

The algorithms are explained in Module 5 and as a single-machine class in Module 3. Here is the comparison that matters for the distributed design.

AlgorithmState per clientAccuracyNotes
Fixed window counter1 counter + window startAllows up to 2× the limit around a window boundarySimplest, cheapest (INCR + EXPIRE)
Sliding window logTimestamp of every requestExactMemory heavy (limit × clients)
Sliding window counterTwo counters (current and previous window)Close approximationGood balance; small state
Token bucketToken count + last refill timeAllows controlled burstsMost popular; two fields per client
Leaky bucketQueue or level + timeSmooth constant output rateGood when the backend needs a steady rate

The boundary problem: with a limit of 100 per minute and a fixed window, a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, which is 200 in two seconds. The sliding window counter estimates the current rate as current + previous × overlap. For example, 30 seconds into a window, with 40 requests in the previous window and 30 in the current one, the estimate is 30 + 40 × 0.5 = 50.

This design uses the token bucket: a bucket of capacity C refills at R tokens per second; each request takes one token; an empty bucket means reject. It allows short bursts up to C and a long-run rate of R.

4. API design

The limiter is usually a library or sidecar inside the API gateway, with an optional internal service for rule lookup. Internal API:

POST /internal/v1/ratelimit/check
{"clientId": "key_8a1f", "rule": "orders-create", "cost": 1}

200 OK
{"allowed": true, "remaining": 87, "limit": 100, "resetMs": 8200}

200 OK
{"allowed": false, "remaining": 0, "retryAfterMs": 1300}

The public API then answers rejected calls like this:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 2
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1762853400

The X-RateLimit-* headers are a widely used convention (not one single official standard); Retry-After is a standard HTTP header.

5. Data model

Two kinds of data. Rules (config): (rule, plan, limit, window or refill), stored in a small database or config service and cached in each limiter instance, refreshed every few seconds. Counters (hot state): a Redis hash per client and rule.

ratelimit:{key_8a1f}:orders-create   (hash)
    tokens = 87.0
    ts     = 1762853392100        (last refill time, ms)
  expire after about 2 x the time to refill a full bucket

6. High-level architecture

7. Deep dive A: atomic checks in Redis

The naive approach is GET then SET from the app. Two gateways do it at the same time, both see 1 token left, and both allow: a race condition. The state change must be atomic. For a fixed window, INCR is atomic by itself. For a token bucket you need several steps (read, refill, subtract, write), so run them as one Lua script; Redis executes a script without interleaving other commands.

local key      = KEYS[1]
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])   -- max tokens
local refill   = tonumber(ARGV[2])   -- tokens added per second
local now      = tonumber(ARGV[3])   -- current time in ms
local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[4])   -- tokens needed for this request

local data   = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1])
local ts     = tonumber(data[2])
if tokens == nil then
  tokens = capacity
  ts = now
end

tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + math.max(0, now - ts) * refill / 1000)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
end

redis.call('HSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, math.ceil(capacity / refill * 2000))
return {allowed, math.floor(tokens)}
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.script.DefaultRedisScript;

public class RedisRateLimiter {
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final DefaultRedisScript<List> script;

    public RedisRateLimiter(StringRedisTemplate redis, String luaSource) {
        this.redis = redis;
        this.script = new DefaultRedisScript<>(luaSource, List.class);
    }

    public boolean allow(String clientId, String rule, int capacity, double refillPerSec) {
        String key = "ratelimit:{" + clientId + "}:" + rule;     // {..} = hash tag
        List<?> r = redis.execute(script, List.of(key),
            String.valueOf(capacity), String.valueOf(refillPerSec),
            String.valueOf(System.currentTimeMillis()), "1");
        return r != null && ((Long) r.get(0)) == 1L;
    }
}

Notes: in Redis Cluster all keys touched by one script must live in the same slot; the {clientId} hash tag guarantees that. Passing time from the gateway means clock differences between gateways add small errors; if that matters, read the time inside the script with redis.call('TIME'). Keep scripts short, since they block the Redis thread while running.

8. Deep dive B: accuracy, latency and failure

  • Centralised vs local limits. Calling Redis on every request adds about a millisecond and makes Redis a dependency. A hybrid cuts both: each gateway keeps a local counter and syncs with Redis every 100 ms or after N requests (batching), or gets a slice of the quota ("you may admit 20 of this client's 100 per minute locally"). It is slightly less exact (a client might exceed by a small percentage) but much cheaper. Say which error you accept.
  • Sharding. Shard Redis by client key with consistent hashing (Module 5); one hot client stays on one shard, so for extreme keys use a local limiter or split the key into sub-buckets.
  • Failure policy. If a Redis call times out (use a very short timeout, 5–20 ms), fail open with a local in-memory limiter as a safety net, and raise an alert. For login or SMS, fail closed. A circuit breaker (Resilience) stops the gateway from waiting on a dead Redis.
  • Replication. Redis replication is asynchronous, so after a failover the counters can roll back a little and clients get a brief extra allowance. For a limiter that is acceptable.
  • Multi-region. Strict global limits need cross-region calls (slow). Usually each region enforces its own share of the limit (for example 50% each) or syncs asynchronously.

9. Deep dive C: where to put it and how to identify clients

  • Placement: at the edge or API gateway (best: reject before doing any work), as a middleware in each service, or both (coarse at the edge, fine-grained per service). Client-side limiting alone is not enough since clients can be hostile.
  • Identity: API key or user id once authenticated; IP address for anonymous traffic (but many users share one IP behind NAT, so be generous), and a combination for login attempts (per username plus per IP).
  • Cost-based limits: let an expensive call take 5 tokens instead of 1.
  • Response: return 429 with Retry-After; well-behaved clients back off with jitter (Retries). Log rejections to spot abusive clients and tune rules.

Bottlenecks and scaling

Add Redis shards as checks per second grow; reduce checks with local batching; keep rules in memory; monitor Redis CPU, command latency and the rejection rate. At 10× traffic (500,000 checks per second) the central-Redis-per-request design needs 10–15 shards, so moving to local batching or quota slices becomes worthwhile.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you stop one tenant using the whole shared quota? (Per-tenant limits plus a global limit.)
  • How would you rate limit by "requests in flight" instead of rate? (A semaphore-style counter that is decremented on completion; needs expiry for crashed requests.)
  • Fixed window vs sliding window: which and why? (Sliding window counter for accuracy at low cost; token bucket for bursts.)
  • How do you test the limiter? (Load test with many parallel clients; assert total allowed ≤ limit plus tolerance.)

Interview angle

  • Say "atomic, so a Lua script" and explain the race in GET-then-SET.
  • State your failure policy (fail open or closed) and justify it per endpoint.
  • Mention the boundary problem of fixed windows and why token bucket or sliding window is better.

Design a notification system (push, SMS, email, in-app)

A notification system accepts "tell user X about Y" requests from many services and delivers them over several channels; the design is a validation layer, per-channel queues with priorities, workers that call external providers with retries and rate limits, and idempotency so nobody gets the same message twice.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Other services (orders, payments, marketing) send notifications through an API or by publishing events.
  • Channels: mobile push (FCM for Android, APNs for iOS), SMS, email and in-app (a bell icon list).
  • Templates with variables ("Your order {{orderId}} is out for delivery").
  • User preferences: opt in or out per channel and per category; quiet hours (do not disturb).
  • Scheduled and bulk (campaign) notifications.
  • Delivery status tracking (queued, sent, delivered, failed, opened) where the provider reports it.

Non-functional: high availability and no loss for important messages (OTP, payment alerts); at-least-once delivery with deduplication so users are not spammed; priority (an OTP must not wait behind a marketing blast); soft real-time (OTP within seconds, marketing within minutes); scalable for burst traffic; respect provider rate limits. Out of scope: building the SMS carrier network, the content of marketing campaigns.

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • 10 million users, on average 5 notifications per user per day → 50 million per day → 50,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 580 per second on average.
  • Burst: a marketing campaign pushes to all 10 million users within 10 minutes (600 seconds) → 10,000,000 ÷ 600 ≈ 16,700 per second. The system must be sized for this, not for the average.
  • Channel mix (assumed): 70% push, 20% email, 5% SMS, 5% in-app only. SMS is 2.5 million per day and costs real money per message, so SMS is the channel to protect with limits.
  • Storage: a log row of about 300 bytes per notification → 50M × 300 B = 15 GB per day. Keep 90 days for support: 90 × 15 GB = 1.35 TB. Older data goes to cheap storage or is deleted.
  • Queue sizing: at the 16,700/s burst with 1 KB messages, throughput is about 17 MB/s, which one small Kafka cluster handles. Workers: if one worker can make 200 provider calls per second, the burst needs about 85 workers, which autoscaling can add.

3. API design

POST /api/v1/notifications
Idempotency-Key: 5d1c0d6e-...
{"userId": 9912,
 "type": "ORDER_SHIPPED",              // maps to a template + category
 "channels": ["PUSH", "EMAIL"],        // optional: otherwise from preferences
 "priority": "HIGH",
 "data": {"orderId": "OD-7731", "eta": "Tomorrow"},
 "sendAt": "2026-11-12T09:00:00+05:30"}   // optional

202 Accepted
{"notificationId": "n_01JC3...", "status": "QUEUED"}

GET  /api/v1/users/9912/notifications?cursor=...&limit=20   (in-app list)
POST /api/v1/notifications/n_01JC3.../read
PUT  /api/v1/users/9912/preferences
     {"email": {"marketing": false}, "quietHours": {"from": "22:00", "to": "07:00"}}

The API answers 202 Accepted because delivery is asynchronous. The caller needs the idempotency key so a retried request does not create a second notification (Idempotency).

4. Data model

CREATE TABLE notification (
    id            VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id       BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    type          VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    channel       VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL,        -- PUSH, SMS, EMAIL, INAPP
    status        VARCHAR(12)  NOT NULL,        -- QUEUED, SENT, DELIVERED, FAILED
    payload       JSONB        NOT NULL,
    attempts      INT          NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at    TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    updated_at    TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_notif_user ON notification (user_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE user_preference (
    user_id BIGINT, channel VARCHAR(10), category VARCHAR(20), enabled BOOLEAN,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, channel, category)
);
CREATE TABLE device_token (
    user_id BIGINT, token VARCHAR(300), platform VARCHAR(10), updated_at TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, token)
);

Preferences, templates and device tokens are small, relational and read-heavy: PostgreSQL or MySQL with a Redis cache in front. The notification log is write-heavy and time-ordered, queried by user and time: a wide-column store (Cassandra) or a partitioned SQL table works. Use SQL first and say when you would move.

5. High-level architecture

Why one queue per channel? Each provider has different speed, cost, failure modes and rate limits. If the email provider is slow, the backlog must not delay push or SMS. This is the bulkhead idea from Resilience. Within a channel, use separate queues (or topics) per priority: OTP and payment alerts on a high-priority queue with dedicated workers, marketing on a low-priority queue that may take hours.

Steps inside the validation stage: authenticate the caller → check the idempotency key → load the user's preferences and quiet hours → pick channels → render the template (language, variables) → write a row as QUEUED → publish to the channel queue. Use the outbox pattern (Outbox) so the row and the queue message cannot disagree.

6. Deep dive A: reliable delivery, retries and duplicates

  • At-least-once. A worker takes a message, calls the provider, and acks the queue only after the call succeeds. If it crashes before acking, the message is redelivered. So duplicates are possible (Delivery semantics).
  • Deduplication. Each notification has an id. Before sending, the worker sets SET sent:<id>:<channel> 1 NX EX 86400 in Redis (or a conditional update in the DB, status QUEUED → SENT). If it already exists, skip. Pass the same id as the provider's idempotency or collapse key when they support one (FCM has a collapse key so repeated messages replace each other). The remaining window (crash after the provider accepted but before recording) gives a rare duplicate; accept it and say so.
  • Retries. Transient provider errors (timeouts, 5xx, 429) are retried with exponential backoff and jitter (Retries), using delayed retry queues (retry after 10 s, 1 min, 10 min) instead of sleeping in the worker. After N attempts, move to a dead-letter queue and mark FAILED. Permanent errors (invalid or unregistered device token, unsubscribed number) are never retried; delete the bad token.
  • Failover between providers. Keep two SMS or email providers; a circuit breaker switches to the second when the first fails.
  • Ordering is not guaranteed and rarely needed across notifications; for status updates on one order, include a version or timestamp so a late "packed" does not overwrite "shipped".

7. Deep dive B: priority, rate limits and bursts

  • Priority: separate queues and consumer groups. Do not use one queue with a priority field on Kafka; consumers read in offset order. RabbitMQ and SQS-style systems have their own priority options, but separate queues are simpler and predictable.
  • Provider limits: providers throttle you. A token-bucket limiter per provider and per sender (Rate limiter) in the workers keeps you under the limit; when the bucket is empty, leave the message in the queue.
  • Per-user limits: cap marketing to, say, 3 per day per user, and collapse bursts ("5 people liked your post" instead of 5 pushes). This protects users from spam, which is also a non-functional requirement.
  • Bulk campaigns: a campaign job reads the audience in pages, creates notifications in batches and feeds the low-priority queue at a controlled rate, never all 10 million at once. Spread sends over time zones.
  • Scheduling: store sendAt and let a scheduler (a DB poller with an index, or delayed messages) enqueue when due. Respect quiet hours by shifting non-urgent messages to the next allowed time.

8. Deep dive C: channel details and tracking

  • Push: the app registers a device token with the backend; the worker sends the token and payload to FCM or APNs. Tokens expire or change; handle "unregistered" replies by deleting the token. Push is best-effort: if the phone is offline, the provider holds the message for a limited time.
  • SMS: costly and regulated (in India, sender id and template registration rules apply for transactional and promotional SMS). Use for OTP and critical alerts; prefer push or email for marketing. Watch for fraud: an attacker triggers OTP SMS to premium numbers (pumping), so rate limit OTP per number and per IP.
  • Email: use a provider (SES, SendGrid and similar); handle bounces and spam complaints via webhooks and stop mailing bad addresses; include an unsubscribe link; set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC so mail is not marked as spam.
  • In-app: write to the notification table and push over the user's open WebSocket if any (see Chat); the bell icon reads the list with cursor pagination and an unread count kept in Redis.
  • Tracking: providers send delivery and open events through webhooks. A callback service updates the status. Treat webhooks as at-least-once too: updates must be idempotent and monotonic (SENT → DELIVERED → OPENED, never backwards).

9. Bottlenecks, scaling and monitoring

  • Scale workers per queue by queue depth (autoscaling on lag). The database write of status rows can become the bottleneck; batch updates and partition by time.
  • Cache preferences and templates in Redis with short TTLs; invalidate on change.
  • Queue brokers are replicated across zones; the API is stateless.
  • Metrics: queue lag per channel, send success rate, provider latency, DLQ size, delivered-to-sent ratio, cost per channel. Alert on lag for high-priority queues and on a sudden drop in the success rate.
  • Security: validate the caller's identity and allowed types so one service cannot message all users; never put secrets or full card numbers in payloads; mask OTPs in logs.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you guarantee an OTP is delivered within 10 seconds? (Dedicated high-priority queue and workers, multiple SMS providers with failover, alert on latency.)
  • What if a user has 3 devices? (One token row per device; send to all active ones, or only the most recent.)
  • How do you support user timezones and localisation? (Store locale and zone; render templates per locale.)
  • How would you avoid sending a "your order was delivered" push twice after a retry? (Idempotency key plus dedupe set, monotonic status.)
  • How do you test without messaging real users? (A sandbox provider and a dry-run mode.)

Interview angle

  • Say early: "async, one queue per channel and priority, at-least-once with dedupe".
  • Size for the campaign burst (16,700 per second), not the average (580).
  • Show you know channel details: device tokens, SMS cost and abuse, email bounces.

Design a chat app (like WhatsApp)

A chat app keeps a WebSocket open from each online user to a gateway, routes each message to the recipient's gateway through a session registry, stores messages durably so offline users catch up when they return, and tracks sent, delivered and read states with acknowledgements.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • One-to-one chat and small group chat (up to a few hundred members).
  • Send and receive text messages in real time; media as links to files (images, video, documents).
  • Message states: sent, delivered, read (the ticks).
  • Online / last-seen status.
  • Messages sent to offline users are delivered when they reconnect, and as push notifications.
  • Chat history synced on a new device (within limits).

Non-functional: low latency (well under a second when both are online), no message loss (durability), per-conversation ordering, high availability, millions of concurrent connections, and security (TLS everywhere; end-to-end encryption is a deep topic, mention it). Out of scope: voice and video calls, stories, payments inside chat.

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • 50 million daily active users, 40 messages sent per user per day → 2 billion messages per day → 2,000,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23,000 per second on average; peak 3× ≈ 70,000 per second.
  • Message size ~100 bytes of text plus ~100 bytes of metadata = 200 B. Per day: 2 × 109 × 200 B = 400 GB; per year ≈ 146 TB; with 3× replication ≈ 440 TB. Media (images, videos) is far bigger and goes to object storage and a CDN, not to the message store.
  • Concurrent connections: if 40% of daily users are online at once → 20 million WebSocket connections. A tuned gateway server can hold on the order of 100,000 idle connections (approximate; depends on memory and kernel tuning) → 20,000,000 ÷ 100,000 = 200 gateway servers, plus headroom.
  • Presence heartbeats: every 30 seconds per connection → 20M ÷ 30 ≈ 670,000 tiny messages per second, handled inside the gateways in memory; only status changes go to shared storage.
  • Bandwidth: 70,000 messages/s × 200 B = 14 MB/s of message payload. Small; connection count and fan-out dominate, not bytes.

3. API design

Chat uses a persistent WebSocket for real-time events, and normal REST for everything else (login, history, media upload). HTTP polling would waste requests, and long polling holds a request open and re-establishes it per message; WebSockets give a two-way channel with little overhead per message.

// client -> server
{"type": "send", "clientMsgId": "c-7f31", "chatId": "ch_88",
 "text": "Reached office", "ts": 1762853392000}

// server -> sender (ack: stored)
{"type": "ack", "clientMsgId": "c-7f31", "msgId": "m_5501772", "seq": 412}

// server -> recipient
{"type": "message", "msgId": "m_5501772", "chatId": "ch_88", "from": 9912,
 "seq": 412, "text": "Reached office", "ts": 1762853392100}

// recipient -> server
{"type": "delivered", "msgId": "m_5501772"}
{"type": "read", "chatId": "ch_88", "upToSeq": 412}
GET  /api/v1/chats/ch_88/messages?afterSeq=400&limit=50
POST /api/v1/media           (returns an upload URL; message then carries the media id)
GET  /api/v1/users/9912/presence

The clientMsgId is an idempotency key generated by the client: if the app resends after a lost ack, the server recognises the duplicate (Idempotency).

4. Data model

Access patterns: "append a message to a conversation" and "read the latest N messages of a conversation, or all after sequence S". Writes are huge and append-only, with reads by chat id in order. That fits a wide-column / partitioned store (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB) with the chat as the partition key and the sequence as the sort key. A single SQL database would need sharding by chat id early.

messages
  partition key : chat_id
  clustering key: seq (ascending)
  columns       : msg_id, sender_id, text, media_id, created_at

user_inbox  (for offline delivery)
  partition key : user_id
  clustering key: msg_id
  columns       : chat_id, seq

chats       : chat_id, type (DIRECT, GROUP), member_ids, created_at
users       : user_id, phone, name, avatar_url, last_seen
receipts    : (chat_id, user_id) -> last_delivered_seq, last_read_seq

Receipts use watermarks (the last sequence delivered or read per user per chat), not one row per message, which keeps group receipts cheap: "read up to 412" marks everything before it.

5. High-level architecture

Send flow:

  1. The sender's app sends the frame over its WebSocket to gateway 1.
  2. Gateway 1 forwards it to the message service, which assigns the next seq for that chat and writes the message to the store. Now it is durable.
  3. The message service replies with an ack (the first tick: "sent").
  4. It looks up each recipient in the session registry (user_id → gateway id, kept in Redis, with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats).
  5. If the recipient is online on gateway 2, the service forwards the message to gateway 2, which pushes it down the socket. The recipient app sends delivered (second tick).
  6. If the recipient is offline, the message stays in their inbox and a push notification is sent through FCM or APNs. On reconnect, the app asks for everything after its last seq.

6. Deep dive A: gateways, routing and scale of connections

  • Stateful connections. A WebSocket is tied to one gateway, so load balancing happens only at connect time (L4 load balancer or a connection router). After that, messages for a user must be sent to their gateway. The session registry gives that mapping. Alternative: publish to a pub/sub channel per user or per gateway and let gateways subscribe (Redis pub/sub, Kafka); simpler but chattier.
  • Gateway failure. Clients reconnect automatically with exponential backoff and jitter (so 100,000 clients lost together do not reconnect at the same millisecond) and then sync from their last seq. No message is lost because messages are stored before being routed.
  • Deploys. Draining a gateway means asking clients to reconnect elsewhere gradually.
  • Group chat. The message service stores one copy under the chat id, then fans out to each member's gateway. For groups up to a few hundred this is cheap. Very large groups or channels need a different design (clients pull, or fan-out through a queue).

7. Deep dive B: ordering, IDs and delivery guarantees

  • Ordering. Global ordering is impossible and unnecessary; users only need order inside a conversation. The message service owns a per-chat counter: all writes for one chat are handled by the same shard or partition (shard key = chat id), so it can assign increasing seq numbers. Clients sort by seq, not by device clock time. Timestamps from phones are wrong too often.
  • IDs. msgId should be unique and time-sortable (Snowflake, see Unique IDs); seq gives dense ordering per chat for gap detection: if the client sees 410, 411, 413 it knows 412 is missing and requests it.
  • Delivery semantics. Client to server and server to client are both at-least-once, with dedupe by clientMsgId and msgId so the user sees each message exactly once (Delivery semantics). The client resends until it gets an ack.
  • Receipts. Delivered and read events travel the reverse path and update the watermark; the sender's app is told by the same routing. Batch read receipts ("read up to seq 412") to avoid sending one event per message. Users can disable read receipts for privacy.
  • Multiple devices. Each device is a separate connection and has its own last-synced seq; the inbox model delivers to all of them.

8. Deep dive C: presence and offline handling

  • Online status. The gateway marks a user online in Redis when the socket opens (SET presence:<id> online EX 60) and refreshes it on each heartbeat. If heartbeats stop (network drop), the key expires and the user becomes offline with last_seen = last heartbeat. This TTL approach copes with crashes where no "disconnect" event arrives (Heartbeats).
  • Who sees presence? Pushing every status change to every contact is a fan-out problem (a user with 500 contacts flickering online/offline). Fetch presence on demand when a chat is opened, and subscribe only for the chats currently on screen. Add a small delay before announcing "offline" so brief network blips do not flicker.
  • Offline users. Messages remain in the inbox until acked as delivered. Push notifications carry no or minimal content (privacy) and wake the app. Limit retention for undelivered messages (for example 30 days) to bound storage.
  • Media. The client uploads the file to object storage (pre-signed URL), gets a media id, and sends a normal message carrying that id and a thumbnail; receivers download via CDN (Module 5).
  • End-to-end encryption (brief): keys live on devices, the server stores and routes ciphertext it cannot read. This makes server-side search, spam filtering and multi-device sync harder, and needs a key exchange protocol (the Signal protocol is the best-known design). Mention it as a design choice with trade-offs.

9. Bottlenecks, scaling and failure

  • Gateways scale by adding servers; the limit is connections per machine. Message store scales by partitioning on chat id. Hot chats (huge groups) may need special handling.
  • Redis session registry: replicate it; if lost, gateways re-register connected users within a heartbeat or two. Rebuildable state is a good property.
  • Overload: rate limit senders to stop spam (Rate limiter), bound per-connection send buffers, drop slow consumers.
  • Monitoring: connected users, message latency end to end, undelivered backlog, reconnect rate, push failure rate.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you support "typing…" indicators? (Ephemeral events through the gateways only; never stored; throttled.)
  • How does search in chat history work? (Local on device for E2E; otherwise an index per user.)
  • How would you design channels with a million members? (Pull-based, fan-out on read, cached latest pages; see News feed.)
  • What if two devices send at the same moment? (Server assigns seq; both messages appear in seq order.)
  • How do you migrate off a failing gateway without dropping messages? (Store-then-route, client resync by seq.)

Interview angle

  • The central trick: store first, then route; then offline and reconnect come almost for free.
  • Do the connection maths: 20 million connections ÷ 100,000 per gateway = 200 servers.
  • Ordering is per conversation (a server-assigned seq), not global and not by phone clocks.

Design a news feed (like Instagram)

A news feed shows each user the recent posts of the people they follow; the core decision is fan-out on write (push each new post into followers' precomputed feeds, fast reads) versus fan-out on read (assemble the feed at request time), and real systems use a hybrid so celebrity accounts do not cause millions of writes.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Users create posts (text, photos, videos).
  • Users follow and unfollow other users.
  • A user opens the app and sees a feed of recent posts from the accounts they follow, newest or best first, loaded page by page (infinite scroll).
  • Likes and comments exist, but the design focus is the feed itself.

Non-functional: feed load in under about 300 ms (reads must be fast), high availability, a new post appears in followers' feeds within a few seconds (eventual consistency is fine; a delay of seconds is not noticed), scalability to hundreds of millions of users, and tolerance for accounts with tens of millions of followers. Strong consistency is not required: seeing a post a little late is acceptable. Out of scope: the ranking model itself (mention the inputs), ads, stories.

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • 100 million daily active users; each opens the feed 10 times a day → 1 billion feed reads per day → 1,000,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11,600 per second; peak 3× ≈ 35,000 per second.
  • 10 million new posts per day → 10,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 116 posts per second.
  • Reads outnumber writes: 11,600 ÷ 116 = 100:1. This strongly favours doing work at write time.
  • Average user follows 200 accounts. Fan-out on write: 10M posts × 200 followers = 2 billion feed insertions per day ≈ 23,000 per second. That is a lot but each is a tiny write (an id into a list), and it runs asynchronously.
  • A celebrity with 50 million followers: one post would need 50,000,000 insertions. At 23,000 per second of system capacity that single post would take about 36 minutes of the total fan-out budget. This is why a pure push model fails for celebrities.
  • Feed cache: keep the latest 500 post ids per active user. Each id 8 bytes → 500 × 8 = 4 KB per user → 100,000,000 × 4 KB = 400 GB (before Redis overhead, which might double it). A sharded Redis cluster of a few nodes with 128 GB each can hold it.
  • Post storage: 10M posts × ~1 KB metadata = 10 GB per day (3.65 TB per year). Media: if 30% of posts carry a 500 KB photo → 3M × 500 KB = 1.5 TB per day in object storage behind a CDN.

3. API design

POST /api/v1/posts
{"text": "Diwali lights", "mediaIds": ["med_88"]}
201 Created   {"postId": "p_91823412", "createdAt": "2026-11-11T09:30:00Z"}

GET /api/v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=p_91823377
200 OK
{"items": [{"postId": "p_91823412", "author": {"id": 7, "name": "Asha"},
            "text": "Diwali lights", "media": ["https://cdn.../med_88.jpg"],
            "likes": 12}, ...],
 "nextCursor": "p_91823101"}

POST   /api/v1/users/7/follow
DELETE /api/v1/users/7/follow

Pagination: use a cursor (the id or time of the last item seen), not page=5 or OFFSET. With offset, new posts push items down and the user sees duplicates or skips; deep offsets are also slow (SQL · Module 5 explains why). Cursor pagination asks for "20 items older than this id", which is stable and uses an index.

4. Data model

users        user_id, name, follower_count, is_celebrity
follows      (follower_id, followee_id)   index both ways
posts        post_id (Snowflake, time-sortable), author_id, text, media_ids, created_at
feed:{user}  Redis sorted set: member = post_id, score = post_id or time
             (latest ~500 entries)
likes        (post_id, user_id) + counter cache
media        media_id -> object-storage path
