  • Posts are written once and read by id, plus "latest posts of author X": a wide-column store or sharded SQL keyed by author_id works, with time-sortable post ids (Unique IDs) so newest-first ordering needs no extra column.
  • Follows is a graph edge list; it needs both "who does X follow" and "who follows X". Store two tables or two indexes. Shard by user id.
  • The precomputed feed is a Redis sorted set per user holding only post ids, not full posts (small, and edits or deletes affect one copy). Hydrate ids into full posts by fetching from a post cache.
  • Counters (likes) are updated asynchronously and cached; approximate counts are acceptable.

5. High-level architecture

Write path: the post service stores the post, then publishes a "post created" event (via an outbox, Outbox). Fan-out workers read the author's follower list in pages and add the post id to each follower's feed sorted set, trimming to 500. Read path: the feed service reads the top 20 ids after the cursor from the user's sorted set, fetches post bodies from the post cache (batch get), fetches author data, and returns the page; images load from the CDN.

6. Deep dive A: fan-out on write vs on read vs hybrid

AspectFan-out on write (push)Fan-out on read (pull)
When feed is builtWhen the post is createdWhen the user opens the app
Read costVery low: read one listHigh: read posts of ~200 followees, merge, sort
Write costHigh: one insert per followerLow: store the post once
Celebrity problem50M inserts per postNone for writes
Inactive followersWasted work filling feeds nobody opensNo waste
FreshnessSeconds of delayAlways current

Hybrid (the usual answer). Use push for normal users and pull for celebrities:

  • If the author has fewer than a threshold of followers (say 100,000, tuned from data), fan out on write.
  • If the author is above the threshold, do not fan out. Store the post only.
  • At read time, the feed service takes the user's precomputed feed (normal accounts) and merges in recent posts from the few celebrities the user follows, fetched from a per-celebrity "recent posts" cache. A user follows few celebrities, so this extra read is small and the celebrity's list is shared by all their followers, so it caches very well.
  • Skip fan-out for inactive users (not opened the app in 30 days). Rebuild their feed on return with the pull method.
public List<PostView> getFeed(long userId, String cursor, int limit) {
    List<Long> ids = new ArrayList<>(feedCache.range(userId, cursor, limit));  // pushed posts

    for (long celeb : graph.celebritiesFollowedBy(userId)) {                  // few of them
        ids.addAll(celebRecent.range(celeb, cursor, limit));                  // pulled posts
    }
    ids.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());          // newest first (time-sortable ids)
    List<Long> page = ids.stream().distinct().limit(limit).toList();
    return postHydrator.load(page);                // batch get from post cache
}

7. Deep dive B: ranking, caching and consistency

  • Chronological vs ranked. A chronological feed is the sorted set as it is. A ranked feed takes candidate posts (say 500 ids), scores each with features (author affinity, recency, past engagement, post type), and returns the top ones. Scoring is a separate service; keep the interface simple: ids in, ordered ids out. In the interview, mention it and keep the focus on retrieval.
  • Hot posts and cache. A viral post is read by millions, so cache the post object with a short TTL, and use a local cache for the hottest ids to avoid a hot key on one Redis shard (Module 5). Media is served from the CDN with long cache lifetimes.
  • Deletes and edits. Because feeds hold ids only, a deleted post disappears when hydration returns "not found" or "deleted"; the feed service filters those out. No need to remove it from 200 feeds immediately.
  • Unfollow and block. Filter at read time by the current follow set (cheap), and lazily clean the stored feed.
  • New follow. Backfill: add the followee's last few posts into the follower's feed.
  • Consistency. The feed is eventually consistent: after posting, the author should see their own post immediately (read-your-writes), so the client inserts it locally or the feed service merges the author's own latest posts. Followers see it within seconds.

8. Deep dive C: the fan-out pipeline at scale

  • Fan-out is a queue-driven job. Split one author's follower list into pages of, say, 1,000 followers; each page is a separate task so many workers share one big fan-out and a failed page can be retried alone.
  • Writes to Redis are idempotent (ZADD of the same member is harmless), so at-least-once processing is fine (Delivery semantics).
  • Use priority: a post by a user with 100 followers should not wait behind a 5-million follower fan-out. Separate queues by author size.
  • Fan-out lag is the key metric: time from post creation to last insertion. Alert when it exceeds a few seconds for normal accounts.
  • Redis memory is the cost driver: trimming to 500 entries and limiting to active users keeps it bounded. If the cache is lost, rebuild feeds lazily by pull.

9. Bottlenecks and scaling

  • Feed cache shards by user id; add nodes with consistent hashing (Module 5).
  • Graph service reads of follower lists are heavy: cache them and page them.
  • Post store shards by author or post id; read replicas for hydration misses.
  • Media is offloaded to object storage and CDN; image resizing happens asynchronously at upload, producing several sizes.
  • Monitoring: feed p99 latency, cache hit ratio for feeds and posts, fan-out lag, queue depth, empty-feed rate (a sign of cache loss).

Follow-up questions

  • Where exactly is the threshold between push and pull, and how do you pick it? (Measure follower distribution and fan-out cost; start near 105 and tune.)
  • How do you show "new posts available" without reloading? (Poll a lightweight count endpoint or use a WebSocket event.)
  • How would you add comments and like counts without hot-row contention? (Sharded counters, async aggregation.)
  • How do you avoid showing the same post twice across pages? (Stable cursor by post id, dedupe in the merge.)
  • How do you handle a user following 5,000 accounts? (Cap, or lean on pull with caching.)

Interview angle

  • Lead with the read:write ratio (100:1) to justify precomputing feeds.
  • Explain the celebrity problem with a number (50 million inserts per post), then the hybrid fix.
  • Store ids, not posts, in the feed; use cursor pagination.

Design a food delivery app (like Swiggy)

A food delivery platform connects customers, restaurants and delivery partners; the design is a restaurant discovery and menu service, an order service driven by a state machine and payment saga, a location service tracking partners, and a matching service that assigns the best nearby partner with a timeout and fallback.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Customer: search and browse restaurants near me, view menus, add to cart, pay, place an order, track it live, rate it.
  • Restaurant: receive orders, accept or reject, update menu and availability, mark order ready.
  • Delivery partner: go online/offline, receive an assignment, accept or reject, pick up, deliver, share live location.
  • Platform: estimate delivery time, handle cancellations, refunds and payouts.

Non-functional: an order must never be lost or charged twice (consistency for orders and payments); browsing can be eventually consistent and must be fast; high availability, especially at lunch and dinner peaks; location updates in near real time; assignment decisions within a few seconds. Out of scope: routing algorithm internals, pricing and surge models, ads.

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • 5 million orders per day nationwide. Average: 5,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 58 per second. Orders cluster in lunch and dinner: assume 60% of orders fall in 4 hours (14,400 seconds) → 3,000,000 ÷ 14,400 ≈ 210 orders per second at peak. Use 250 with headroom.
  • Browsing: each order comes from about 20 sessions that search and browse, with several requests each → peak read traffic on the order of 20 × 210 = 4,200 sessions/s, say 20,000 read requests per second. Heavily cached.
  • Delivery partners: 100,000 online at peak. Location update every 5 seconds → 100,000 ÷ 5 = 20,000 location writes per second. Each update ~50 bytes (partner id, lat, lng, time) → 1 MB/s. Only the latest position matters for matching, so this is an overwrite workload, not an append workload.
  • Order storage: 5M orders/day × 2 KB (order, items, history) = 10 GB per day → 3.65 TB per year. Manageable in sharded SQL.
  • Menu catalogue: 300,000 restaurants × 100 items × 1 KB = 30 GB. It fits in memory caches easily.

3. API design

GET  /api/v1/restaurants?lat=12.9716&lng=77.5946&cuisine=south&cursor=...
GET  /api/v1/restaurants/812/menu

POST /api/v1/orders
Idempotency-Key: 1f6c...
{"restaurantId": 812, "items": [{"itemId": 55, "qty": 2}],
 "addressId": 301, "paymentMethodId": "pm_9"}
201 Created
{"orderId": "o_7731", "status": "PLACED", "total": 41800, "currency": "INR"}

GET  /api/v1/orders/o_7731                 (status, partner, ETA)
POST /api/v1/orders/o_7731/cancel
POST /api/v1/restaurant/orders/o_7731/accept
POST /api/v1/partners/me/location          {"lat": 12.97, "lng": 77.59}
POST /api/v1/partners/me/assignments/a_1/accept

Amounts are in paise (integers), never floating point. Order creation takes an idempotency key (Idempotency) so a double tap on the pay button creates one order.

4. Data model

  • Orders, payments, users, partners: relational (PostgreSQL / MySQL) because an order involves several related rows and needs transactions and constraints. Shard by city or by customer id when needed.
  • Restaurants and menus: read-heavy, rarely changed, read as a document. Store in the database, index into a search engine (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) for text and filter queries (cuisine, rating, veg only), with a geo filter for distance.
  • Live partner locations: an in-memory geo store (Redis GEO or a geohash/H3 grid), with the latest location only. History can be sampled into a log store for analytics and disputes.
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id   BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    restaurant_id BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    partner_id    BIGINT,
    status        VARCHAR(24)  NOT NULL,
    total_paise   BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    created_at    TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    updated_at    TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE order_item (
    order_id VARCHAR(20), item_id BIGINT, qty INT, price_paise BIGINT,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, item_id)
);
CREATE TABLE order_status_history (
    order_id VARCHAR(20), status VARCHAR(24), at TIMESTAMP, actor VARCHAR(20)
);

Price is copied into order_item at order time, so later menu price changes do not alter past orders (the deliberate duplication from Monolith vs microservices).

5. High-level architecture

6. Deep dive A: the order lifecycle as a state machine

  • One service owns the state (order service). Others send events; the order service validates that a transition is legal (for example, you cannot go from DELIVERED to PREPARING) with an optimistic-lock update: UPDATE orders SET status = 'ACCEPTED' WHERE order_id = ? AND status = 'PAID'. Zero rows updated means a stale or duplicate event; ignore it.
  • The flow is a saga (Saga): reserve/authorise payment → ask the restaurant to accept → find a partner. Compensation: if the restaurant rejects or does not respond within, say, 3 minutes (a timer in a scheduler or a delayed message), refund and cancel. If no partner can be found, retry matching with a wider radius, then cancel and refund.
  • Reliable events via the outbox pattern (Outbox); every consumer is idempotent.
  • Keep the status history table for support and for showing the customer a timeline.

7. Deep dive B: location tracking and nearby search

  • Ingestion. 20,000 updates per second go to a location service that overwrites each partner's latest position in an in-memory geo store. Use a lightweight protocol (HTTP/2 or MQTT; a WebSocket works too). Batch and reduce the rate when the partner is idle or stationary. Update the geo index only when the cell changes or every N seconds.
  • Nearby query. Redis GEO stores points in a sorted set using a geohash score and supports a radius query around a point (GEOSEARCH in current Redis versions). Alternative: bucket space into geohash or H3 cells and keep a set of partners per cell; to find partners within 3 km, query the cell and its neighbours. The deep treatment of geohash and quadtrees is in Ride sharing.
  • Live tracking for the customer. While the order is PICKED_UP, the customer app polls GET /orders/{id} every few seconds or holds a Server-Sent Events / WebSocket stream. The tracking service reads the partner's latest location and an ETA. Polling every 5 seconds from 500,000 simultaneous deliveries is 100,000 requests per second, so a push channel and a small cache are cheaper.
  • ETA = restaurant preparation time + partner travel time to restaurant + travel time to the customer. Use a maps/routing service with live traffic; add a learned correction from past orders. State this as an estimate with error bars.

8. Deep dive C: partner matching

When an order becomes ACCEPTED, start matching so that a partner arrives as food becomes ready (not too early; waiting partners waste capacity).

  1. Candidates: query the geo index for available partners within a radius of the restaurant (start with 2–3 km).
  2. Filter: online, not already carrying too many orders, right vehicle type, not recently rejected this order.
  3. Score: distance or ETA to the restaurant, current load, rating, acceptance rate, and whether the delivery direction fits an order they already carry (batching).
  4. Offer: send the best candidate an assignment with a timeout (10–15 seconds). Create the assignment in the database with state OFFERED. If accepted, atomically update partner_id where it is still null (a conditional update prevents two partners getting one order). If rejected or timed out, offer to the next candidate.
  5. Fallback: if nobody accepts after K attempts, widen the radius, add an incentive, or alert operations.

Avoid assigning the same partner to two orders at once by marking the partner as reserved during an offer; use a short lease with a TTL, not a lock that can get stuck (Coordination). Global optimisation (batching many orders and many partners and solving an assignment problem every few seconds) beats greedy one-by-one matching but is more complex; mention it as an improvement.

9. Bottlenecks, scaling and failure

  • Peaks: lunch and dinner. Pre-scale before the peak, cache restaurant lists per area, and shed non-essential features (recommendations) first (Resilience).
  • Sharding: by city for orders, restaurants and partners; each city is nearly independent, which also limits the blast radius of a failure.
  • Search: read replicas of the search index; update it asynchronously when menus change.
  • Payments: use the idempotent flow in Payments; never store card data yourself.
  • Failure cases: restaurant tablet offline (fallback: call, auto-cancel after timeout); partner phone loses network (last known position, reassign after a timeout); duplicate events (idempotent handlers).
  • Monitoring: order success rate, time to restaurant accept, time to assign a partner, delivery time vs ETA, location staleness, cancellation reasons.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you handle a restaurant going out of stock after an order? (Item-level substitution/refund flow; short menu cache TTL; push availability changes.)
  • How do you show "restaurants open now within 5 km, sorted by rating"? (Search index with geo-distance filter and sort, ranked results, cached per area.)
  • How do you prevent a partner's duplicate location updates from corrupting state? (Last-write-wins by timestamp; discard older updates.)
  • What happens if the order service restarts mid-saga? (State is in the database; resume from the last persisted status; timers are persisted.)
  • How would you support batching two orders for one partner? (Matching scores route overlap and time windows.)

Interview angle

  • Draw the order state machine; interviewers like it because it exposes failure paths.
  • Separate consistency needs: orders and payments strong, browsing and tracking eventual.
  • Explain matching as candidates → filter → score → offer with timeout → fallback.

Design a ride-sharing app (like Uber or Ola)

Ride sharing needs a fast geospatial index of live driver locations (geohash cells or a quadtree), a matching service that offers the trip to nearby drivers with timeouts and atomic assignment, a trip state machine, and a real-time channel that streams the driver's position to the rider.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Rider: enter pickup and drop, see fare estimate and nearby vehicles, request a ride, see the driver arrive on the map, pay, rate.
  • Driver: go online, receive a request, accept or decline, navigate, start and end the trip.
  • Platform: match riders to drivers, compute ETA and fare, handle cancellations.

Non-functional: match within a few seconds; location updates in near real time (the car on the map should lag by seconds, not a minute); high availability in each city; a driver must never be assigned two rides at once, and a ride must never be given to two drivers (consistency for assignment); scalability to hundreds of thousands of online drivers. Out of scope: the routing engine, surge pricing model, fraud detection (mention briefly).

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • 20 million rides per day → 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 230 per second on average; peak 3× ≈ 700 ride requests per second.
  • 1 million drivers online at peak. Each sends its location every 4 seconds → 1,000,000 ÷ 4 = 250,000 location updates per second. Each update ~50 B → 12.5 MB/s. This is the dominant load; it is write-heavy and overwrites the previous value.
  • Location store size: 1,000,000 drivers × 100 B = 100 MB of latest positions. It fits in memory on a single machine; throughput, not size, forces sharding (split by city or by geohash prefix).
  • Nearby-driver reads: each ride request queries nearby drivers a few times, and riders opening the app also see nearby cars (say 10 map refreshes per ride request) → around 700 × 10 = 7,000 geo queries per second. Moderate.
  • Trip records: 20M × 2 KB = 40 GB/day. GPS trail kept for disputes: 20-minute trips sampled every 4 s = 300 points × 30 B = 9 KB per trip → 20M × 9 KB = 180 GB/day, stored cheaply (log store or object storage) and kept for a limited time.
  • Concurrent trips in progress: 700/s × average trip 20 min (1,200 s) ≈ 840,000 trips at peak, each streaming a position to a rider every few seconds → about 200,000+ messages per second to riders.

3. API design

POST /api/v1/rides/estimate
{"pickup": {"lat": 12.9352, "lng": 77.6245}, "drop": {"lat": 12.9784, "lng": 77.6408}}
200 OK  {"options": [{"type": "AUTO", "farePaise": 14500, "etaMin": 4},
                      {"type": "SEDAN", "farePaise": 21000, "etaMin": 6}]}

POST /api/v1/rides
Idempotency-Key: 9a0d...
{"pickup": {...}, "drop": {...}, "type": "SEDAN", "paymentMethodId": "pm_2"}
202 Accepted  {"rideId": "r_3301", "status": "SEARCHING"}

GET  /api/v1/rides/r_3301              (status, driver, ETA)
POST /api/v1/rides/r_3301/cancel

POST /api/v1/drivers/me/status         {"online": true}
POST /api/v1/drivers/me/location       {"lat": 12.94, "lng": 77.62, "heading": 80}
POST /api/v1/drivers/me/offers/of_1/accept
POST /api/v1/rides/r_3301/start        (driver, after OTP check)
POST /api/v1/rides/r_3301/end

The ride request returns 202 because matching happens asynchronously; the app listens on a WebSocket for status changes. The driver location endpoint is called often, so it should be a persistent connection or a very light request.

4. Data model

  • Rides/trips, riders, drivers, payments: relational, with strong consistency, sharded by city or ride id. Trip rows carry the state machine status and timestamps.
  • Live driver locations: an in-memory geo index (Redis GEO or a custom service) holding only the latest point per driver with a TTL (a driver who stops updating disappears after 30 seconds).
  • Location history: append-only into Kafka, then to cold storage for analytics, disputes and ETA model training.
CREATE TABLE ride (
    ride_id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    rider_id     BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    driver_id    BIGINT,
    status       VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,   -- SEARCHING, ASSIGNED, ARRIVED, STARTED, ENDED, CANCELLED
    pickup_lat   DOUBLE PRECISION, pickup_lng DOUBLE PRECISION,
    drop_lat     DOUBLE PRECISION, drop_lng   DOUBLE PRECISION,
    fare_paise   BIGINT,
    requested_at TIMESTAMP,
    ended_at     TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE driver (
    driver_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80), vehicle_type VARCHAR(10),
    rating NUMERIC(3,2), state VARCHAR(12)  -- OFFLINE, AVAILABLE, ON_TRIP
);

5. High-level architecture

6. Deep dive A: geospatial indexing (geohash vs quadtree)

The question "which drivers are within 2 km of this point?" cannot use a plain index on latitude and longitude, since that checks one coordinate at a time and scans a huge band. We need a structure that maps 2D space into something searchable.

Geohash. A geohash encodes a latitude/longitude pair into a short string by repeatedly halving the world (alternating longitude and latitude bits) and writing the bits in base 32. Longer strings mean smaller cells, and cells that share a prefix are near each other. Approximate cell sizes:

Geohash lengthCell size (approx.)Use
5about 4.9 km × 4.9 kmCoarse area, city districts
6about 1.2 km × 0.6 kmTypical "nearby drivers" bucket
7about 150 m × 150 mFine pickup points

Index: keep a map from geohash (length 6) to the set of available drivers in that cell. To find drivers near a rider: compute the rider's cell and its 8 neighbours (a driver just across a cell edge has a different prefix, so neighbours are required), union their sets, then compute exact distance and filter by radius. Updating a driver: if the cell changed since the last update, remove from the old set and add to the new one. A geohash is also a good shard key: partition drivers by a coarse prefix so each shard handles one area.

Quadtree. A tree where each node covers a rectangle. If a node has more than N drivers (say 500), split it into four children (NW, NE, SW, SE). Dense downtown areas get deep, small cells; empty suburbs stay as big cells. To search, walk down to the leaf containing the point, then check neighbouring leaves until enough drivers are found. It adapts to density, unlike fixed-size geohash cells, but is harder to update at 250,000 moves per second and to distribute across servers (usually rebuilt in memory and partitioned by region).

AspectGeohash gridQuadtree
StructureFixed-size cells, string keysAdaptive tree
Update costCheap: change a set if the cell changedMove between leaves, maybe split/merge
Density handlingPoor: crowded cells are big setsGood: splits where crowded
DistributionEasy: shard by prefix; works in RedisHarder
Edge casesMust query neighbouring cellsMust query neighbouring leaves

Most practical answers use a geohash-style or hex grid (Uber published the H3 hexagonal grid for this) kept in memory; mention both and pick one with a reason: "geohash in Redis, simple and shardable".

7. Deep dive B: location updates at 250,000 per second

  • Reduce the rate. Update every 4 seconds while available or on a trip, every 15–30 seconds when idle. Send only when the driver moved more than a few metres. Adaptive rates cut the load a lot.
  • Writes go to memory. The location service overwrites the driver's entry in a sharded in-memory store; it does not touch the SQL database. Redis GEO (GEOADD) or per-cell sets work; shard by city or geohash prefix so each node takes tens of thousands of writes per second.
  • Persistence is secondary. If the in-memory store is lost, drivers re-send within 4 seconds, so it rebuilds itself. Meanwhile, a copy of every update goes to Kafka for history.
  • Staleness. Use a TTL or timestamp check; ignore drivers whose last update is older than ~15–30 seconds when matching.
  • Protocol. A persistent connection (WebSocket, MQTT) avoids repeated TLS handshakes and headers for a tiny payload; HTTP works at smaller scale.

8. Deep dive C: matching, assignment and the trip lifecycle

  1. The ride service stores the ride as SEARCHING and calls the matching service with pickup, type and time.
  2. Matching asks the geo index for available drivers of the right type within a starting radius (for example 2 km); if too few, widen it step by step.
  3. Rank candidates by road ETA, not straight-line distance (a driver 500 m away across a river may be 15 minutes away), using the routing service on the top 10–20 candidates only because routing is expensive. Also consider rating, acceptance rate and fairness.
  4. Offer the ride to the best driver with a 10–15 second timeout. Alternatives: offer sequentially (simple, slower) or to the top 3 at once (faster, wastes some driver attention).
  5. On acceptance, assign atomically: UPDATE ride SET driver_id = ?, status = 'ASSIGNED' WHERE ride_id = ? AND driver_id IS NULL and set the driver to ON_TRIP in the same transaction, or use a short Redis lease on the driver while the offer is open. One row updated means success; zero means someone else won the race (Coordination).
  6. If no driver accepts after a few rounds, widen the search; after a limit (say 2 minutes), tell the rider and cancel.
  • Real-time updates. The rider's app keeps a WebSocket to a realtime gateway (Chat describes the gateway and session registry pattern). During ASSIGNED and STARTED, the driver's updates are republished to the rider's channel every 2–4 seconds, and the app animates the car between points. Status changes (ASSIGNED, ARRIVED) are pushed too, with a push notification as a backup.
  • Fare. Estimate before the ride (distance × rate + time × rate + base + surge multiplier), compute the final fare from the actual trip. Surge: compare demand (requests) and supply (drivers) per cell over a sliding window and raise a multiplier; smooth it to avoid flapping.
  • Payment at trip end uses an idempotent charge (Payments).

9. Bottlenecks, scaling and failure

  • City sharding: riders and drivers in one city rarely interact with another city, so shard the geo index, matching and ride data by city (or region). A city outage then affects only that city.
  • Hot spots: airports and stadium exits have thousands of requests in a small area. Use finer cells there and queue requests per pickup zone.
  • Driver app offline: if heartbeats stop mid-trip, keep the trip alive, store the trail on the phone and upload later; notify support after a long gap.
  • Duplicates: accept and end calls carry idempotency keys; transitions are conditional.
  • Monitoring: time to match, offer accept rate, location staleness, cancellations by reason, geo query latency.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you handle a driver near a geohash cell boundary? (Search the 8 neighbouring cells too.)
  • Why not store driver positions in the SQL database? (250,000 writes per second of overwrites; memory store fits better; durability not needed.)
  • How do you pool shared rides? (Extend matching to combine requests with compatible routes and time windows; more complex optimisation.)
  • What if two riders are matched to one driver at the same instant? (Conditional update; the loser re-matches.)
  • How do you compute ETA accurately? (Road graph with live traffic, learned corrections, cached for popular segments.)

Interview angle

  • Explain why lat/lng cannot use a normal index and how a geohash grid fixes it, including the neighbouring-cells detail.
  • Give the location-update arithmetic: 1 million drivers ÷ 4 s = 250,000 per second, and say it lives in memory.
  • Mention atomic assignment and the trip state machine.

Design a video streaming platform (like YouTube)

A video platform splits into an upload pipeline (upload to object storage, transcode into many resolutions and small segments in parallel, publish) and a playback path (CDN serving adaptive-bitrate segments chosen by the player), because storage and bandwidth, not request counts, dominate the design.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Users upload videos (large files) with title, description and thumbnail.
  • Viewers search, open a video and watch with smooth playback on phones, laptops and TVs, on fast and slow networks.
  • Seek anywhere in the video; the video starts quickly.
  • View counts, likes and comments (basic). Recommendations are out of scope.

Non-functional: very high availability for playback; start-up delay of about a second or two; no buffering on stable networks; uploads must be reliable and resumable; uploaded videos must not be lost (durability); cost efficiency (storage and bandwidth are the bill); eventual consistency is fine for counts and for "video is processing" delays. Out of scope: live streaming, DRM details, recommendation models.

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • 100 million daily active users watching 5 videos each → 500 million views per day → 500,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 5,800 video starts per second.
  • Average watch time 5 minutes (300 s). Total viewing per day = 500M × 300 s = 150 billion seconds. Divide by 86,400 seconds in a day: average concurrent streams = 150,000,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1.7 million; peak 3× ≈ 5 million.
  • Average stream bitrate 2.5 Mbps (megabits per second) → 2.5 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.31 MB/s. Peak egress = 5,000,000 × 2.5 Mbps = 12,500,000 Mbps = 12.5 Tbps (about 1.6 TB per second). No origin can serve this; the CDN must carry nearly all of it.
  • Uploads: 100,000 new videos per day → about 1.2 per second. Average raw size 500 MB → 100,000 × 500 MB = 50 TB per day raw, about 18 PB per year.
  • Transcoded versions: say 6 renditions (240p to 1080p) with the total close to the raw size → another ~50 TB per day, so roughly 100 TB per day, ~36 PB per year of video storage (approximate; codecs, lengths and ladders change this a lot). Object storage with tiering (hot, cold) is the only option.
  • Metadata: 100,000 videos × 2 KB = 200 MB per day. Tiny. Views: 5,800 counter increments per second, handled by batching.

Conclusion: request QPS is modest; bytes (storage and egress) and compute for transcoding drive the architecture.

3. API design

POST /api/v1/videos/uploads
{"title": "Bengaluru metro vlog", "sizeBytes": 734003200, "contentType": "video/mp4"}
201 Created
{"videoId": "v_8F3k1", "uploadUrl": "https://storage.../raw/v_8F3k1?signature=...",
 "partSizeBytes": 8388608}

PUT   {uploadUrl} + part number       (client uploads parts directly to object storage)
POST  /api/v1/videos/v_8F3k1/complete {"parts": [{"n": 1, "etag": "..."}, ...]}
202 Accepted {"status": "PROCESSING"}

GET   /api/v1/videos/v_8F3k1
200 OK {"title": "...", "status": "READY",
        "manifestUrl": "https://cdn.example/v_8F3k1/master.m3u8",
        "thumbnailUrl": "...", "views": 1520}

GET   /api/v1/search?q=metro&cursor=...

The video bytes never pass through the API servers. The client uploads in parts straight to object storage with a pre-signed URL, which gives resumable uploads (retry only the failed part) and keeps the application tier light.

4. Data model

  • Metadata (videos, channels, comments): SQL or a document store; read-heavy and cached. Videos table: video_id, owner_id, title, description, status, duration, created_at with status UPLOADING, PROCESSING, READY, FAILED.
  • Video files and segments: object storage. Layout: raw/<id>/original.mp4 and vod/<id>/<resolution>/seg_00001.ts (or .m4s), plus manifests.
  • Search: an inverted index (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) over titles, descriptions and tags, updated from a stream of metadata changes.
  • Counters: view and like counts aggregated from events; stored in a counter table or Redis and flushed periodically.

5. High-level architecture

6. Deep dive A: the upload and transcoding pipeline

Raw uploads come in many formats, sizes and bitrates. Transcoding turns each into a set of standard versions so every device can play something suitable. It is CPU-heavy, so it is done in parallel by many workers.

  1. Upload complete: an object-storage event (or the complete call) puts a job on a queue and sets status PROCESSING.
  2. Validate: check the file type, duration limits, run a virus/abuse and copyright scan (fingerprint matching), and extract metadata.
  3. Split the source into chunks of a few seconds on keyframe boundaries (groups of pictures). Each chunk can be encoded independently, so a long video is processed in parallel.
  4. Encode each chunk into every rendition of the bitrate ladder (for example 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, optionally 4K) with a modern codec (H.264 is the universal baseline; VP9/AV1/HEVC give better compression at higher compute cost). This is a DAG of tasks: split → encode chunk × rendition → merge → package.
  5. Package into segments of 2–6 seconds and write a manifest: HLS uses .m3u8 playlists, MPEG-DASH uses .mpd. The master manifest lists the available renditions and their bandwidth.
  6. Extras: thumbnails and preview sprites, captions, audio tracks.
  7. Publish: write segments to the encoded bucket, set status READY, index it for search, and notify the uploader (Notifications).
  • Make every task idempotent (output path derived from video id, rendition and chunk number, so a retried task overwrites the same file) and retry failed chunks only (Retries). Use a workflow/orchestrator to track the DAG state (Orchestration).
  • Use spot or preemptible compute for workers, since tasks are retryable, to save cost.
  • Prioritise: short videos and new uploads from verified creators first; a backlog metric shows when to add workers.
  • Encode popular renditions first (so playback can start sooner) and add the rest later; or encode lazily the rarely used ones on demand.

7. Deep dive B: adaptive bitrate streaming and the CDN

Adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming. The video is available in several renditions, each cut into short segments. The player downloads the manifest, starts with a medium rendition, and downloads segment after segment over plain HTTP. It measures download speed and buffer level; if the network slows, it switches to a lower rendition for the next segment, and switches back up when the network recovers. The user sees quality change, not buffering. Seeking is easy: compute the segment number from the time (time ÷ segment length), and fetch from there. Because segments are ordinary files over HTTP, they are cacheable by any CDN.

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2800000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
1080p/index.m3u8

CDN. Playback traffic (12.5 Tbps at peak in our estimate) is served by edge servers near viewers (Module 5). Segments are immutable, so they cache perfectly with long TTLs. Design points:

  • Pull CDN with an origin shield: an edge miss asks a mid-tier cache, which asks the origin only if it also misses. This collapses many edge misses into one origin read.
  • Popularity is skewed: a small share of videos gets most views, so edge caches hold the popular head, and the long tail is fetched from origin storage on demand. For an expected hit (new release), pre-warm (push) segments to edges.
  • Multiple CDNs or ISP-embedded caches for cost and resilience; steer clients by DNS or manifest URLs.
  • Cost: egress dominates the bill, so a high cache hit ratio directly lowers cost. Efficient codecs reduce bytes per second.
  • Security: signed, expiring URLs for private or paid content; hotlink protection.

8. Deep dive C: metadata, search, counters and consistency

  • Metadata path. The video page API reads the cached metadata (Redis) and returns the manifest URL. Metadata is small, so a replicated SQL database with a cache is enough; shard by video id if needed.
  • View counts. 5,800 starts per second would hammer one row per popular video. Players emit view events into a stream; consumers aggregate in windows and add to counters periodically. Counts are approximate and a few minutes late; dedupe or filter bot traffic. Show rounded numbers in the UI.
  • Search. Index text fields; rank by relevance and engagement. The index is updated asynchronously from the metadata change stream (CDC, Outbox and CDC), so a new video becomes searchable after a short delay.
  • Resume playback. Store the last position per user and video, written every ~10–30 seconds from the client; a key-value store is enough.
  • Thumbnails and previews are small images served by the CDN, cached aggressively.
  • Deletion and takedown. Mark deleted in metadata (immediate effect on the API), purge CDN objects, then delete files in the background.

9. Bottlenecks, scaling and failure

  • Transcode backlog after a surge of uploads: autoscale workers on queue depth; show "processing" and let low-resolution renditions publish first.
  • Origin load during a viral spike of a new video: pre-warm the CDN, use an origin shield, and rely on request collapsing (many simultaneous misses become one origin fetch).
  • Storage cost: tier old and rarely watched videos to cheaper storage; drop unused high renditions for cold videos and re-create on demand.
  • Regional failure: replicate object storage across regions; multi-region CDN.
  • Failure cases: corrupt upload (validate and mark FAILED with a reason); worker crash (retry the chunk); manifest published before all segments exist (publish the manifest last).
  • Monitoring: start-up time, rebuffer ratio, CDN hit ratio, transcode queue lag and failure rate, bytes served per region.

Follow-up questions

  • How would you support live streaming? (Ingest by RTMP/WebRTC, near-real-time packaging into short segments, low-latency HLS, a very different latency budget.)
  • Why short segments? (Faster adaptation and seeking vs more requests and manifest overhead; 2–6 s is a common range.)
  • How do you reduce start-up time? (Start at a low rendition, small first segments, CDN proximity, preload the manifest.)
  • How do you protect paid content? (Signed URLs, token auth, DRM licences.)
  • How would you detect duplicate or copyrighted uploads? (Content fingerprinting at the validation step.)

Interview angle

  • Do the bandwidth arithmetic (5 million concurrent × 2.5 Mbps = 12.5 Tbps) to justify the CDN.
  • Explain the pipeline in order: pre-signed upload → queue → chunked parallel transcode → segments plus manifest → CDN.
  • Describe ABR in two sentences: renditions, segments, the player switches per segment.

Design payments and e-commerce checkout

Checkout must never charge twice or sell stock you do not have; the design uses idempotency keys on every money-moving call, a payment state machine confirmed by gateway webhooks, a double-entry ledger as the record of truth, atomic stock reservation with expiry, and daily reconciliation against the payment provider.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Customer reviews the cart and places an order: choose address and payment method (UPI, card, net banking, wallet, cash on delivery).
  • The system reserves inventory, takes payment through an external payment gateway, and confirms the order.
  • Failed or abandoned payments release the stock. The customer can retry payment.
  • Refunds (full and partial) and order cancellation.
  • Payment status is visible to the customer and to support; finance can reconcile and settle.

Non-functional: correctness over speed: no double charge, no lost payment, no overselling, a complete audit trail. Strong consistency for money and stock. High availability for checkout, but when in doubt, fail safe (refuse rather than guess). Peak traffic during sales. Security and compliance: never store raw card numbers or CVV (use the gateway's hosted fields or tokens; PCI DSS rules apply to card data). Out of scope: building a bank or card network, tax and invoice rules in detail, fraud model internals.

2. Capacity estimates (assumptions)

  • 1 million orders per day → 1,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 12 orders per second on average. A big-sale hour might carry 100× the normal rate for popular items: assume 1,500 checkout attempts per second at the sale peak (several attempts per successful order, since many payments fail or are abandoned).
  • Payment attempts: about 1.5 attempts per order → 1.5M per day, 17 per second average, up to 2,000 per second at the peak.
  • Ledger: each completed order creates about 4 ledger entries (customer payment, merchant payable, platform fee, tax) of ~100 B → 1M × 4 × 100 B = 400 MB per day ≈ 146 GB per year. Small. Because it is append-only and critical, keep it forever in a durable relational store.
  • Inventory contention: a flash sale of 1,000 phones with 100,000 users trying at once is 100 requests per unit. The stock row is a hot row; the hard problem is contention, not volume.
  • Gateway calls are slow (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds) and rate limited, so they must be asynchronous-friendly and protected with timeouts and circuit breakers.

3. API design

POST /api/v1/checkout/orders
Idempotency-Key: 3b7e...
{"cartId": "c_55", "addressId": 301}
201 Created
{"orderId": "o_9012", "status": "PENDING_PAYMENT", "totalPaise": 249900,
 "reservedUntil": "2026-11-11T09:45:00Z"}

POST /api/v1/orders/o_9012/payments
Idempotency-Key: 8c21...
{"method": "UPI", "returnUrl": "https://shop.example/pay/return"}
201 Created
{"paymentId": "pay_771", "status": "REQUIRES_ACTION",
 "gatewayRedirectUrl": "https://gateway.example/pay/..."}

GET  /api/v1/orders/o_9012            (order and payment status)
POST /api/v1/orders/o_9012/refunds    {"amountPaise": 50000, "reason": "damaged"}

POST /webhooks/gateway                (called by the gateway; signed)
{"event": "payment.captured", "gatewayPaymentId": "gw_1", "orderRef": "pay_771", ...}

Both create calls need Idempotency-Key (Idempotency): the order call so a double-click makes one order, and the payment call so a retry after a timeout does not start a second payment. The same key is passed to the gateway when it supports one. Money is always an integer in the smallest unit (paise) plus a currency code. Webhooks are verified with a signature and are idempotent too.

4. Data model

Use a relational database with ACID transactions for orders, payments, stock and the ledger.

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id   BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    status        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,   -- PENDING_PAYMENT, CONFIRMED, CANCELLED, REFUNDED
    total_paise   BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    reserved_until TIMESTAMP,
    created_at    TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE payment (
    payment_id    VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    amount_paise  BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    method        VARCHAR(12) NOT NULL,
    status        VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,   -- CREATED, PENDING, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED, FAILED, REFUNDED
    gateway_ref   VARCHAR(64),
    version       INT         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    updated_at    TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE idempotency_key (
    key VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, request_hash CHAR(64), response_code INT, response_body TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE stock (
    sku VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, available INT NOT NULL CHECK (available >= 0)
);
CREATE TABLE stock_reservation (
    order_id VARCHAR(20), sku VARCHAR(20), qty INT, expires_at TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)
);
CREATE TABLE ledger_entry (
    entry_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, txn_id VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    account  VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,   -- e.g. customer:9912, merchant:44, platform_fee
    direction CHAR(1)    NOT NULL,   -- D debit, C credit
    amount_paise BIGINT  NOT NULL CHECK (amount_paise > 0),
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

5. High-level architecture

6. Deep dive A: the checkout flow, idempotency and unknown outcomes

  • Why not trust the browser? After paying, the customer may close the tab before returning to your site. The webhook from the gateway (server to server, signed) is the source of truth for the outcome; the browser return only triggers a status check. Deliveries can repeat or arrive out of order, so the handler is idempotent and applies only valid state transitions.
  • The unknown outcome. You call the gateway and the request times out. Did the money move? You do not know. Never assume failure and never blindly retry without the idempotency key. Mark the payment PENDING, then query the gateway status by your reference, and let the webhook arrive. A periodic job polls payments stuck in PENDING for more than a few minutes. This is the central lesson of payment design: handle "I don't know" as a first-class state.
  • State machine. Payment moves CREATED → PENDING → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED, or → FAILED, and later → REFUNDED. Transitions use conditional updates / optimistic locking (UPDATE payment SET status = 'CAPTURED', version = version + 1 WHERE payment_id = ? AND status IN ('PENDING','AUTHORIZED') AND version = ?), so a duplicate webhook changes nothing.
  • Authorise then capture (cards): authorise at checkout to hold funds, capture when the item ships; void if cancelled. UPI and many methods capture immediately.
  • Saga and compensation. Order, stock and payment are separate services, so this is a saga (Saga): if payment fails or times out, release the stock and cancel; if the order cannot be confirmed after payment, refund. Events are published with the outbox (Outbox) so a captured payment always produces an PaymentCaptured event.
  • Double-click and retries: the client generates the idempotency key when the user starts the payment attempt and reuses it on each retry of the same attempt; a new attempt (after a failure) gets a new key.

7. Deep dive B: inventory without overselling

Two customers both see "1 left" and both pay. The check and the decrement must be one atomic step:

UPDATE stock
   SET available = available - 2
 WHERE sku = 'SKU-1' AND available >= 2;     -- affected rows: 1 = success, 0 = out of stock
INSERT INTO stock_reservation (order_id, sku, qty, expires_at)
VALUES ('o_9012', 'SKU-1', 2, now() + interval '15 minutes');
  • Reserve, then commit. Reserving at order time and holding it for 15 minutes balances two risks: no reservation means many paid orders you cannot fulfil; reserving forever lets abandoned carts block stock. A scheduled job releases expired reservations (add the quantity back) and cancels the pending order.
  • Hot rows. In a flash sale, one row takes thousands of updates per second and locks serialise them. Options: put the sale stock in Redis with an atomic DECR (a Lua script that checks and decrements) and sync to the database asynchronously; split stock into N buckets (sub-rows) and pick one at random; or queue purchase requests and process them in order, returning "you are in line". Use a waiting room to control entry (Rate limiter).
  • Overselling vs underselling. Redis-first approaches can lose a decrement on a crash; choose which error is acceptable. For limited drops, prefer underselling (a few units re-released later) to overselling (apologies and refunds).

8. Deep dive C: the ledger and reconciliation

Do not model money as a mutable balance column that you overwrite. Use a double-entry ledger: every money movement is a transaction with at least two immutable entries, a debit and a credit, which add up to zero. Balances are computed from entries (and cached or snapshotted).

txn_idaccountdirectionamount (paise)
t_1gateway_clearingD249,900
t_1merchant:44 payableC224,900
t_1platform_feeC25,000

Debits 249,900 equal credits 224,900 + 25,000 = 249,900. A refund is a new transaction with the opposite entries; you never edit or delete old rows. Benefits: a full audit trail, easy to prove where every rupee went, and errors are corrected by adding entries. Write the ledger entries in the same database transaction as the payment state change, so they cannot disagree.

Reconciliation. Your records and the gateway's records must match. A daily (or more frequent) job downloads the gateway's settlement report and compares it with your payments by gateway reference and amount. It reports: payments you think succeeded but the gateway has no record of; payments the gateway captured that you marked failed (the unknown-outcome cases); amount mismatches; fee differences. Mismatches create tickets or automatic fixes (refund the stray capture, or mark the order paid). Reconciliation is the safety net for every bug and every lost webhook.

9. Consistency, failure and scaling

  • Consistency model. Strong (ACID) inside each service's database for its own data; eventual consistency between services through events. Show the customer the real state ("payment pending") instead of guessing.
  • Gateway failure. Protect calls with timeouts and a circuit breaker (Resilience); offer a second gateway for routing/fallback; show a clear message and allow retry later. Do not retry charges blindly.
  • Scaling. Services are stateless; payment DB sharded by payment or order id if needed; read replicas for status queries (but read your own writes from the primary right after payment); cache the cart and product data, never the payment status.
  • Security. TLS everywhere, signed webhooks, secrets in a vault, tokenised card data via the gateway, least-privilege access, audit logging, rate limits on payment attempts per user to stop card testing by fraudsters.
  • Monitoring: payment success rate by method and bank, PENDING age, webhook delay, reconciliation mismatches, reservation expiry count, stock vs reservations drift.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the webhook never arrives? (Poll the gateway status; reconciliation catches the rest.)
  • What if the customer pays twice from two tabs? (Idempotency key per attempt; detect a second capture for the same order and auto-refund.)
  • How do you handle partial refunds and partial shipments? (Refund transactions in the ledger per item; order lines have their own status.)
  • Cash on delivery? (No payment capture up front; collection by the delivery partner is recorded and settled later; higher return/fraud risk.)
  • How do you support multiple currencies? (Store amount plus currency; convert only at defined points; never use floats.)

Interview angle

  • Say the four words early: idempotency, webhook, ledger, reconciliation.
  • Treat "unknown outcome after a timeout" as a first-class state, and say what you do about it.
  • Explain the atomic conditional update for stock and the reservation expiry.

Interview questions — HLD interview practice

How do you structure a 45-minute HLD interview?

Requirements and scope (5 minutes), capacity estimates (5), API and high-level design (10–15), data model (5), deep dive on the hardest part (10–15), then trade-offs, failures and scaling (5). Narrate your choices, check in with the interviewer at phase ends, and tie each component to a requirement or a number.

What clarifying questions would you ask first?

Who are the users and what are the core actions; expected scale (users, requests per day, read:write ratio); which features are in scope; latency and availability targets; consistency needs (can data be slightly stale); durability (can we lose data); single or multi-region; and constraints such as abuse, privacy and retention. Then write functional, non-functional and out-of-scope lists.

URL shortener: how do you generate the short code?

Three options: a unique counter encoded in base62 (no collisions, short, but sequential and needs a counter service; ranges per server remove the bottleneck), a hash of the URL truncated to 7 characters (no coordination but collisions must be handled), or pre-generated random keys (fast, unguessable, needs a key service). With 6 billion URLs, 627 ≈ 3.5 trillion gives ample room. I would pick pre-generated keys or a counter with a reversible shuffle.

301 or 302 for a URL shortener?

301 is permanent and browsers cache it, so later clicks bypass you: cheaper, but no analytics and the target cannot change or expire. 302 (temporary) sends every click through your server, enabling click counting, edits and expiry at the cost of more load. If analytics or expiry matter, use 302.

Pastebin: why not store paste content in the database?

Pastes can be up to megabytes. Large rows bloat the buffer cache, backups and replication and cost more per GB. Store metadata (key, owner, size, expiry, blob path) in the database and the text in object storage, served via a CDN since pastes are immutable. Expire with lazy checks on read plus a background cleaner or lifecycle rule.

How do you build a distributed rate limiter and make it atomic?

Keep a token bucket or counter per client in Redis, sharded by client key. The read-modify-write must be atomic, so use a Lua script (or INCR for a fixed window); otherwise two gateways both read "1 token left" and both allow. Decide the failure policy: fail open for most APIs, fail closed for login or SMS, with a local limiter as a fallback. Return 429 with Retry-After.

Notification system: how do you avoid duplicates and handle bursts?

Delivery is at-least-once, so give every notification an id and dedupe before sending (a conditional status update or a Redis SET NX), and pass idempotency or collapse keys to providers. For bursts, use one queue per channel and per priority so an OTP never waits behind a campaign, throttle against provider rate limits, retry with backoff and jitter, and move poison messages to a DLQ. Size for the campaign burst, not the average.

Chat: how does a message reach an online user and an offline user?

The sender's WebSocket gateway forwards the message to the message service, which assigns a per-chat sequence number and stores it durably, then acks the sender. A session registry maps the recipient to their gateway, and the message is pushed down their socket. If they are offline, it stays in their inbox and a push notification is sent; on reconnect the client asks for everything after its last sequence number.

Chat: how do you order messages and show delivered / read ticks?

Order per conversation using a server-assigned sequence number, not phone clocks and not globally. Delivered and read are acknowledgements from the recipient app; store them as watermarks per user per chat ("read up to seq 412") rather than a row per message. Clients dedupe by message id because delivery is at-least-once.

News feed: fan-out on write or on read?

Fan-out on write precomputes each follower's feed when a post is created, making reads very cheap, which suits a 100:1 read-heavy workload, but a celebrity with 50 million followers makes one post cost 50 million writes. Fan-out on read has no write cost but slow reads. Use a hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull and merge celebrity posts at read time, skip inactive users. Store post ids in the feed and use cursor pagination.

Ride sharing: how do you find nearby drivers fast?

A normal index on latitude and longitude cannot do a 2D radius search. Use a geospatial index: a geohash or hex grid with a set of drivers per cell, or a quadtree. Query the rider's cell plus its eight neighbours, then filter by exact distance and rank by road ETA. Keep latest positions in memory (Redis GEO), sharded by city; 1 million drivers updating every 4 seconds is 250,000 writes per second.

Video streaming: what happens between upload and playback?

The client uploads in parts to object storage using a pre-signed URL. A job queue triggers transcoding: the video is split into chunks, each encoded in parallel into several resolutions, packaged into short segments and HLS/DASH manifests, and published. Playback uses adaptive bitrate streaming: the player picks a rendition per segment based on bandwidth. A CDN serves nearly all bytes because the egress is enormous.

Payments: how do you prevent a double charge when a request times out?

The client sends an idempotency key per payment attempt and reuses it on retries; the server stores the key and result in a dedupe table and passes the key to the gateway. On a timeout, the payment is marked PENDING (unknown), not failed; the gateway status is queried and the webhook updates the state with conditional transitions. A reconciliation job against the gateway's settlement report catches whatever slips through.

Why a double-entry ledger instead of a balance column?

Each movement is an immutable pair of debit and credit entries that sum to zero, so you keep a full audit trail, can prove where money went, and correct mistakes by adding reversing entries instead of editing history. Balances are derived from entries. Entries are written in the same transaction as the payment state change.

The interviewer asks: "what if traffic grows 10 times?"

Redo the numbers to find the first bottleneck, then go inwards from the edge: CDN and caching, more stateless app servers, a larger cache with a better hit ratio, read replicas, sharding for writes and storage, queues for slow work, and protection with rate limits and load shedding. Then say what breaks next at 100 times.

Cheat sheet — HLD interview practice

  • Time plan requirements 5, estimates 5, design 10–15, data 5, deep dive 10–15, trade-offs 5
  • Estimate shortcut per second = per day ÷ 86,400 (about 105); peak 2–3× average
  • Always say assumptions, one number per component, one trade-off, one failure case
  • URL shortener 40 writes/s, 4,000 reads/s, 6B URLs, 627 ≈ 3.5T, ~3 TB, cache-aside
  • 301 vs 302 301 cached by browsers (no analytics); 302 every click hits you
  • Pastebin metadata in DB, text in object storage + CDN; lazy expiry + cleaner job
  • Rate limiter token bucket in Redis, atomic Lua, shard by client, fail open or closed, 429
  • Notification API → validate/prefs/template → queue per channel and priority → workers → provider
  • Notification safety at-least-once + dedupe id, backoff + jitter, DLQ, provider rate limits
  • Chat WebSocket gateways, session registry, store then route, per-chat seq, inbox for offline
  • Chat numbers 20M connections ÷ 100K per gateway = 200 gateways
  • Receipts sent → delivered → read, kept as watermarks per chat
  • News feed 100:1 reads; push for normal users, pull for celebrities; ids in Redis sorted sets
  • Pagination cursor (last id), not offset
  • Food delivery order state machine + payment saga; geo index of partners; match with timeout
  • Ride sharing geohash cell + 8 neighbours or quadtree; 250K location writes/s in memory
  • Assignment conditional update (driver_id IS NULL) so only one driver wins
  • Video pre-signed multipart upload → queue → parallel chunk transcode → HLS/DASH → CDN
  • ABR several renditions, 2–6 s segments, player switches per segment
  • Video numbers 5M concurrent × 2.5 Mbps = 12.5 Tbps; CDN is mandatory
  • Payments idempotency key, state machine, webhook = truth, ledger, reconciliation
  • Unknown outcome timeout means PENDING, then query gateway; never assume failure
  • Stock UPDATE ... WHERE available >= n; reserve with expiry; hot rows need buckets or Redis
  • 10× traffic CDN, stateless scale-out, cache, replicas, shard, queue, shed load
  • Mistakes no requirements, no numbers, over-engineering, ignoring failure, name-dropping

Practice — HLD interview practice

  1. Warm-up arithmetic. Without notes, redo the estimates for the URL shortener and the chat app on paper (QPS, storage, connections). Done when your numbers match the notes within a factor of 2 and you can say what each number implies for the design.
  2. The 45-minute URL shortener. Set a timer and design a URL shortener out loud, on a whiteboard or paper, using the six phases. Record yourself or practise with a friend. Done when you finish all phases inside 45 minutes, covered code generation, 301 vs 302 and caching, and named two failure cases.
  3. Build the core. Implement a small URL shortener in Spring Boot: POST to create, GET /{code} to redirect, PostgreSQL for storage, Redis cache-aside, base62 encoding. Done when 10,000 redirects in a load test show a high cache hit ratio and creation is idempotent with an Idempotency-Key header.
  4. Atomic rate limiter. Implement the Redis token-bucket Lua script from the notes and call it from a Spring filter. Fire 200 parallel requests at a limit of 100. Done when at most about 100 succeed and the rest get 429 with a Retry-After header.
  5. Draw all ten. For each of the ten problems, draw the architecture flowchart from memory on one page and write three bullet points for its hardest deep dive. Done when each page has a diagram, two numbers and one trade-off, and you can explain each in two minutes.
  6. Queue and cache discussion (Project 4). Take your Project 4 and prepare a five-minute explanation of where it uses a cache and a queue: why, which pattern (cache-aside, TTL, invalidation), delivery guarantee, retry and dead-letter handling, and what happens when each fails. Done when you can answer follow-ups on stampede, duplicates and ordering.
  7. Mock the hard follow-ups. Ask a friend to challenge you with "what if traffic grows 10×", "what if the cache dies" and "what if the database is down" on any two problems. Done when each answer follows the edge-to-database walk and names a first bottleneck.
  8. Payments walkthrough. Write the sequence diagram for checkout with a gateway timeout in the middle and mark where each state is persisted. Done when it shows the idempotency key, the PENDING state, the status poll, the webhook and the reconciliation fix.
  9. Peer review. Give one of your designs to a friend with the rubric from the method article and ask for scores on requirements, numbers, depth, failure thinking and communication. Done when you have one improvement noted per area and redo the weakest phase.
